[{"suffix": "", "text": "Revealing statistically robust strain rate effects on mechanical \nperformance of pristine single fiber aramids   \n \nAtik Faisal1, Alexander K Landauer2, Walter Adamy Jr1, Dumbari David Kabari1, Kathleen A. Lamkin-\nKennard*1, Amanda L. Forster2, Amy Engelbrecht-Wiggans1 \n1. Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York, USA \n2. National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, Maryland, USA \n \n*Corresponding author; kaleme@rit.edu \nAtik Faisal ORCiD 0000-0003-2221-5320 \nAlexander K. Landauer ORCiD 0000-0003-2863-039X \nAmanda L. Forster ORCiD 0000-0001-7397-4429 \nKeywords: Aramid fibers; Tensile testing; Strain rate sensitivity; Kolsky bar; High strength fiber; Body \nArmor; High strain rate \nAbstract \nHigh-performance synthetic fibers, especially aramid fibers, are widely used for body armor applications \nfor their strength, stiffness, and excellent strength-to-weight ratio. Among those, Kevlar and Twaron \n(hereafter Aramid A and Aramid B, respectively) are extensively used for their superior thermal stability, \nhigh modulus, and proven ballistic performance. However, their tensile behavior under high strain rate \n(HSR) conditions approaching ballistic impact rates remains insufficiently characterized due to \nexperimental challenges in measuring stress and strain at break at the single-fiber level. Previous studies \nhave suggested moderate strain rate sensitivity in aramid-based fibers, but small sample sizes and limited \naccuracy in failure strain measurement under HSR have constrained the statistical robustness of the \nfindings. In this study, a custom single-fiber tensile Kolsky bar instrument was configured for HSR tensile \ntesting with accurate specimen alignment, gripping, and pulse quality. A rigid-body digital image \ncorrelation (DIC) method was implemented to track relative grip displacements and measure the strain at \nfailure, enabling accurate measurements of failure force, strain, and strain rate at the single-fiber level. \nUsing 62 samples per fiber at HSR and 100 per group under quasi-static (QS) conditions, clear strain-rate-\ndependent strengthening was observed in both fiber types. Maximum force, failure stress, and failure \nstrain increased by approximately 28.5 % to 35.6 % under HSR compared to QS. The large sample size \nenabled a statistically robust assessment using distributional and non-parametric analyses, showing that \nAramid B exhibited more uniform failure distributions than Aramid A. The approach establishes a \npractical framework for quantifying single-fiber strain-rate sensitivity.\n\n1 \n \n1. Introduction \nBallistic-resistant, flexible body armor, often referred to as soft body armor, is critical for protecting \nemergency responders, including military personnel, police officers, firefighters, and emergency medical \nresponders. According to the International Association of Chiefs of Police and the DuPont Kevlar \nSurvivors’ Club, body armor has saved over 3100 officers since 1975 [1]. Body armor effectiveness is \ncommonly assessed using the destructive ballistic limit (V50) test, defined as the projectile velocity at \nwhich penetration occurs in 50 % of cases [2]. Soft body armor typically consists of multi-layered fabrics \nor flexible fiber composites. Among the fibers used in body armor, poly-paraphenylene terephthalamide \nor PPTA, was first developed by DuPont in the 1960s and marketed as Kevlar1 [3]. A similar aramid fiber \nwith the same chemical structure, Twaron, was subsequently developed by Teijin [4]. These are the most \ncommon aramid fibers used in flexible body armor today, composed of highly oriented PPTA molecular \nchains with para-linkages that provide high axial strength and stiffness, making the fibers highly \nanisotropic [5], [6] and thermally stable, with decomposition around 500 °C [7], [8]. The ballistic \nperformance during V50 testing of this class of armor largely derives from the mechanical performance of \nindividual fibers during tensile loading [9]. However, fibers within the impact zone also experience \ncomplex multiaxial loading, including transverse compression, shear, and localized axial compression \n[10], [11]. Because PPTA fibers are much weaker in compression than in tension, compressive \ndeformation can produce kink-band formation and fibrillation that reduce the residual tensile strength of \nthe fibers [12], [13]. While this compressive behavior plays a direct role in energy dissipation and governs \nhow much tensile capacity can be realized at the impact site [8], [11], axial tension remains the dominant \nmechanism and ultimate failure mode [8]. Consequently, ultimate tensile properties remain the primary \ninputs for ballistic performance models and are the focus of this work.  \nMechanical performance characterization of body armor fibers is often conducted under quasi-static (QS) \nconditions, many orders of magnitude slower than the strain rates experienced during ballistic impacts. \nSince the polymer fibers exhibit viscoelasticity, a number of studies have examined the effect of strain \nrate using high strain rate (HSR) tensile testing methods to characterize the response of ballistic fibers \nunder more realistic loading conditions. To study single fiber behavior under HSR conditions, the split \nHopkinson (Kolsky) pressure bar technique was adapted by several groups for single fiber tensile testing \n[14]. Studies using similar systems on PPTA-based aramid fibers showed a modest effect on tensile \nstrength, modulus, and toughness, increasing as strain rate increased [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20]. \nHowever, the magnitude, consistency, and statistical robustness of the reported rate effects in aramid \nfibers remain less clear. For example, Cheng et al. [19] reported only about 4 % increase in strength for \nKevlar KM2. Others, such as Kim et al. [18] found an approximately 14 % increase, while Lim et al. [16] \nobserved 6 % to 12 % increases across three aramid fiber types, and Sanborn and Weerasooriya [20] \nreported an 18.6 % increase for unwoven Kevlar KM2 fibers, based on mean failure stress values of (4.30 \n± 0.49) GPa at QS rate and (5.10 ± 0.41) GPa at HSR. \n \n1 Certain equipment, instruments, software, or materials are identified in this paper in order to specify the \nexperimental procedure adequately.  Such identification is not intended to imply recommendation or endorsement  of \nany product or service by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, nor is it intended to imply that the \nmaterials or equipment identified are necessarily the best available for the purpose.  \n \n\n2 \n \nAramid fiber rate sensitivity and viscoelasticity arise through a combination of mechanisms during tensile \nloading from the anisotropy crystallinity introduced during the drawing process and the presence of both \ncovalent bonds and weaker secondary bonds [21]. The covalent bonds within the molecular chains deform \nelastically, while secondary bonds undergo viscoelastic shear deformation. The secondary interactions \nweaken and eventually lead to fiber fracture as shear stress increases [22]. During tensile loading under \nHSR, molecular chains have insufficient time for rearrangement, leading to reduced intermolecular slip. \nAs a result, fewer hydrogen bonds between adjacent PPTA chains break and more load transfers to \nprimary covalent bonds, increasing the likelihood of covalent bond rupture and crystallite fracture [23], \n[24]. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations by Tan et al. [24] support this, showing longer \nfibrils at low strain rates and shorter fibrils at about 1000 s⁻¹, consistent with a shift from secondary to \nprimary bond failure. Since primary bond scission requires greater strain energy than secondary bond \nfailure, this transition can also lead to higher failure strains at elevated loading rates [24]. The shift in \nload-bearing behavior results in a transition from viscoelastic to elastic behavior at HSR [8]. \nPrior studies have generally had limitations, including small sample sizes (typically between 10 and 16 \nspecimens at HSR), indirect strain measurement techniques, and a lack of direct comparison to fiber-\nmatched QS testing and diameter measurements [16], [18]. To overcome these limitations, in this work, \nextensive QS fiber testing was paired with testing on a specialized miniaturized Kolsky tension bar [25], \nknown as the \"Mini-Kolsky Bar,\" specifically designed for HSR tensile testing of single fibers. The main \ncontribution of this work is a set of methodological advances that improve the accuracy and statistical \nrobustness of single-fiber HSR characterization and comparison to lower rate testing. First, the NIST \nMini-Kolsky Bar configuration was optimized, and a paper-frame templating technique was used to \nreduce grip-induced compliance, eliminate localized slipping, and minimize slack and gauge-length \nartifacts. Second, a rigid-body digital image correlation (DIC) method was implemented to measure grip \ndisplacement and failure strain directly, rather than deriving strain indirectly from bar signals as in most \nprior work. Third, failure stress was obtained using a paired-sampling approach with propagated \nmeasurement uncertainty, enabling for the first time a direct fiber-matched comparison between QS and \nHSR conditions. For high-strength single-fiber testing, at least 100 samples are preferable to ensure \nstatistical robustness [26], and thus this study employed substantially larger sample sizes than prior work \n(n = 62 per fiber at HSR, n = 100 per QS condition) to provide a statistically robust characterization of \nrate-dependent mechanical behavior. Because these advances are not specific to PPTA, this approach is \nbroadly applicable to HSR tensile characterization of other high-performance single fibers. By improving \nthe accuracy and dataset size of single-fiber Kolsky bar testing methods for PPTA, the work aims to \ncontribute to the development of lighter, more flexible, and more effective body armor systems. \n2. The reactive mono-\nmers generally have low viscosity and can be readily infused\ninto a network of stiﬀ, high-strength fibers or inorganic filler\nparticles and then thermally cross-linked around the fillers to\ncreate a polymer matrix composite. One of the most widely\nutilized strategies in polymer matrix composites is to combine\nthermosetting epoxy resins with high strength carbon fibers to\nrealize high-strength, light-weight systems. Carbon fiber-epoxy\ncomposites are increasingly used in a range of commercial and\nmilitary applications related to buildings and construction,\ntransportation and vehicles, aerospace, athletics, and protective\nequipment. In many of these applications, it is desirable to\nhave the composite maintain its performance over a wide range\nof temperatures, extending from the deeply sub-ambient to\ntemperatures that can exceed 200 1C. One of the most impor-\ntant properties for a structural composite material is mechan-\nical toughness. Retaining toughness across such a broad\ntemperature range is a challenge for most epoxy resins. Lower\nTg epoxy formulations that oﬀer toughness under ambient\nconditions often become embrittled at sub-ambient tempera-\ntures. High Tg epoxy formulations that oﬀer strength and\nthermal stability unfortunately tend to be brittle and lead to\npoor fracture resistance of the resulting composite. This lack of\ntoughness becomes especially problematic at the ultra-high\nrates of deformation that are associated with ballistic impacts.\nOver the past decade, several studies have focused on quanti-\nfying the level of energy dissipation in a wide range of cross-\nlinked thermoset network polymers under ballistic impact con-\nditions across an extreme range of temperatures.1–8 These studies\nhave mostly focused on the neat resin, without fibers or fillers, to\ndevelop a molecular understanding of what gives rise to energy\ndissipation, and therefore toughness, at the rates of deformation\nthat are relevant for ballistics,i.e., strain rates in excess of 106 s/C01.\nThe ability of an epoxy formulation to dissipate energy at these\nballistic rates is operationally defined by making multiple panels\nof the same material and shooting identical projectiles, each at a\nfresh panel, with increasing incident velocities until the point at\nwhich 50% of the panels are penetrated by the projectile. This\ncritical velocity is defined as V50.B yk n o w i n gt h em a s so ft h e\nprojectile and V50, one can define KE 50 as the ballistic impact\nresistance, the kinetic energy of a projectile needed to penetrate\n50% of the panels. KE50 is an operationally defined performance\nmetric relevant to ballistic impact resistance, but not a true\nmeasurement energy dissipation or material toughness.\nThis manuscript focuses on the mechanisms that dissipate\nenergy and contribute to the toughness of cross-linked thermo-\nset glasses. For decades it has been appreciated that relaxations\nin the glassy state are important for mechanical toughness in\npolymers, i.e., that having an active mechanical relaxation is\nimportant for energy dissipation. 9–12 Seminal works by Boyce,\nusing a variety of impact testing configurations that push the\ndeformation rates into the sub-ballistic regime (strain rates\nnominally up 10 4 s/C01) have shown that when the rate of\nmechanical deformation exceeds the characteristic relaxation\ntime of the sub- Tg relaxation (often called the b relaxation) in\nthe polymer glass, the stiffness and yield strength of the\nmaterial goes up. 13–15 The interpretation is that when you\ndeactivate the energy dissipation mechanism by not giving\nthe material enough time to respond to the impulse, the glass\nbecomes stiffer but also more brittle. However, there is still a\ndisparity between the time and length scales of the molecular\nmechanisms that dissipate energy under ballistic rates of\ndeformation, in excess of 10 6 s/C01, and the characterization\ntechniques that are used to quantify the relevant relaxations.\nAs a general statement, we still cannot predict the ballistic\nresponse of glassy polymers from our current knowledge of\npolymer relaxations.\nWe recently initiated an eﬀort to close this gap by exploring\ncorrelations between the level of anharmonicity in the atomic\nmean square displacement, hu2iexcess, of polymer glasses as\nquantified by incoherent neutron scattering and their corres-\nponding toughness.16 Across a homologous series of polycarbo-\nnates (PCs) with systematic variations in their toughness, we\nobserved a strong correlation between hu2iexcess and the quasi-\nstatic impact strength. Our assertion was that the large ‘‘excess’’\nmean-square atomic displacements measured in the tough PCs,\nreflecting collective molecular relaxations on the sub-ns time-\nscale, are the signature of incipient dissipative relaxations. How-\never, these measurements based on a Debye–Waller analysis of\nthe elastic incoherent neutron scattering intensities did not\nprecisely resolve the timescale of the motions, beyond identifying\nthat they were faster than the approximately 1 ns resolution of the\nspectrometer. In a second manuscript, 17 we quantified the full\nenergy spectra of the scattered neutrons to better define the\ndynamical processes and relevant time scales that underpin these\nobserved motions in the quiescent glass. This is the\ntypical order of magnitude for the fast beta relaxation time that is\nseen in neutron scattering. 19,20 The onset of this relaxation\ncoincided with the BDT temperature, suggesting that many-\natom, collective relaxations underpin macroscopic toughness.\nIn our previous publication, we estimated that the size of these\ncollective motions was on the order of (5 to 20) nm 3, and noted\nthese dimensions were on par with the activation volume of\nyielding in typical polymer glasses.17\nWith respect to our goal to develop a general understanding\nof the ballistic impact resistance in polymer glasses, the study\nhere contains two important extensions from our previous\npublications on correlating quasielastic neutron scattering with\nmechanical properties. Many of the reading assignments this term will be \ntaken from a new textbook by Ken Dill and Sarina Bromberg. 2 This text is focused on applications for physical \nchemists and biologists, but has excellent explanations and many simple numerical examples that you may find \nhelpful. The text by Denbigh 3 is a traditional text on classical thermodynamics - it is very rigorous, but in some \n5parts difficult for a newcomer to thermodynamics. Zemansky’s text 4 and the text by Lupis are a good place to go \nfor alternate explanations of difficult concepts, and are rooted in practical examples. The text by Bent 6 provides a \nvery physical description of concepts and uses simple examples to help explain concepts. It teaches \nthermodynamics from a composite statistical mechanics/classical thermodynamics approach. For practice with \npractical problems, a good textbook is Ga skell7, which has answers for the problems at the end of each chapter \nprovided. \nThe text by Hill8 is an introduction to statistical mechanics, but like Denbigh, its rigor may be difficult for you \nto follow at this stage. Callen 9 is a somewhat advanced treatment of classical thermodynamics, and likewise \nChandler10 is a somewhat advanced modern treatment of statistical mechanics. \n1.\t Carter, W. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Resistivity\nResistivity is the material property that pertains to how difficult it is for electrical current to flow through said material.\nMaterials with high resistivity are known as insulators while materials with low resistivity are known as conductors.\nSpanning from 10  Ωm to 10  Ωm (see Figure ), resistivity possess the largest range of values for any physical\nproperty. Resistivity is essential in many material applications including resistors in electrical circuits, dielectrics,\nresistive heating, and superconducting.\nFigure :  Regimes of materials according to resistivity.\nIntroduction\nThe fundamental relationship that explores a materials opposition to electron flow was first derived in 1826 by Georg\nOhm, a German physicist and mathematician. Ohm's Law is represented by the following equation:\nwhere\nV [Volts: J/C] is the voltage applied to the material,\nI [Amperes: C/s] is the electrical current flow, and\nR [ohms: V/A] is the resistance of the material specimen.\nIt is important to note that resistance is dependent on the specific geometry of a material specimen as seen in Figure 2.\nFigure  Material specimen dimensions that relate resistance to resistivity.\nTo represent the electrical resistivity as an intrinsic material property, the voltage must be divided by the length L at\nwhich it is applied to and the current must be divided by the area A it flows through to produce an electric field  and\ncurrent density J respectively. This translation to electric field and current density yields the following equation for\nresistivity:\nwhere  is the resistivity of a material . When comparing materials, it is common to invert the value of resistivity to\nmake conductivity  [Siemens] which can easily be used to rank materials on the basis of how well each conducts\nelectrons. Due to the significant temperature dependence on resistivity and conductivity, a material's resistiveness\nmeasured at room temperature [20°C].\nAs mentioned above, materials are broken into three essential regimes: insulators, semiconductors, and metals. The\nmanifestation of resistivity in conducting materials, metals and semiconductors, can be fully realized by evaluating the\nbehavior of electrons at the quantum mechanical level.\nResistivity of Pure Metals\nMetals are structured by a lattice of atoms that are metallically bonded to one another. The sea of delocalized electrons\nfound in metallic bonding is created by having a high density of states (i.e. electrons) at the Fermi level which are easily\nexcited into the conduction band. From this bonding, electrons a can be thought of as free electrons moving through the\nmetal matrix. As the electron flows, it will interact with individual atoms, causing scattering events, which decrease the\neffectiveness of electrons at traversing the metal. The mobility of the electrons play an important role in quantifying the\nresistivity of a metal as seen in the following equation:\n-8 20\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\n9/30/26, 2:11 PM Resistivity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Resistivity 1/4\n\nwhere e is the charge of an electron,  Fermi velocity of a conduction electron, τ is the relaxation time between\nscattering events, and  is the population density of electrons at the Fermi energy. Additionally, it is seen that the\npopulation density of electrons at the Fermi level is taken in to account as opposed to the total number of valance\nelectrons, which explains the exceptionally low resistivity of silver, copper and gold.\nTemperature Dependence\nThe equation above shows that the resistivity of a metal is inversely proportionally to the relaxation time. This means\nthe number of scattering events plays a substantial role in the resistivity of a metal. A large contributor to the number\nof scattering events iin a metal is the thermal vibrations of each atom in the lattice. As the temperature of a material\nincreases, each atom beings to oscillate about its central position, increasing the probability that an electron would\ncollide with it. This relationship is visualized by measuring the resistivity of silver as a function of temperature, Figure\n.\nFigure :  Resistivity of bulk silver as a function of temperature.\nMetals exhibit a minimal resistivity at temperatures approaching 0 Kelvin, known as a residual resistivity, and a linear\nincrease in resistivity as the metal reaches its melting point.\nResidual Resistivity and Matthiessen's Rule\nAt low enough temperatures, the degrees of thermal vibration are not yet activated meaning the residual resistivity of a\nmetal is a collection of all other scattering sites present in the material specifically defects and impurities. With\npolycrystalline metals, there will be a number of sources of defects in the microstructure including Grain boundaries,\ndislocations, and vacancies. Along with defects, impurities in a metal can host a scattering site. In 1864 Augustus\nMatthiessen, a British chemist and physicist, was the first to incorporate all of these aspects into the resistivity of a\nmetal. Matthiessen's Rule is as follows:\nwhere  is the resistivity due to temperature,  is the resistivity due to impurities and  is the the resistivity due\nto defects. While temperature, defects, and impurities do in fact contribute to resistivity, some deviation from the\nsimple summation postulated by Matthiessen has been reported for specific metals.\nResistivity of Alloys\nFrom Matthiessen's Rule it was seen that the resistivity of a metal was influenced by the impurities present. This\nportion of the resistivity begins to have a significant contribution when metals are alloyed together. An alloy can be\nviewed as a metal with a large number of impurities, meaning there is a great deal more scattering sites to increase the\nresidual resistivity of the metal. The result of this increase is a translation of the plot in Figure  upward. At varying\ncompositions of a simple binary alloy, the resistivity of the system is a linear interpolation of the resistivity of each pure\nmetal. If the system exhibits an energetically favorable phase transition that results in a more ordered structure than\nthat of the solute atoms in solution, a drop in resistivity at that composition will be observed. An example of a binary\nsystem that has ordered phases that affect resistivity is copper and platinum.\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\n9/30/26, 2:11 PM Resistivity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Resistivity 2/4\n\nFigure :  Resistivity of the binary system of copper and platinum at 500 K as a function of\ncomposition. The dashed line models standard linear interpolation of the two pure metals while the solid line\nrepresents the actual resistivity due to the formation of ordered phases.\nThe plot of the copper platinum binary system demonstrates the result of the ordered phases  and . Similar to the\ndeviations from Matthiessen's Rule, formulation of the relationship of resistivity of any alloy has not been adequately\ndeveloped because of the complexity of the structures created by any given alloy system. Several rules have been\ncreated with little implication because each emphasizes a specific subset of alloys with particular characteristics.\nResistivity of Semiconductors\nThe primary distinguishing factor between metals and any other material is that metals do not possess a band gap or a\nrange of energy levels that are not allowed for electrons to inhabit. It has been observed that the size of the band gap of\na material how insulative it is and at low enough band gaps, the material can be partially conductive. These materials\nare, of course, semiconductors. During the region of temperatures when\nthe resistivity is not changing, the number of electrons being thermally excited to the conduction band is not yet large\nenough to influence the resistivity as much as the extrinsic doping has. Eventually the number of excited electrons\nbecomes great enough to resume the intrinsic temperature dependent trend.\nQuestions\n1. What distinguishes resistance from resistivity? [{"suffix": "", "text": "3.012 PS 3            3.012 \nIssued: 10.03.05          Fall 05 \nNot due \n \n \n \n \nBONDING \n \nThese questions cover several topics presented in class – use them as a checklist to highlight areas \nthat need more work. \n \n1. What is the wavelength of a photon that has an energy of 1 eV ? \n2. Describe the concept of linear superposition, and what we mean by destructive interference. \n3. What is the wavefunction for a free electron in 3 dimensions ? Show that it satisfies either the \nstationary Schroedinger equation, or, if you write also the time-dependent term, that it \nsatisfies the full, time-dependent Schroedinger equation. \n4. What is the momentum, and what is the wavelength of an electron that has a kinetic energy \nof 1 eV ? \n5. How can you derive the stationary Schroedinger equation from the time-dependent \nSchrodinger equation ? \n6. What are the eigenfunctions and the eigenstates of an electron confined in 3-dim in a square \nbox of radius a ? \n7. How does the STM works ? \n8. What is a linear operator ? \n9. What is an expectation value ? \n10. What is the surface of the earth, if its radius is 6,400,000 m ? \n11. What is, in cartesian coordinates, the angular momentum operator ? Used with permission.\n\nDetermining Active Slip System\n There are two methods to determine which slip \nsystem is active\n Brute Force Method- Calculate angles for each slip \nsystem for a given load and determine the maximum \nSchmid Factor\n Elegant Method- Use stereographic projection to \ndetermine the active slip system graphically\n\nStereographic Projection Method\n1 Identify the triangle containing the tensile axis\n2 Determine the slip plane by taking the pole \nof the triangle that is in the family of the slip \nplanes (i.e. for FCC this would be {111}) and \nreflecting it off the opposite side of the \nspecified triangle\n3 Determine the slip direction by taking the \npole of the triangle that is in the family of \ndirections (i.e. for FCC this would be <1-10>) \nand reflecting it off the opposite side of the \nspecified triangle\nCourtesy of DoITPoMS, University of Cambridge.\n\nRotation of Crystal Lattice Under an \nApplied Load\n With increasing load, the slip plane and slip direction \nalign parallel to the tensile stress axis\n This movement may be traced on the stereographic \nprojection\n The tensile axis rotates toward the slip direction \neventually reaching the edge of the triangle\n Note that during compression the slip direction rotates away \nfrom the compressive axis\n At the edge of the triangle a second slip system is \nactivated because it has an equivalent Schmid factor\n\nMore Physical Examples\n Initial Elastic Strain- results from bond stretching (obeys \nHooke’s Law)\n Stage I (easy glide)- results from slip on one slip system\n Stage II- Multiple slip systems are active. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Review\nRobotic sorting and artificial intelligence in material recovery facilities: a \nreview of published research and expert perspectives\nTanmay Haldankar a,b, Kelsea Schumacher b,*\na University of Maryland, College Park, College Park 20742, MD, USA\nb National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg 20899, MD, USA\nARTICLE INFO\nKeywords:\nAutomation at materials recovery facilities\nAI sorting in recycling\nRobotic waste sorting\nRobotic integration challenges\nABSTRACT\nMaterial Recovery Facilities (MRFs) are essential to municipal recycling infrastructure, but face difficulties in \nsorting due to the growing complexity of recyclable material streams and contamination in their inputs. The \nlimitations of traditional sorting technologies and reliance on manual sorters at MRFs have driven interest in \nintegrating robotic systems that combine artificial intelligence (AI) detection with robotic actuation. This paper \npresents a review of AI and robotic sorting at MRFs, based on insights from recent literature and expert con-\nsultations. The literature review uncovered advances in AI algorithms and datasets, application of new sensors \nand multi-modal sensing systems, and novel robotic gripping and grasping strategies. Expert consultations \nidentified a shift toward deploying AI systems as standalone detection tools, particularly for quality control and \nfacility monitoring, and a movement away from robotic integration due to limitations in speed, reliability, and \ngripper effectiveness. The analysis reveals three key challenge areas: (1) practical deployment and economic \nviability of robotic sorting systems, (2) limitations in AI performance and data availability, and (3) robot-specific \nchallenges related to gripping and grasping. The paper outlines future research directions to address these \nchallenges and advance the field.\n1. Introduction\nThe U.S. municipal recycling system consists of three primary stages: \ncollection, processing, and remanufacturing (U.S. Environmental \nProtection Agency, 2025). Materials recovery facilities (MRFs) serve \nas processing facilities that sort and separate collected recyclables into \ncompacted bales to be sold to secondary markets. Unlike ‘dirty’ MRFs, \nwhich aim to separate recyclables from the municipal solid waste (MSW, \ni.e., black bag garbage) stream, ‘clean’ MRFs handle source-separated \nrecyclables from residential areas, i.e., materials consumers have \nalready sorted from the MSW stream, typically in blue or green bins. \nThere are over 400 MRFs operating in the United States, collectively \nprocessing more than 37 million tons of packaging material annually, \ncollected primarily from identified sources, and often require techno-\nlogical upgrades to improve operational efficiency and material recov-\nery rate (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2024). This paper \nfocuses on clean MRFs, which are the predominant type in the US and, \nfor simplicity, will be referenced henceforth as “MRFs”.\nSource-separated collection and clean MRF-style processing are also \npracticed in other regions, like the European Union, where Extended \nProducer Responsibility (EPR) regulations and deposit-return schemes \nshape accepted material streams and bale quality standards are different \nfrom the U.S. context, as well as Australia and parts of Asia. Regional \ndifferences in accepted materials, bale market specifications, and policy \ndrivers mean that findings from one system are not always directly \ntransferable between regions.\nA major challenge for MRFs is contamination in the incoming ma-\nterial stream. This includes both non-recyclable items as well as impu-\nrities on otherwise recyclable items, such as labels, food residue, or \nliquids. A common contributor to the former is “wish cycling,” where \nconsumers place non-accepted items in recycling bins in the hope that \nthey will be recycled. Products that are generally not accepted at MRFs, \nsuch as packaging made from certain plastics (e.g., PVC, PS), plastic film \nand bags, or products requiring disassembly, complicate the sorting \nprocess. For example, flexible plastics like grocery bags and film can \nentangle sorting equipment, leading to mechanical failures and down-\ntime (Lubongo and Alexandridis, 2022). Hazardous materials, including \nbatteries and medical waste, further increase operational risk. Lithium- \nion batteries are particularly dangerous, as they can ignite when \ndamaged (Plasticsrecycling.org, 2025). Contamination not only disrupts \n* Corresponding author.\nE-mail address: Kelsea.Schumacher@nist.gov (K. Schumacher). \nContents lists available at ScienceDirect\nWaste Management\njournal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/wasman\nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.wasman.2026.115830\nReceived 1 April 2026; Received in revised form 15 June 2026; Accepted 21 August 2026  \nWaste Management 226 (2026) 115830 \nAvailable online 1 September 2026 \n0956-053X/Published by Elsevier Ltd. \n\nMRF operations but also reduces the quality of their output, and MRF \nbales may be rejected by downstream processors due to high contami-\nnation levels (Lubongo and Alexandridis, 2022).\nMRFs use a combination of automated and manual sorting systems to \nseparate incoming recyclables. Facilities equipped with older sorting \ntechnology often rely on manual labor to sort complex material streams, \nsuch as mixed plastics. Manual sorting is also essential across MRFs to \naddress contamination and prevent operational disruptions. This reli-\nance on human labor can slow processing and increase operating costs. \nHigh employee turnover is common at MRFs due to difficult working \nconditions that include elevated temperatures, strong odors, and phys-\nically demanding tasks. Worker safety is a persistent concern due to \nexposure to hazardous materials, such as sharp objects and medical \nwaste, as well as the risk of equipment-related injuries (Rosengren, \n2019).\nThe need to enhance sorting efficiency and reduce dependence on \nmanual labor has made material sorting at MRFs a popular application \nfor robotic system development. In this context, robotic sorters refer to \nintegrated systems that combine artificial intelligence (AI)-driven \ndetection with robotic manipulation. These advanced systems integrate \nperception technologies, such as cameras and AI algorithms, to identify \nrecyclables on conveyor belts and use robots to physically separate the \ndetected materials. Robotic sorters can identify and locate materials \nbased on visual features such as shape and color, flexibly pick items from \nconveyor belts, and integrate into the spatially constrained environ-\nments of existing MRFs. Through continuous, real-time training, they \ncan adapt to changing material streams and exhibit sorting capabilities \nthat resemble those of human workers. These systems also offer addi-\ntional functionality, such as operational monitoring, data collection, and \nthe ability to sort items by product brand.\nSeveral reviews have previously examined AI and robotic sorting in \nthe broader waste management context. Fang et al. (2023) provide a \ncomprehensive overview of AI applications for waste management in \nsmart cities, covering collection, transportation, and sorting across \ndiverse waste streams, establishing the wider landscape within which \nMRF sorting sits. Lu and Chen (2022) systematically assess computer \nvision methods for solid waste sorting, and Kroell et al. (2022) survey \noptical sensors and machine learning for material flow characterization. \nMaier et al. (2024) offer a broad survey of sensor-based sorting tech-\nnology across industrial applications, while Kiyokawa et al. (2024)\nsurvey robotic sorting challenges specifically for mixed industrial waste. \nOur paper complements these works by focusing specifically on clean \nMRFs, with the operational context grounded primarily in the United \nStates. The AI and robotics literature reviewed is intentionally broad and \nspans literature about kitchen waste facilities in China, European in-\ndustrial sorting plants, and synthetic datasets because no MRF-specific \nliterature exists for many of the technical areas covered. Where \nstudies originate from non-U.S. or non-MRF settings, they are treated as \nproviding transferable but indirect evidence and their testing context is \nnoted in Table 2. The paper addresses three aspects not well covered in \nthe existing literature: (1) the deployment and economic barriers that \nshape real-world adoption of AI and robotic systems at MRFs; (2) the \nemerging industry trend of decoupling AI detection from robotic sort-\ning/actuation, with AI increasingly deployed alongside optical sorters \nrather than integrated with robots; and (3) expert perspectives on \noperational constraints like throughput limitations, gripper reliability, \nand facility economics, that are not yet well represented in the published \nliterature.\nDespite their potential, robotic sorters face significant challenges \nwhen integrated at MRFs. MRFs present highly unpredictable environ-\nments, characterized by a wide variety of items densely gathered on fast- \nmoving conveyor belts, requiring robotic sorters to effectively separate \nmaterials at high speeds. The objective of this work is to assess the \ncurrent state of robotic sorters deployed at MRFs and identify challenges \nthey face with the intent to inform future research. The rest of the paper \nis structured as follows: Section 2 details the methodology used for the \nresearch; Section 3 provides background information regarding MRFs \nand their sorting operations; Section 4 presents descriptions of imple-\nmentations of robotic and AI sorting systems discovered from the liter-\nature review and expert consultations; Section 5 outlines the challenges \nidentified from both sources; and Section 6 offers a discussion based on \nthe findings.\n2. Methodology\nThe research methodology involved two phases: literature review \nand discussions with industry experts. The literature review included a \nstructured search conducted in 2024 across three major academic da-\ntabases, Engineering Village, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. These \ndatabases were selected for their broad and overlapping coverage of \nengineering, computer science, and applied science literature relevant to \nthe topic. The following search string was used to gather relevant \nstudies: (robot OR “computer vision” OR vision* OR “machine learning” \nOR “deep learning” OR “artificial intelligence” OR “learning” OR \n“grasping” OR “grasp planning” OR gripp*) AND (recycl* OR “mixed \nindustrial waste” OR waste OR “materials recovery facilities” OR MRF \nOR MSW OR “municipal solid waste”) AND (sort* OR separat*) AND \n(challenge* OR survey OR review*). It should be noted that the inclusion \nof 'challenge OR survey OR review*' in the final AND clause may have \nintroduced a bias toward problem-focused literature and deployment \nstudies that do not use these terms in titles or abstracts may have been \nmissed. This is acknowledged as a limitation of the search strategy.\nThe search query resulted in 974 papers, which were initially \nscreened for relevance based on titles and abstracts by the lead author. \nThe gathered articles can be categorized into review articles and papers \nthat develop robotic sorting implementations. Survey/review papers \nprovide comprehensive overviews of prior research in the field and help \nsummarize key challenges in the literature. The implementation papers \npresent the latest methods for robotic sorting of MSW at recycling fa-\ncilities and help clarify current research trends.\nPapers that focused on automated sorting in other waste streams, like \nconstruction and demolition (C&D) waste or electronic waste, and other \nrobotic applications, such as smart bins and mobile sorting robots

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Effect of Ionic Liquids on the Structure of Ionomer Inks\nTyler B. Martin* and Kimber Stamm Masias*\nCite This: Macromolecules 2025, 58, 8288−8294\n ReadOnline\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: This study investigates the impactof ionic liquids (ILs) on the structure\nand performance of catalyst inks used in proton exchange membrane fuel cells\n(PEMFCs). Using contrast variation small-angle neutron scattering (CV-SANS), we\nelucidate the structural interactions between ionomers, Pt/C catalyst particles, and ILs.\nThe analysis reveals that IL composition significantly influences the arrangement of\nionomersandtheirinteractionswithotherinkcomponents.Inparticular,oneoftheILs\n([BMIM][C4]) exhibited stronger associations with both ionomer and catalyst\nparticles, resulting in reduced availability of platinum catalytic sites and lower PEMFC\nperformance. These findings demonstrate the structural origins of electrochemical\nperformance variations, providing insights into the design of improved ionic liquid formulations for enhanced fuel cell efficiency.\n■INTRODUCTION\nProton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC) convert\nchemicalenergyfromthereactionofH2 andO2 intoelectricity,\npresenting a low emission route to a carbon neutral energy\nsource. A major component of a PEMFC is the membrane\nelectrodeassembly(MEA)whichconsistsofgasdiffusionlayers,\ncatalyst layers, and the polymer electrolyte membrane. While\nreducingtheunitcostbyreplacingtheplatinum(Pt)catalystisa\nlargeandongoingfocusofresearchers,otherchallengespersist.\nEfficiency of PEMFCs is hampered by energy losses at the\ncathode during the oxygen reduction reaction,1 opening the\ndoor to investigation of non-Pt catalysts,2 shape-controlled\ncatalysts,3 alternative ionomers for proton transport,4 and\nimproving the triple phase boundary between carbon, Pt, and\nionomer.\nSearching for ever-better performance, researchers have\ninvestigated the inclusion of ionic liquids (ILs) in the ionomer\ncomplexwiththeaimofimprovingtheefficiencyofO2 diffusion\nthrough the polymer by modifying the ionomer-Pt catalyst\ninterface.5−8 Severalinvestigationshaveshowntheinclusionof\nILsimprovestheO2 transportkineticsaswellastheaccessibility\nofPtcatalystsites.Severalelectrochemicaloriginsforthechange\nin performance can be proposed, including changes in\nhydrophobicity that impact proton transport or variations in\ntheO2 transportkinetics.Structuraloriginsfortheperformance\nimprovement, such as changes in the association between the\nionomer side chain thiol groups and the Pt catalyst, are also\nplausible.Theseexplanationshavebeenconsideredinthedried\ncatalyst layer of the MEA but theimpact of including the ionic\nliquidintothecatalystinkusedtocreatetheMEAhavenotbeen\nexplored.\nInordertofabricateafunctionalMEA,allcomponentsofthe\nMEAaremixedandsuspendedinacatalystinkusingwaterand\nalcohol as solvents. The structure and eventual function of the\nMEAisdirectlyimpactedbythepropertiesoftheink,including\nthe coating of the ionomer onto the carbon-supported Pt\ncatalyst (Pt/C) and the subsequent aggregation of the catalyst\nparticles themselves. Identifying the impact of the ILs on the\nordering and aggregation of the ink components will allow a\nbetter understanding of the structural rearrangements of the\nrealized MEA thatmodify itselectrochemical performance.\nMeasuring the arrangement of the catalyst ink components\nusing traditional techniques, such as small-angle scattering, is\nchallenging.Thecontrastandfractalassemblyofthecarbonand\nPt components of the ink dominate the signals of both small-\nangle X-ray and neutron scattering (SAXS and SANS,\nrespectively). Even attempting to leverage simple contrast\nmatching techniquesinSANSfails duetothestrongscattering\nand neutronSLDof thecarbonand Pt.\nTo overcome this, previous studies have used contrast\nvariation SANS (CV-SANS) to study the catalyst layer inks\n(without ionic liquids).9−12 Using CV-SANS, these authors\nwereabletoidentifythestructuralarrangementoftheionomers\nintheirinks,despiterawSANSintensitybeingdominatedbythe\nPt/C. The CV-SANS approach takes the SANS pattern of a\nmaterial measured at several contrast conditions and decom-\nposes the scattering into individual component scattering\nfunctions. This allows for the understanding of not only the\noverall solution structure of the ink, but also the relative\narrangement of the individual components (e.g., IL, ionomer,\nPt/C).\nIn this study, we use CV-SANS to determine the impact of\nmultipleionicliquidsonthestructureofaliquidphasecatalyst\nReceived: March 14, 2025\nRevised: July 17, 2025\nAccepted: July 17, 2025\nPublished: July 28, 2025\nArticlepubs.acs.org/Macromolecules\n© 2025 The Authors. Note that (a) is an equation in individual \noperations, not symmetry elements. \n \n \nc. The three-dimensional space lattices may be derived by “stacking” the two \ndimensional plane groups. (These give the set of symmetries that require all possible \ntypes of two-dimensional lattices.  Symmetry and the “special” geometry of a lattice \nare two inseparable aspects of a pattern.  For example, a 2-D lattice is square only if \nthere is a 4-fold axis present that demands that this be so, and if a 4-fold axis is \npresent it requires that, if it is combined with translational periodicity, that the lattice is \nexactly square.)   \n \nCombining a third translation that is not coplanar with plane group P4 will, therefore, \n“stack” the square nets above one another. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Identifying the chemical gel point of epoxy-fumed silica composites using optimally windowed chirp measurements \nStian K. Romberg† (ORCID: 0000-0003-1026-2023)\nSarah Lehrman†‡\nJonathan Seppala† (ORCID: 0000-0002-5937-8716)\nAnthony P. Kotula†* (ORCID: 0000-0002-0830-2869) \n†Materials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, United States of America\n‡University of Maryland Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD 21250, United States of America\n*Email of corresponding author: anthony.kotula@nist.gov\n\n\n\nAbstract\nThe chemical gel point that occurs in the resin matrix of thermoset composites is crucial to the design of manufacturing process parameters. However, the formation of a physical network of filler material can affect the viscoelastic response of the composite so strongly that conventional rheological indicators of the chemical gel point (like power-law stress relaxation) are no longer observed. Additionally, many industrially relevant thermoset composites have a small linear viscoelastic region, limiting the utility of the high-strain multiwave measurement approach that was developed to monitor the frequency-dependent behavior of rapidly evolving materials. Here, we pair frequency-dependent properties obtained by low-strain Optimally Windowed Chirp (OWCh) measurements with existing rheology-conversion relationships to apply time-cure superposition to the loss tangent of epoxy-amine resins filled with unreactive particles. We show that this advanced rheological approach allows us to track the relative change in the relaxation time, providing another way to identify the elusive chemical gel point of these thermoset composites. The results allow us to assess the applicability of several gel point criteria to crosslinking composites, including the G'-G'' crossover, frequency-independent tan δ, peak in tan δ, and divergence of the relaxation time. Investigation of a resin with a weak filler network reveals all of these gel point criteria, with the frequency-independent tan δ providing the best agreement with the easily identifiable gel point of the neat resin. For resins with a strong physical filler network, frequency independence of tan δ does not occur, but the divergence of the relaxation time matches the gel point of the neat resin and the peak in tan δ. \nKeywords: optimally windowed chirp (OWCh); thermoset composite; gel point; time-cure superposition; relaxation time\nIntroduction\nThe critical gel point associated with the formation of a space-spanning network of chemical crosslinks (referred to here as the “chemical gel point” to distinguish it from physical gelation processes) informs processing parameters that are important in many manufacturing processes that use thermoset composite resins (Athanasiou et al. 2024; Duty et al. 2018; Kim et al. 2022; Kinjo et al. 1989; Macosko 1989; Rau et al. 2023; Romberg and Kotula 2023). These particle-filled resins are processed in an initially uncured state, where manufacturers take advantage of the yield stress properties of the physical gel particle network in the uncured composite resin to flow the material into a desired shape that is then held once the physical network recovers. The flowability of this composite resin persists until the matrix resin forms a chemical gel, after which point the yielding of this composite requires the irreversible breaking of covalent bonds in the matrix. The chemical gel point in these composite resins is also associated with significant changes in overall material properties. For example, in direct ink write (DIW) additive manufacturing, the chemical gel point represents an exponential increase in the structural stability of parts (Rau et al. 2023), after which parts can be moved or temperature can be increased without risking collapse (Romberg and Kotula 2023). Semiconductor packaging provides even more examples with processes like underfilling, encapsulation, transfer molding, and application of thermal interface materials, which consist of a dispersion of filler particles and additives in a matrix resin. In these techniques, the dispersion must reach its intended location (for example, it must fully fill the transfer mold) before flow halts at the chemical gel point (Kinjo et al. 1989). This point also marks the moment that the dispersion can support a load and cure shrinkage begins to manifest as residual stress (Kim et al. 2022). The chemical gel point is essential in many other industries that also utilize thermoset composites, like marine applications (Athanasiou et al. 2024) or high throughput molding (Macosko 1989).\nOne of the initial approximations used to identify the chemical gel point in unfilled resins was the first crossover of the storage modulus Gʹ and the loss modulus Gʺ (i.e., loss tangent tan δ = 1) during a single-frequency measurement (Winter 1987). While this approximation is useful in designing curing schedules, it makes several assumptions about the stoichiometry and behavior of the material, restricting its applicability to a narrow set of materials (Chambon and Winter 1987). Perhaps the most limiting assumption is that Gʺ is greater than Gʹ at the beginning of the cure. This is not true for many thermoset composites (Chapartegui et al. 2012; Corder et al. 2020; Hayaty et al. 2011; Meng et al. 2005; Nohales et al. 2013; Raghavan et al. 1996) which are filled with particles to improve structural stability in the uncured state or reduce the coefficient of thermal expansion of the fully cured product. In the absence of this simple approximation, previous work used the peak in the loss tangent to estimate the chemical gel point (Hayaty et al. 2011) but did not present independent measurements to verify or evaluate this criterion. For neat resins, a peak in the loss tangent late in the cure can represent vitrification; however, an additional peak may appear earlier in the cure for composite resins (Hayaty et al. 2011; Nohales et al. 2013; Romberg and Kotula 2023). Hayaty et al. associated the earlier peak with the chemical gel point. Other approaches estimate the chemical gel point from single-frequency measurements by identifying the shoulder in the loss modulus (Romberg and Kotula 2023) or by modeling the rheological evolution using the chemical gel point as a fitting parameter (Romberg et al. 2024). But again, these criteria are not presented with complementary results that indicate they correspond to the chemical gel point.\nMulti-frequency measurements of rheological properties reveal the viscoelastic relaxation spectrum, which provides a more general definition of the chemical gel point in unfilled resins. Winter and Chambon developed and verified a theory that determines the chemical gel point by identifying the moment that the loss tangent becomes frequency independent (Chambon and Winter 1987; Winter and Mours 1997). Previous research suggests that some composite resins may not exhibit the expected frequency independence at the chemical gel point of the matrix resin (Becker et al. 2003; Burroughs et al. 2022; Chiou et al. 2001; Corder et al. 2020; Hayaty et al. 2011; Nohales et al. 2013). In these cases, enough filler was added to form a space-spanning particle network (often referred to as a particulate gel (Larson 1999) or a physical gel (Winter and Mours 1997)). These physical gels have a low frequency plateau modulus, due to the particle network, that masks the frequency independence associated with the chemical gel point of the matrix resin. Since the chemical gel point in unfilled resins is also characterized by a divergence in the characteristic relaxation time (Winter and Mours 1997), measurement and analysis methods that can detect this divergence may be able to identify the chemical gel point in thermoset composites. Unfortunately, capturing the “instantaneous” relaxation time near the gel point is experimentally challenging because the material appreciably cures during the long duration required to directly measure diverging relaxation times (Adolf and Martin 1990). Horizontal shift factors used to achieve time-cure superposition of the frequency-dependent tan δ offer a way to track the relative change in relaxation time of the material, providing a faster alternative to monitor the evolution of this property. While time-cure superposition has been successful in identifying the gel point during crosslinking or the sol-gel process (Adolf and Martin 1990; Eom et al. 2000; Hodgson and Amis 1990; Lee and McKenna 1988; Plazek 1966; Simon et al. 2000; Winter and Mours 1997), it has not been applied to curing thermoset composites. \nTable 1 lists the tan δ-based chemical gel point criteria that will be discussed in the results of this work, as well as an abbreviation for each criterion.\nTable 1: Challenges and limitations of tan δ-based chemical gel point criteria\nChemical gel point criteria\nAbbreviation\nReferences\nChallenges/limitations\ntan δ = 1\nTD1\n(Winter 1987)\nObserved in neat resins\nOnly for balanced stoichiometry or other special cases\nAssumes Gʺ > Gʹ before curing\ntan δ ≠ f(ω)\nTDFI\n(Chambon and Winter 1987; Winter and Mours 1997)\nObserved in neat resins\nRequires multi-frequency measurements that are traditionally slow or apply large strains\nRequires tan δ be frequency independent in the measured frequency range\ntan δ peak\nTDP\n(Hayaty et al. 2011)\nObserved in composite resins\nNot verified with independent measurements\nDivergence of relaxation time\nDRT\n(Adolf and Martin 1990; Winter and Mours 1997)\nObserved in neat resins\nRequires multi-frequency measurements that are traditionally slow or apply large strains\nRequires time-cure superposition of tan δ\n\nTechniques like time-cure superposition require measurements of viscoelastic spectra over (in the ideal case) the widest frequency range in the shortest measurement duration possible. The slowest approach – a traditional frequency sweep – can take minutes to hours to complete and will provide unreliable measurements for resins that evolve quickly (Athanasiou et al. 2024). A faster approach, called Fourier Transform Mechanical Spectroscopy (Holly et al. 1988) or “multiwave” testing, applies superimposed sinusoidal strain waves of varying frequencies to the sample and measures the resulting stress response. The measurement duration is then set by the period of the lowest frequency. Multiwave testing is successful for materials with generous linear viscoelastic regions (Tanaka et al. 2012); however, the strain for each frequency is additive, leading to large total applied strain values that can exceed the modest linear viscoelastic strain amplitude limit (referred to here as the “critical strain”) frequently observed in thermoset composites (Athanasiou et al. 2024; Larson 1999; Romberg and Kotula 2023). Ghiringhelli et al. (Ghiringhelli et al. 2012) and Curtis et al. (Curtis et al. 2015) developed another way to quickly measure the viscoelastic spectrum via Optimal Fourier Rheometry (OFR) measurements, which utilize frequency modulated chirp waveforms. Rather than superimposing sinusoidal waves with different frequencies, OFR measurements smoothly transition between frequencies within a single measurement cycle, decoupling the amount of applied strain from the number of frequencies tested. Inspired by this work Geri et al. (Geri et al. 2018) developed Optimally Windowed Chirp (OWCh) measurements, which refined OFR by incorporating amplitude modulation to maximize the signal to noise ratio and avoid spectral fluctuations. OWCh measurements are both fast and minimize applied strain, making this approach a promising candidate to observe the evolution of the viscoelastic spectrum of thermoset composites during curing, as has recently been demonstrated by Athanasiou et al. (Athanasiou et al. 2024).\nHere, we build on the work of Athanasiou et al. (Athanasiou et al. 2024) by performin

Explain your choice of true/false (in 1 or 2 brief sentences), and if\nnecessary, show an equation that supports your statement.\n i. A first-order phase transition can be identified by a discontinuous increase in\nthe value of several variables of a system at the transition temperature,\nincluding volume, heat capacity, enthalpy, and entropy.\nFalse.  First-order phase transitions are characterized by a discontinuity in each of these functions;\nhowever, the heat capacity may jump to a higher or lower value after the phase transition (e.g.,\ntransformation from a liquid to a gas), and volume also is not constrained to jump to a higher value\n(e.g. ice has a larger molar volume than liquid water).\n ii. If the entropy change of a first-order phase transformation at constant\npressure ΔStrans is positive for stability, then the enthalpy of transformation\nΔHtrans must also be positive.\nTrue.  At a first-order phase transition at constant pressure, the enthalpy change and entropy\nchange are related to one another by \n€ \nΔHtrans=dqrev,trans=TtransΔStrans.  Since the absolute temperature\nmust be positive, the sign of the enthalpy and entropy changes must be the same.\n iii. Minimizing the Helmholtz free energy of the system + its surroundings under\nconditions of constant temperature and volume to determine the equilibrium\nstate is equivalent to maximizing the entropy of the universe, in obedience to\nthe second law.\nFalse.  Minimizing the free energy of the system alone at constant temperature and volume is\nequivalent to maximizing the entropy of the universe in a spontaneous process.\n iv. The entropy of materials decreases as temperature decreases, but if a hot\nliquid is placed in thermal contact with a cold reservoir, the liquid will\nspontaneously cool to the temperature of the reservoir, and this spontaneous\nprocess will not violate the second law.\nTrue.  Though the entropy of the material will be decreased in this process, the entropy of the\nsurroundings will substantially increase in the process of accepting heat from the system (heat must\nleave the system in this process).  Thus the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) will\nincrease.\n\n3.012 Quiz 2 2 of 4 10/27/04\n v. The work of polarizing an anisotropic single-crystal material by application of\nan electric field will depend on the direction in which the field is applied relative\nto the crystal orientation.\nTrue. For an isolated system of two materials A and B brought into thermal contact,\nthe entropies of the subsystems will be maximized at equilibrium, but the\ninternal energies will not necessarily reach a maximum or minimum.\nFalse.  The entropies of the individual subsystems will not necessarily be maximized- the sum of\nthe entropies of the two subsystems will be maximized, according to the second law.\n\n3.012 Quiz 2 3 of 4 10/27/04\nb. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Lattice Vibrations\nAlmost all solids with the exception of amorphous solids and glasses have periodic arrays of atoms which form a\ncrystal lattice . The existence of the periodic crystal lattice in solid materials provides a medium for characteristic\nvibrations. Between the lattice spacing, there are quantized vibrational modes called a phonon.  The study of phonon\nis an important part of solid state physics, as they play an essential role in the physical properties of solids, the thermal\nand electrical conductivity of the materials. The long wavelength property of phonon also gives attributes to sounds in\nsolids. Phonons are also a quantum mechanical version of a special type of vibrational motion. This type of vibrational\nmotion is called a normal mode (elementary blocks of lattice vibration), which is a pattern of motion in which all parts\nof the system move in a sinusoidal fashion, with the same frequency . An example of a normal mode is a standing\nwave, which is a continuous form of normal mode and all space elements, (x, y and Z co-ordinates) are oscillating at the\nsame frequencies, and phase but different amplitude.\nFigure  Standing Wave Standing wave in stationary medium. The red dots represent the wave nodes.\nThe general form of a standing wave is:\nwhere  represents the dependence of amplitude on location and the cosine and sine are the oscillations in time.\nA  represents the amplitude of the cosine waves.\nLattice Vibrations\nLattice vibrations can explain sound velocity, thermal properties, elastic properties and optical properties of materials.\nLattice Vibration is the oscillations of atoms in a solid about the equilibrium position. For a crystal, the equilibrium\npositions form a regular lattice, due to the fact that the atoms are bound to neighboring atoms. The vibration of these\nneighboring atoms is not independent of each other. A regular lattice with harmonic forces between atoms and normal\nmodes of vibrations are called lattice waves. Lattice waves range from low frequencies to high frequencies on the order\nof 1,013 Hz or even higher . However, the wavelengths at extremely high frequencies are of the order of inter atomic\nspacing. Due to the shortness of these wavelengths, the motion of the neighboring atoms is uncorrelated; with each\natom moving about its average position in three dimensions with average vibrational energy, which is usually 3kT,\nwith ‘ ’ representing the Boltzmann constant and ' ' the absolute temperature. Lattice vibrations can also interact with\nfree electrons in a conducting solid which gives rise to electrical resistance .\nCompared to the static lattice model that deals with the average positions of atoms in a crystal; lattice dynamics\nworks towards extending the concept of crystal lattice to an array of atoms with finite masses capable of motion.\nThe motion of masses is a superposition of vibrations of atoms around the equilibrium sites induced by the\ninteraction with neighboring atoms. The collective vibration of the atoms within the crystal forms a wave of\nallowed wavelength and amplitude. For example, as we know that light is said to be a wave motion composed of\nphotons, we can also think of the normal modes of vibration in a solid as being a particle. However, lattice dynamic,\noffers two different ways of finding the dispersion relation within the lattice .\n1. Quantum-mechanical approach: Quantum-mechanical approach can be used to obtain phonon's dispersion\nrelation. In order to do so, the solution to the Schrödinger equation for the lattice vibrations must be solved. The\nquantum-mechanical operators for the normal mode coordinates are substituted in the phonon Hamiltonian by\nthe creation and annihilation operators.\n2. Semi-classical treatment of lattice vibrations: The semi-classical treatment gives classical mechanics the use of\none additional postulate taken from quantum mechanics, mainly that the energy of lattice vibrations is\nquantized. However, there is a need to evaluate the feasibility of mitigation techniques for \nexisting structures containing pyrrhotite aggregate but have not yet shown signs of deterioration. \nEfforts at NIST have focused on evaluating the potential of concrete sealants, which can reduce \nor entirely eliminate the ingress of water and air into the concrete. Since pyrrhotite requires both \noxygen and water to react, one or both component ’s concentrations can be reduced to delay \npyrrhotite oxidation for some amount of time. One methodology being vetted for characterizing \nthe performance of  mitigating sealants is air permeability  test. This report details efforts to \nvalidate changes made to a commercially available air permeameter to better facilitate NIST’s \nneeds. This validation testing was generally conducted in two parts. Part 1 focused on validating \nas-received equipment for use with 152.4 mm (6-inch) diameter concrete cores, which is the size \nthe commercially available set -up is made to test. Part 2 focused on validating retrofitting the \nequipment to test 101.6 mm (4-inch) diameter cores, the common diameter used for laboratory \nand field-cast concrete specimens.  \n \nKeywords \nAir Permeability; Concrete; Pyrrhotite; RILEM-Cembureau Permeability \n\nNIST TN 2382 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. As the commercial space sector grows, this “ take-make-use-\ndispose” paradigm is increasingly challenged by the economic  and operational realities of long -\nduration space activity.  This report captures key themes from the 2025 Building an In -Space \nCircular Economy seminar series, convened by the Department of Commerce Office of Space \nCommerce and the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The seminars examined the \ntechnical, regulatory, and economic requirements needed to support a transition toward circular \nspace operations. Major themes include the need for streamlined regulations alongside \ngovernment procurement strategies that establish dependable demand , clarification of salvage \nrights and ownership transfer pathways, and the development of standards to support servicing, \nrefueling, reuse, recycling, and data exchange. Additionally, the report highlights the importance \nof orbital infrastructure, including servicing hubs, modular platforms, recycling architectures, \nlogistics networks, and energy systems, as well as the critical role of materials science and \nmanufacturing innovation. Key c oncepts such as design for circularity, materials passports, \nfeedstock processing, and in-space manufacturing are identified as enabling tools for extending \nthe value of space assets. The multidisciplinary nature of the participants, presentations, and \ndiscussions highlighted that building an in -space circular economy will require coordina tion \namong policy, finance, technology, and standards organizations. \nKeywords \nCircular space economy ; design for circularity; in-situ resource utilization; in-space \nmanufacturing; in -space recycling; in -space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing ; \ninteroperability; interoperability standards; modularity; orbital infrastructure; space policy; \nspace resource utilization; space sustainability; standards. \n \n\nNIST SP 1500-39 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \nExecutive Summary ................................ ................................ ................................ ............................ 1 \n1. Poster: \nConceptualization, Supervision, Validation, Writing-Reviewing and Editing. \n\nNIST SP 1500-39 \nSeptember 2026 \n1 \nExecutive Summary \nSpace is a resource -constrained environment because nearly all materials  and equipment \nmust currently be launched from Earth. Although commercial launch services have reduced \ntransportation costs, delivering mass to orbit remains expensive and logistically challenging. As \ncommercialization of the space industry continues to expand, the traditional single mission, \nlinear operational model is increasingly challenged. Historically, spacecraft are designed, \nlaunched, operated, and then deorbited or moved to graveyard orbits. However, a n in -space \ncircular economy model could reduce dependence on terrestrial resupply by extending asset \nlifetimes and enabling the inspection, servicing, repair, reuse, repurposing, recycling, and \nremanufacturing of materials and systems already in space. \nThe 2025 Building an In -Space Circular Economy seminar series, convened by the U.S. \nDepartment of Commerce Office of Space Commerce and the National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, brought together representatives from government, industry, academia , and \nnonprofit organizations.  Each seminar attracted more than 300 registered attendees, roughly \nhalf of whom represented industry . Participants examined the technical, regulatory, economic, \ninfrastructure, and standards -related conditions needed to transition towards  circular space \noperations. A central finding was that circularity requires many elements to work together. It \ndepends on coordinated circular design practices, clear ownership pathways, and strong market \ndemand. Additionally, it needs physical and digital infrastructure, financing m echanisms, and \ntrusted operational standards. \nCircularity must begin during the design of space systems. Future assets developed with \ndefined pathways for servicing, repair, and upgrades  are essential. Modular components, \nstandardized interfaces, accessible attachment points, reduced material complexity, and digital \nrecords such as ‘materials passports’ are needed to make future servicing and recovery feasible. \nWithout these provisions, assets remain difficult or uneconomical to repair, repurpose, or \nrecycle. This perpetuates the traditional linear operating model. \nPolicy and regulatory uncertainty remain a significant barrier. Circular a ctivities such as \ninspection, servicing, and debris capture do not fit cleanly within regulatory systems originally \ndeveloped for launch, reentry, remote sensing, and spectrum use. Companies face overlapping \njurisdictions, uncertain authorization pathways, and unpredictable timelines.
