[{"suffix": "", "text": "A model of the heat sealing process for multilayer films with molecular detail\nMarat Andreeva#, Chinmay Gangala#, Anthony P. Kotulab, Jeffrey D. Weinholdc,\n Jonathan Moored, Gregory C. Rutledgea*\naDepartment of Chemical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA\nbNational Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD\ncDow Inc., Lake Jackson, TX\ndDow Inc., Midland, MI\n*corresponding author. Contact at rutledge@mit.edu\n#Authors with equal contribution\nAbstract\nHeat sealing of multilayer polymer films is a critical step in the packaging of food, consumer products, and various other commercial items.  Each layer comprises a resin that is specifically designed to impart a particular property to the final package.  The sealant layer, in particular, must provide the package with a hermetic seal of sufficient strength to hold the product, and it must do so fast enough to accommodate high throughput.  The toughness layer provides overall strength to the film. Recently, packaging manufacturers have sought  to create all-polyethylene packaging. Polyethylene resins are tailored for different roles through adjustments in molecular weight and short-chain branching (SCB) distributions. To facilitate the design of resins for such multilayer packages, we develop a model for the heat sealing operation that accounts for the thermo-rheological behavior of the different crystallizable resins comprising the multilayer film, based on molecular level characterization.  The crystallizable discrete slip-link model (cDSM), modified to account for partial crystallinity, is used to describe the rheology of each resin as it melts and recrystallizes.  Melting and crystallization are modeled using the Toda and Nakamura models, which have been expanded to accommodate distributions of melting points associated with SCB in high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE) resins. The heat sealing model is validated using results for hermeticity obtained from multilayer films processed in industrial packaging machines. \nIntroduction\nFigure 1: a) Vertical form fill and seal machine (VFFS) b) pillow pouch highlighting the sealing regions of the folded fin and triple point; c) edge-on view of the folded fin and triple point before sealing.Figure 1: a) Vertical form fill and seal machine (VFFS) b) pillow pouch highlighting the sealing regions of the folded fin and triple point; c) edge-on view of the folded fin and triple point before sealing.Heat sealing is a common industrial process for hermetically sealing flexible packaging made from polymer films. The sealed package protects and preserves the content against environmental conditions and frequently carries a graphic image to identify and advertise the product. A typical heat sealing operation is shown in Figure 1a. In this vertical form, fill and seal (VFFS) operation, the film is first converted into a tube by forming a fin seal, and then two hot seal bars apply pressure and heat to form the seal. After that, the machine cuts the film to create individual pouches. The pouches, as depicted in Figure 1b, have the fin folded to the side during sealing.  Within the top and bottom seal regions, the folded fin creates a challenge for producing a fully hermetic seal. The initial heat and pressure applied by the seal bars are focused on the fin and underlying layers, as this region is twice the thickness of the rest of the pouch.  As melting and squeeze flow proceed, the thickness of the fin and underlying film decreases enough for the rest of the seal region to make full contact with the seal bars.  Squeeze flow slows due to the larger area of contact; however, the final step of sealing requires sufficient volume of molten polymer to flow into the triple point, closing off the channel (shown in Figure 1c) adjacent to the fold.  \n\nFigure 1: a) Vertical form fill and seal machine (VFFS) b) pillow pouch highlighting the sealing regions of the folded fin and triple point; c) edge-on view of the folded fin and triple point before sealing.\n\nFigure 1: a) Vertical form fill and seal machine (VFFS) b) pillow pouch highlighting the sealing regions of the folded fin and triple point; c) edge-on view of the folded fin and triple point before sealing.\nThe polymer films are typically multilayer films, wherein different layers serve different purposes and comprise different polymer resins designed for each purpose. In its simplest form, the multilayer structure is a bilayer that consists of a toughness layer and a sealant layer. The toughness layer has a relatively high melting temperature and provides mechanical strength to the film; for example, it might be a resin designed for puncture- and tear-resistance. The sealant layer has a relatively low melting temperature. It melts when the hot seal bars are applied, flows under the applied pressure to fill any gaps between the two multilayer films, and forms a weld after the seal bars are removed, as it cools down and recrystallizes. Typically, multilayer films may have additional layers, such as a barrier layer to ensure product preservation, a printing layer to carry graphics, or layers that serve other, more subtle and proprietary purposes. However, the different purposes of layers are usually achieved with chemically different polymers, which are later hard to separate, limiting recyclability. All-polyethylene packaging seeks to improve recyclability by sourcing only polyethylene resins, such as high density (HDPE) and linear low density (LLDPE) polyethylenes, for the different layers. The differences between resins lie in their molecular-level details: specifically, molecular weight and short-chain branching (SCB) distributions, which translate to differences in rheological properties, melting temperatures, and crystallization rates. Generally, polyethylenes with more SCB have lower melting temperatures, while those with less SCB have higher melting temperatures and make denser, harder materials. Molecular weight controls the viscosity of molten polymers; lower molecular weight polymers flow faster, while higher molecular weight polymers have a more elastic response to deformation. The ability to manipulate these molecular characteristics allows tuning of resins for heat sealing performance.   \nThe speed of the heat sealing operation is critical for the overall efficiency of the packaging line. The seal bars are in contact with the film, applying heat and pressure for the time interval known as the dwell time tdwell. The bar temperature has to be high enough, and the dwell time has to be long enough, to melt the sealant layer and for polymer chains in the melt to interdiffuse through the interface and create a strong weld[1,2]. The time required to form a strong weld can be reduced by raising the seal bar temperature Tbar. The molten sealant layer flows in response to the pressure applied by the seal bars, Pbar. The maximum throughput, or minimum cycle time, of a packaging line is often determined by the ability of certain layers of the film to melt quickly and provide a large volume of flow. We define fractional flow volume Vf as the volume of material squeezed out from the seal area divided by the total volume of material; in previous work, this quantity was called “squeeze-out”[3]. The flow volume is necessary to fill any gaps between the films, including filling of the triple point, and ensure a hermetic seal. However, excessive flow can lead to insufficient sealant between films and cause seal failure. Thus, flow volume is important for seal integrity and depends on operating conditions, such as seal bar temperature, seal bar pressure, and dwell time, and the properties of the several resins that constitute the multilayer film. Hermeticity maps are often used to understand a film’s ability to form a hermetic seal as a function of the primary packaging machine parameters. However, generating these maps can be time-consuming. For this purpose, computational methods are beneficial.  \n A model for the heat sealing process must consider rheology, heat transfer, and phase transition. In their seminal work, squeeze-out was studied by Morris and Scherer[3], who modeled the flow of polymer melt between the seal bars under constant compressing force. This model assumes no-slip boundary conditions at the bars and allows the strain rate to vary across the film thickness. The polymer melt rheology was modeled using the Carreau-Yasuda model, which accounts for shear-thinning behavior. Steady state operation was assumed, precluding any description of the initial elastic response of the polymer or time-varying rheology such as that associated with the melting of a semicrystalline polymer upon application of the hot seal bars. The model did not consider heat transfer, assuming instead a constant temperature across the film's thickness. Variations in temperature would change the strain rate profile, as pointed out by the authors[3] . The authors compared the model results with experimental data. The model was found to underestimate squeeze-out significantly, but the effect of bar temperature on squeeze-out was captured qualitatively. \nThe build-up of strength in the seal was studied by Morris[4], who developed a transient model that considers heat transfer but not flow. The transient behavior includes stages of heat-up, constant temperature, and cool-down. It also accounts for the generation and removal of latent heat associated with melting and recrystallization. To model seal formation, the author correlated the diffusion distance of polymer chains across the weld interface with the experimentally observed seal strength. Considering the entire heating cycle is important since significant diffusion across the interface occurs during heat-up and cool-down, as pointed out by the author[4]. \nFurther work on modeling the heat sealing process was done by Aghkand et al.[5], and Aghkand and Ajji[6] who studied linear low density polyethylenes (LLDPEs) as sealant layers in a bilayer film. In the former work, the authors focused on the heat-transfer boundary condition from the seal bar and neglected the squeeze flow in their model completely. In the later work, squeeze flow was modeled under the assumption that the sealant layer is completely molten, using either a power law or Carreau-Yasuda model for the melt rheology. Both approaches, while qualitatively accurate, failed to predict squeeze out at the bar temperatures studied. Since a lag time would be required to reach the melting temperature of the sealant, the authors used a shift factor in time to revise the estimates for squeeze flow. Thus, a more accurate description of the range of melting temperatures in LLDPE resins and the rheology of the sealant at intermediate crystallinities is needed to model the heat sealing process.\nIndeed, both transient thermal and rheological models are  required for flow volume calculations. The latent heat of melting and recrystallization affects heat transfer, while the associated destruction and creation of rigidifying crystallinity affect the rheology and, by extension, the onset or cessation of flow. For layers with melting transitons well above Tbar, it may be reasonable to treat them as fully rigid throughout all stages of a transient model, but for those with melting transitions in the vicinity of or below Tbar, a more detailed description that accounts for both the effects of crystallinity on flow and the affects of flow on crystallization kinetics may be required. Such is clearly the case for multilayer films comprising LLDPE resins wherein the sealant layer melts and recrystallizes.  These resins are disperse in molecular weight and in the distribution of short chain branches, arising from the incorporation of hexene or octene monomers in the polyethylene chain. As a result, LLDPEs – especially those used as sealant resins – display a melt

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Compressed Qubit Noise Spectroscopy:\nPiecewise-Linear Modeling and Rademacher Measurements\nKaixin Huang,1, 2,∗ Demitry Farfurnik,3, 4 Dror Baron,3 and Yi-Kai Liu2, 5\n1Joint Quantum Institute (JQI), NIST/University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA\n2Joint Center for Quantum Information and Computer Science (QuICS),\nNIST/University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA\n3Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering,\nNorth Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, 27695, USA\n4Department of Physics, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, 27695, USA\n5Applied and Computational Mathematics Division,\nNational Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Gaithersburg, MD 20899, USA\n(Dated: September 29, 2026)\nRandom pulse sequences are a powerful method for qubit noise spectroscopy, enabling efficient\nreconstruction of sparse noise spectra. Here, we advance this method in two complementary di-\nrections. First, we extend the method using a regularizer based on the total generalized variation\n(TGV) norm, in order to reconstruct a larger class of noise spectra, namely piecewise-linear noise\nspectra, which more realistically model many physical systems. We show through numerical simula-\ntions that the new method resolves finer spectral features, while maintaining an order-of-magnitude\nspeedup over conventional approaches to noise spectroscopy. Second, we simplify the experimental\nimplementation of the method, by introducing Rademacher measurements for reconstructing sparse\nnoise spectra. These measurements use pseudorandom pulse sequences that can be generated in\nreal time from a short random seed, reducing experimental complexity without compromising re-\nconstruction accuracy. Together, these developments broaden the reach of random pulse sequences\nfor accurate and efficient noise characterization in realistic quantum systems.\nI. I NTRODUCTION\nCharacterizing the spectral properties of environmen-\ntal noise is essential for understanding and mitigating\ndecoherence in quantum systems. In particular, the accu-\nrate reconstruction of the noise spectral density,S(ω), in-\nforms both noise-resilient control protocols and error mit-\nigation strategies in quantum technologies [1–3]. Dynam-\nical decoupling (DD) techniques enable indirect access\ntoS(ω) by modulating a system’s sensitivity to environ-\nmental fluctuations via tailored control sequences. How-\never, conventional methods of DD often rely on coarse\nfrequency resolution or assumptions of spectral smooth-\nness, limiting their effectiveness in resolving structured\nand non-smooth features [4–8].\nTo improve the resolution and resource efficiency of\nnoise spectroscopy, compressed sensing (CS) has emerged\nas a powerful framework for spectral reconstruction in\nquantum noise spectroscopy, particularly when the spec-\ntrum possesses sparse structure in a suitable representa-\ntion [9, 10]. Recent work has introduced random pulse se-\nquences as a tool for the direct measurement of arbitrary\nlinear functionals ofS(ω), enabling the CS reconstruction\nof sharp spectral peaks with fewer measurements [11].\nWhile this approach is effective for perfectly sparse\nspectra, it leaves two key challenges unresolved: can this\nmethod be applied to a larger class of noise spectra that\nare not perfectly sparse? And can the practical difficulty\n∗ kxhuang@umd.edu\nof applying the desired random pulse sequences in an ex-\nperiment be reduced? This paper addresses both of these\nchallenges separately.\nA. A Larger Class of Noise Spectra\nMany realistic noise processes, including charge and\nmagnetic noise in solid-state qubits, exhibit more com-\nplicated spectral features rather than sparse peaks rep-\nresented by simple delta functions [12, 13]. For example,\nthe spectra of quantum dot systems often combine nar-\nrow resonances with broad, slowly varying backgrounds.\nThis motivates the need for models that retain sparsity\nwhile capturing richer structures. Piecewise-linear, and\nmore generally piecewise-polynomial, functions provide\nsuch a representation.\nIn this work, we develop a CS protocol for reconstruct-\ning piecewise-linear noise spectra by enforcing sparsity\non the second derivativeS′′(ω). Specifically, we apply an\nL1-norm regularization onS′′(ω), which promotes recon-\nstructions that are globally continuous but exhibit sparse\ncurvatures. This approach aligns with recent advances\nin total generalized variation (TGV) [14–16] and higher-\norder sparse regularization techniques for inverse prob-\nlems [17, 18]. It can also be viewed as an extension of\nwell-known work on compressed sensing in the context\nof medical imaging, for piecewise-constant images in two\ndimensions, based on regularization using the total vari-\nation (TV) norm [19–22].\nOur method extends this to the problem of compressed\nsensing of a piecewise-linear function using TGV regu-\n\n2\nlarization, in one dimension. This particular setting ap-\npears to be more challenging from a theoretical perspec-\ntive, and beyond the scope of the above works. Nonethe-\nless, our numerical simulations on simulated spectra with\nvarying degrees of piecewise-linearity demonstrate high-\nfidelity reconstructions.\nB. Simpler Pulse Sequences\nNext, we consider the experimental implementation of\nrandom pulse sequences, which can be resource-intensive.\nIn particular, previous work proposed the use of random\npulse sequences with complex, long-range correlations,\nwhich are difficult to generate in real time. Instead, the\nentire pulse sequence typically had to be generated “of-\nfline,” using a desktop computer, then transferred to an\narbitrary waveform generator (AWG), before being ap-\nplied to a physical qubit. The loading and storage of a\ngreat number of different pulse sequences creates a bot-\ntleneck in experiments.\nTo address this bottleneck, we introduce a simplified\nvariant of the method, using uncorrelated random pulses,\nwhich we call Rademacher measurements. These pulse\nsequences are easier to generate in real time, using a short\nrandom seed and a high-quality pseudorandom number\ngenerator [23], so that the entire pulse sequence never has\nto be stored in memory. This opens up the possibility\nof generating the random pulse sequences “on the fly”\nusing a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), without\nany need for an AWG.\nIn this scheme, the total evolution time is divided into\nequal segments indexed by m = 1, 2,...,M, each time\nsegment is assigned a Rademacher random variable Um\n(i.e., an independent random variable that takes on the\nvalues 1 and−1 with equal probability), and rotation\nπ-pulses are applied to the qubit whenever Um+1̸=Um.\nAt first glance, it may seem that these pulse sequences\nconsist of nothing more than white noise, and thus can\nonly measure a single degree of freedom of the environ-\nment of the qubit. We get around this difficulty by using\na simple trick: we perform many measurements using\nthe same realization of the random variablesUm (i.e., by\nrunning a pseudorandom number generator many times\nusing the same seed). This lets us measure the signal\nassociated with the fluctuations in a single realization of\nthe pulse sequence. By repeating this measurement with\ndifferent fluctuations, we collect enough information to\nfully characterize the environment of the qubit.\nDespite their simplicity, we show via theory and simu-\nlations that Rademacher measurements retain the same\ncompressed-sensing efficiency as Fourier-based random\npulses [11], while substantially reducing experimental\ncomplexity. Interestingly, these Rademacher measure-\nments are similar in spirit to Gaussian measurements in\ncompressed sensing, which are well-studied [24, 25]. But\nour Rademacher measurements have an unusual feature,\nwhich is different from these older works on compressed\nsensing: our measurements depend quadratically (rather\nthan linearly) on the random variables Um, as shown\nin Eq. (14). For this reason, our recovery guarantee\nfor Rademacher measurements relies on more recently-\ndeveloped techniques, involving the recovery of struc-\ntured low-rank matrices [26, 27].\nC. Application to Quantum Dots\nFinally, we extend our investigation to realistic phys-\nical systems, focusing on the noise spectra of self-\nassembled quantum dots [13]. We demonstrate the ef-\nficiency of the TGV-based CS method, combine it with\nthe Rademacher measurements technique, and demon-\nstrate its potential for rapidly reconstructing realistic\nnoise spectra. We also explore modifications of the pro-\ntocol that further reduce the number of control pulses\nwithout significant loss in reconstruction accuracy. These\nresults broaden the applicability of random-pulse-based\nnoise spectroscopy and improve its practicality for near-\nterm quantum devices.\nThe remainder of the paper is organized as follows.\nThe basic model and background are introduced in\nSec. II. The two main techniques of the paper are de-\nveloped in detail in Secs. III and IV. We explore appli-\ncations of our techniques on realistic systems in Sec. V.\nWe conclude with a summary and a discussion of open\nproblems in Sec. VI.\nII. Landauer  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nalexander.landauer@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0003-2863-039X \n \nKarl F. Schoch, Jr. \nMaterials and Processes, \nNorthrop Grumman \nBaltimore, MD, USA \nk.eric.schoch@ngc.com \nHuong Giang Nguyen  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nhuong.nguyen@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0002-1052-7565 \nGale Holmes  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \ngale.holmes@nist.gov      \nORCID: 0000-0002-5639-4112  \nGery Stafford  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \ngery.stafford@nist.gov   \nORCID: 0000-0003-3445-9402  \n \nAbstract—Residual stresses inevitably develop in \nthermosetting materials used for semiconductor packaging during \nthe curing process and in service. Understanding the development \nof these deleterious stresses is necessary for improving predictive \nmodels and engineering design. Here, we present a suite of \nmetrologies and methodologies, including advanced thermal \nanalysis, rheological ch aracterization, shrinkage, and evolved \nstress measurements, to link residual stress development  with \nfundamental material properties in a commercial liquid \nencapsulant.  \nKeywords—liquid encapsulant, cure kinetics, rheology, cure \nshrinkage, residual stress \nI. INTRODUCTION \nSemiconductor packaging materials  are typically \nthermosetting polymer formulations with multiple components. \nIn these materials, residual stress es develop during the curing \nprocess and are closely linked with the reaction kinetics, liquid-\nto-solid transition, and cure-induced shrinkage [1]. Residual \nstresses continue to evolve in the cured material in response to \nhygrothermal conditions during service [2]. Characterizing these \nbehaviors is often challenging due to the complex formulations \nused in the semiconductor industry. However, understanding the \ndevelopment of residual stresses is necessary to inform \npredictive models and thus improve the engineering design and \nmanufacturing productivity of semiconductor assemblies. \nHere, we present a suite of advanced metrologies and \nmethodologies to measure and analyze the fundamental material \nproperties of a commercial liquid encapsulant. Thermal analysis \nis used to measure and accurately model the cure kinetics  for \ncomplex mechanisms. Rheological measurements supplement \nthe cure kinetics study and are used to identify the liquid-to-solid \ntransition during curing.  Thin film curvature measurements \ndemonstrate that this transition accurately predicts the  \ndevelopment of residual stress caused by the observed cure-\ninduced shrinkage. Stress measurements on the post -cured \nmaterial further reveal the effect of hygrothermal conditions on \nthe mechanical response. Taken together, this metrology suite \nties fundamental to part -scale measurements for a holistic \nunderstanding of the evolution of residual stresses during curing \nand in service, an essential step for improving predictive models.    \nII. EXPERIMENTAL \nA. Chemical Composition \nAll experiments are performed on a commercial liquid \nencapsulant designed for semiconductor devices. As shown in \nTable I, the formulation comprises multiple epoxy resins with \nvarying concentrations. It also includes a reactive diluent to \nreduce the resin viscosity while still participating in the curing \nprocess [3], an adhesion promoter to couple organic and \ninorganic components [4], and inorganic silica fillers to match \nthe coefficient of thermal expansion of the encapsulant with \nother device components  [5]. The encapsulant is stored in a freezer at -40 °C and \nallowed to thaw to room temperature before use. \nB. Curing Schedule \nThe stress and strain developed in polymeric materials are \ndependent on the curing process. Therefore, all samples are \ncured in air according to the supplier recommendation of \n60 min at 100 °C followed by 60 min at 165 °C. Rheological \nexperiments to determine the liquid -to-solid transition are \nperformed at 100 °C for 100 min. \nIII. METROLOGY SUITE \nA. Differential Scanning Calorimetry for Cure Kinetics \nDifferential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is widely used \nwithin the semiconductor community to investigate  the cure \nkinetics of  electronic packaging materials  [5], [7]–[9]. Prior \nwork by Tao et al.  [7] outlines several best practices for DSC \nmeasurements on epoxy molding compounds, which we \nimplement to study the liquid encapsulant. All measurements \nare performed using a DSC equipped with a refrigerated \ncooling system under nitrogen  purge gas . About 10 mg to \n15 mg of uncured encapsulant samples are sealed in 40 µL \nhermetic pans for measurement. The heat flow (𝑄̇ ) is measured \nas a function of temperature (T) by heating samples from -40 °C \nto 300 °C at constant heating rates b = (0.5, 1, 5, and 10 ) \n°C min-1. The standard uncertainties for temperature and heat \nflow are approximately ±  1 % and ±  3 %, respectively. The \ndegree of cure or conversion as a function of temperature , \nα(𝑇) = ∫ 𝑄̇ 𝑑𝑇/\tβ\t∆𝐻! , is calculated by integrating the \nexothermic reaction peaks starting from a temperature below \nthe onset of the reaction, dividing by the total heat of reaction \n(∆HT), and normalizing by the heating rate. The conversion rate \nis given by dα/dt. To replicate the recommended curing \nschedule, we perform an isothermal DSC test at 100 °C for 60 \nmin, followed by a second isothermal test at 165 °C for 60 min. \nModel-based kinetics analysis and simulation are performed \nusing a commercial  software following ICTAC \nrecommendations for the analysis of multi-step kinetics [10].  \nB. Rheometry for Liquid-Solid Transition \nRheometry is a versatile technique for measuring the time-\nevolving material properties of various materials, including  \nviscoelastic liquid encapsulants. Using a rotational rheometer, \nwe measure the viscoelastic storage (G') and loss (G\") moduli \nof the uncured encapsulant by deforming a small sample \nbetween two 8-mm disposable aluminum parallel plates  \naccording to a user -defined oscillating profile of strain \namplitude (g) and angular frequency (w). The instrument has a \nminimum resolvable torque of ±  0.05 μN m and angle of \n± 0.04 μrad. The storage and loss moduli represent the elastic \nand dissipative behavior, respectively, and arise due to the \nstress-strain phase lag inherent to viscoelastic materials. We \nidentify the critical strain below which the viscoelastic moduli \nare strain-independent, i.e., the linear viscoelastic region [11], \nby conducting amplitude sweep experiments where g is varied \nfrom 0.1 % strain to 100 % strain at isothermal temperatures up \nto 100 °C. The critical strain is temperature-dependent, with the \nlowest value (g » 0.3 % strain) occurring at 100 °C. Therefore, \nwe maintain the strain amplitude well below this critical value \nin consecutive experiments to measure the linear viscoelastic \nmoduli.  \nTo investigate the temperature evolution of the moduli \nduring the first heating ramp, we heat a sample from nominally \n40 °C to 100 °C at 5 °C min-1, hold at 100 °C for 5 min, then \ncool back down to 40 °C at 5 °C min-1. As will be further \ndiscussed in a later section, the material exhibits rapid gelation \nkinetics, which makes it difficult to identify the liquid-to-solid \ntransition. Therefore, we use a nascent approach called \noptimally windowed chirps (OWCh), which involves applying \na frequency -varying deformation profile to obtain \nmeasurements at significantly faster acquisition times \ncompared to the classical single -frequency method [12]. The \nOWCh parameters can be designed to apply much lower strain \namplitudes than rapid 'multiwave' methods  [13], allowing for \nmeasurements well below the critical strain. We measure the \ntime evolution of the moduli at 100 °C by continuously \napplying a modulated deformation profile, where g << 0.3 % \nstrain and w is varied from 0.9 rad s-1 to 25.2 rad s-1. The time \ncorresponding to the liquid-to-solid transition is defined when \nthe loss tangent, tand = G\"/G', is independent of frequency [12]. \nC. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Journal of Chromatography A 1730 (2024) 465115\nAvailable online 23 June 2024\n0021-9673/Published by Elsevier B.V.\nOn-line coupling of hollow-fiber flow field-flow fractionation and \ndepolarized multi-angle static light scattering (HF5/D-MALS). Proof \nof principle \nAndr´e M. Striegel \nChemical Sciences Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), 100 Bureau Drive, MS 8390, Gaithersburg, MD 20899-8390, USA   \nARTICLE INFO  \nKeywords: \nHollow-fiber flow field-flow fractionation \nDepolarized multi-angle static light scattering \nOn-line coupling \nDepolarization ratio \nTeflon latex \nABSTRACT  \nIntroduced here is the on-line coupling of hollow-fiber flow field-flow fractionation (HF5) to depolarized multi- \nangle static light scattering (D-MALS). HF5 is a size-based separation alternative to size-exclusion and hydro-\ndynamic chromatography and asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation. HF5 can separate larger sizes than its \nchromatographic counterparts and provides several advantages over its fractionation counterpart, including \nreduced sample consumption and greater ease of operation. D-MALS is a variant of MALS in which the depo-\nlarized scattering from the analyte solution is measured at a variety of angles simultaneously. Measurements of \ndepolarized scattering have previously been employed in studying the optical properties of solutions or sus-\npensions, to determine the length of rod-like analytes, and to gain increased accuracy in the determination of \nanalyte molar mass. The coupling HF5/D-MALS allows for the depolarization ratio of a solution or suspension to \nbe measured continuously across the fractogram. This is demonstrated here for a Teflon latex the size range of \nwhich extends beyond that accessible to commercial size-exclusion columns. The results presented provide the \nfirst reported on-line HF5/D-MALS coupling, showing the feasibility of the technique as well as its realized \npotential for providing continuous depolarization measurements, inter alia.   \n1. Introduction \nSize-based separations are among the most used methods for \nmacromolecule characterization. Among these techniques, size- \nexclusion chromatography (SEC) is employed far more than any other \n[1]. SEC is not without its limitations, however [2], one of these being \nthe analysis of very large and/or very fragile analytes. In this limiting \nregime, other techniques such as hydrodynamic chromatography (HDC) \nand flow field-flow fractionation (flow FFF) can often be successfully \nemployed [3-5]. Variants of the latter include the more popular asym-\nmetric flow FFF (AF4) and the generally underutilized hollow-fiber flow \nFFF (HF5) [6,7]. \nIn HF5, solutions or suspensions flow through a hollow fiber with \nsemi-permeable walls encased within a solid housing. Suction is applied \nconcentrically to the fiber, causing analytes to migrate to and focus on \nthe fiber walls, the latter being the FFF accumulation wall. As in AF4, \ncross-flow programming can be employed in HF5 to improve resolution \nand to ensure retention and elution within a given timeframe and within \nthe given volume constraints of the hollow fiber. \nSome potential advantages of HF5 vis-`a-vis AF4 are the possibility of \nachieving higher sensitivity in the former, as a result of lower analyte \ndilution because of the smaller volume in the hollow fiber versus in an \nAF4 channel; a lower propensity for overloading and, thus, for analyte \naggregation in HF5, given the much lower concentrations employed, \nabout one-third those employed in AF4; and a less complicated experi-\nmental set-up, as HF5 cartridges are easily installed and removed as a \nsingle unit, as opposed to the assembly and disassembly required for \nmembrane installation and replacement in AF4 channels. One notable \ndrawback of HF5 is its generally lower signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) as \ncompared to AF4, due to the lower concentrations employed in HF5 and \nthe lower amount of analyte injected in this technique [8]. \nAmong the most popular on-line detection methods for macromo-\nlecular separations is multi-angle static light scattering (MALS). With an \naccompanying concentration-sensitive detector, MALS is normally \nemployed to determine the molar mass and size of a sample [1,9]. A less \npopular use for MALS has been to study the depolarization state of dilute \npolymer solutions, as to do this requires the use of depolarized MALS \n(D-MALS). This latter detection method offers the possibility of \nobserving the angular dependence of the optical behavior of dilute \npolymeric or colloidal solutions, of calculating the length of rod-like \nE-mail address: andre.striegel@nist.gov.  \nContents lists available at ScienceDirect \nJournal of Chromatography A \njournal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/chroma \nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2024.465115 \nReceived 6 June 2024; Received in revised form 20 June 2024; Accepted 22 June 2024   \n\nJournal of Chromatography A 1730 (2024) 465115\n2\nobjects, and more, including allowing for more accurate calculations of \nanalyte molar mass and of the Rayleigh factor of solvents. D-MALS dif-\nfers from depolarized dynamic light scattering. The former measures the \ndepolarized time-averaged fluctuations of the light scattered by a dilute \nanalyte solution. The latter measures the depolarized time-dependent \nfluctuations of this scattered light and is used to disambiguate from \neach other the translational and rotational diffusion coefficients of \nanalytes and to assist when evaluating the angular dependence of decay \nrates in dynamic light scattering, among other applications. \nOn-line D-MALS was introduced as a detection method for SEC over \ntwo decades ago and applied to a variety of macromolecular scenarios \n[10,11]. Its use since appears to have languished, however. With the aim \nof reintroducing this detection method to a new generation of separation \nscientists, coupled to a technique which extends into a higher size \nregime than does SEC, we have attempted the on-line coupling of HF5 to \nD-MALS. The principles of D-MALS are explained in [12] within the \ncontext of on-line detection and, in more fundamental but off-line, \nbatch-mode fashion, also in [13]. As such, only a brief introduction is \ngiven here. Our test analyte is a Teflon emulsion with average diameter \nranging from 0.1 µm to 0.5 µm [14], i.e., with an upper size limit \ngenerally exceeding that of commercially available SEC columns [15]. \nWe hope that this demonstration of the feasibility of performing on-line \nHF5/D-MALS will encourage others to attempt these types of experi-\nments for their own purposes. \n2. Experimental \n2.1. Materials \nNa2HPO4 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), NaN3 (J.T. Baker, Phil-\nlipsburg, NJ, USA), Brij-35 (Honeywell-Fluka, Morris Plains, NJ), so-\ndium dodecyl sulfate (Polysciences, Warrington, PA, USA). The Teflon \nlatex employed was Algoflon #D60 V (Solvay, Baltimore, MD, USA), \nkindly provided by Paul Russo (Georgia Institute of Technology) and \nRafael Cueto (Louisiana State University). \n2.2. HF5/D-MALS analysis \nThe HF5 analyses were carried out using an Agilent 1260 isocratic \nHPLC pump and autosampler (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, \nUSA), an Eclipse DualTec FFF control module (Wyatt Technology Co., \nSanta Barbara, CA, USA), and an on-line MALS photometer (DAWN \nHELEOS-II, Wyatt). While an on-line DRI detector (T-rEX, Wyatt) was \nalso part of the system, injected concentrations were too low to yield \nusable concentration data. \nThe HF5 cartridge contained a 17-cm-long polyethersulfone fiber of \n≈ 0.8 mm inner diameter and 1.3 mm outer diameter, with a nominal \ncut-off of 10 kDa (Wyatt). The HF5 analysis conditions are summarized \nin Table 1. A linearly decaying cross-flow starting from 0.2 mL min 1 \nwas employed. All the analyses were carried in out in triplicate using \nMilli-Q (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) H2O + 0.02 % NaN3 + 0.002 mol \nL 1 HNa2PO3 + 0.2 % Brij-35 + 0.05 % sodium dodecyl sulfate, an \neluent previously used successfully for the HDC separation of various \ntypes of latexes [16,17]. Detectors were temperature-regulated at (25.0 \n± 0.1) ◦C, while the HF5 fiber temperature was ambient. Fiber flow was \n1 mL min 1; injection volume was 5 µL. \nOn-line D-MALS employed the same MALS detector as described \nabove, which generates a vertically polarized laser beam. In this de-\ntector, odd-numbered photodiodes are located on one side of the cell and \neven-numbered ones on the other. For D-MALS, two strips of Polaroid \nfilm (Wyatt), one with vertical polarization axis and one with horizontal \npolarization axis, are placed around the sides of the MALS flow cell and \nmaintained tightly in place by a grooved cell retainer attached to the \ncell. The strips thus play the role of analyzer in the optical train of the \nsystem. Two sets of experiments are performed, first with the vertically \npolarized Polaroid strip facing the odd-numbered photodiodes and the \nhorizontally polarized strip facing the even-numbered ones. The posi-\ntion of the strips is then reversed, and the experiment is repeated. Great \ncare must be taken during installation and removal of the strips, to \nensure their snugness around the cell, to avoid or at least minimize \n“leaking” of light around the strips as well as kinking of the strips, and to \navoid touching them or the MALS flow cell with one’s fingers (the use of \nsoft-tipped tweezers is recommended, as is an anti-static strap). It should \nbe noted that the same dissolutions of sample were analyzed in both \nmodes, i.e., with both Polaroid strip positions, as well as without the \nstrips in place. \n3. Results and discussion \nFor a completely isotropic analyte, the dipole induced by interaction \nwith incident radiation will be parallel to the electric vector E0 of said \nradiation. If the analyte is non-absorbing, then only the component of \nthe scattered light which is parallel to the transmission axis of the \nanalyzer (in the present case, the Polaroid strips), E0cosϕ, will pass \nthrough the strips onto the MALS photodiodes. (The angle ϕ is that be-\ntween the polarization and transmission axes). The intensity I(ϕ) of the \nscattered light reaching the photodiodes is given by [18]: \nI(ϕ)= cε0\n2 E2\n0cos2ϕ (1)  \nwhere c is the speed of light in vacuum and ε0 is the permittivity of free \nspace. The intensity of the scattered light which is transmitted by the \nanalyzer reaches a maximum, Imax =\n\ncε0E2\n0\n)\n/2, when ϕ = 0o; \nconversely, I = 0 when ϕ = 90o. When an isotropic analyte in the MALS \nflow cell scatters the vertically polarized incident laser light, all of the \nscattered light should then reach the photodiodes facing the Polaroid \nstrip with vertical polarization axis, and none of the scattered light \nshould reach the photodiodes facing the strip with horizontal polariza-\ntion axis. Depolarizing analytes will alter these relations, displaying \nanywhere from mild to strong (depending on the system) scattering in \nso-called “cross-polarization” mode, i.e., the intensity of scattered light \nreaching the photodiodes facing the Polaroid strip with horizontal po-\nlarization axis will be greater than zero (when vertically polarized \nincident radiation is employed, as is the case here). It should be noted \nthat, in reality, not all the scattered light will reach the photodiodes in \n“aligned-polarization” mode (i.e., when the transmission axis of the \nanalyzer is aligned with the polarization axis of the incident radiation), \ndue to an approximately 10 % to 20 % absorption of light by the Polaroid \nfilters. An a posteriori route for correcting for this absorption during data \ntreatment, derived for SEC/D-MALS but also potentially applicable to \nother types of on-line D-MALS experiments, was presented in [11]. \nRe

Perform the same exercise for Zn, and \nconvince yourself that in a polycrystal with randomly oriented grains, Zn will twin in \ntension but not in compression. \n2.\t At the ideal c/a ratio achieved for close-packed HCP hard spheres, will twinning occur in \ncompression or tension?  Explain your thought process. \n3.\t An HCP metal with ideal c/a ratio is loaded in tension on the [2111] axis. If this metal \ncan only slip on the basal plane, which slip system operates first?  Explain how you \narrived at your answer. \n4.\t For FCC crystals the twinning system is (111), [112].  In other words, K1 = (111). If K2 \n= (11 1)  is the second undistorted plane, calculate the twinning shear strain. \n5.\t For an FCC crystal loaded in tension, what is the largest possible rotation angle that the \ncrystal can sustain during single slip? \n6.\t Two identical pieces of an unknown pure metal are given to you in an annealed state.  \nYou deform both of them in the same way, and they become work hardened.  Then, you \ntake the first of the two samples and anneal it, for 1 hour at 1000º C.  You find that the \nstrength has dropped by a factor of two as a result of the anneal.  With the second sample, \nyou anneal at a slightly higher temperature, say, 1015º C, and you find that it takes only \nhalf as long to reduce the strength by a factor of two!  Based on this data, infer what the \nunknown metal must (or may) be.  (Hint: you will need some diffusion data for this one- I \nrecommend the Smithell’s Metals Reference Book in the library). \n7.\t Look up the melting point of the metal you identified for problem 4.  In light of the \nmelting point, does the recovery data given make sense?  Explain. \n\nMIT OpenCourseWare\nhttp://ocw.mit.edu \n3.40J / 22.71J / 3.14 Physical Metallurgy \nFall 2009 \nFor information about citing these materials or our Terms of Use, visit: http://ocw.mit.edu/terms."}]

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Responses to Thermo Recitation 2 “Muddy Cards” \nThe most common remark was lingering confusion about reversible versus \nirreversible processes, and calculation of the work thereof: e.g., when are \nwhich work equations used? A related question that has come up in office \nhours is the difference between Pext and P. \nFirst, realize that P refers to the pressure of the system – such as the gas – always. Pext \nrefers to the pressure being applied to the system by the surroundings. In a reversible \nprocess they must be equal (in equilibrium) at all times; hence, you can substitute an \nequation of state such as the ideal gas law in for P. In an irreversible process, Pext may \nchange more quickly than P is able to catch up, so to speak; since it is Pext that determines \nmechanical work performed, if it is constant, it is readily taken outside the integral sign. \nMy answer regarding when one should assume a process is reversible is a pragmatic one: \ndo so when you need to do so to solve the problem. In an isobaric process you never do. \nIn an isochoric process there is no work. Along an isotherm, it is useful to do so, and \nprobably not a bad assumption, due to already needing to keep the system in equilibrium \nwith respect to one variable - T. Finally, in this course, we will not be studying adiabatic \nexpansions/compressions (section 2.10 the book if you are interested). \nRelatedly, how does one calculate work done when changing temperature? \nWork is only done inasmuch as the temperature change causes a corresponding volume \nchange, if it does so. This will typically be calculated from a constitutive equation (e.g., \nPV = nRT). But a temperature change may transfer heat without the transfer of work. \nWhere does U = 1.5 nRT come from? \nThis is true only for an ideal gas (monatomic, at that). It can be derived from statistical \nmechanics and the kinetic theory of gases, as shown in chapter 33 of Engel & Reid. \nRecall that dU = CvdT, so that tells you something about its relation to classical thermo. \nWhy is it useful that mixed partial derivatives of exact differentials are equal? \nI hope that my solution to problem I.3 cleared this up in part. First of all, it makes a \nuseful test for whether something is a state function or not – circular, I know. Second of \nall, some partial derivatives are much easier to calculate than others! One may be equal \nto a property like Cv, whereas another is basically gibberish, conceptually speaking. In \nother words: it allows you to solve problems given physical data. \nWhat is specific heat? How does heat capacity relate to boiling points? \nSpecific heat is just another name for heat capacity. It is often given in units of energy \nper mass per temperature, rather than energy per mole per temperature. At phase \n\nchanges, heat capacity is considered undefined (or infinite), because it is the ratio of \ndifferential heat transferred and differential temperature change – which is zero. \nHigh boiling points and high heat capacities can be related. In the case of water, both are \ndue to the extensive hydrogen bonding network: it must be broken for evaporation (i.e., \nboiling) to occur, and energy input to heat liquid water to a higher temperature may be \n‘wasted’ on bending of hydrogen bonds. \nRegarding the “units?” question – please be more specific next time, as I’m not \nsure what in particular you are asking. \nRegarding pedagogical suggestions: thank you, I will try to incorporate them."}]

[{"suffix": "", "text": "1 Phase-Change Polymer−Metal Composites with Tunable Thermal\n2 Conductivity and Their Additive Manufacturing\n3 Jinyu Bu,# Robsun Gina,# Naifu Shen, Fan Zhang, Atik Faisal, Ran Tao,* and Weinan Xu*\nCite This: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsaenm.5c01153\n Read Online\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\n4 ABSTRACT: Polymer−metal composites that combine a soft polymer\n5 matrix with low-melting-point metal/alloy particles that can be melted\n6 within a compatible temperature range hold great promise for\n7 multifunctional additive manufacturing (AM). The reversible melting−\n8 solidification phase transition of the metal component, coupled with the\n9 mechanical flexibility and stretchability of the polymer matrix, enables\n10 thermally responsive and mechanically tunable composites suitable for\n11 3D printing. However, a fundamental understanding of their thermal,\n12 rheological, and morphological behaviors remains limited. In this work,\n13 we investigate a series of polymer−metal composites composed of\n14 Field’s metal (FM) and thermoplastic elastomers (TPE), with the goal\n15 of elucidating the critical structure−property relationships for material\n16 extrusion-based AM. Thermo-rheological analyses reveal distinct\n17 temperature-dependent transitions strongly influenced by FM content and processing conditions. X-ray diffraction and electron\n18 microscopy further demonstrate significant process-dependent morphological evolution. Notably, these composites exhibit highly\n19 tunable thermal conductivity, achieving values up to 19 W m−1 K−1 after the postprinting processing. Successful 3D printing via\n20 pellet extrusion reveals substantial differences in thermal, rheological, and mechanical properties compared to solution-cast\n21 counterparts, primarily due to shear-induced morphological rearrangement during printing. The insights gained into the key\n22 structure−property relationships of these 3D-printable multifunctional FM−TPE composites pave the way for their potential\n23 applications in thermal management, soft electronics, and robotics.\n24 KEYWORDS: additivemanufacturing,multifunctionalcomposites,lowmeltingpointalloy,phasechangematerial,phasetransition,\n25 thermalconductivity,thermoplasticelastomer\n1. form\n32 factor.6−9 Among polymer 3D printing technologies, material\n33 extrusion (MEX) is one of the most widely adopted.10,11 It\n34 operates by extruding melted polymer filaments or pellets\n35 through a heated nozzle in a layer-by-layer fashion, with each\n36 layer cooling and solidifying on the print bed to form the\n37 desired structure.12 However, due to the intrinsic limitations of\n38 polymer materials�such as relatively low strength and limited\n39 temperature stability, as well as low electrical and thermal\n40 conductivity,13−15 �the practical use of 3D-printed polymer\n41 structures remains constrained despite the ease of 3D\n42 printing.16,17 To address these, significant efforts have been\n43 directed toward incorporating functional inorganic materials\n44 into polymer-based feedstocks to enhance their overall\n45 performance.18−20 Among these, polymer−metal composites\n46stand out for their improved mechanical strength and\n47conductivity. 21 Although interest in 3D printing such\n48composites has increased over the past decade, their\n49implementation remains relatively limited, with only a few\n50studies demonstrating promising applications in electronics,\n51robotics, and aerospace.22−24\n52Representative examples of AM technologies that utilize\n53polymer−metal composites as precursors for metal 3D printing\n54include metal fused filament fabrication or bound metal\n55deposition.25−27 However, in these approaches, the polymer\n56serves solely as a sacrificial binder, and the process requires\n57energy- and cost-intensive high-temperature sintering�often\n58exceeding 1300 °C for steel�to produce the final metal\n59parts.28 To overcome these limitations, low-melting-point\nReceived: December 2, 2025\nRevised: January XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX\ntsu00 | ACSJCA | JCA11.2.5208/W Library-x64 | manuscript.3f (R5.2.i3:5013 | 2.1) 2022/08/03 13:05:00 | PROD-WS-121 | rq_5056943 | 1/26/2026 17:13:06 | 10 | JCA-DEFAULT\n\n60 metals high-temperature sintering-based methods that fully\n64 eliminate the polymer phase, composite systems based on low-\n65 melting-point metals can retain both components�preserving\n66 the polymer for mechanical flexibility or structural support, and\n67 the metal for electrical, thermal, or mechanical functionality.\n68 This strategy enables the full realization of polymer−metal\n69 synergy, rather than relegating the polymer to a purely\n70 sacrificial role.\n71 Most previous studies on low-melting-point metals−based\n72 composites and additive manufacturing have focused on\n73 gallium-based liquid metals (LM).31−34 Direct ink writing 3D\n74 printing with LM and its composites have been extensively\n75 studied,35−38 many of them demonstrated high electrical\n76 conductivity,39,40 and one report also showed enhanced\n77 thermal conductivity.41 However, the low melting point\n78 (Tm), often below room temperature, of these metals presents\n79 a bottleneck for 3D printing with conventional methods, as\n80 they cannot maintain complex geometries without the aid of a\n81 supporting matrix.42,43 It is noted that some recent reports\n82 demonstrated the extrusion of LM structures without\n83 supporting materials such as by creating LM foams,44 or\n84 depositing viscous and oxidized LM on supporting tem-\n85 plates.45,46 But the 3D printability and complex geometry\n86 fabrication remain limited.\n87 Field’s metal (FM), a eutectic alloy of bismuth, indium, and\n88 tin, has aTm of 62 °C, and is advantageous for extrusion-based\n89 3D printing due to its rigidity at room temperature and readily\n90 accessible melting transition.47,48 Several studies have reported\n91 the fabrication of FM−polymer composites with unique\n92 mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties.49−52 However,\n93 research into 3D printing with FM and its composites is still in\n94 its early stages.53,54 In our recent work,55 we developed a novel\n95 3D-printable polymer−metal composite system by integrating\n96 thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) with FM. These composites\n97 can be conveniently printed using MEX method under mild\n98 conditions, without the need for high energy input or extensive\n99 postprinting processing.\n100 Despite the significant potential and growing interest in 3D\n101 printing of polymer−metal composites, fundamental under-\n102 standing of the key structure−property relationships governing\n103 their printability and performance remains limited. In\n104 particular, critical properties such as thermal transitions,\n105 rheological behavior, internal morphologies, phase transitions,\n106 and interfacial interactions between the polymer and metal\n107 components have not been systematically investigated. This is\n108 especially important for composites incorporating low Tm\n109 metals such as FM, where multiple thermal transitions�\n110 arising from both polymer softening and metal melting�occur\n111 during the printing process. These properties are highly\n112 interrelated and strongly influence both processability and\n113 functional performance of the printed structures.\n114 To bridge this knowledge gap, we present a comprehensive\n115 investigation of the fundamental properties of 3D-printable\n116 FM−TPE composites and demonstrate their printability via a\n117 scalable pellet-extrusion method. We show that the solid-\n118 ification behavior of the FM phase from the melt within the\n119 TPE matrix is strongly influenced by FM particle size, loading\n120 fraction, and the composite processing method. The shear\n121 storage and loss moduli of the FM−TPE composites are highly\n122 dependent on both composition and processing conditions\n123(i.e., 3D printing vs solution casting). Furthermore, we\n124demonstrate that the thermal conductivity of these composites\n125can be effectively tuned over a broad range by adjusting the\n126composition, modifying the internal structure, and applying\n127postprinting processing. These insights establish foundational\n128design principles for 3D-printable polymer−metal composites\n129that retain the merits of both constituents, i.e., the mechanical\n130flexibility of the polymer and the excellent physical properties\n131of the metal. In particular, the high thermal conductivity\n132achieved in these phase-change composites is promising for\n133thermal management applications. The combination of phase-\n134changing metallic phase with high thermal conductivity and a\n135flexible, elastic TPE matrix makes FM−TPE composites highly\n136attractive as thermal interface materials (TIMs), especially\n137where mechanical compliance and conformability are required.\n138FM also serves as a phase-change material (PCM) with a low,\n139accessible melting point, allowing these composites to function\n140as effective thermal buffers that mitigate temperature spikes\n141and improve device reliability.\n2. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Vol.:(0123456789)\nAnalytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry \nhttps://doi.org/10.1007/s00216-025-05851-x\nRESEARCH PAPER\nPyrolysis-GC/MS differentiates polyesters and detects additives \nfor improved monitoring of textile labeling accuracy and plastic \npollution\nJosh Forakis1 · Jennifer Lynch1,2\nReceived: 15 January 2025 / Revised: 17 March 2025 / Accepted: 20 March 2025 \n© The Author(s) 2025\nAbstract\nPolyesters comprise the greatest proportion of textile fibers and are found in various everyday goods; hence, polyester fibers \nare a significant source of microplastic pollution and textile waste. The specific chemical composition of commercial polyes-\nter fibers is often proprietary and mostly assumed to be poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET). Polyester is a class of polymers \nthat include poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT), poly(cyclohexylenedimethylene terephthalate) (PCT), and poly(ethylene \nnaphthalate) (PEN), as well as biodegradable polymers. Our study aims to clarify whether household polyester products are \nprimarily PET, are labeled accurately, or contain phthalate additives by applying double-shot pyrolysis–gas chromatography/\nmass spectroscopy (Py-GC/MS). We analyzed four scientific-grade polyester reference standards, 52 manufacturer-grade \npolyester fibers or pellets, and 229 samples from 193 consumer polyester products. From the pyrograms, samples were \npredominantly identified as PET (87.4%, 95% CI [93.5–81.3%]), but five samples were identified as a different polyester, \nnine as non-polyester polymers, and 23 as a blend of PET with another polymer. From the thermal desorption chromato-\ngrams, diethyl phthalate was the most frequently detected phthalate, found in 23.3% (95% CI [17.3–29.3%]) of the consumer \nproducts, including children’s toys. Double-shot py-GC/MS advantageously results in these empirical data that (1) counter \nthe assumption that products labeled polyester are always PET, (2) emphasize the importance of creating spectral libraries \nwith well-characterized materials for accurate polymer identification of unknown plastic particles, and (3) demonstrate that \nphthalates are common additives in household products.\nKeywords Microfibers · Polyesters · Py-GC/MS · Polymer identification\nIntroduction\nMicrofibers, defined by pollution researchers as natural \nor synthetic fibrous materials of a thread-like structure \nwith a diameter of less than 10 μm, a length between 1 \nμm and 5 mm, and a length-to-width ratio greater than \n100, are becoming the most abundant form of microparti-\ncle pollution identified in the natural environment [1 , 2]. \nWhole fabrics are also found as marine debris or plastic \npollution, impacting coral reefs and other ecosystems. \nMany common textile materials shed microfibers during \nproduction, use, and end-of-life [3 , 4]. Natural fibers, like \ncellulose and silk, are biodegradable, so they are less of an \nenvironmental concern [5 ]. Still, synthetic textiles, com-\nmonly made of polyester, acrylic, nylon, or polyolefins, are \ndesigned to last, and thus, those products or microfibers \nthat leach from them persist in the environment. Micro-\nfibers have been identified in all environmental matrices, \nincluding the atmosphere, wastewater, sludge, and marine \nsediment [6–9]. In addition, 0.28 million tons of microfib -\ners is estimated to be released into aquatic environments \nyearly [10]. Aquatic organisms can mistake microfibers for \nfood, which can negatively impact ecological and human \nhealth by leaching small-molecule contaminants, diluting \nnutrients, and bioaccumulating or biomagnifying plastic \nparticles in biota and up the food chain [11, 12].\n * Josh Forakis \n jforakis@hpu.edu\n1 Center for Marine Debris Research, Hawaii Pacific \nUniversity, 41-202 Kalanianaole Hwy #9, Waimanalo, \nHI 96744, USA\n2 National Institute of Standards and Technology, 41-202 \nKalanianaole Hwy #9, Waimanalo, HI 96744, USA\n\n J Forakis, J. Lynch  \nThe production rate of synthetic fiber textiles exceeds \nthat of natural fibers and continues to grow. Polyester \naccounted for 54% of all globally produced fibers in 2022 \n(not just synthetic), and polyester textiles are used in vari-\nous everyday products, including clothing, carpets, cur -\ntains, and toys [13]. The traditional definition of a poly -\nester is any polymer with an ester group in the repeating \nunits of the main polymer chain [14]. Polyesters can be \nfurther categorized into those containing a difunctional \nester of an aromatic substituted carboxylic acid (usually \nterephthalic acid) and those with an ester group but no \nsubstituted aromatic carboxylic acid monomer. The cat -\negory with a substituted aromatic carboxylic acid mon -\nomer is the most common for commercial textile fiber \napplications. These polyesters include poly(ethylene tere -\nphthalate) (PET plastic resin code #1) and poly(butylene \nterephthalate) (PBT), which do not biodegrade in the \nenvironment [15]. Polyesters with an aliphatic carboxylic \nacid monomer, or aliphatic polyesters, are primarily hydro-\nphobic, biodegradable or compostable polymers because \ntheir ester groups are readily hydrolyzed by microbes in \nthe decomposition process [16, 17]. Figure  1 displays an \noverview of the two categories of polyesters. Only aro-\nmatic polyesters are considered for this study, as these are \nthe most relevant regarding microfiber pollution.\nAromatic polyesters are copolymers containing two \nmonomer types: a substituted aromatic carboxylic acid and \na glycol, joined via condensation polymerization [14]. Dif-\nferent types of aromatic polyesters were designed by making \nminor structural alterations to the carboxylic acid or, more \ncommonly, the glycol monomer. Table 1 gives an overview \nof four common aromatic polyesters: PET, PBT, poly(1–4 \ncyclohexylenedimethylene terephthalate) (PCT), and \npoly(ethylene naphthalate) (PEN). PET, PCT, and PBT con-\ntain the same carboxylic acid monomer but contain different \nglycol monomers: ethylene glycol, cyclohexanedimethanol, \nand 1,4-butanediol, respectively. PEN is made with eth-\nylene glycol but has an altered carboxylic acid monomer, \ndimethyl-2,6-naphthalenedicarboxylate. Due to the chemical \ndifferences in their polymer backbone, different polyesters \noffer a range of mechanical and chemical properties, includ-\ning heat and chemical resistance and the ability to be molded \ninto different products [18, 19].\nVarious analytical techniques have been employed to \nidentify and quantify environmental microfibers [20]. \nSpectroscopic techniques are the most common, but they \nare limited in their ability to differentiate polymers with the \nsame functional groups [21]. This means that the spectra of \nthe different polymers in the same group, such as polyesters \nand polyamides (nylon), look similar and may only differ by \nminor, easy-to-miss spectral features [22, 23]. Furthermore, \na low-quality spectrum of one polymer type might cause \nit to register as a different polymer according to a spectral \ncorrelation search. In addition, plastic pollution laborato-\nries, like ours, create spectral libraries using consumer goods \nlabeled with their polymer composition. Since polyester is \na common label on textile goods, spectra of these materials \nare entered into libraries under this umbrella term. Polyester \ncan also be found in commercial spectral libraries without \nexplaining the specific polymer used in that entry. Plastic \npollution pieces often match these polyester spectra, which \ndoes not provide complete chemical information about the \npollution.\nThermal decomposition methods such as Py-GC/MS and \nthermal extraction and desorption GC/MS (TED-GC/MS) \noffer advantages for plastic pollution analysis [20, 24–26]. \nBreaking the bulk polymer chain into characteristic frag-\nments provides more detailed information on the sample’s \nchemical structure, including specific monomer subunits. \nUnlike spectroscopic methods, they destroy the sample, \nrequire a small amount of material, and provide polymer \nmass rather than particle count. TED-GC/MS is a two-step \nFig. 1  Two types of polyester compounds. Polyesters often comprise \ntwo monomers: a difunctional carboxylic acid (acid monomer) and a \ndifunctional alcohol (glycol monomer). These monomers can undergo \na condensation polymerization reaction to create polyester com-\npounds, releasing water as a byproduct. The acid component contains \nan aromatic functional group for aromatic polyesters, and the result-\ning polymer is not biodegradable. Aliphatic polyesters are typically \nbiodegradable and do not contain aromatic functional groups in their \nacid monomer\n\nPyrolysis-GC/MS differentiates polyesters and detects additives for improved monitoring…\ntechnique combining thermo-gravimetric analysis and \nsolid-phase absorption with thermal desorption GC/MS. \nThis method allows for sample sizes up to and above 100 \nmg, but is less straightforward than Py-GC/MS, with TED-\nGC/MS requiring solid-phase extraction before desorbing \nand analyzing fragments. Py-GC/MS directly pyrolyzes the \nsample in a furnace before passing the compounds through \nthe GC/MS system, but is limited to samples less than 0.5 \nmg. Py-GC/MS is a useful technique when the sample is \nrelatively pure and requires little preparation. Py-GC/MS \ncan differentiate polymers with the same functional groups, \nincluding polyesters, and it has been employed in micro-\nfiber research to characterize textile fibers and quantify fiber \nrelease from laundering polyester clothes [27, 28].\nThe precise bulk polymer composition of polyester prod-\nucts is often undisclosed, most frequently labeled “100% \npolyester fibers” or something similar. From the perspec-\ntive of the plastic pollution research community, this can \ncause challenges when building or using infrared or Raman \nspectral libraries to quantify and characterize environmental \nmicrofibers [29, 30]. Researchers rely on spectral libraries \nto assign a polymer identity to unknown plastic samples, \noften making their spectral libraries from readily available \nconsumer goods and naming that spectra the polymer or \nmaterial type printed on the label. Reference spectra from \npolyester-labeled materials are ambiguous to the actual \npolymer. For example, several microplastic studies have \nreported detecting both polyester and PET [31– 34], which \nimplies that they are using a library that contains a spectrum \nfrom an ambiguous polyester material and cannot identify \nall of the polyester particles to a specific polymer. Accurate \nenvironmental monitoring depends on quality reference \nlibraries made with the most fully characterized materials.\nThus, this study was designed to test a common assump-\ntion that most polyester products, and therefore pollution, \nconsist of PET [3 , 35, 36]. While PET is the most com-\nmonly produced polyester, assuming all polyesters to be PET \noverlooks the diversity of polyester polymers and may affect \naccuracy of plastic pollution studies. This study employed \nPy-GC/MS to identify the precise bulk polymer composition \nof four scientific standard polyesters, 52 polyester fibers rep-\nresentative of a wide array of commercially available fibers \nfrom numerous producers across the globe (Forensic Fiber \nReference Collection by Microtrace LLC), and 229 samples \nfrom consumer goods labeled “100% polyester.” While we \npredicted most polyesters would be identified as PET, no \nprevious study has applied the advantages of Py-GC/MS to \nempirically identify the polymer of scientific-grade, manu-\nfacturer, and consumer-good polyester fibers. These data are \na necessary contribution towards harmonizing plastic pol-\nlution analysis and improving the accuracy of microfiber \nquantification. Furthermore, the thermal desorption chro-\nmat

Microwave absorption: Oxygen has weak absorp-\ntion at visible and infrared frequencies, but there is\na strong peak near 60 GHz [2].\nMathar’s tool hitran2refr [3] calculates refrac-\ntive index as a superposition of independent oscil-\nlators.
