[{"suffix": "", "text": "4th International Conference on Natural Hazards & Infrastructure  \n29 June – 2 July 2026, Chania, Greece \n \nAdvancing Resilience Across Lifeline Infrastructure \nSystems: The Need for Consistent Guidance \n \nCraig A. Davis, P.E., G.E., Ph.D.,  \nC. A. Davis Engineering \n \nKatherine J. Johnson, Ph.D.,  \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology \n \nAyse Hortacsu, P.E., \nApplied Technology Council \n \nLaurie Johnson, Ph.D.,  \nLaurie Johnson Consulting \n \nThomas D. O’Rourke, Ph.D.,  \nCornell University, Professor Emeritus \n \nKent Yu, P.E., S.E., Ph.D.  \nSEFT Consulting Group \n \n \nABSTRACT \n \nConsistent resilience guidance is needed  to address the performance and recovery of lifeline \ninfrastructure systems during and after hazard events. Lifeline  infrastructure systems (e.g., \nwater, wastewater, electric power , gas and liquid fuel,  communication, and transportation \nsystems) are interconnected and interdependent; each cannot operate normally or recover after \nan event without the services of the others. Social and economic activities also depend on \nlifelines and c ommunities cannot be resilient if the infrastructure  system services are not \nrestored in a timely manner. Unfortunately, no system -level guidelines or standards exist to \nmaintain service continuity and achieve rapid  recovery following hazard  events. Advancing \nresilience across lifeline  infrastructure sectors requires improvements in (a) objectives for \nproviding interdependent services needed by users during and after various hazard  events, \n(b) design guidance for new and existing infrastructure to achieve those objectives, and \n(c) identifying and prioritizing organizational actions to support performance and recovery \nobjectives. Formulating these into an overarching process helps each lifeline achieve consistent \nperformance and service recovery. Lifeline -focused guidance then outline s asset and \norganizational action procedures, respectively, for designing the connecting components within \neach system and establishing strategies for the essential organizational groups. This guidance \nalso provides direction for modifying existing or developing new system, component, and \norganizational group level guidelines and standards. NIST SP 1310 and 1311, entitled “ Initial \nFramework to Design Lifeline Infrastructure for Post -Earthquake Functional Recovery,” uses a \nsimilar approach for water, wastewater, and electric power systems, which is explored in this \npaper. This work also shows how the framework for post-earthquake recovery can be extended \nto other hazards and systems. \n \nKeywords: Guidelines, Lifeline Infrastructure, Resilience, Performance, Recovery \n\nINTRODUCTION \n \nLifeline infrastructure  systems (e.g., water, wastewater, energy , communication, and \ntransportation systems) provide services to meet social and economic needs of  communities. \nLifeline infrastructures are socio-technical systems that provide services through the integration \nof physical infrastructure and the human agency that operates it. To support community hazard \nresilience, service disruptions should be limited, and recovery activities should address societal \nneeds. Resilience thinking acknowledges that service disruption from infrastructure  systems \ncannot be completely prevented in a severe hazard  event, but service recovery to customers \nand users when needed can be managed.   \nThe performance of infrastructure under normal operating conditions as well as extreme loading \nis a key consideration in assessing and enhancing community  resilience. Accordingly, lifeline \ninfrastructure system resilience deals with the restoration of disrupted services and recovery of \nsystem reliability after hazard events to support impacted communities. However, current codes \nand standards generally do not explicitly consider the function of an infrastructure system or its \ncomponents in establishing  the desired performance in hazard events. Usually, safety is the  \nprimary, and often the only, criterion (RRMC, 2019). The lifeline infrastructure performance and \nservice recovery objectives should be dictated by community resilience goals, yet most \ncommunities have never established any.  A major challenge related to the  development of \ncommunity-resilience-based performance guidelines and standards is ensuring  consistency in \nthe performance assessment metrics and methods across different lifeline infrastructure system \nsectors (RRMC, 2019). \nLifeline infrastructure  systems are interconnected and interdependent because e ach provides \nservices to the others, and many are co-located. This means that the operation and provision of \nservices from one depends on, or is critical to, the other systems. As a result, their designs and \norganizational actions must have consistency to meet a minimum performance  level and the \nability to recover services in an orderly manner to support the resilience of communities to \nhazards. NIST SP 1310 and 1311 presented the first framework of its kind to provide guidance \non how to design lifeline infrastructure systems and align their performances and functional \nrecoveries to meet societal needs following an earthquake.  \nThis paper addresses the need for overarching guidance and presents processes to establish \nconsistent procedures for designing, upgrading, and operating across all lifeline infrastructure \nsectors in response to hazard events. Consistency is necessary to align their performances and \nprovide the orderly recovery of disrupted services to support community functions. The \nrelationship between lifeline infrastructure services and essential community functions is \nreviewed. A linkage between community, building, and lifeline infrastructure system objectives \nis summarized. From this , processes are presented to create consistent procedures for  lifeline \ninfrastructure design and organizational actions . The processes first cover overarching design \nand organizational action procedures applicable to all lifeline infrastructure. The next part of the \nprocesses covers preparation of consistent design and organizational action procedures specific \nfor each  lifeline sector  that is enabled by the overarching  guidance. The  third part of the \nprocesses addresses components and organizational groups making up each lifeline to \nrespectively entail specific specialized designs and organizational policies and strategies  \nconsistently across the systems. The procedures can be documented in guidelines and standards. \nIn this context, the term ‘design’ refers to developing new and upgrading existing infrastructure \ncomponents and systems in the same way that policies and strategies may apply to existing \norganizational groups or the creation of new ones. \nRecent frameworks (NIST 20,24a; Davis et al., 2023; ALA, 2005) prepared for seismic hazards \nare described to illustrate how the processes and procedures can be applied to improve  lifeline \ninfrastructure earthquake resilience. Methods for addressing other hazards are also considered.   \n \nDEVELOPING LIFELINE INFRASTRUCTURE RESILIENCE GUIDANCE  \n \nDuring and following damaging natural hazard events, performance of each lifeline infrastructure \nsector and interaction among multiple sectors is of critical importance to community resilience.  \nDesigning each of these interdependent systems and their components and establishing related \n\norganizational actions for a set of coherent objectives can help them operate as intended before, \nduring, and after hazard events. The designs and organizational actions  need to address how \nthe infrastructure will perform (1) during events , in terms of potential for damage , service \ndisruption, and operational continuity, and (2) following events, in terms of service recovery and \nrestoring long-term functional and operational reliability. \nCommunity-Level Resilience Goals \nIdeally, community-level resilience goals for the various social and economic systems would first \nbe established  and applied across communities , from which lifeline infrastructure objectives \nwould be developed and aligned with similar objectives for building clusters (RRMC, 2019). \nAlthough guidance on planning for community resilience exists (e.g., NIST, 2015 ; Rockefeller \nFoundation and ARUP, 2014), not all community resilience plans establish a set of performance \nand recovery goals, but the plans may identify that goals need to be documented (e.g., City of \nLos Angeles, 2018). Additionally, a systematic consensus -driven process for establishing links \nfrom community resilience goals to building and lifeline infrastructure objectives is not yet \navailable (RRMC, 2019); because of its complexity and enormity, these proposed formal links \nare difficult to achieve and require significantly more research. Furthermore, most communities \nare not yet developing resilience goals, while interest and demands for improving lifeline \ninfrastructure resilience are intensifying and spreading as the impacts from hazards increase \naround the world (United Nations, 2016). Even if all communities established their own resilience \ngoals as proposed by NIST (2015) , it would be difficult for lifeline infrastructure that serves \nmultiple communities to meet a differing set of goals created by each  community at different \ntimes. As a result,  coordinated guidance for improving resilience for all infrastructure \nsectors must proceed now by incorporating flexible methods to meet the needs of vital \ncommunity functions during and following hazard events. It is believed that a well -\nthought-out process can be implemented  based on a premise that most vital or \nessential community functions are similar across communities (e.g., a hospital is \ncritical to community recovery no matter where it is located) . The lifeline infrastructure \nobjectives can later be  synchronized with future community-level consensus driven processes \nfor developing community resilience goals.  \nThe approach presented in this paper was originally created for an existing lifeline infrastructure \nsystem using performance-based design processes for earthquakes (Davis, 2017; Davis, 2019; \nLADWP, 2019) in the absence of community resilience goals.   \n \nFigure 1. Process linking community -level resilience goals with building s and lifeline \ninfrastructure performance and recovery objectives and targets (modifications from RRMC, 2019 \nshown in blue). \nFig. 1 shows an aspirational approach  for establishing resilience objectives  for buildings and \nlifeline infrastructure from community -level resilience goals  modified from RRMC’s (2019) \noriginal vision. The goals, objectives, and targets in Fig. 1 are shown in an ascending order with \nCommunity-Level Resilience Goals \nPerformance & Recovery Objectives for \nVital Community Functions \nPerformance & Recovery Objectives \nfor Building Clusters \nPerformance & Recovery Objectives for \nLifeline Infrastructure Systems \nPerformance & Recovery Targets for \nIndividual Buildings \nPerf. & Rec. Targets for Lifeline Infrastructure \nComponents and Organizational Groups \n\nhighest importance at the top, and each level giving direction for the next. First, a policy-driven \nprocess is carried out to establish community -level resilience goals, which are used to derive \nperformance and recovery objectives for a set of vital community functions and their supporting \ninfrastructure (i.e., the building clusters and lifeline  infrastructure) and link with performance  \nand recovery  targets for individual buildings and lifeline infrastructure components  and \nassociated organizational groups . Building clusters are defined as a set of buildings serving a \ncommon function, such as housing, healthcare, or retail, without necessarily being \ngeographically collocate

[{"suffix": "", "text": "NIST Technical Note \nNIST TN 2384\nNIST Transactive Energy Market \nFederate         \nA TE Market for GridLAB-D Co-Simulations \nDavid Holmberg \nThomas Roth \nThis publication is available free of charge from: \nhttps://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2384 \n\n\nNIST Technical Note  \nNIST TN 2384 \nNIST Transactive Energy Market \nFederate         \nA TE Market for GridLAB-D Co-Simulations \n \nDavid Holmberg \nBuilding Energy and Environment Division  \nEngineering Laboratory  \n \nThomas Roth \nWireless Networks Division \nCommunications Technology Laboratory \n \n \n \nThis publication is available free of charge from:  \nhttps://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2384 \nSeptember 2026 \n \n \n \n \n \nU.S. Department of Commerce  \nHoward Lutnick, Secretary \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology  \nArvind Raman, NIST Director and Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology\n\n\nNIST TN 2384 \nSeptember 2026 \n \n   \nCertain equipment, instruments, software, or materials, commercial or non-commercial, are identified in this \npaper in order to specify the experimental procedure adequately. Such identification does not imply \nrecommendation or endorsement of any product or service by NIST, nor does it imply that the materials or \nequipment identified are necessarily the best available for the purp ose.  \nPublication History \nApproved by the NIST Editorial Review Board on 2026-09-17 \n \n \nHow to Cite this NIST Technical Series Publication \nHolmberg D, Roth T (2026) NIST Transactive Energy Market Federate: A TE Market for GridLAB-D Co-Simulations.      \n(National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD), NIST Technical Note (TN) NIST TN 2384. \nhttps://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2384. \nAuthor ORCID iDs \nDavid Holmberg: 0000-0002-1738-8190 \nThomas Roth: 0000-0002-9986-7784 \n \n\nNIST TN 2384 \nSeptember 2026 \n \ni \nAbstract \nThe NIST Transactive Energy Market (TEM) federate was developed to simulate a local \ndistribution electricity market. For a typical distribution grid customer’s electricity tariff, utility \npower is offered at some price (whether a fixed or dynamic price) in unlimited quantities with \nthe assumption that congestion is neglectable. However, in practice, there may be significant \ncongestion, with overloading and voltage problems on a distribution circuit. Congestion could \nbe tied to increasing electrification, including the addition of electric vehicle (EV) charging, \nwhile overvoltage may be tied to excess photovoltaic (PV) generation. It is possible that a local \ntransformer serving four homes may be overloaded on a hot summer afternoon when each \nhouse has electric heat pumps, electric water heaters, and EV chargers consuming power. The \naggregated load may also challenge the available capacity on the wider grid.  \nThe TEM implements a market using the OASIS Common Transactive Services (CTS) standard \nframework with a TE Market Agent (TEMA) as the market operator and TE User Agents (TEUA) \nthat buy and sell energy on behalf of loads, storage, and generation assets behind customer \nmeters. The TEMA receives bids and offers, issues quotes and transactions and tracks the \nposition of each market participant. The TEUA may represent a single distributed energy \nresource (DER; smart load, generator, or storage) or aggregate the load curves of multiple \nbuilding systems. The TEUA may serve as an intelligent agent (e.g., estimating future load based \non historical consumption and other data), and may additionally have access to house meter \ndata and the ability to track position for different loads. The TEUA may buy and sell power in \nforward and real-time markets to optimize energy use. Behind the TEUA interface, controllers \nmanage devices based on their understanding of device flexibility and owner priorities.  \nIn initial simulation experiments, the NIST TEM implements a day-ahead hourly congestion-\npricing-based quote-driven market. Market participants include all devices behind a specific \nservice transformer. Initial prices of hourly power for the next day are set based on the bulk \nDay Ahead Market clearing price. Initial quotes are for a limited quantity of 75 % of the service \ntransformer power flow rating. If the full amount of power available at this initial price is \ntransacted (purchased by market participants) for some hour, then additional power (of a \nsmaller quantity) is offered to the market for that hour at a higher price. Devices participating \nin the market may choose to pay the higher price for power in that hour, to move the load in \ntime to a lower-price time interval, or to curtail. The market iterates until all devices have \nacquired power to meet their power needs according to their individual comfort and flexibility \nlimits.  \nThis paper introduces the NIST TEM design and implementation.  \nKeywords \nco-simulation; Common Transactive Services; electricity markets; market agent; transactive \nenergy; user agent. \n  \n\nNIST TN 2384 \nSeptember 2026 \n \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. Introduction \n What is TE and why does it matter? \nTransactive Energy (TE) is a concept where markets are used as the mechanism for negotiating \nenergy use and prices, recognizing that energy’s value changes with time of day [1]. Existing \nwholesale energy markets provide a good example, and the goal is to bring energy markets to \nthe distribution level, providing local optimization of distributed resources. Energy markets can \nprovide an optimal solution to match supply and demand while providing good forward signals, \ne.g., price signals offering energy for sale for time intervals tomorrow. In the case of TE, offers \nto sell some quantity of energy for some price motivate investment in storage and provision of \ncustomer flexibility to meet grid reliability and capacity needs. A key concept in TE is the use of \nmarkets to expose the value of energy in time to incentivize provision of flexibility. Flexibility is \nthe ability of a customer facility/device to shift, shed/add, or modulate energy use [2]. TE \nbecomes the mechanism to incentivize, manage and pay for customer flexibility, including \nbattery storage.  \nAnother key TE concept is service orientation—allowing the customer to control his or her own \ndevices and to provide grid services. In a market environment, the customer is presented with \nthe economic value of energy now and in the near future to inform decisions about energy \nusage, or when to charge and discharge storage. The market allows the customer to optimize \nenergy use to maximize personal or organizational benefit, minimizing energy cost while \nproviding needed services in the building or home. That is, a homeowner needs to keep the \nhouse comfortable, provide hot water, charge the EV, etc., but one homeowner has a different \nidea of comfort and a different EV driving schedule compared to their neighbor. It is not ideal to \nhave some external service provider control equipment in a house. An external actor would \ngenerally know less than the homeowner about planned schedules, comfort parameters and \ndaily needs. External control may also present safety concerns, and additionally, a direct control \nconnection is more difficult to maintain given a heterogenous ecosystem (APIs, network \nconnections, security architectures, patches, etc.). For these reasons, it is better for the \ncustomer to maintain control and provide services to the grid based on perceived value. \nTE provides a path for the local distribution utility to procure flexibility from the customer in a \nrelatively simple way that does not require a variety of custom programs and specialized tariffs \n(e.g., different pricing for EV charging). A single TE local-market-based tariff may simultaneously \naddress every smart device in the customer’s home or facility. The retail market becomes the \ntool used to guide the battery when to charge and discharge, guide the EV to charge on low \nprices, and guide the heat pump to avoid running during peak prices, etc. Markets can also be \nused for frequency response services or voltage control. TE can replace specialized tariffs (e.g., \nfor EV charging), support grid reliability and local resilience, improve voltage management, \nadapt to renewable energy use, and reduce infrastructure build-out by improving the capacity \nfactor of the grid. \nTE incentivizes the customer to invest in intelligent agents that can respond to prices to shift \nload and save money, while benefitting the grid. The price signals that incentivize local storage \n\nNIST TN 2384 \nSeptember 2026 \n \n2 \nand load shifting expose the value to customers and promote a healthy balance between grid-\nscale and customer-owned storage and generation.  \n The TE Market (TEM) Simulation Federate and NIST TE Co-simulation \nThe NIST TEM is an implementation of a TE market that runs together with GridLAB-D (GLD) \ngrid simulation and Flexible Resource Controller (FRC) [3] within the NIST TE Testbed, as seen in \nFig. 1. The TEM takes baseline load and generation power profiles as input and uses the market \nand device energy cost algorithms to adjust the power profiles to minimize local congestion, \nsave money for the device owner, and meet owner service requirements. For example, if an EV \nmust charge overnight, the market will help the EV charger find the lowest-cost hours to charge \nwhile still getting the required charge quantity. The market enables neighbors to indirectly \nnegotiate charging schedules such that one charges now and the other later; both neighbors \nand the grid benefit.  \n  \nFig. 1 High-level co-simulation federates and data flow directions. \nThe TEM outputs are updated power profiles to pass to the FRC. The FRC then passes power \nand temperature set points into the ongoing GLD simulation. GLD in turn outputs transformer \npower flow, metered energy at each house and voltages at each meter, and that data is used to \nevaluate performance of the TEM versus other pricing approaches, as well as for load \nforecasting and billing (settlement, comparing market transactions versus metered usage). \nMore details on the data that is exchanged and subcomponents in the simulation are provided \nin the following sections. \nThe TE Testbed with the federates shown in Fig. 1 uses a middleware based on the High Level \nArchitecture (HLA) standard described in [4] to communicate and coordinate between \nfederates. For improved scalability to large distribution grids, there is a single aggregate FRC \nfederate that controls all customer resources in GLD. Additional details on the implementation \nare provided in later sections.   \nThe TEM operates as a day-ahead hourly congestion market. A market cycle begins when, at \nsome time before 5:00 p.m. each day, the wholesale day-ahead market clearing prices (DAP) \nare distributed to all market participants as a quote for some initial quantity of energy tied to \n\n\nNIST TN 2384 \

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Spatial heterogeneity in polymer blends and its impact on dynamics\nBret W. Tantorno a,1\n , Tuyen T.T. Truong a,1, Lori M. Hoover a, Gregory B. McKenna a,*\n ,  \nRan Tao b, Fan Zhang b\na Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, 27695-7905, USA\nb Materials Measurement Science Division, Material Measurement Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD, 20899, USA\nARTICLE INFO\nKeywords:\nPolymer blend\nPMMA\nPEO\nDynamic heterogeneity\nMiscibility\nDSC\nRheology\nWAXS\nSAXS\nUSAXS\nABSTRACT\nThe relationship between dynamic and spatial heterogeneity in polymer blends is still not fully understood, yet it \nplays a crucial role in our understanding of their viscoelastic properties. Here, we report the results of an \ninvestigation of the viscoelastic response of a set of poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO)-poly(methyl methacrylate) \n(PMMA)-dimethylacetamide (DMAc) ternary blends, with emphasis on the nominally miscible regime. The work \nreveals interesting deviations from time-temperature superposition (TTS) as evidenced through van Gurp-Palmen \n(vGP) analysis. While previous rheological studies on such systems have focused on the terminal regime, our \nwork extends through the Rouse- and towards the glassy-regime to broaden the range of dynamic behavior \nprobed. We find that PEO:PMMA(DMAc) blends show thermal and rheological compatibility at PEO mass \nfractions below 30 % in the rubbery and terminal regimes. However, as the system dynamics go through the \nRouse-regime and approach the glassy or α-relaxation (glass transition regime) the vGP plots no longer form a \nsingle curve, thus revealing a breakdown in TTS. These results both suggest that small-scale heterogeneities with \ndistinct temperature dependencies exist, i.e., the blends are immiscible, and that the vGP plots are much more \nsensitive to breakdown of TTS than is the creation of the master curves themselves. Thus, it appears that the vGP \nanalysis provides a sensitive measure of dynamic heterogeneity, highlighting subtle deviations that are not seen \nin standard TTS analysis. Additionally, in the system studied here, the ternary nature of the blends (PMMA- \nDMAc-PEO) includes a solvent and this alters the Tg and relaxation dynamics, and we describe how this im-\npacts the reported outcomes. Our findings suggest that, as the polymer blends approach the α-relaxation, small- \nscale heterogeneities influence the dynamics such that they show different temperature dependencies, leading to \ndynamic heterogeneity. We also show results from wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS), small-angle X-ray \nscattering (SAXS), and ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering (USAXS) investigations that support the observations \nfrom the viscoelastic measurements.\n1. Introduction\nThere is a growing body of evidence suggesting that subtle deviations \nfrom time-temperature superposition (TTS) or frequency-temperature \nsuperposition (FTS) in polymers can be more effectively analyzed \nusing van Gurp-Palmen (vGP) plots than through traditional double- \nlogarithmic representations of viscoelastic master curves [1–5]. By \nexamining the phase angle (δ) as a function of the logarithm of the \nmagnitude of the complex modulus (|G*|), vGP analysis can potentially \nprovide a sensitive means of identifying dynamic heterogeneity in \ncomplex fluids [5]. This approach offers a promising framework for \nidentifying such heterogeneities and their relationship to underlying \nspatial heterogeneity in complex systems, including polymer blends and \nblock copolymers, where the interplay of microstructure and dynamics \nis of fundamental interest.\nPoly(ethylene oxide):poly(methyl methacrylate) (PEO:PMMA) \nblends have been extensively studied, with their thermodynamic \nmiscibility well-documented in terms of composition and temperature. \nAbove PEO's melting point, techniques such as differential scanning \ncalorimetry (DSC), small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) [6–9], and \nsmall-angle neutron scattering (SANS) [10] demonstrate miscibility \nacross the entire composition range. Below the melting point, however, \nPEO tends to phase separate and crystallize, with PMMA interfering with \ncrystallization [11–13]. Conversely, complementary investigations \n* Corresponding author.\nE-mail address: gbmckenn@ncsu.edu (G.B. McKenna). \n1 These two authors made equal contributions to the work.\nContents lists available at ScienceDirect\nPolymer\njournal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/polymer\nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymer.2026.130287\nReceived 7 February 2026; Received in revised form 16 May 2026; Accepted 24 May 2026  \nPolymer 360 (2026) 130287 \nAvailable online 28 May 2026 \n0032-3861/© 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license ( http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by- \nnc-nd/4.0/ ). \n\nusing DSC, dielectric spectroscopy [14], density analysis [15], \nFourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) [16], and 13C solid-state \nnuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) [17,18] reported no PEO phase \nseparation and crystallization for blends containing less than 30 % mass \nfractions of PEO, below the melting point of PEO, suggesting that these \nblends are miscible at lower PEO concentrations. These studies were \nconducted on PEO:PMMA samples in which PEO crystallized, because \nthe cooling process was not rapid enough to avoid crystallization. If the \nPEO phase separation and crystallization could be prevented, the blends \nmight retain their miscibility, though this was not attempted.\nThe prior studies focused on the thermodynamic miscibility of the \nPEO:PMMA blends, while the dynamic compatibility (or heterogeneity) \nremains less explored. However, rheological studies, including those by \nvan Gurp and Palmen [19], as well as Colby [20], have reported that \nPEO:PMMA blends do not follow TTS under miscible conditions, i.e., \nabove the melting point of PEO. This incompatibility was attributed to \nthe large difference in relaxation times between PEO and PMMA, and \nthe conclusion has also been supported by infrared dichroism and \nbirefringence studies performed simultaneously with dynamic studies \nconducted by Zawada et al. [21] Furthermore, prior studies have \nexplored dynamic heterogeneity through the use of Cole-Cole plots [22], \nwhere a slight breakdown in TTS can be observed in the terminal \nregime. However, we contend that the vGP plot is superior for repre-\nsenting the broad range of dynamics investigated here where we \nexamine the behavior from terminal to glassy relaxations. Due to the \nvast range of modulus magnitudes, the Cole-Cole type of analysis ne-\ncessitates multiple “zoomed-in” subplots to capture the full breadth of \nthe data, while the vGP plot provides a visualization of the entire range \nof data in one plot.\nThe apparent discrepancy between thermodynamic miscibility and \nthe observation of dynamic heterogeneity under identical conditions, \nyet using different experimental techniques, may arise from nanoscale \nheterogeneities that are undetectable by conventional techniques like \nDSC but become evident in NMR experiments [17,18] that detect \npossible heterogeneity below a length scale of 20 nm. By leveraging vGP \nanalysis to probe such possible subtle heterogeneities, we offer a new \nperspective on the miscibility of PEO:PMMA blends and the broader \nimplications of polymer blend design. In the present study, DMAc was \nincorporated into the PMMA phase to lower the glass transition tem-\nperature of neat PMMA closer to that of PEO, thereby preventing po-\ntential PEO degradation in the terminal regime, as shown subsequently. \nThe present work uses the ternary PEO:PMMA(DMAc) blend to broaden \nthe range of dynamics investigated. In the prior work on binary PEO: \nPMMA blends, the studies focused on the terminal behavior. The current \nwork extends the prior studies by examining both the full range of dy-\nnamics from terminal, to rubbery, to Rouse, and towards the glassy (or \nα-relaxation) regimes, thus providing insights into our understanding of \nthe interplay between microstructure and viscoelastic dynamics. These \nternary blends exhibit apparent TTS compatibility in their dynamics, \nunlike the prior work on binary PEO:PMMA blends which show TTS \nbreakdown. However, they also show anomalous behavior in the cor-\nresponding vGP plots. Specifically, deviations in the phase angle from \nexpected trends suggest the presence of nanoscale dynamic heteroge-\nneities. Such anomalies provide an alternative route to characterizing \nblend miscibility and homogeneity, with implications for understanding \nand tuning the properties of polymer blends. It also provides insights \nrelated to conventional frequency-temperature superposition analysis. \nIn addition to the blend rheology, we also employed synchrotron-based \nWAXS and SAXS measurements to examine a subset of the nominally \ncompatible blends and these results further support our conclusions.\n2. Experimental methods\n2.1. Sample preparation\nPolyethylene oxide (PEO, Mw = 125,000 g/mol, PDI = 1.88), poly \n(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA, Mw = 100,000 g/mol, PDI = 1.33), and \ndimethylacetamide (DMAc) were purchased from Thermo Fisher Sci-\nentific Inc.2 The molecular weight and polydispersity index (PDI) were \ndetermined by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) from Resolve-\nMass Laboratories Inc. (Supplemental Information). Polymer blend \nplaques of PEO:PMMA(DMAc) were prepared by a solvent casting pro-\ncedure as shown in Fig. 1. First, the polymers were dissolved in DMAc by \ncontinuous stirring at 50 ◦C for 24 h. Then, the pure polymer solutions of \nPEO and PMMA were mixed at the appropriate ratios to produce mix-\ntures of 0 % to 100 % mass fractions of PEO to PMMA in 10 % mass \nfraction increments. An additional plaque of PEO at a mass fraction of 5 \n% was made as well. The PEO:PMMA(DMAc) blends with varying mass \nfractions are denoted as PEO:PMMA(DMAc) for simplicity, representing \nthe mass fraction ratios of PEO to PMMA that were mixed. The actual \ncompositions of the ternary blends are given in Table 1. The mixtures \nwere then stirred for an additional 24 h at 50 ◦C to ensure uniform \nmixing. After mixing, the solutions were poured onto a Teflon evapo-\nration disk and transferred to a 60 ◦C oven for 2 days to dry. Similar \ntreatments were applied to the pure PMMA and PEO materials to un-\nderstand the impact of solvent on the results. The as-cast plaques had \nthicknesses of approximately 750 μm and were cut out with an 8 mm \nhole punch. Also, neat PMMA and neat PEO as received were used \nwithout solvent treatment for comparison. [{"suffix": "", "text": "A Metrology Development Platform for Digital Image \nCorrelation-Based Measurement of Thermal \nExpansion and Cure Shrinkage in Epoxies\nAlexander K. Landauer  \nNational Institute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nalexander.landauer@nist.gov  \n0000-0003-2863-039X \n       \nAbstract—NIST is developing  a suite of material metrology \ntools to understand and characterize the development of residual \nstresses during epoxy curing. In this work, the application of  \ndigital image correlation (DIC)-based metrology for coefficient of \nthermal expansion (CTE) and (effective) cure shrinkage (E)CS is \ndescribed. The DIC setup and experimental considerations are \nexplained in detail.  An example analysis of CTE for  a prototype \ntest material, also under development, is discussed with example \nCTE data shown. This contribution helps the interested reader to \nunderstand the basic design decisions for establishing DIC -based \nmetrology for epoxy cure, and future developments may include \nrobotic calibration, humidity control and epoxy confinement. \nKeywords—epoxy packaging, digital image correlation, cure \nshrinkage, coefficient of thermal expansion \nI. INTRODUCTION \nThe increasing complexity of chip assemblies as the \nsemiconductor industry moves toward 3D heterogeneous \narchitectures has led to increased introduction of sophisticated \nepoxies into build ups [1]. With such a substantial use of epoxy, \nquantifying thermo-chemo-mechanical properties such a s \n(effective) cure shrinkage [(E)CS] and coefficient of thermal \nexpansion (CTE) is an important step for developing predictive \nmodels of these systems. Mechanical properties  such as \nstrength, toughness, and adhesion  are important primary \nperformance measures, but calibrated CS and CTE mismatch are \nimportant parameters for informing models to predict warpage \nand other downstream challenges [2-4]. Here, the focus is on a \ndevelopment platform for digital image correlation (DIC)-based \nmetrology for quantification of (E)CS and CTE , which can be \nused to study in situ curing.  \nDigital image  correlation-based technique s have been \napplied to measure CS, CTE, and similar properties in various \nprevious works , e.g.,  [5-9]. Package w arpage is also \ncharacterized with  DIC and it is recognized a s a possible \napproach for package warpage measurement by JEDEC \nstandard JESD22-B112C [10-11]. C ommercial instrument s \nutilizing DIC for displacement and strain measurements  are \navailable from packaging metrology companies  [3]. S everal \nDIC vendors have been commissioned or sell specialized \nsystems for measuring packa ge warpages and packaging \nmaterials with DIC.  Since the use o f DIC for these \nmeasurements is becoming widespread, this project aims to \ndemocratize access, explore the potential of the technique,  and \nprovide insight into the metrological details.  \nTo address the multifaceted characterization needs  for \npacking epoxies a suite of test methods is under development by \na broader project team at the National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology (NIST) [12]. These test methods encompass a wide \nrange of chemical, thermal, and  mechanical assays from \nmolecular-scale to part-scale. The DIC system that is the focus \nof this work, shown in Fig. 1, embodies one of the tools in this \nsuite, which was briefly discussed in Centellas et al. [12]. This \nproject focuses on describing development of the DIC platform, \nexploring challenges,  and discussing methodologies for the \nsystem to quantify (E)CS and CTE with sufficient fidelity and \nwith in situ  capabilities to inform reliable predictive models. \nUsing a simple, well-controlled test material as a baseline, this \nwork discusses the application of this DIC system to (E)CS and \nCTE measurements. Since both measurements are similar, the \nexample application highlighted focuses on CTE measurement \nand changes to the methodology needed for (E)CS are noted.  \nII. EXPERIMENTAL \nA. Material \nA prototype test material (TM01) under development by \ncolleagues at NIST  is used a s the example case for the \nremainder of this paper. This is a highly simplified model \nmaterial of an underfill -like epoxy. It consists of bisphenol F \nepoxy resin cured with diethyl toluene diamine, which are  \nconstituents foundational to advanced underfill formulations . \nNotably, no additional modification agents or fillers are \nincluded in this formulation.  After formulation, the material is \nstored at about 4  °C in a lab refrigerator until about 20 min \nbefore use. \nB. Specimen Design and Fabrication \nFor (E)CS and CTE measurements with DIC,  specimen \ndesign and fabrication are critical to measure meaningful, \nrepresentative data on the material behavior. DIC is a  \nnoncontact surface-type measurement in contrast to, e.g.,  fiber \nOfficial contribution of the National Institute of Standards and Technology; \nnot subject to copyright in the United States. \nThis work was performed with funding from the CHIPS Metrology Program, \npart of CHIPS for America, National Institute of Standards and Technology, \nU.S. Department of Commerce. National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology Award # 70NANB24H283. \n\n   \n \n \nBragg [13], [14]  or TMA [3] experiments where a sensor is \ntouching or embedded into the material . A relatively small \nquantity of material (ca. 50 mg) is sufficient for (E)CS and CTE \nmeasurements for this DIC method. To decouple the specimen \nfrom a stiff back er, which could influence the total strain \nresponse after the material passes its gelation point, a thin and \nrelatively compliant high-temperature polymer backer sheet is \nused. Depending on  the material under stud y and thermal \nprofile different backer sheet polymers are needed. In our \nprevious work, a  nominally 0.02 mm p olyetherimide (PEI) \nsheet was used effectively [12]. For TM01, the low surface free \nenergy and hydrophilic nature of the PEI resulted in flow of the \nTM01 during curing. Instead, a high-temperature polyethylene \nterephthalate (PETE) sheet (ca. 0. 03 mm) was used for this \nstudy. This provided a surface on which the liquid epoxy \nbeaded during the transient low viscosity portion of curing, i.e., \nwhen at elevated temperature with low degree cure.  \nAfter synthesis of the prepolymer, it is stored in a laboratory \nrefrigerator until about 5 min before use. Preliminary data \nindicates that moisture uptake in the epoxy during long term \n(i.e., more than  four weeks) storage of prepolymer or cured \nresin may affect characteristics such as CTE , residual stress,  \nand viscoelastic moduli. Thus, specimens for the example data \nshown were fabricated within three weeks of synthesis, cured \nwithin 30 min of fabrication, and tested within five days of \ncuring. To make a specimen, a n approximately 5 cm by 5  cm \nsquare of the selected backer material is cut from the as -\nreceived material. Depending on the viscosity evolution during \ncure and surface interaction of the epoxy and backer, a 3D \nprinted die mold can be used to press a containment feature into \nthe backer. For the example TM01 experiments a  die with a  \n7 mm inner diameter, 11  mm outer diameter,  and 2 mm tall \nridge was used to press a containment feature into the backer. \nDuring cure the PETE relaxes this plastic strain, and it re -\nflattens. However, i n conjunction with the surface energy \neffects, it is sufficient to produce a suitability repeatable \ngeometry for CTE measurement. This strain relaxation disrupts \nquantitative determination of the stress onset during cure  for \n(E)CS measurements, and thus the containment feature may not \nbe suitable when  adopting this approa ch. Once the backer is \nprepared, a scoopula is used to deposit a drop of the prepolymer \non the backer. This is typically 40 mg to 45 mg of material. For \nthe (E)CS experiments  the specimens are speckled  (see Sect. \nII.D.), then cured (see Sect. II.C.) while collecting DIC data on \nboth the  specimen and the  surrounding backer. For the CTE \nmeasurements, the specimens are cured prior to speckling (in \nthis case using the same oven  as DIC ), speckled , left at lab \ntemperature (ca. 22  °C) for the paint  to dry overnight, then \nplaced in the oven for temperature cycling.  \nC. Preliminary \nmeasurements conducted by a collaborator using a stress bench \nmeasurement based on the instrument described in [12] showed \nlinear behavior for the range  25 °C to 150  °C, thus for the \nexamples used here a limited range is used. \nD. [{"suffix": "", "text": "A practical guide to hydrogel working curves for bioprinting \nRion J. Wendland1*, Thomas J. Kolibaba1, Kristan S. Worthington2, Jason P. Killgore1* \n1. Applied Chemicals and Materials Division, National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, Boulder, CO USA \n2. Roy J. Carver Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA \n \n* Corresponding Authors: RJW: rion.wendland@nist.gov, JPK: jason.killgore@nist.gov  \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n\nAbstract: \nThe working curve is a widely implemented, but presently not standardized, method of assessing \nresin printability for photopolymer additive manufacturing technologies. While the working \ncurve has been studied and refined for plastic resins, application to hydrogel materials used in \nbioprinting has been limited. Hydrogels present measurement challenges due to their decreased \nsolids content, compliant nature, and significant swelling. Here, adapting lessons learned from \ninterlaboratory studies on plastic working curves, we assess various techniques for hydrogel \nworking curve measurements. Notably, across several formulations with various molecular \nweights and solids content, hydrogels exhibit near ideal log-linear behavior consistent with the \nJacobs model when measured appropriately. However, certain measurement modalities (such as \ncontact-based and rheological) can indicate Jacobs-like behavior, but with systematic errors in \nthe cure depth compared to non-contact optical methods. Overall, this work highlights the \nchallenges when conducting hydrogel working curve measurements and provides several \nconsiderations to help further develop and standardize measurements across 3D bioprinting \napplications. \n \n \n \nKeywords: \nHydrogels; working curve; Jacobs equation; photopolymerization; 3D printing \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n\n1. Introduction: \nThe use of photopolymer additive manufacturing (PAM) is widely established in the \nbiomedical field, with applications including tissue engineered cell scaffolds, pharmaceutical \ndelivery platforms, and microfluidic organ-on-a-chip devices [1-5]. Specifically, vat \nphotopolymerization, which includes stereolithography and digital light processing systems, \nenables the creation of complex parts and structures in a fast and reproducible manner. Given the \ngrowth and impact of bioprinting on the healthcare system, it is imperative to develop \nmeasurement techniques to compare bioprinting materials accurately and reproducibly across \nlaboratories and research groups.  \nIn vat photopolymerization, an established measurement of photopolymer resin \nprintability is the working curve. A common model used to understand the working curve is the \nJacobs model. This model defines a relationship between Beer-Lambert light absorption and the \ncritical exposure of light Ec necessary for liquid-to-solid polymerization [6]:  \n𝐶𝑑 = 𝐷𝑝ln⁡ (𝐸0\n𝐸𝑐\n) \nHere, Cd is the cure depth or thickness of a sample and E0 is the incident radiant light exposure. \nWhen cure depth as a function of incident radiant exposure is determined experimentally, a log-\nlinear plot produces slope Dp (light penetration depth: where light intensity attenuates to 1/e ≈ 37 \n%) and x-intercept Ec (Figure 1). While historically E0 is referred to as a “dose” rather than \n“radiant exposure”, a “dose” is not consistent with the SI unit system. Here, we use “radiant \nexposure” or “exposure” to refer to the area-normalized optical energy input into the system[7]. \nIdeally, measuring a resin’s working curve can enable users to determine suitable printing \nparameters (e.g., light intensity, cure time, layer thickness) for specific resins. Practically, these \nvalues can also be used as a quality control metric across resin batches, as well as an estimation \nof a resin’s z-resolution and throughput capabilities. \n  \nFigure 1. Example schematic of a working curve experiment. A) Photopolymer formulations are \nirradiated for discrete exposure durations in isolated areas of a methacrylate-functionalized glass slide and \n\n\nthe resulting cure depths are measured. B) Cure depths are plotted against radiant exposure on a log-linear \nplot: Dp is the slope of the regression while Ec is the x-intercept. \n \nIn the field of plastic PAM (i.e. PAM wherein plastic or elastomeric materials are \nprinted), the working curve has been the focus of many studies related to new measurement \ntechniques [8-10], assumptions of the Jacobs equation [11-14], or characterizations of new \nphotopolymer resins [15-18]. Despite the importance of the working curve, this measurement has \nyet to be standardized. For example, a recent interlaboratory study highlighted the variation of \nworking curve measurements across laboratories, with up to a 7-fold and 70-fold difference in \nreported Dp and Ec values, respectively [19]. Importantly, some of this variation can be attributed \nto spectral variability of commercial printers, most notably broadband light sources and variable \nexposure across the resin vat [20]. As such, the use of a well characterized and reproducible light \nsource is vital for standardized working curve measurements. This is clearly demonstrated in the \nmost recent interlaboratory study on plastic working curves, which made use of a standardized \nand well characterized LED light engine. This protocol resulted in significant improvements to \nthe variations in Dp from 7-fold down to 1.6-fold and Ec from 70-fold down to 2.1-fold [21]. \nThe rapid adoption of vat photopolymerization for bioprinting has accelerated the need \nfor robust hydrogel characterization methods. Bioprinting typically uses hydrogel resins for their \nadvantageous properties such as biodegradability, biocompatibility, and close approximation of \nnatural tissue mechanics [22-24]. These hydrogel precursor materials can be synthetic (e.g., \npolyethylene glycol, polyacrylamide, polycaprolactone) or natural (e.g., gelatin, silk, hyaluronic \nacid) which each come with corresponding advantages and disadvantages [25, 26]. The working \ncurve measurement could provide a means of comparing resins properties and print-relevant \nparameters between different materials, batches, or laboratories. Additionally, the magnitude of \nDp and Ec can provide important insights to bioprinting with live cells. For example, many live \ncell printing applications look to minimize the total energy exposure per layer to mitigate \npotentially harmful effects to the cells. Resins with low Ec would be prime candidates for live \ncell printing, as less energy exposure is needed to polymerize the layer. Likewise, high Dp resins \nwould potentially minimize the overall radiant exposure to the cells but may negatively impact \nthe achievable resolution of the printed structure. Regardless of material, implementing working \ncurves on hydrogels requires rethinking of the cure depth (thickness) measurement due the low \nstiffness samples (kPa to MPa) that could be easily deformed or damaged by typical contact-\nbased thickness measurement tools like handheld micrometers [27-29]. As an alternative, some \ngroups have used non-contact methods such as microscopy or photorheology to measure working \ncurve behavior on a variety of photopolymer materials [10, 19, 30, 31]. However, there remains a \ngap in understanding and quantifying how different measurement methods influence hydrogel \nworking curves and Jacobs parameters.  \nHere, we present a guide to practical considerations for measuring working curves on \nhydrogel systems. We use a model acrylate polymer, polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA), at \nvarious molecular weights and concentrations to compare how different cure depth measurement \ntechniques influence hydrogel working curve fit parameters. For all measurement techniques, we \n\nuse an identical light source to ensure that true comparisons can be made between methods. \nImportantly, we show that working curve measurements of photopolymer hydrogels cured with a \nwell-calibrated, narrowband LED light source produce the log-linear working curve relationship \npredicted from the Jacobs model. However, working curves and the extracted Ec and Dp \nparameters are strongly dependent on the measurement method. Contact methods substantially \ncompress soft samples, resulting in an underestimation of cure depth which effects the Dp and Ec \nvalues extracted from the Jacobs model fits. On the other hand, optical methods do not \nsubstantially deform samples but require appropriate contrast and analysis techniques to \naccurately determine cure depth. Gap-dependent photorheology is also investigated as a \ncandidate measurement technique, but the resultant cure profiles do not predictably correlate to \neither the contact or optical methods. Overall, the results presented here can be applied to all \nhydrogel photopolymer 3D printing applications, helping to further develop and standardize \nworking curve measurements across the field. \n \n2. Materials and Methods: \nCertain commercial equipment, instruments, or materials are identified in this paper to specify \nthe experimental procedure adequately. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Piezoelectricity\nPiezoelectricity is the effect of mechanical strain and electric fields on a material; mechanical strain on piezoelectric\nmaterials will produce a polarity in the material, and applying an electric field to a piezoelectric material will create\nstrain within the material. When pressure is applied to a piezoelectric material, a dipole and net polarization are\nproduced in the direction of the applied stress. Piezoelectricity has many applications in regards to electrical\ntransducers and signal devices.\nIntroduction\nBrothers Pierre and Jacques Curie published the first paper on the direct piezoelectric effect in 1880; they applied\nstresses to crystals without a center of symmetry, and observed a surface charge on these crystals. Piezoelectricity\ncomes from a Greek word; \"piezo\" means \"to press\" or \"push\"; therefore, piezoelectricity is creating electricity by\napplying pressure. Gabriel Lippmann predicted a \"reverse\" piezoelectric effect, and the Curie brothers later verified\nthat to be the converse piezoelectric effect. This eventually gave rise to the reversibility of the piezoelectric effect and its\napplications.\nCenter of Symmetry\nMaterials must not have a center of symmetry in order to act as piezoelectric materials. In a material with a center of\nsymmetry, the center of masses of the positive and negative charges coincide at the center of symmetry with or without\nmechanical strain, keeping zero net polarization. In the case of piezoelectric materials, when stress is applied, the center\nof masses of the positive and negative ions change depending on the direction the stress is applied; a net polarization is\nproduced, creating a voltage difference between the two surfaces of the crystal the stress is being applied on.\nFigure :  A non-piezoelectric material with a center of symmetry.\nIn Figure , no force is applied to the non-piezoelectric material; no polarization is induced, as the centers of mass for\nboth the positive and negative ions coincide at point C.\nFigure :  A force is applied on a non-piezoelectric material with a center of symmetry.\nIn Figure , a force is applied to the non-piezoelectric material; no polarization is induced, as the centers of mass for\nboth the positive and negative ions still coincide at point C.\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\n9/30/26, 2:11 PM Piezoelectricity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Piezoelectricity 1/5\n\nFigure :  A piezoelectric material with no center of symmetry.\nIn Figure , a piezoelectric material is shown with no force applied to it. The centers of mass for both the positive and\nnegative ions coincide at point O.\nFigure :  A piezoelectric material compressed on the top and bottom.\nIn Figure , when a vertical force is applied, the centers of mass for both the positive and negative ions shift, creating a\nnet polarization as shown in the middle of the material. This process cancels out within the material until the ends of\nthe material's surface.\nFigure :  A piezoelectric material compressed on the sides.\nIn Figure , when a horizontal force is applied, the centers of mass for both the positive and negative ions still coincide\nwith each other, producing no net polarization; a net polarization will be induced depending on the crystal structure,\nthe direction the force is applied onto the material, and the material's Poisson ratio.\nMechanism\nWhen a stress is applied to a piezoelectric material, the dimensions of the material changes. Depending on the direction\nthe stress is applied, the resulting change in dimensions can shift the centers of mass for the positive and negative ions;\nthis produces a dipole throughout the material. The dipoles inside the material cancel each other out, but on the surface\nof the material the dipoles are not canceled out, producing a polarity given by.\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\n9/30/26, 2:11 PM Piezoelectricity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Piezoelectricity 2/5\n\nwhere T is the mechanical stress, P is the induced polarization, and d is the piezoelectric coefficient.\nFigure :  The piezoelectric effect is shown above; mechanical tension or compression on a\npiezoelectric will induce a current depending type of stress and direction.\nPolarization charge is given by\nwhere\n is the charge and\n is the cross-sectional area of the piezoelectric material the stress is applied on.\nThe polarization induces a voltage due to the given by\nwhere\n is the vacuum permittivity,\n is the relative permittivity,\n is the length of the piezoelectric material, and\n is the capacitance.\nOn the other hand, if an electric field is applied to the piezoelectric material, it produces a strain given by\nwhere  is the applied electric field,  is the produced strain, and d is the same piezoelectric coefficient as above. This is\nalso known as the converse piezoelectric effect. In this case, negative ions would tend to move towards the positive end\nof the electric field, and the positive ions towards the negative end. As a result of the shift of the positive and negative\nions, the dimensions of the material change, creating a strain within the material.\nThe piezoelectric coefficient is the same for both the direct and converse piezoelectric effect at the same magnitude of\neither electric field and induced strain or mechanical stress and induced polarization.\nPoisson's ratio can also play a factor into piezoelectricity; if a piezoelectric material is compressed in one direction, it\nmay expand in the other two directions. An ideal piezoelectric material\nwould have a Poisson ratio of 0, effectively removing its effect on the polarization.\nPiezoelectric Materials\nPiezoelectric materials require a lack of a center of symmetry. In the case of microphones, the vibrations of the sound waves are\nconverted into electric signals. Loudspeakers do the opposite, converting those electrical signals into sound waves.\nPiezoelectric transducers, rather than being used in audible wave ranges, find use on ultrasonic wave ranges.\nPiezoelectric transducers are useful in ultrasonic wave applications. The Young's Modulus of a solid can be determined\nby finding the ultrasonic velocity of the wave traveling through the solid which is then converted to an electric signal\nread on an oscilloscope. lf there are cracks and defects within the material, the ultrasonic waves will either reflect or\nscatter; this allows for material failure analysis because the ultrasonic waves keep the material's structural integrity\nintact.\nThe Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) device was produced primarily for its use as a filter; by interacting with the surface\nwaves on circuit boards, one can either enhance or reduce certain frequencies produced by electric devices.\nOther uses of piezoelectrics are transformers (to raise or lower electric voltages) and pressure sensors (using the\npiezoelectric effect to produce an electric response in the event of a pressure or frequency change).\nQuestions\n1. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Journal of Chromatography A 1730 (2024) 465115\nAvailable online 23 June 2024\n0021-9673/Published by Elsevier B.V.\nOn-line coupling of hollow-fiber flow field-flow fractionation and \ndepolarized multi-angle static light scattering (HF5/D-MALS). Proof \nof principle \nAndr´e M. Striegel \nChemical Sciences Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), 100 Bureau Drive, MS 8390, Gaithersburg, MD 20899-8390, USA   \nARTICLE INFO  \nKeywords: \nHollow-fiber flow field-flow fractionation \nDepolarized multi-angle static light scattering \nOn-line coupling \nDepolarization ratio \nTeflon latex \nABSTRACT  \nIntroduced here is the on-line coupling of hollow-fiber flow field-flow fractionation (HF5) to depolarized multi- \nangle static light scattering (D-MALS). HF5 is a size-based separation alternative to size-exclusion and hydro-\ndynamic chromatography and asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation. HF5 can separate larger sizes than its \nchromatographic counterparts and provides several advantages over its fractionation counterpart, including \nreduced sample consumption and greater ease of operation. D-MALS is a variant of MALS in which the depo-\nlarized scattering from the analyte solution is measured at a variety of angles simultaneously. Measurements of \ndepolarized scattering have previously been employed in studying the optical properties of solutions or sus-\npensions, to determine the length of rod-like analytes, and to gain increased accuracy in the determination of \nanalyte molar mass. The coupling HF5/D-MALS allows for the depolarization ratio of a solution or suspension to \nbe measured continuously across the fractogram. This is demonstrated here for a Teflon latex the size range of \nwhich extends beyond that accessible to commercial size-exclusion columns. The results presented provide the \nfirst reported on-line HF5/D-MALS coupling, showing the feasibility of the technique as well as its realized \npotential for providing continuous depolarization measurements, inter alia.   \n1. Introduction \nSize-based separations are among the most used methods for \nmacromolecule characterization. Among these techniques, size- \nexclusion chromatography (SEC) is employed far more than any other \n[1]. SEC is not without its limitations, however [2], one of these being \nthe analysis of very large and/or very fragile analytes. In this limiting \nregime, other techniques such as hydrodynamic chromatography (HDC) \nand flow field-flow fractionation (flow FFF) can often be successfully \nemployed [3-5]. Variants of the latter include the more popular asym-\nmetric flow FFF (AF4) and the generally underutilized hollow-fiber flow \nFFF (HF5) [6,7]. \nIn HF5, solutions or suspensions flow through a hollow fiber with \nsemi-permeable walls encased within a solid housing. Suction is applied \nconcentrically to the fiber, causing analytes to migrate to and focus on \nthe fiber walls, the latter being the FFF accumulation wall. As in AF4, \ncross-flow programming can be employed in HF5 to improve resolution \nand to ensure retention and elution within a given timeframe and within \nthe given volume constraints of the hollow fiber. \nSome potential advantages of HF5 vis-`a-vis AF4 are the possibility of \nachieving higher sensitivity in the former, as a result of lower analyte \ndilution because of the smaller volume in the hollow fiber versus in an \nAF4 channel; a lower propensity for overloading and, thus, for analyte \naggregation in HF5, given the much lower concentrations employed, \nabout one-third those employed in AF4; and a less complicated experi-\nmental set-up, as HF5 cartridges are easily installed and removed as a \nsingle unit, as opposed to the assembly and disassembly required for \nmembrane installation and replacement in AF4 channels. One notable \ndrawback of HF5 is its generally lower signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) as \ncompared to AF4, due to the lower concentrations employed in HF5 and \nthe lower amount of analyte injected in this technique [8]. \nAmong the most popular on-line detection methods for macromo-\nlecular separations is multi-angle static light scattering (MALS). With an \naccompanying concentration-sensitive detector, MALS is normally \nemployed to determine the molar mass and size of a sample [1,9]. A less \npopular use for MALS has been to study the depolarization state of dilute \npolymer solutions, as to do this requires the use of depolarized MALS \n(D-MALS). This latter detection method offers the possibility of \nobserving the angular dependence of the optical behavior of dilute \npolymeric or colloidal solutions, of calculating the length of rod-like \nE-mail address: andre.striegel@nist.gov.  \nContents lists available at ScienceDirect \nJournal of Chromatography A \njournal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/chroma \nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.chroma.2024.465115 \nReceived 6 June 2024; Received in revised form 20 June 2024; Accepted 22 June 2024   \n\nJournal of Chromatography A 1730 (2024) 465115\n2\nobjects, and more, including allowing for more accurate calculations of \nanalyte molar mass and of the Rayleigh factor of solvents. D-MALS dif-\nfers from depolarized dynamic light scattering. The former measures the \ndepolarized time-averaged fluctuations of the light scattered by a dilute \nanalyte solution. The latter measures the depolarized time-dependent \nfluctuations of this scattered light and is used to disambiguate from \neach other the translational and rotational diffusion coefficients of \nanalytes and to assist when evaluating the angular dependence of decay \nrates in dynamic light scattering, among other applications. \nOn-line D-MALS was introduced as a detection method for SEC over \ntwo decades ago and applied to a variety of macromolecular scenarios \n[10,11]. Its use since appears to have languished, however. With the aim \nof reintroducing this detection method to a new generation of separation \nscientists, coupled to a technique which extends into a higher size \nregime than does SEC, we have attempted the on-line coupling of HF5 to \nD-MALS. The principles of D-MALS are explained in [12] within the \ncontext of on-line detection and, in more fundamental but off-line, \nbatch-mode fashion, also in [13]. As such, only a brief introduction is \ngiven here. Our test analyte is a Teflon emulsion with average diameter \nranging from 0.1 µm to 0.5 µm [14], i.e., with an upper size limit \ngenerally exceeding that of commercially available SEC columns [15]. \nWe hope that this demonstration of the feasibility of performing on-line \nHF5/D-MALS will encourage others to attempt these types of experi-\nments for their own purposes. \n2. Experimental \n2.1. Materials \nNa2HPO4 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO), NaN3 (J.T. Baker, Phil-\nlipsburg, NJ, USA), Brij-35 (Honeywell-Fluka, Morris Plains, NJ), so-\ndium dodecyl sulfate (Polysciences, Warrington, PA, USA). The Teflon \nlatex employed was Algoflon #D60 V (Solvay, Baltimore, MD, USA), \nkindly provided by Paul Russo (Georgia Institute of Technology) and \nRafael Cueto (Louisiana State University). \n2.2. HF5/D-MALS analysis \nThe HF5 analyses were carried out using an Agilent 1260 isocratic \nHPLC pump and autosampler (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, \nUSA), an Eclipse DualTec FFF control module (Wyatt Technology Co., \nSanta Barbara, CA, USA), and an on-line MALS photometer (DAWN \nHELEOS-II, Wyatt). While an on-line DRI detector (T-rEX, Wyatt) was \nalso part of the system, injected concentrations were too low to yield \nusable concentration data. \nThe HF5 cartridge contained a 17-cm-long polyethersulfone fiber of \n≈ 0.8 mm inner diameter and 1.3 mm outer diameter, with a nominal \ncut-off of 10 kDa (Wyatt). The HF5 analysis conditions are summarized \nin Table 1. A linearly decaying cross-flow starting from 0.2 mL min 1 \nwas employed. All the analyses were carried in out in triplicate using \nMilli-Q (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA) H2O + 0.02 % NaN3 + 0.002 mol \nL 1 HNa2PO3 + 0.2 % Brij-35 + 0.05 % sodium dodecyl sulfate, an \neluent previously used successfully for the HDC separation of various \ntypes of latexes [16,17]. Detectors were temperature-regulated at (25.0 \n± 0.1) ◦C, while the HF5 fiber temperature was ambient. Fiber flow was \n1 mL min 1; injection volume was 5 µL. \nOn-line D-MALS employed the same MALS detector as described \nabove, which generates a vertically polarized laser beam. In this de-\ntector, odd-numbered photodiodes are located on one side of the cell and \neven-numbered ones on the other. For D-MALS, two strips of Polaroid \nfilm (Wyatt), one with vertical polarization axis and one with horizontal \npolarization axis, are placed around the sides of the MALS flow cell and \nmaintained tightly in place by a grooved cell retainer attached to the \ncell. The strips thus play the role of analyzer in the optical train of the \nsystem. Two sets of experiments are performed, first with the vertically \npolarized Polaroid strip facing the odd-numbered photodiodes and the \nhorizontally polarized strip facing the even-numbered ones. The posi-\ntion of the strips is then reversed, and the experiment is repeated. Great \ncare must be taken during installation and removal of the strips, to \nensure their snugness around the cell, to avoid or at least minimize \n“leaking” of light around the strips as well as kinking of the strips, and to \navoid touching them or the MALS flow cell with one’s fingers (the use of \nsoft-tipped tweezers is recommended, as is an anti-static strap). It should \nbe noted that the same dissolutions of sample were analyzed in both \nmodes, i.e., with both Polaroid strip positions, as well as without the \nstrips in place. \n3. Results and discussion \nFor a completely isotropic analyte, the dipole induced by interaction \nwith incident radiation will be parallel to the electric vector E0 of said \nradiation. If the analyte is non-absorbing, then only the component of \nthe scattered light which is parallel to the transmission axis of the \nanalyzer (in the present case, the Polaroid strips), E0cosϕ, will pass \nthrough the strips onto the MALS photodiodes. (The angle ϕ is that be-\ntween the polarization and transmission axes). The intensity I(ϕ) of the \nscattered light reaching the photodiodes is given by [18]: \nI(ϕ)= cε0\n2 E2\n0cos2ϕ (1)  \nwhere c is the speed of light in vacuum and ε0 is the permittivity of free \nspace. The intensity of the scattered light which is transmitted by the \nanalyzer reaches a maximum, Imax =\n\ncε0E2\n0\n)\n/2, when ϕ = 0o; \nconversely, I = 0 when ϕ = 90o. When an isotropic analyte in the MALS \nflow cell scatters the vertically polarized incident laser light, all of the \nscattered light should then reach the photodiodes facing the Polaroid \nstrip with vertical polarization axis, and none of the scattered light \nshould reach the photodiodes facing the strip with horizontal polariza-\ntion axis. Depolarizing analytes will alter these relations, displaying \nanywhere from mild to strong (depending on the system) scattering in \nso-called “cross-polarization” mode, i.e., the intensity of scattered light \nreaching the photodiodes facing the Polaroid strip with horizontal po-\nlarization axis will be greater than zero (when vertically polarized \nincident radiation is employed, as is the case here). It should be noted \nthat, in reality, not all the scattered light will reach the photodiodes in \n“aligned-polarization” mode (i.e., when the transmission axis of the \nanalyzer is aligned with the polarization axis of the incident radiation), \ndue to an approximately 10 % to 20 % absorption of light by the Polaroid \nfilters. [{"suffix": "", "text": "IN-SITU 2D AND 3D MEASUREMENTS OF PROCESS AND \nPERFORMANCE IN ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING: APPLICATIONS IN \nPOLYMERS AND METALS \n \nOrion L. Kafka1, Jake Benzing1, Nicholas Derimow1, Newell Moser1, Nikolas \nHrabe1, Callie Higgins1, Jason Killgore1 \n1Applied Chemicals and Materials Division \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology \nBoulder, CO, USA \n \nINTRODUCTION \nAcross the spectrum of 3D printing, or Additive \nManufacturing (AM), understanding of the \nprocess-structure-process-performance (PSPP) \nrelationships depend on accurate \nmeasurements. The materials made are 3D, and \nso 3D measurements, in addition to 2D \nmeasurements, provide great insight throughout \nthe PSPP chain. This work will provide an \noverview of several measurement technologies \nthat have recently been deployed in our project to \ntake such measurements, and include relevant \nfindings of these measurements. The \nmeasurement systems can be categorized based \non the point in the manufacturing and use \nprocess in which they are used. In-situ process \nmeasurements refer to those measurements \ntaken during the material manufacturing . \nAlternatively x-ray computed tomography (XRCT) \nwith in -situ mechanical testing , refers to the \nprocess of taking 3D images during deformation \nof an already-produced part. \n \nPROCESS-STRUCTURE MEASUREMENTS \nThe first class of measurements elucidate the \nmanufacturing process, for which there are two \nexamples in our recent wor k. The first is  atomic \nforce microscope (AFM) -based measurements \n[1], which can be used in-situ to deduce changes, \nsuch as viscosity and thin-film compliance which \nare indicative of chemical changes in the resin \nand cure. This can be used to, e.g., measure \nconversion ratio. See Figure 1 for a schematic of \nthe experiment.  Using this modality, \nmeasurements of the local conversion inform \nprocessing choices – when geometric features \nmatch diffusion lengths, geometric aberrations \nwere observed to increase.  For instance, even \nwith equal dose, higher irradiance was shown to \ndecrease the fidelity of a  patterned ring  due to \nunintended polymerization. Figure 2, reproduced \nfrom [2], demonstrates the measurement of this \neffect in-situ, shortly after UV exposure. Detailed \nmeasurement of the UV cure process enabled    \nby in -situ AFM can thus reveal fundament al \nlimitations and opportunities in the high -\nresolution fabrication of complex, 3D objects with \nstereolithographic techniques. While this first \nform works will for polymers, its application to \nmetals is practically impossible. In order to \nachieve similar i nsights for metals, in-situ \nsynchrotron-based measurements of single -\ntrack, laser-based powder melting is conducted. \nIn our work, we have recently been considering \ndifferences in factors such as substrate \ngeometry, chemistry, and powder size [ 3]. See \nFigure 3 for an example of these images.  Larger \npowder sizes tended to have more internal pores, \nwhich remained trapped in the melt pool and \neventually contributed to final porosity in the \nsolidified melt tracks. Cover gas chemistry did not \nseem to significantly impact the melting behavior, \ndespite differences in heat transfer coefficient. \n \n \nFIGURE 1. Schematic illustration of in -situ \npolymer cure experiment combining UV \nillumination, a photocurable resin , and an AFM  \nwith the tip immersed in the resin . See [1] for \ndetails. \n \n\n\n \nFIGURE 2. Plots of height versus position \nmeasured in -situ with the AFM instrument; this \ndemonstrates the different polymerization profiles \nachieved with varying irradiance and same total \ndose. Reproduced from [2] with permission. \n \n \nFIGURE 3. In-situ melting of two different particle \nsize distributions a) 45 µm to 75 µm, b) 75 µm to \n106 µm. Reproduced from [2] with permission. \n \nSTRUCTURE-PROPERTIES \nMEASUREMENTS \nThe second class of measurements ut ilize micro \nx-ray computed tomography (XRCT) and a load \nframe mounted inside the XRCT instrument to \nmake interrupted in -situ measurements during \nload progression . We have done these \nexperiments on several classes of materials . For \ninstance, using this method we can measure pore \ndeformations during uniaxial tensile loading of an \nIN718 specimen created with laser powder bed \nfusion (PBF -LB/M), along with digital image \ncorrelation to measure surface strains \nconcurrently with the in -situ experiment [ 4]. See \nFigure 4 for demonstration pore and surface \ndeformation measurements.  From this, factor  \ninfluencing local mechanics such as pore grow  \nand deformation localization  can be computed. \nThe pore deformation data is informative in term \nof ductile behavior, and can inform and serve to \nvalidate computational models with high fidelity.  \nSimilar experiments could be conducted in \ncompression and fatigue loading. \n \n \nFIGURE 4. Example pore deformation \nmeasurements throughout loading, along with \nsurface strain maps [3 ], reproduced with \npermission. \n \nSTRUCTURE-PROPERTIES-PERFORMANCE \nMEASUREMENTS \nAlthough ex -situ, before -and-after 3D imaging \ncan also be informative. For instance, a series of \n3D XRCT measurements taken before fatigue \ntesting can be correlated with fatigue \nperformance and post -failure fractographic \nanalysis to determine probable -cause failure \nsites and furthermore develop a more nuanced \n\n\nunderstanding of the impact surf ace features \nhave upon fatigue life, at least in the context of \nrotating bending fatigue with as -printed surface \nfor PBF -LB/M IN718 [ 5]. Figure 5, reproduced \nfrom [5], shows surface profiles made from XRCT \nscans of fatigue coupons, and the resulting lives \nof a number of such coupon. Figure 6 relates \nfailure cite to the surface measured before \ntesting, and demonstrates that simply identifying \nthe deepest not may not be sufficient – the failure \ninitiating feature was not the deepest one. \n \n \nFIGURE 5. Surface profiles measured from \nXRCT on top; stress -life chart with different \nsurface characteristics. Reproduced from [5] with \npermission. \n \n \nFIGURE 6. a) Surface profile map with deepest \nfeature (orange arrow) , and failure initiating \nfeature (red arrow) marked; b) SEM image of \nfracture surface and specimen surface near \nfracture surface, for comparison to d), the pre-test \nXRCT image used to identify the deepest surface \nnotch, which is rendered in 3D in c). Reproduced \nwith permission from [5]. \n \n \nCONCLUSIONS \nAlthough a range of technologies have been \ndiscussed, the overall take -away is that careful \n3D experiments throughout the PSPP workflow \nhelp to understand key mechanics across the AM \nportfolio, matching the pro duction capabilities to \nthe measurement capabilities.  These \nmeasurements serve to inform better AM builds \nin terms of resolution, fidelity, and material quality \nand density. They also allow for more rigorous \nunderstanding of the material deformation \ncharacteristics, which may inform more predictive \nmodels. Finally, they can elucidate the failure \nmodes in novel ways, such that build choices and \nmodels can be made to optimize factors such as \nproduction rate, fatigue life, and part/feature \nresolution. \n \nREFERENCES \n[1] Higgins CI, Brown TE, Killgore JP. Building on the 2023 PAMA Workshop, \nthe 2025 iteration brought together leaders from industry, national laboratories, academia, \nstandards organizations, and startups to assess the current state and future trajectory of PAM, \nalso known as vat photopolymerization (VPP).  \n \nThe workshop centered on four panels themed around the state-of-the-field and outlook, novel \nmaterials and metrology, and safety and standards, with a final panel focusing on an innovative \nVPP newcomer, volumetric additive.
