Building on the 2023 PAMA Workshop, \nthe 2025 iteration brought together leaders from industry, national laboratories, academia, \nstandards organizations, and startups to assess the current state and future trajectory of \nphotopolymer additive manufacturing (PAM), also known as vat photopolymerization (VPP).  \nFigure 1: Welcome and registration table at the third bi-annual PAMA Workshop. \n \nAt the outset, PAMA leadership outlined a strategic framework aimed at strengthening the \norganization's role in supporting the responsible growth of the PAM ecosystem. Key goals \ninclude leveraging the complementary strengths of NIST and the RadTech community to \nadvance safe materials handling and processing knowledge, improve transparency and \neducation around material safety data (MSDS), and collaborate with stakeholders to develop \nstandards for materials, hardware, and pre- and post-processing. PAMA emphasized its role as \na trusted forum to discuss emerging global regulations and identified membership growth and \nbroader industry engagement as priorities to increase the organization's impact. \n \nTo support these goals, PAMA introduced an action plan focused on strengthening PAM \ninformation infrastructure and outreach. Initiatives include redesigning the PAMA website to \nimprove access to technical resources, clarifying the value proposition for membership, \nstreamlining enrollment, and developing partnerships with other associations and PAM-\nadjacent conferences. These collaborations are intended to expand participation, expedite \n\n\nNIST AMS 100-78 \nJune 2026 \n2 \n \nstandards development, and facilitate educational activities across the field. \n \nFigure 1: (left) Panel II- Regulation, Safety, and Standards moderator, Michael Gould, preparing \nto introduce his panelists. (right) Stakeholders participating in the PAMA 2025 by percentage. \n \nDuring the four panels, participants examined barriers to adoption, evolving regulatory and \nsustainability pressures, materials and hardware innovation, and the urgent need for \nstandardization, particularly in light of NIST interlaboratory studies underscoring significant \ndiscrepancies in cure depth measurements. A central theme was that PAM is transitioning from \nan innovation-driven field toward a manufacturing-driven ecosystem where reliability, safety, \nregulatory readiness, and data transparency are increasingly critical. \n \nPanel discussions highlighted that although PAM has achieved strong adoption in applications \nsuch as dental, footwear, and sports equipment, broader industrial deployment remains limited \nby fragmentation, post-processing challenges, and consumer misconceptions. At the same time, \nadvances in high-throughput experimentation, machine learning, and AI-driven materials \ndiscovery offer new opportunities for accelerated innovation, provided they are supported by \nshared data standards and cross-sector collaboration. \n \nRegulatory considerations emerged as an increasingly important driver of industry direction. \nGrowing scrutiny of photoinitiators, hazardous classifications, and photopolymer waste is \nincreasing demand for safer chemistries, improved hazard communication, and harmonized \nglobal standards. Participants emphasized that early engagement with regulators is essential to \nensure policies support both safety and continued innovation. \n \nDiscussions of the materials innovation pipeline noted that acrylate-based systems continue to \ndominate PAM but may be approaching the limits of incremental improvement. Future \nadvances are likely to involve alternative chemistries, hybrid cure mechanisms, and dual-\nreaction systems, alongside hardware innovations that expand the feasible materials space \n\n\nNIST AMS 100-78 \nJune 2026 \n3 \n \nthrough improved thermal control, viscosity handling, and exposure architectures.1–6 \n \nThe workshop also featured PAMA's first focused discussion on volumetric additive \nmanufacturing (VAM), a rapidly emerging approach that challenges conventional layer-based \nassumptions about exposure and resolution. Participants emphasized that measurement \nframeworks, terminology, and materials characterization standards must evolve quickly to \nsupport the scalable adoption of this technology. \n \nAcross all four panels, seven strategic themes (Appendix 1) emerged as foundational priorities: \n1. Materials Evolution Beyond Incremental Improvement \n2. Regulatory Readiness and Sustainability as Design Drivers \n3. Data Infrastructure, Digitalization, and AI-Enabled Discovery \n4. Standards and Metrology as Enablers of Scale \n5. Hardware–Materials Co-Design and Process Integration \n6. Application-Driven Commercialization and Validation \n7. Collaboration as Core Infrastructure \n \nThese themes reinforced that the next phase of PAM growth will depend on coordinated \nprogress across materials science, hardware development, regulatory science, data \ninfrastructure, and standards development. Achieving this vision will require sustained \ncollaboration across industry, academia, and government; an effort that PAMA aims to support \nby serving as a trusted platform for dialogue, education, and coordinated standards \ndevelopment. \n \n\nNIST AMS 100-78 \nJune 2026 \n4 \n \n \nFigure 2: A subset of the 2025 Workshop Attendees posing outside of the conference venue \nwith the CU Boulder campus and Flatirons in the background. \n\n\nNIST AMS 100-78 \nJune 2026 \n5 \n \n1. Discussions focused on persistent adoption bottlenecks, increasing \nsustainability pressures abroad, and the emergence of new technology platforms, such as high-\nthroughput material screening and AI-driven discovery, that could reshape how PAM materials \nand processes are developed. Prabhu*\nCite This: ACS Macro Lett.2025, 14,962−968\n ReadOnline\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: We report that polar cosolvent−water mixtures\noffer a unique approach to controlling the liquid−liquid phase\nseparation (LLPS) of polyelectrolyte complex solutions formed\nfrom degree of polymerization-matched mixtures of strong and\nweak polyelectrolytes�respectively, quaternary poly(N,N-dime-\nthylaminoethyl methacrylate chloride) (qPDMAEMA) and\nsodium poly(acrylate) (PA). As observed in prior work, associative\nLLPS in water exhibits an upper-critical salt concentration with\nstoichiometric complexes and lower-critical solution temperature\n(LCST) behavior, where electrostatic correlations are believed to\ndrive phase behavior. However, upon addition of a miscible\ncosolvent prior to mixing the individual polyelectrolytes at room\ntemperature, we observe a shift in the LCST and the appearance of an upper-critical solution temperature (UCST). This new UCST\nfeature corresponds to a segregative LLPS, whereby the polycation partitions out of the polyanion-rich dense phase and into the\nsupernatant. This behavior arises with cosolvents that decrease (e.g., ethylene glycol) or increase (e.g., N-methyl formamide) the\naverage solvent dielectric constant, suggesting that electrostatic correlations may not primarily control the phase behavior for\ncosolvated coacervate systems. A conceptual 3D phase surface summarizing these observations for the cosolvated system suggests\nthat two distinct surfaces with critical lines appear on the polymer−salt−temperature phase diagram.\nP\nolyelectrolyte complex (PEC) coacervation is of interest in\nboth biophysics, where liquid−liquid phase separation\n(LLPS) leads to membraneless organelles, and advanced\nmaterial applications, with efforts predominantly covering the\neffects of added salt,1−11 charge density of the polyelectro-\nlytes,9−11 and occasionally temperature.12−15 The propensity of\na PEC to resist dissolution is often referred to as “salt\nresistance”�PEC dissolution is favored at high salt concen-\ntration,lowpolyelectrolytechargedensity,andlowtemperature\nasaresultofincreasedcharge-screeningbysaltionsordecreased\nelectrostatic attraction between polyions.16,17 Solvent quality\nproves to be another way of tuning PEC solubility, although\nquantifyingthiseffectintermsofinteractionparametersremains\na challenge.18,19 Nonaqueous solvents, such as deep eutectics20\nand fluorinated alcohols,21 can increase the solubility and\nprocessability of PEC under low salt conditions. Salt\n(salinity)22−24 and pH shifts25−27 in aqueous PEC solutions\nareusedtoformporousandbiocatalyticmembranesinamanner\nsimilar to non-solvent-induced phase separation. PEC in\nnonaqueous or aqueous miscible cosolvent mixtures may offer\nadditional pathways to form membranes. Herein, extensive molecular dynamics (MD) simula-\ntions of a model OMIEC representing various electrochemically\ngated states are reported that reveal charge state-dependent\ncounterion condensation. X-ray diﬀraction simulations based on\nthe MD data predict a measurable change in the scattering intensity\nat the counterion absorption edge, indicative of counterion repo-\nsitioning with charging. We leverage an operando resonant X-ray\nscattering technique to experimentally corroborate the simulated\nscattering and report excellent agreement between predicted and\nexperimental data, confirming that counterions preferentially\nreside in the lamellar mid-plane of crystallites at low doping, and\nnear the polymer backbone at higher doping. On the modelling side, all- atom and coarse-grained mole-\ncular dynamics (MD) simulations have been applied to elucidate\nmorphological changes induced by doping and/or de-doping\nin various conjugated polymer electrolytes. These include\nthe swelling of a glycolated polythiophene (p(gT2)), 9 poly(3,4-\nethylene dioxythiophene) Tosylate (PEDOT:Tos) 10 and poly(3,4-\nethylene dioxythiophene) poly(styrene sulfonate) PEDOT:PSS, 11\nthe substrate-dependent structural phase transition in 2,5-bis-\n(thiophenyl)-1,4-bis(2-(2-(2-methoxyethoxy)ethoxy)-ethoxy)benzene\n(PB2T-TEG),12 or the effect of various solvents, salts and salt\nconcentrations on the microstructural features of poly(3,4-\npropylenedioxythiophene) (PProDOT). 13 Modelling has also\npredicted strong interactions of glycolated thiophenes with\ncations and water. 14,15 Experimentally, ion mobility has been\nmeasured directly on the device scale, 16 strongly affects device\nresponse time asymmetry, 17 and does not limit doping at low\nvoltages.18 It has also been shown that ions typically enter the\nfilm with an electrolyte concentration and ion type dependent\nhydration shell. 19,20 Experimental technique development\nhas aided in improving the understanding of such processes,\nfor example, operando nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) has\nshed insight into charge coupling efficiency and local ion\nenvironments in PEDOT:PSS.21 In addition, photoinduced force\nmicroscopy (PiFM) and photoluminescence have shown that,\nduring charging, ions are initially injected into crystalline\ndomains,22,23 in agreement with the assumption that lower\nbandgap regions of the film are doped first.\nYet, knowledge about the precise location of ions is limited,\nespecially with respect to electronic charge transporting con-\njugated polymer backbones. While some polymers are rigid-rod\nlike and conduction is determined by short contacts, 24 most\nother OMIECs are semi-crystalline. 6 Therein, such aggregates\nand/or crystalline domains are a dominant contributor of the\npercolative charge transport network and may be leveraged to\nshed light on processes occurring in amorphous domains. It is\nessential to determine counterion position with respect to these\nordered assemblies since the distance between the electronic\nand ionic charges strongly impacts interfacial capacitance and\ncould create traps for hole/electron transport. 25 Despite the\ncounterion-hole (or electron) separation being unknown, some\nsynthetic design strategies presumed that it could strongly\naﬀect charge transport and that separating the holes/electrons\nfrom counter ions ( e.g., by adding alkyl spacers) could be a\nstrategy towards improved performance. 26,27 Recently, it has\nbeen established that grazing incidence resonant X-ray diﬀrac-\ntion (GIRXRD) can quantitatively determine the location of\ncounter ions in a semicrystalline polymer OMIEC. 28 Initial\nex situ (dry) measurements established that, counter to naı ¨ve\nexpectation, the counter ion resides near the lamellar half-\nplane (far from the charge carrier). However, the operando state,\nwhere solvent swelling occurs, is vastly disparate in terms of\npolymer structure 29–31 and the dielectric environment of sol-\nvated ions; therefore, determining counterion position during\noperation is a critical need.\nWe report here on a novel MD model designed to closely\nreplicate experimental operando doping conditions for a model\nsemi-crystalline polymer OMIEC. To the best of our knowledge,\nno numerical simulations have yet been reported that replicate\nthe experimental conditions of ion insertion and their spatial\norganization into crystalline domains as a function of electrical\ncharging. Starting from a well-defined structure of the polymer\ncrystallites, our MD simulations successfully capture the inser-\ntion of ions, surrounded by their hydration spheres, into the\ncrystallites as a function of the doping state of the polymer\nbackbones. We find that the average position of the ions with\nrespect to the lamellae varies dramatically with degree of\ncharging, exhibiting condensation near the backbone at high\ndegrees of doping. We then generated synthetic grazing-\nincidence resonant X-ray diﬀraction (GIRXRD) data based on\nthe MD simulations that show that counterion condensation\nnear conjugated polymer backbones should be measurable.\nOperando GIRXRD experiments corroborate predicted results,\nshowing excellent agreement between MD and experiment. The\nfindings demonstrate that ion condensation is strongly influ-\nenced by the polymer’s charge state and the nature of the\nanionic species. We marry the complementary approaches to\nboth verify the interpretation of experimental data and to gain\ninsights about ion–polymer interactions that were previously\ninaccessible. Finally, we leverage the MD simulations to gain\nmechanistic insight into the driving forces for ion condensa-\ntion. This work thus emphasizes the importance of simulated\ndata and suggests important implications for materials design\nand electrolyte choice in mixed conductors towards improved\nmaterials performance.\nComputational insight into charged\nstructures\nTypically, when p-type accumulation mode OMIECs are oxi-\ndized, water and charge compensating anions are injected from\nsurrounding electrolyte reservoirs into the polymer micro-\nstructure.4,32 While the bulk of this swelling does not happen\nin the highly ordered regions of the polymer, some fraction of\nthose ions and water will intercalate in the interlamellar space\nof crystallites. 5,30,33 The expansion of these regions can be\nmeasured with conventional monochromatic X-ray scattering,\nbut information about where ions reside within the crystallites\nis inaccessible. Accelerating the materials innovation lifecycle from\nfundamental understanding to product-on-market is crucial to\nmeeting the challenges of energy, water, health, and environ-\nment required by the growing global population. Efforts to\naccelerate this lifecycle, such as the Materials Genome\nInitiative,1 have largely focused on harnessing advanced\nmodeling and modern informatics to supplement human\nexpertiseindecidingwhichexperimentstoperformtoproduce\nthe maximum measurement value from the minimum number\nofexperiments.Suchworkflowsandrelated in silicoinformatics\napproaches have been transformative in exploring the\nequilibrium phase diagrams of hard materials, such as metals\nand ceramics, and some nonequilibrium materials processing.\nIncontrasttometalsandceramics,wherecompositionswith\nfive elemental components are considered highly complex,2,3\nliquid formulations regularly consist of tens to hundreds of\ncomponents withthe physicsofstructure formation driven by\neach component. Formulated products span the breadth of\nmodernsociety,frompharmaceuticals,personalcareproducts,\nand food and beverage to drilling fluids and industrial\nmaterials. Despite the success of advanced modeling and\nclosed-loop studies in other areas, most formulations are\ndeveloped using human expert intuition or, at best, design-of-\nexperiments (DOE) strategies focused on phenomenological\nor structural properties. This gap originates in several\nfundamental features of formulations: they are nearly always\nhighly multicomponent, their structures are often far-from-\nequilibrium with significant processing pathway dependence,\nand their structure−property relationships are frequently\nhighly complex and poorly theoretically understood. The\ndifferencebetweenanautomatedplatformandanautonomous\none is the decision-making agent that optimally guides the\ncourse of an experiment.\nFor hard materials science and small molecule chemistry,\nagent-guided closed-loop autonomous experiments have\nshown great value in discovering new materials, optimizing\nmaterialproperties,and mappingphase boundaries.5−12 Many\nof these studies have moved past the simple application of\nblack box machine learning techniquesand have attempted to\nincorporatematerialormeasurementphysicsintotheiragents.\nThis can include incorporating thermodynamic constraints\n(e.g., Gibbs phase rule), knowledge of crystallographic\nconcepts like peak shifting, or knowledge about the potential\nmathematicaldescriptionsofphysicalphenomena.5,8,12 Others\nhave sought to add explainability to their agents, such as\nthrough interpretable constraints applied to latent spaces of\nknown variables.13 Frameworks have been developed for\nallowing multiple autonomous agents to interactively collab-\norate.14 Additionally, there is a growing conversation in the\nautonomous experimentation community on how to imple-\nment “human-machine teaming” concepts where autonomous\nagents collaborate with humans to combine the speed of\nautonomous agent decision making with human knowledge\nand intuition.15−18\nComparatively, the application of active learning and\nautonomous techniques to polymer and soft material systems\nis less developed. Several groups have identified reversible\naddition−fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) polymer syn-\nthesis as being highly amenable to flow geometries and\ntherefore automation.19−22 These studies sought to optimize\nmaterialpropertiesbytuningthepolymersynthesistocontrol\nthe polymer sequence or molecular weight distributions of\ntheir polymers. There have been a smaller number of studies\non polymer property optimization of polymer formula-\ntions.23−26 These studies optimize material properties by\ntuningcompositionratherthansynthesis.Ofparticularinterest\nare studies that take industrial interests into account, such as\nthe cost of the formulation chemistry.26\nHere we report the development of a modular active\nlearning agent that leverages small-angle scattering (SAS)\nmeasurementsforphasediscovery.Ouragentisdesignedtobe\ngeneral-purpose such that it can be applied to scattering (and\nnonscattering) instruments and a range of material systems\nwithout prior knowledge of a system’s phase behavior. In the\nfollowing sections we discuss the design of the agent, our in\nsilico tuning approach, and finally closed-loop experimental\nFigure 1. Schematic overview of the active learning agent. [{"suffix": "", "text": "The importance of branch placement on the\ndilute solution properties of comb-like\nmacromolecules\nRobert J. S. Ivancic, ∗,† Chase B. Thompson,‡ Devin A. Golla,¶ Bintou Koroma,§\nJack F. Douglas,† Sara V. Orski,† and Debra J. Audus †\n†Materials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and\nTechnology, Gaithersburg, Maryland 20899, United States\n‡Leidos Inc., 1750 Presidents Street, Reston, Virginia 20190, United States\n¶Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, University of Pennsylvania,\nPhiladelphia, Pennsylvania 19104, United States\n§Fischell Department of Bioengineering, University of Maryland, College Park, Maryland\n20742, United States\nE-mail: robert.ivancic@nist.gov\nAbstract\nBranch density and length substantially impact the properties of comb-like poly-\nmers. Scientists often use the dilute solution properties of these materials to quantify\ntheir architecture. As branch spacing decreases and branch length increases at a fixed\nmolecular mass, dilute solution properties such as the radius of gyration, intrinsic vis-\ncosity, and hydrodynamic radius typically decrease because the length of the backbone\ndecreases. However, this decrease is only partially driven by this change in backbone\nlength, even for relatively short branches. While many models focus on predicting the\n1\n\ndilute solution properties of these materials with fixed branch spacing, most comb-like\npolymers exhibit statistical branch spacing which leads to non-trivial changes in ex-\ncluded volume effects. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we show how changing\nthe distribution of branches from fixed to statistical and then to diblock affects the di-\nlute solution properties of a coarse-grained linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), a\ncanonical comb-like polymer, in 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene, a standard good solvent. This\napproach explicitly accounts for excluded volume interactions that were not included\nin prior theories. We extend our previous theoretical work to account for statistical\nbranch spacing and test prior renormalization group estimates of diblocks in good sol-\nvent to show that it is consistent with our numerical results. Our approach provides\na framework for a more quantitative understanding of chain architecture from dilute\nsolution properties, yielding better structure-property relationships.\nIntroduction\nComb-like polymers, linear polymers with linear side chains, have various applications, such\nas conductive textiles,1 paint,2 drug delivery3 and chemotherapy.4 One reason these polymers\nare attractive is that varying the length and spacing of the side chains can lead to substan-\ntial changes in properties. 5,6 A classic, industrially important example of this effect is linear\nlow-density polyethylene (LLDPE). As the side chains get longer, LLDPE impact strength,\nductility, and impact fatigue life increase. 7,8 As the density of side chains increases, i.e., the\naverage branch spacing decreases, melt temperature, crystallization temperature, and lamella\nthickness decrease precipitously.9 While the architecture of comb-like polymers is critical to\ntheir resulting properties, accessing their detailed structure can be challenging even with\nwell-known synthesis techniques. Thus, the development of better methods to probe this\nstructure is essential to making better materials and characterizing them accurately.\nOne way to interrogate the structure of polymers is to take a sample, dissolve it in a good\nsolvent, and then investigate its dilute solution properties, such as its radius of gyration (Rg),\n2\n\nintrinsic viscosity ([η]), and hydrodynamic radius (Rh). In a good solvent, these properties\nscale as\np =KpMνp (1)\nwhere M is the molar mass, νp is the scaling exponent of property p (=Rg, [η], or Rh) and\nKp is a prefactor. In the case of intrinsic viscosity, this function is known as the Kuhn-Mark-\nHouwink-Sakurada equation.10 We expect linear polymers to scale asνRg≈ 0.588,ν[η]≈ 0.7,\nand νRh≈ 0.6 in a good solvent. 11–13\nChain architecture can dramatically affect these properties. A standard method to quan-\ntify these changes is examining the contraction factor of propertyp (gp), the ratio of branched\nto linear dilute solution properties at the same mass. This representation enhances prop-\nerty changes resulting from the chain architecture, in this case branching. Specifically, we\nconsider\ngp = pb\npl\n(2)\nwhere the subscripts l and b denote whether we measure the property for the correspond-\ning/equivalent linear or branched polymers, respectively. This notation follows that of Dou-\nglas and coworkers, and we point out that most of the theoretical work on these quantities\ninvolves the assumption of Gaussian chains and the hydrodynamic preaveraging approxima-\ntion, making them somewhat unreliable.14,15 Moreover, the mass dependence of this equation\ndrops out if the scaling exponents ( νp) are the same for the branched and linear polymers.\nWhile it is widely observed that these factors are less than unity for many comb-like polymers\ndue to the increased linear density of the chain, the exact origin of this decrease remains\npoorly understood. 16–18 This lack of understanding hinders the mapping from dilute solution\nproperties to the underlying architecture of the comb-like macromolecule, thereby limiting\nthe use of this method for probing chain architecture.\nTheorists have previously proposed several useful scaling models to address this challenge.\nThese models often attempt to predict the polymer’s radius of gyration based on the Flory\n3\n\napproximation, which assumes strong hydrodynamic interactions and a linear scaling between\ndifferent measures of polymer size. These models imply scaling relationships in powers of the\nbranch length (L) and spacing (S), i.e.,LβLSβS. 19–22 These theories often distinguish between\nthe comb-like regime in which branches weakly interact of interest here and the bottlebrush\nregime (L≫ S) in which branches strongly interact. Recently, Pan and coworkers tested\nmany of these models experimentally, finding that Rg∼ (L/S)0.37. 23,24 Molecular dynamics\nsimulations20,25 have also proven valuable tools to test these theories.\nIn addition to the above theories, we previously introduced a semi-empirical model for\ncomb-like polymers with precise branch spacings (S) and lengths (L). We subsequently tested\nour model against molecular dynamics simulations. 26 This model accounts for changes in the\npersistence length from two effects. As with previous models, it suggests a scaling of the\nradius of gyration with increasing branch length but also incorporates short-ranged repulsion\nbetween the backbone and the branch directly into the model. Moreover, it uses empirical\nscaling relationships to predict intrinsic viscosity and the hydrodynamic radius from the\nradius of gyration.\nWhile these models offer predictions for the dilute solution properties of polymers, they\nassume fixed branch spacing or do not depend on the placement of branches along the\nbackbone. Although carefully designed experiments meet the condition of fixed branch\nspacing, 17 most industrial comb-like polymers, e.g., LLDPE, and many experimental ar-\nchitectures22,23,27 have side chains placed in an uncontrolled or statistical manner along\nthe backbone. To investigate whether branch placement changes dilute solution properties,\nThompson and Orski synthesized two sets of LLDPE, diblocks and statistical copolymers\nof LLDPE to investigate this effect further. 28 They synthesized the diblocks using a one-\npot sequential ring-opening metathesis polymerization of 1-butyl- trans-cyclooctene and 1,5-\ncis,cis-cyclooctadiene. When they compared these\ntwo polymer architectures at the same branch density, they exhibited substantially different\nintrinsic viscosities.\nOn a theoretical level, it is unsurprising that branch placement has a substantial effect on\nthe dilute solution properties of polymers. Though few have considered the dilute solution\nproperties of statistical copolymers, many have looked into the more tractable problem\nof diblocks. Mondescu and Muthukumar have developed an analytical theory for many\ndynamical properties of diblock copolymers in good solvents. 29 Douglas and Freed have\nconsidered a renormalization group description for the radius of gyration in a good solvent,30\nand their solution was consistent with earlier Monte Carlo simulation estimates by Tanaka\net al. 31 These results and recent experiments 28,32 suggest that the distribution of branches\nalong the polymer backbone plays a role in determining the dilute solution properties of a\ngiven polymer architecture.\nHere, we summarize our model for predicting dilute solution properties of comb-like\nmacromolecules with fixed branch spacing and length. 26 We build upon this work to design\na model for statistically placed branches similar to many industrial cases. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Extreme Size and Irradiance Dependence in High-Resolution Vat \nPhotopolymerization of Hydrogels \n \nRion J. Wendland*, Orion L. Kafka, Thomas J. Kolibaba, Callie I. Higgins, Grant Draper, Nick \nClinton, Raghuveer Lalitha Sridhar, Kalyan Vydiam, Daniel Backman, Aman Kaur, Matt Gelber, \nMatthew Bedell, Scott Turner, Jason P. Killgore* \n \nR.J. Wendland, O.L. Kafka, T.J. Kolibaba, C.I. Higgins, J.P. Killgore: Applied Chemicals and \nMaterials Division - National Institute of Standards & Technology, Boulder, CO USA \nG. Draper, N. Clinton, M. Gelber, S. Turner: 3D Systems, San Diego, CA USA \nR.L. Sridhar, K. Vydiam, D. Backman, A. Kaur, M. Bedell: United Therapeutics, Manchester, \nNH USA \n*Corresponding authors: rion.wendland@nist.gov, jason.killgore@nist.gov  \n \nKeywords \nVat photopolymerization, working curve, hydrogels, optical coherence tomography, bioprinting, \ndead zone, oxygen inhibition, cure depth \n \nAbstract \nVat photopolymerization is a high-resolution and high-throughput technology used in many \nbiomedical applications. However, achieving geometric precision in printed devices with \nfeatures spanning orders of magnitude in length scale is non-trivial. Here, a new characterization \ntool combining fast, high-resolution optical coherence tomography imaging with a high-powered \ndigital light processing projector enables real time measurements of photopolymer curing. The \ndirect, quantitative measurement of hydrogel working curves (the relationship between cure \ndepth and light exposure) shows that the critical energy for gelation (Ec) exhibits extreme size \ndependence, demanding a rethinking of gray-scaling light intensity for achieving predictable \nvoxel formation at high resolutions. This in situ method also enables measurement of size-\ndependent working curves and dead zone thicknesses using oxygen permeable window materials, \nwhich is impossible via ex situ methods. Generally, size sensitivity is amplified at low irradiance, \nhigh dye-loading, and in the presence of oxygen permeable windows. Despite the extreme size \nsensitivity, calibrating the light exposure to the size dependent Ec allows a 3x improvement in \nlayer-growth uniformity compared to a naïve approach. Overall, these results highlight the \nchallenges in high-resolution printing of hydrogels and provide a framework to measure and \naccount for size dependence. \n\n1. Introduction \nBioprinting is at the forefront of medical research, enabling breakthroughs in tissue \nengineering, regenerative medicine, and pharmaceutical screening.1–3 Many of the advantages \nenabled by bioprinting address the fabrication of tissue-like 3D structures, which more closely \nmimic the human body than traditional 2D cell cultures on plastic materials.4–6 One of the \nultimate goals of bioprinting remains the manufacturing of functional human organs, which \nwould significantly improve health outcomes and end the reliance on donor organs. An important \naspect of these functional organ systems is the size scale and resolution needed to mimic the \ninherent complex geometries displayed by these systems. For example, blood (arteries to \ncapillaries) and air (trachea to bronchioles) pathways can range from micrometers to centimeters \nin thickness and diameter.7,8 While the highest resolutions in additive manufacturing have been \nachieved with two-photon polymerization, the serial nature of the method typically limits total \npart size. Given the requirement to print relatively large scaffolds and organs while retaining \nmicron-scale fidelity, vat photopolymerization with digital light processing (DLP) or liquid \ncrystal display (LCD) technologies is a promising fabrication technique for bioprinting. By \nindividually addressing the pixels in the light engine, tens of millions of simultaneous reactions \ncan be controlled in a single layer. The size of the projection dictates the maximum lateral part \ndimensions, while the pixel size and pitch dictate theoretical resolution. Despite high theoretical \nhardware resolution (e.g., single micrometer projector resolution is commercially available), \nrealizing that resolution in a complex 3D bioprint demands optimization of material and process.  \nIn vat photopolymerization of plastic resins, numerous studies have highlighted the \ndependence of voxel formation kinetics on programmed feature size (i.e. the size of the feature in \nthe digital mask). Repeatedly, smaller features have been shown to cure slower than larger \nfeatures.9–13 Thus, the exposures that precisely produce small features will overcure large \nfeatures. The size dependence has been attributed to both light engine and resin characteristics. \nFor the light engine, pixels may be considered as individual gaussian emitters with spatially \nvarying intensity. When pixels are combined in a larger area, the tail from one gaussian adds to \nthe peaks of neighboring pixels, producing a higher effective irradiance.10 For the resin, size \ndependence could arise from increased diffusion of species into or out of the voxel, resulting in \nalteration of the polymerization reaction.12,14 Additionally, studies in plastic resins have \nhighlighted differences in curing kinetics based on light irradiance levels.14–19 This phenomenon \nhas been attributed to different rates of radical generation for different irradiances. Higher \nirradiances increase the rate of radical generation, which can increase the likelihood of radical \nterminations and decrease the ratio of propagation to termination rate.19–22 Previous studies have \nadjusted radiant exposure to account for light scattering effects (specifically with cell-laden \nresins) on printed resolution and fidelity of hydrogels.23,24 Here, we extend that approach to \nconsider size- and irradiance-dependent effects that must be considered in higher resolution \nprinting of hydrogel materials. \nTo date, size- and irradiance-dependence in plastic resins has largely been studied ex situ, \nusing plan view optical microscopy and measurement of cure depth Cd. Typical optical \nmicroscopy measurements have considered the lateral dimensions of a features in a single \n\nprinted layer relative to the dimensions programmed in the photomask.25,26 Cure depth \nmeasurements have revealed size dependence by comparing feature thickness for the same \nexposure, at different lateral feature size. The exposures can be cured into a comparatively deep \npool of resin, resulting in unbounded vertical growth of the layer. For cure depth measurements, \nthe thickness (and often sidewall profile) of a single layer printed feature is often determined via \nmicrometer, stylus profilometer, optical profilometer, or oblique microscopy.9,20,27 The resultant \ncure depth data can be considered directly, or interpreted via the Jacob’s working curve:  \n𝐶d = 𝐷p ln (𝐸0\n𝐸c\n) (1) \nwhere, Dp is the depth of light penetration corresponding to 1/e light absorption, E0 is the \nincident radiant exposure used to cure the measured feature, and Ec is the critical exposure \nrequired to achieve gelation at zero cure depth.28 For working curve measurements, the Cd \nmeasurements are made at a range of discrete E0 such that Dp and Ec can be determined by the \nslope and intercept of the semi-log plot, respectively. To date, Ec has been strongly revealing of \nsize dependence in plastics, while Dp shows more modest dependence. \nThough refinement of this method can produce highly reproducible data, it can be time \nand resource intensive. As such, recent efforts have been made to study photopolymerization \nreactions in situ.14,29–32 These real-time microscopy-based measurements have the potential to be \nhigher throughput, while also being capable of observing transient phenomena that are missed \nduring the interval from processing to characterization. While previously studied in plastic \nresins, optical microscopy techniques are uniquely suited for hydrogel resins, as we recently \ndemonstrated by exploring bulk hydrogel working curve measurements.33 Contact methods (such \nas micrometers) can impart significant deformation and be prone to moisture dependent \nproperties if performed ex situ, resulting in inaccurate working curves compared to non-contact, \noptical methods. Given the challenges and unknown size-effects associated with high-resolution \nhydrogel bioprinting, we introduce an in situ microscopy technique using optical coherence \ntomography (OCT) to measure size- and irradiance-dependence of hydrogels in a high-\nthroughput, high-resolution, and real-time manner. OCT is a noninvasive imaging technology \nthat uses galvo-scanning near-infrared low-coherence interferometry to detect optical interfaces \nthroughout a structure. In photopolymer and bioprinting applications, OCT has previously been \nused to measure ex situ cure depths of plastic and hydrogel resins,33,34 characterize surface \nroughness of dental prosthetics,35 perform 3D analysis of extrusion printed contructs,36,37 and \nvisualize resin flow rate in injection continuous liquid interface printing.38,39 \nIn this study, we develop a hybrid instrument combining a 5.4 µm resolution, high power \nprojector with a custom sample stage and OCT imaging system to enable real time visualization \nof voxel gelation in hydrogels. To enable visualization with OCT, we designed a hydrogel resin \nthat scatters significantly more infrared light upon gelation compared to unpolymerized material. \nAs such, feature cure depths versus radiant exposure (i.e., the working curve) can be measured in \na high-throughput, accurate manner (Figure 1). Using this system, we compare in situ hydrogel \nworking curves (and the subsequent Jacobs fit parameters) as a function of lateral boundary \nconditions (feature width wf and feature spacing sf) and light irradiance. We then investigate the \n\nsize dependencies under print relevant conditions including resin formulation (dye loading) and \nwindow material (oxygen permeable versus non-permeable). Lastly, we demonstrate that \ncalibrating the light exposure to the size dependent Ec in a single- and multi-layer printed part \nsignificantly improves the cure depth uniformity compared to a naïve, single exposure approach. \nOverall, these results demonstrate the capabilities of in situ photopolymerization measurements \nand establish the size dependencies of hydrogel materials, helping to overcome the challenges of \nhigh-resolution bioprinting.  \n \n \n \n\n\nFigure 1. Despite remarkable performance and response speed advance-\nments enabled by novel OMIECs, research has predominantly centered \non device metrics, often neglecting the broader requirements for \nreal-world applicability. To enable practical use of OECT-based bio-\nsignal monitoring devices, efforts must prioritize both long-term reli-\nability and high performance. Despite \nachieving high transconductance values exceeding 400 mS [3], a sig-\nnificant limitation of depletion-mode PEDOT:PSS is its imbalance in \ntransduction capability, restricting effective biosignal transduction to \nthe negative potential range. Recent advancements have demonstrated \nhigh μC* values exceeding 700 F cm 1 V 1 s 1, which was record-high \nmaterial characteristic that facilitates efficient charge transport and \nionic coupling, resulting in transconductance values of 6.1 mS, under-\nscoring the potential of n-type OMIECs for sensitive and efficient bio-\nsignal monitoring applications [7–9].\nHowever, developing biosignal recording devices based on n-type \nmaterials still remains challenging. The key characteristics essential for \ntheir successful application in real-world scenarios such as record-high \ntransconductance, superior stability, and skin-conformal stretchability \nare difficult to be simultaneously satisfied from a single active material. \nA primary obstacle in advancing n-type depletion-mode OMIECs is the \nenergetic position of their lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) \nlevels, which often lie near the oxygen reduction potential. This makes \nn-type materials highly vulnerable to oxidative degradation, severely \nlimiting their long-term operation in ionic aqueous solution [7,10,11]. \nAdditionally, channel materials must endure external environmental \nstresses, such as UV exposure or autoclaving, which are essential for \nmaintaining device cleanliness and sterility before attachment. Without \nproper sterilization, bacterial and microbial accumulation may pose \nsignificant health risks [5,12–14]. These processes are standard sterili-\nzation procedures applied to help remove bacteria and contaminants for \ndevices/gadgets that function in contact with human bodies, but many \norganic channel materials cannot endure these harsh conditions due to \ntheir weak intermolecular bonding, leading to degradation and \ncompromising stability. Furthermore, the dynamic, microstructured, \nand constantly changing surface of the skin demands materials that can \nachieve conformal adhesion. Skin motion and deformation can signifi-\ncantly affect the device performance, making it crucial to design mate-\nrials and devices that maintain reliable adhesion and prevent stress \nconcentration during mechanical deformation, thereby ensuring dura-\nbility under strain.\nIn this work, we present an ultraflexible 4-terminal vertical Corbino \nOECT (4-T vcOECT) featuring an n-doped poly(benzodifurandione) (n- \nPBDF) film, which is a highly conductive (~4038 S/cm) n-type polymer \n[15,16]. By capitalizing on our 4-T device structure [3], μC* value was \nmeasured to be 1787 F cm 1 V 1 s 1, yielding a gm of 374 mS in the \nvertically structured Corbino device. This configuration achieved cutoff \nfrequencies (fc) up to 1.2 kHz with negligible on-current variation after \n4000 on/off cycles. The device maintained both current and gm values \neven after 1000 cycles of repetitive tensile strain testing at a tight \nbending radius of 5 μm, which is attributed to the isotropic stress dis-\ntribution accommodating strains of up to 200 %. Additionally, the de-\nvices exhibited exceptional shelf-life stability, with gm values showing \nnegligible changes after 8 h under conditions of 85 % relative humidity, \nimmersion in aqueous electrolyte (0.1 M NaCl), and phosphate-buffered \nsaline (PBS). The devices also endured UV- and autoclave sterilization \nconditions, showing negligible performance changes. This stability was \nattributed to the low LUMO level of  4.94 eV. Notably, the 4-T vcOECT \nsuccessfully recorded electrocardiogram (ECG) signals at an operational \nvoltage of just 10 mV, delivering a signal-to-noise ratio of 38.1 dB over 7 \ndays. This achievement represents a significant step toward the practical \napplication of long-term biosignal monitoring devices using n-type \nOMIECs.\n2. Conversely, under positive potential, the \npolaronic peak diminished, and the neutral peaks recovered in the in-\ntensity, reflecting the subsequent oxidation of the n-PBDF film. This \nelectrochemical behavior demonstrates the reversible doping and \ndedoping capabilities of n-PBDF, validating its suitability as an active \nlayer for OECT devices.\nTo enhance charge and ion transport properties, the n-PBDF polymer \nwas incorporated into a vertical Corbino device structure (Figs. 1b and \n1c), forming a film on the planar (region I) and vertical (region II) \nchannel areas (Fig. 1d). The channel length and width were precisely \ncontrolled by the thickness of the parylene-C (PaC) layer between the \ntop and bottom metal electrodes and the perimeter of the via hole, \nrespectively. Orski*\nCiteThis:J.Am.Chem.Soc. 2025, 147, 46061−46074\n ReadOnline\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: Over 50% of plastic waste comes from a single class\nof polymers called polyolefins. Most recycling strategies fail to\npreserve the broad molecular mass distribution of these polyolefins,\nfrom which they derive their unique combination of processability\nand mechanical strength. Here, we show that incorporation of\nurethane-based dynamic bonds into high-density polyethylene\n(HDPE) can circumvent this issue, by strengthening the\namorphous phase through interchain supramolecular interactions,\nas opposed to traditional entanglements from high molecular mass\nchains. We show that many key properties of these dynamic HDPE\npolymers, including percent crystallinity, melting temperature,\nlamellae and amorphous thicknesses, and bond association, are\ndetermined by the distribution of bond-to-bond spacings along the chain backbone and are predicted using polymer physics theories.\nMoreover, we find that a mixed backbone HDPE dynamic polymer exhibits mechanical properties that exceed HDPE and approach\nthe strain-hardening behavior seen in ultrahigh molecular weight polyethylene along with a unique display of long-range\nsupramolecular order that persists in the melt state. This work illuminates key principles governing how the placement of dynamic\nbonds influences bulk material properties and provides a framework for toughening semicrystalline polymers and designing chemical\nrecycling processes based on controlling bond-spacing distributions.\n■INTRODUCTION\nThe use of polyolefin thermoplastics within the US, including\nhigh-density polyethylene (HDPE), low-density polyethylene\n(LDPE), linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE), and\npolypropylene (PP) resulted in about 15,000 U.S. tons (or\n∼30 million pounds)collected for recycling in 2018 and 22,000\nU.S. tons (or ∼43.2 million pounds) discarded.1 This large\namount of discarded plastic, including losses between collection\nand recycling, has a significant impact in community waste\nmanagement, economic opportunity losses, and the environ-\nment.2−5 Even as efforts to improve collection, sortation, and\nmechanical recycling of polyolefins are emphasized, multiple\ntechnological and engineering approaches are needed to address\nthe large scale of polyolefin waste, which remain highly desirable\nmaterials due to their chemical resistance and excellent\nmechanical and barrier properties.\nChemical recycling can address many of the limitations of\ndirect mechanical recycling, particularly heterogeneous mixtures\nthat may result in phase separation and inferior mechanical\nproperties, previously recycled resins, undesired cross-linking\nand chain scission during reprocessing, and separation and\npurification challenges. Different approaches have been\ninvestigated to chemically recycle plastic waste including:\nconversion back to monomers and repolymerization, 6−9\nadditives into virgin plastics to introduce cleavable groups e.g.,\nesters, alkenes, or thionolactones into the backbone,10−12\ndeconstruction to oils and other products,13−15 and upcycling\nby direct functionalization or oligomerization and recombina-\ntion into mechanically recyclable products.16−22 The latter\napproach, in which polyolefin waste is upcycled into a new\nproduct that can then be mechanically recycled, is promising\nsince it works for both existing and future waste and also reduces\nthe total energy use and carbon footprint of the process.23,24\nNonetheless, this upcycling approach is constrained by a\nsignificant limitation−chain scission during reprocessing leads\nto selective loss of high molar mass chains, producing inferior\nmechanical properties after recycling.25 Moreover, any mecha-\nnism that reduces polyolefin chains into shorter oligomers,\nthrough processes such as dehydrogenation and cross meta-\nthesis,17,26 and then repolymerizes them with degradable units\nwill remove the highest molecular mass chains (Figure 1a).\nReceived: August 6, 2025\nRevised: October 25, 2025\nAccepted: October 27, 2025\nPublished: December 4, 2025\nArticlepubs.acs.org/JACS\nNot subject to U.S. Copyright. Such relationships are needed to properly tune bulk\nproperties and, ideally, to be able to predict them a priori.\nQuantifying tolerance for functional group integration and the\ndistribution of functional groups on resultant polymer proper-\nties (mechanical and in the melt) can help streamline research\nfocus areas and facilitate shorter paths to commercial adaptation.\nThis will allow these new methods to be strategically targeted to\nfill in gaps in expanding an efficient materials economy, where\nintegrated approaches can guide creative, functional chemistries\ninto upcycling polyolefins into high value applications, integrate\nwith industrial infrastructure, and facilitate rapid commercializa-\ntion.\nHere, we demonstrate a promising option based on the\nincorporation of dynamic bonds into HDPE (Figure 1a). [{"suffix": "", "text": "Ferroelectricity\nFerroelectricity is a property observed in certain materials characterized by the presence of a spontaneous electric\npolarization without the presence of an electric field, much like how ferromagnetism is characterized by a spontaneous,\npermanent magnetic field. A subclass of piezoelectric and pyroelectric materials, ferroelectric materials are\nnoncentrosymmetric crystals, where some atoms in the unit cell are misplaced to create a permanent electric dipole due\nto the imbalances observed in the distribution of electric charge. Barium titanate (BaTiO ), a common ferroelectric\nmaterial with the perovskite crystal structure, portrays this property by displacing the titanium ion at body center\n0.05Å along the +b direction and the oxygen atoms 0.08Å in the -b direction, creating a slight dipole moment (figure 1).\nThis displacement, coupled with the relatively small size of the Ti  ion, makes it difficult for the titanium ion to bond\nwith all of the oxygen ions.\nFigure : : Crystal structure of barium titanate below its Curie temperature. Green circles represent Ba2+ ions, blue\ncircles O2- ions, and the red circle represents the Ti4+ ion.\nCrystal Structure and Material Preparation\nFerroelectricity is a displacive phenomenon where ions within the unit cell are placed asymmetrically, creating dipole\nmoments. These asymmetries may form in two different ways, either displacively or by order-disorder. Ferroelectrics\nwith the perovskite crystal structure, like barium titanate (BaTiO ) and lead titanate (PbTiO ), are commonly\ndisplacive-type ferroelectrics, where at temperatures below the Curie temperature, ions are displaced slightly from\nequilibrium to create an asymmetry in the electron population densities, which leads to the permanent dipole moment.\nIn order-disorder ferroelectrics, like NaNO , the dipoles are present at all temperatures, but are randomly oriented\nabove the Curie temperature. The dipoles align after the temperature is brought below the threshold.\nFigure : a & 2b: Representations of the polar axes of a ferromagnetic material before (left) and after (right) heat\ntreatment under an applied field.\nWhile the individual unit cells of a ferroelectric material possess their own dipole moment, without the presence of an\nexternal electric field these moments do not align with each other to produce any long-range symmetry (figure 2a).\nWithin individual grains the polar axes are aligned but across the bulk of the sample there is no net polarization. At\nsufficiently high temperatures for the grains to break down, and in the presence of an electric field, the polar axes may\nrealign to match the field. If the material is cooled under this field, the polar axes remain aligned, thus forming a\nsubstance that has an observable, spontaneous electric dipole (figure 2b). In the case of barium titanate, the titanium ion\nis displaced in the direction of the electric field and the oxygen ions displaced against it, creating the dipole. With\nsubsequent inputs of alternating electric fields, the dipoles realign by shifting the titanium ion to the other side of the\nunit cell.\n3\n4+\n3 3\n3\n9/30/26, 2:10 PM Ferroelectricity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Ferroelectricity 1/3\n\nProperties\nFerroelectricity is characterized by the presence of a spontaneous electric dipole while not exposed to an external\nelectric field, much like how ferromagnetism is characterized by a spontaneous magnetic dipole. Above a certain\ntemperature, called the Curie temperature (T ), ferroelectric materials lose this polarization and behave like\nparamagnetic or diamagnetic materials. At the Curie temperature, the energy within the crystal allows the ions to\narrange themselves in a stable equilibrium, eliminating the polarization caused by the displacement of one or more\nions.\nFigure : : The hysteretic relationship between applied electric field and ferroelectric polarization. At the origin, the\nferroelectric material is unpolarized and in a zero field. Applying a positive E-field polarizes it positively until its\npolarity changes linearly with applied field. Applying the reverse field does not unpolarize the ferroelectric until it\nreaches a certain magnitude, where the left-side of the loop reaches P=0. (source: commons.wikimedia.org)\nThe change in polarity of ferroelectrics with an applied electric field is observed to follow a simple hysteresis loop\n(figure 3). If the crystal structure of a ferroelectric has been broken down in high heat and not in the presence of an\nelectric field., it is unpolarized as seen in the origin of figure 2. With an applied field, the polarization quickly\napproaches a point where the polarization is linearly proportional to the applied electric field. If an opposite electric\nfield is applied, the polarity does not change significantly until the field reaches a relatively large magnitude, and the\npolarity of the ferroelectric reverses and levels off. This loop can be repeated numerous times to alter the polarity of the\nferroelectric, often to the order of 10 cycles depending on the material.\nThe polarization of ferroelectrics is a non-volatile property once the polarization is set. External electric fields are\nunable to change the polarization direction unless the magnitude of the field reaches the required threshold, and\nmagnetic fields have negligible effects on the electronic polarization observed.\nApplications\nMany application of ferroelectric materials utilize the polarization reversal, or switching effect, that the materials\nexperience when exposed to powerful electric fields. This switching effect is utilized in digital memory applications, as\nreversing the polarity of the material allows for the creation of 0 and 1 bits in computing. As the polarization of\nferroelectrics is nonvolatile and does not require extra input to remain polarized, ferroelectrics possess an advantage\nover traditional semiconductors when it comes to digital storage. Dielectric random access memory (DRAM) in a\ncomputer relies on electricity to maintain its storage, and unexpected shutdowns or power outages cause loss of\ninformation, allowing the short-term memory modules in computer to behave like back-up long-term memory banks.\nThis property also makes ferroelectrics ideal for electronic access cards, like keycards or transit cards, as their polarized\nstates are not disrupted by magnetic fields and do not decay over time. The ability to maintain its polarization without\noutside input also means ferroelectric random access memory (FeRAM) only requires energy when it is read or written,\nwhile DRAM requires a constant energy input to maintain the information stored. The energy-saving possibilities of\nFeRAM are therefor highly researched and a leading reason for the development of more efficient FeRAM assemblies.\nThe hysteretic behavior of the polarization of ferroelectrics also makes them very good candidates for alternatives to\ndielectrics in capacitors. As the polarization of ferroelectrics can reach very high levels, as well as the possibility of\ntuning the strength of the dipole according to the strength of the input electric field. As dielectric capacitors cannot be\ntuned like ferroelectric capacitors, the latter are capable of being made much smaller in comparison to the former.\nQuestions\n1. At T>T , a certain ferroelectric material displays no ferroelectric properties, and through sensitive imaging\ntechniques, it is determined that the material displays a perfect perovskite crystal structure. When T<T , imaging\nreveals that the ions within the crystal have shifted slightly and no longer indicate a perfect perovskite crystal, as the\nions at body-center have shifted slightly towards individual sides of the unit cells. What kind of ferroelectric phase\ntransformation is observed in this material?\n2. You have grown a BaTiO  crystal and apply an electric field to it in order to produce a net dipole. However, when\nyou try to measure the moment there is nothing to be seen. Assuming that your measurement equipment is working\nproperly, what might be the issue with your sample and how might you go about fixing it?\n3. A brand new ferroelectric has just recently been discovered and you are tasked with determining its viability as a\nnew material to make FeRAM out of. You develop a prototype device and subject it to conditions (rate of electric\nCurie\n16 \nC\nC\n3\n9/30/26, 2:10 PM Ferroelectricity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Ferroelectricity 2/3\n\ninput, temperature) that RAM modules often experience in computers. The grains within the sample may not have their polar axes aligned, so attempts to polarize it are not effective.\nIncreasing the temperature, exposing the substance to an electric field, and then cooling it while in the field will\nalign the polar axes to a certain degree, allowing them to produce a net electric dipole moment.\n3. [1,2]\nChemical doping and dedoping oﬀer ef-\nfective solutions for doping level control,\nwhich can tailor the performance of con-\njugated polymers for speciﬁc applications\nto achieve optimal performance in vari-\nous organic devices.[3–5] Highly doped con-\nducting polymers ﬁnd their application as\ntransparent conductors in optical electron-\nics due to their high electrical conductiv-\nity and transparency in the visible wave-\nlength region.[6,7] However, a high doping\nlevel is not always desirable in all types\nof applications. For example, in solar cells,\nthe doping level of conducting polymer\ncharge transport layers needs to be prop-\nerlytunedtoalignwiththeenergeticsofthe\nadjacent layers to facilitate eﬃcient charge\ntransport.[8,9] In organic thermoelectrics,\nthe ﬁgure of merit, power factor, is de-\ntermined by both the Seebeck coeﬃcient\nand electrical conductivity, necessitating an optimized doping\nlevel to maximize device performance.[10,11] Furthermore, un-\ndopedconjugatedpolymersarepreferredinorganicelectrochem-\nicaltransistors(OECTs)tolowerenergyconsumptionduringde-\nvice operation.[12–14] Whilecontrollingthedopinelevel ofp-type\npolymers, such as poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) doped with\npoly(styrenesulfonate)(PEDOT:PSS),hasbeenextensivelystud-\nied, developing n-type conducting polymer systems with tun-\nable doping levels remains challenging.[15,16] Most reported n-\ntypeconductingpolymerssuﬀerfromlowperformanceandlim-\nitedstability.[17]\nThe recent discovery of n-doped Poly (3,7-dihydrobenzo[1,2-\nb:4,5-b′]difuran-2,6-dione) (poly(benzodifurandione), n-PBDF)\nhas presented exciting opportunities in the ﬁeld of printed elec-\ntronics and related areas. In the synthesis of PBDF, the lowest\nunoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) level allows forin-situ n-\ndoping and charge compensation by protons, eliminating the\nneed for additional doping steps.[18,19] This feature makes the\nn-PBDF solution processable, stable under ambient conditions,\nAdv. Initially, n-PBDF is naturally n-\ndoped (reduced) after synthesis. The dedoping process involves\nextractingelectronsfromn-PBDFusingdedopants.Variousoxi-\ndants were evaluated for their ability to induce the dedoping re-\naction. If it is \nequal, then the trial wavefunction must coincide with the ground state eigenfunction of the \nSchrödinger equation, and the expectation value of the energy will obviously be the ground \nstate eigenvalue. \nThe variational principle has both practical and conceptual consequences; e.g. it \nallows us to find good approximate solutions to problems we would not be able to solve \nexactly if formulated as a differential equation. It also allows us to study most many-electron \nproblems using trial wavefunctions that are simple  linear combinations of atomic orbitals. It \nactually provides a justification for the concept of “hybridization” of atomic orbitals, and allows \nto explore ground and excited states of molecules and solids as simple linear combinations of \natomic orbitals (LCAO for molecules, “tight-binding” for solids). \nFor this problem we’ll go back to the hydrogen atom, and will consider a trial \nwavefunction Ψ= C exp (−αr ) ; different values of α  will correspond to different shapes of α \nΨ  (i.e. different decays towards large r). α can be considered a “tunable handle” that allows α \nus to explore all possible wavefunctions in a class (here, that of simple decaying exponentials \nas a function of the polar coordinate r). Note that the only role of the multiplicative constant C \nis to “normalize” the solution, so that the integral over all space of the square modulus of the \nwavefunction is equal to 1 (i.e. we are 100% certain to find an electron somewhere). Franaszek, P. Piliptchak and K. S. Saidi \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, USA  \nE-mail: marek@nist.gov \n \n \nSummary: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) can segment novel, previously unseen objects from 2D images. This \ncapability is especially important in automated bin picking applications, where low-volume and high-variability scenarios are \ncommon. When prompted by a point, SAM outputs three masks with varying confidence scores. Prior research indicates that \nSAM's performance depends on the type of parts in a bin: for parts that are visually decomposable into subcomponents, \ncorrectly segmented masks are more often associated with a medium confidence score. Conversely, for parts that are not readily \nvisually decomposable into subcomponents, correct masks are typically associated with the highest confidence score. We \ninvestigated the transition from visually decomposable to non-decomposable part categories in simulation by using  \ncomputer-aided design (CAD) models with gradually altered geometric features. Differences in the dimensions of these \ngeometric features cause corresponding differences in grayscale images. We found that this transition occurs within a relatively \nnarrow range of feature modifications and image intensities. This demonstrates the strong sensitivity of SAM to the specific \ntypes of parts within a bin. Consequently, prior knowledge of a part's complexity can be leveraged to better tune the processing \nof SAM's output. \n \nKeywords: Foundation models, Segment anything model, Robotic bin picking. \n \n \n1. Introduction \n \nThe successful deployment of bin picking systems \nto automate manufacturing tasks, such as assembly or \nkitting, depends strongly on vision system \nperformance. The vision system must segment the \nacquired depth images to determine the six degree -of-\nfreedom (6DoF) pose of individual parts, enabling the \nintegrated robot to execute tasks successfully. \nAccurate instance segmentation of unorganized \npiles of manufacturing parts remains especially \nchallenging. While early segmentation algorithms \nrequired model retraining for different parts [1], the \nemergence of foundation models such as the Segment \nAnything Model (SAM) has made retraining for novel \nparts almost obsolete [2]. When prompted by a point \nin a query image or a bounding box, SAM outputs \nthree binary segmentation masks with distinct \nconfidence scores. \nContinued research on prompts has led to the \nadoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), which \nallow the use of text -based prompts to obtain \nsegmentation masks for specified objects [3 -5]. These \nnew Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) \ntechniques have yielded promising results for semantic \nsegmentation when tested on Common Objects in \nContext (COCO) -style databases [6]. However, \nextensive testing on images of industrial parts \nrandomly filling a bin still needs to be conducted. \nAnother kind of prompt in the form of a  \ncomputer-aided design (CAD) model was recently \nproposed [7]. It is especially useful for bin picking \napplications where CAD models of the parts filling the \nbins are usually available. A modified version of SAM \n(SAM3) [5] was trained on synthetic images cre ated \nwith the NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulator [8], which was \nused to build multi -object scenes utilizing CAD \nmodels from the ABC dataset of industrial parts [9]. It \nwas tested on two standard industrial benchmark \ndatasets, T -LESS and ITODD, which do not contain \nmany heavy clutter scenes typical of bin picking \napplications [10, 11]. \nCurrently, using point prompts in depth images \nremains the easiest way to obtain instance \nsegmentation masks. To maximize the efficiency of \nrobotic path planning, the vision system should \nprovide as many correct masks as possible, prompted \nfrom points scat tered across the entire image area. \nPrevious work demonstrated that SAM's performance \ndepends heavily on the type of parts in the bin [12]. For \nparts that are visually decomposable into \nsubcomponents (as in Fig. 1(a)), accurate masks from \nSAM’s multi-mask output were most often associated \nwith the medium (second -highest) confidence score. \nFor parts lacking obvious subcomponents (as in  \nFig. 1(b)), accurate masks typically correlated with the \nhighest confidence score. \n \n \n   \n(a)                         (b) \n \nFig. 1. Examples of two types of parts: a) visually \ndecomposable into subcomponents (drawn with different \ncolors); b) not readily decomposable into subcomponents. \n \n \nPreviously, the distinction between the two types \nof parts was based on subjective, unquantifiable \n\n\nXII International Conference on Sensors and Electronic Instrumentation Advances (SEIA' 2026)  \n30 September – 2 October 2026, Granada, Spain \n9 \nevaluation. In this study, a more objective metric is \nformulated. We systematically investigate how SAM's \nperformance shifts during the transition from one type \nof part to another by gradually altering the geometric \nfeatures of the part within a simulated bin. Our results \nsuggest that this transition occurs over a relatively \nnarrow range of geometric changes. Those changes \nresult in corresponding changes in the 8 -bit grayscale \nintensity of depth images. We found that two compact, \nadjacent regions on a depth  image whose intensities \ndiffer by less than 15 will most likely be segmented as \none region that stretches over both adjacent areas. \nThus, a part represented in a depth image as a patch \nwhere no compact subregions can be identified with \nintensity differences greater than ∆𝐼 =  15, should be \nclassified as non-decomposable part. \nPatches consisting of subregions with intensity \ndifferences much larger ( ∆𝐼 ≫ 15) correspond to \ndecomposable parts for which binary masks associated \nwith the medium score will be more accurate. Our \nresults reveal a specific range of differences in \ngeometric features, along with a corresponding range \nof intensities in a grayscale image , where no single \nstrategy (strongest vs. medium score mask) is \npreferred. In such mixed regions, to maximize the \nnumber of correctly segmented parts in a bin, masks \nassociated with both the strongest and medium \nconfidence scores may need to be analyzed. \nThus, prior knowledge of a part's dimensions and \nshape can be utilized to optimize the processing of \nSAM's output, thereby improving overall bin picking \nsystem performance. \n \n \n2.
