The reactive mono-\nmers generally have low viscosity and can be readily infused\ninto a network of stiﬀ, high-strength fibers or inorganic filler\nparticles and then thermally cross-linked around the fillers to\ncreate a polymer matrix composite. One of the most widely\nutilized strategies in polymer matrix composites is to combine\nthermosetting epoxy resins with high strength carbon fibers to\nrealize high-strength, light-weight systems. Carbon fiber-epoxy\ncomposites are increasingly used in a range of commercial and\nmilitary applications related to buildings and construction,\ntransportation and vehicles, aerospace, athletics, and protective\nequipment. In many of these applications, it is desirable to\nhave the composite maintain its performance over a wide range\nof temperatures, extending from the deeply sub-ambient to\ntemperatures that can exceed 200 1C. One of the most impor-\ntant properties for a structural composite material is mechan-\nical toughness. Retaining toughness across such a broad\ntemperature range is a challenge for most epoxy resins. Lower\nTg epoxy formulations that oﬀer toughness under ambient\nconditions often become embrittled at sub-ambient tempera-\ntures. High Tg epoxy formulations that oﬀer strength and\nthermal stability unfortunately tend to be brittle and lead to\npoor fracture resistance of the resulting composite. This lack of\ntoughness becomes especially problematic at the ultra-high\nrates of deformation that are associated with ballistic impacts.\nOver the past decade, several studies have focused on quanti-\nfying the level of energy dissipation in a wide range of cross-\nlinked thermoset network polymers under ballistic impact con-\nditions across an extreme range of temperatures.1–8 These studies\nhave mostly focused on the neat resin, without fibers or fillers, to\ndevelop a molecular understanding of what gives rise to energy\ndissipation, and therefore toughness, at the rates of deformation\nthat are relevant for ballistics,i.e., strain rates in excess of 106 s/C01.\nThe ability of an epoxy formulation to dissipate energy at these\nballistic rates is operationally defined by making multiple panels\nof the same material and shooting identical projectiles, each at a\nfresh panel, with increasing incident velocities until the point at\nwhich 50% of the panels are penetrated by the projectile. This\ncritical velocity is defined as V50.B yk n o w i n gt h em a s so ft h e\nprojectile and V50, one can define KE 50 as the ballistic impact\nresistance, the kinetic energy of a projectile needed to penetrate\n50% of the panels. KE50 is an operationally defined performance\nmetric relevant to ballistic impact resistance, but not a true\nmeasurement energy dissipation or material toughness.\nThis manuscript focuses on the mechanisms that dissipate\nenergy and contribute to the toughness of cross-linked thermo-\nset glasses. For decades it has been appreciated that relaxations\nin the glassy state are important for mechanical toughness in\npolymers, i.e., that having an active mechanical relaxation is\nimportant for energy dissipation. 9–12 Seminal works by Boyce,\nusing a variety of impact testing configurations that push the\ndeformation rates into the sub-ballistic regime (strain rates\nnominally up 10 4 s/C01) have shown that when the rate of\nmechanical deformation exceeds the characteristic relaxation\ntime of the sub- Tg relaxation (often called the b relaxation) in\nthe polymer glass, the stiffness and yield strength of the\nmaterial goes up. 13–15 The interpretation is that when you\ndeactivate the energy dissipation mechanism by not giving\nthe material enough time to respond to the impulse, the glass\nbecomes stiffer but also more brittle. However, there is still a\ndisparity between the time and length scales of the molecular\nmechanisms that dissipate energy under ballistic rates of\ndeformation, in excess of 10 6 s/C01, and the characterization\ntechniques that are used to quantify the relevant relaxations.\nAs a general statement, we still cannot predict the ballistic\nresponse of glassy polymers from our current knowledge of\npolymer relaxations.\nWe recently initiated an eﬀort to close this gap by exploring\ncorrelations between the level of anharmonicity in the atomic\nmean square displacement, hu2iexcess, of polymer glasses as\nquantified by incoherent neutron scattering and their corres-\nponding toughness.16 Across a homologous series of polycarbo-\nnates (PCs) with systematic variations in their toughness, we\nobserved a strong correlation between hu2iexcess and the quasi-\nstatic impact strength. Our assertion was that the large ‘‘excess’’\nmean-square atomic displacements measured in the tough PCs,\nreflecting collective molecular relaxations on the sub-ns time-\nscale, are the signature of incipient dissipative relaxations. How-\never, these measurements based on a Debye–Waller analysis of\nthe elastic incoherent neutron scattering intensities did not\nprecisely resolve the timescale of the motions, beyond identifying\nthat they were faster than the approximately 1 ns resolution of the\nspectrometer. In a second manuscript, 17 we quantified the full\nenergy spectra of the scattered neutrons to better define the\ndynamical processes and relevant time scales that underpin these\nobserved motions in the quiescent glass. These measurements\nwere performed as a function of temperature (T)f r o md e e pi nt h e\nglassy state to well above room T, traversing the brittle-to-ductile\ntransition (BDT) of a tough PC glass. We observed that the onset\nof nonlinear anharmonic fluctuations as quantified by hu2iexcess\n(relative to the low T harmonic vibrations that contribute to an\nincrease of hu2i that evolves linearly with T) coincides with the\nemergence of a relaxation process with a characteristic time scale\nof t E 3 ps that starts to dominate the QENS spectra. This is the\ntypical order of magnitude for the fast beta relaxation time that is\nseen in neutron scattering. 19,20 The onset of this relaxation\ncoincided with the BDT temperature, suggesting that many-\natom, collective relaxations underpin macroscopic toughness.\nIn our previous publication, we estimated that the size of these\ncollective motions was on the order of (5 to 20) nm 3, and noted\nthese dimensions were on par with the activation volume of\nyielding in typical polymer glasses.17\nWith respect to our goal to develop a general understanding\nof the ballistic impact resistance in polymer glasses, the study\nhere contains two important extensions from our previous\npublications on correlating quasielastic neutron scattering with\nmechanical properties. The standardization\napproach puts ﬂow cytometric data from different instrument platforms on the\nstandardized ERF scale.\nDiscussion: To overcome the challenge of instrument-driven variability, this ILS\nutilizes a human TBMNK cell assay to establish and validate a new standardization\nframework. By reporting results in SI-traceable units, this work demonstrates that\ncomparable measurements of viable, non-apoptotic TBMNK subsets are\nachievable across different cytometer s. Over the past few years, the\ntechnology has evolved from a gold standard method for CD4 +\nlymphocyte counting for monitoring of HIV/AIDS ( 1) and for\nCD34+ cell counting for hematopoietic stem cell transplant ( 2), a\ncritical tool for diagnosing and classifying various types of blood\ncancers ( 3, 4) and hematological and autoimmune diseases ( 5), to\nan essential technique for characterizing advanced live cell-based\ndrugs (6) with the ability to measure up to 50 markers at the single\ncell level ( 7).\nThe 2024 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Guidance\nDocument on Considerations for the Development of Chimeric\nAntigen Receptor (CAR) T Cell Products ( 8) recognizes ﬂow\ncytometry as a critical analytical tool for cell viability, identity,\npurity, and potency. FDA recommends that the initial investiga-\ntional new drug (IND) submission includes detailed information on\nﬂow cytometric assays, such as description of assay, instrument\ncalibration and quality control (QC), assay controls, assay standard\noperating procedure (SOP), antibody titration, direct detection of\nCAR, and comprehensive assay validation for lot release to support\nlicensure. These recommendations have drastically increased the\nneed for high quality, robust, and validated ﬂow cytometric assays.\nDespite many efforts toward ﬂow cytometry instrument cali-\nbration and standardization as well as assay harmonization ( 9, 10),\nchallenges remain due to the complexity of the technology and the\nlack of reference standards, and particularly with respect to mea-\nsurement conﬁdence and comparability from different instruments,\nsites and over time. These challenges hinder consistent critical\ndecision-making in research, manufacturing, and clinical applica-\ntions. Furthermore, high-quality, well-annotated ﬂow cytometric\ndatasets are sparse in the public domain which limits the develop-\nment of arti ﬁcial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML)\napproaches. It also impedes integration of ﬂow cytometry datasets\nwith omics datasets to support system biology approaches for\nprecision medicine.\nTo address these unmet challenges, NIST launched the Flow\nCytometry Standards Consortium (FCSC) ( 11) in 2020 to work\nwith key stakeholders to jointly develop standards and\nmeasurement solutions to support the broad adoption of quantita-\ntive ﬂow cytometry technologies. At present, ﬁve working groups\n(WGs) are working to advance 1) instrument calibration and\nstandardization, 2) cytometric assay standardization, 3) centralized\ndata analysis, 4) measurement assurance issue on various gene\ndelivery systems, and 5) AI/ML approaches to ﬂow cytome-\ntry applications.\nThis manuscript presents the ﬁndings of the ﬁrst\ninterlaboratory study (ILS) led by Working Group 2 (WG2) to\nstandardize cell count and health assays, utilizing a ﬂow cytometry-\nbased T/B/Monocyte/Natural Killer (TBMNK) as the primary\nmodel ( Figure 1 ). Four objectives were set for the ILS: 1) to\ndesign the assay with ﬁxed variables including test samples, assay\npanel, and instrument control materials, 2) to develop common\nstudy SOPs that will enable result comparability in standardized\nunits across instrument platforms, 3) to generate data for evaluating\nsuitability of test materials as potential future reference standards,\nand 4) to produce high-quality dataset for data analysis studies to\nidentify reference data standard. Here, we present a comparative\nanalysis of the data produced and subsequently analyzed by\nparticipants following provided SOPs (Supplemental documents).\nThe site-reported manual analysis results on percentages of cell\nsubsets are compared with those from centralized automated data\nanalysis (CDA) procedures conducted by WG3 (Working Group 3)\nthat is ongoing to demonstrate approaches to standardizing cell\npopulation identiﬁcation from cross-platform ﬂow cytometry data.\nExpected ILS outputs include assay standardization approach,\nSOPs, and reference dataset.\n2 Methods\n2.1 Study designs\nThis study used a 10-marker, 8-color TBMNK cell assay\nincluding viability and apoptosis markers. System Classification (open, closed, isolated, adiabatic): state your assumptions! \n1.\t What kind of system is a well-insulated thermos filled with hot tea and ice cubes? \nWhat happens to the energy distribution of the material in the thermos over time? \nWhat happens to the entropy? \nIsolated system, with an energy distribution that flattens out over time (due to change \nfrom multi-phase to single-phase system), while entropy increases. \n1.\t What kind of system is a greenhouse? What category of energy is relevant? \nClosed, assuming a sealed greenhouse. Specifically, heat is exchanged (not work). \n1.\t What type of system is a balloon filled with helium? How would you describe its \nwalls? \nOpen.  Gas exchange goes on over time (so the balloon sinks), and it is theoretically \npossible that the gases may carry heat; this is because the walls are semi-permeable. \n1.\t What type of system is a hollow ball made of a thick but flexible rubber? \nIf we can imagine the object above, it is an adiabatic system. Mechanical work may \nbe performed by pressing on the ball, but heat cannot travel through the insulating \nrubber. Also note that this system is closed to matter. \n1.\t What type of system is the earth? \nThe earth is approximately a closed system, assuming transfer of matter with the \nuniverse is fairly negligible, whereas the energy term is certainly large. \n\nPart II. Thermodynamic Processes. \n1.\t Explain the differences between a reversible and irreversible gas expansion. \nImagine a process for each (real or idealized). For the reversible process, the piston would move very slowly \nand be frictionless, while for the irreversible process the piston would move quickly \nand experience friction. Differences between the processes are summarized below: \nReversible\t Irreversible \nExactly reverse process is possible. One-way process only. \nSystem at (or infinitesimally near) System may be far from equilibrium, but \nequilibrium at all times (t). will reach equilibrium at long t (final state). \nTD variables (P, V) change slowly. TD variables may change quickly, even as \n(Infinitesimally-slowly moving piston.) immediate step-changes.\nNo dissipative processes (e.g., friction). Energy ‘loss’ to surroundings is typical.\nNo permanent change in surroundings Causes permanent change in universe –\nor system – may return to initial state. including entropy increase.\nNote: many of these differences are inter-related. \n2.\t  Give an example of a natural process that happens spontaneously. Is it obvious \nhow entropy increases in this system? What dissipative process may be at play? \nConsider the bouncing ball discussed in class and in the supplementary reading. \nThermal energy is dissipated through friction and sound waves, and increases the \nentropy of the universe by this random thermal motion."}]

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Thermoelectrics\nThermoelectrics (TEs) are materials that convert heat to electricity via the Seebeck effect. This unique ability of TEs is\ndependent upon electronic and thermal properties. The dimensionless figure of merit (zT) is used to quantify TE\nperformance, and is related to the conversion efficiency (η). TEs optimizing energy conversion are currently used in\nradioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) to generate electricity for spacecraft and other inaccessible power\nsystems. As Figure 1 shows, TE generators consist of the series of n-type and p-type materials bridging the gap between\na heat source and heat sink to create a current.\nMaterial Properties\nThe performance of TEs is related to their Seebeck coefficient, electrical conductivity, and thermal conductivity. The\nSeebeck coefficient relates change in voltage to change in temperature, and is given by the equation:\nwhere  is the Boltzmann constant,  is the elementary charge of an electron, and  is the Fermi energy at 0K.\nThe electrical conductivity σ of materials is given by the Drude conductivity equation:\nWhere n is the concentration of charge carriers and μ is the drift mobility of charge carriers. As  approaches infinity,  approaches the Carnot efficiency (i.e., the thermodynamic efficiency limit) of a\nreversible process.\nWhile the Carnot efficiency is a theoretical upper limit of TE performance, complications arising from interrelated\nproperties affecting zT obstruct TE optimization. Semiconductor materials are typically used as TEs because the\nelectronic properties of semiconductors can be manipulated easily. In particular, the carrier concentration and Fermi\nenergy of bulk semiconductors can be adjusted with doping to maximize electrical conductivity and the Seebeck\ncoefficient. Semiconductors also have lower thermal conductivity than metals. Because the Seebeck coefficient and zT\nare proportional to temperature and  is proportional to the Seebeck coefficient squared, higher temperatures result in\nhigher . Temperature’s proportionality to electron thermal conductivity and inverse proportionality to electrical\nconductivity (in semiconductors) results in a competing temperature dependence in  that limits TE performance.\nTE performance has also been limited by structure. Crystalline materials have long-range order that result in relatively\nhigh electrical conductivity, as charge carriers can move directionally within the lattice with minimal restriction.\nBecause electrical conduction contributes to thermal conduction, higher crystallinity in a material correlates to higher\nthermal conductivity. Conversely, the amorphous structure of glasses results in low electrical conductivity and low\nthermal conductivity. In contrast, TEs for power generation are designed to maximize\nzT. TEs are most commonly used in RTGs for long-term space missions like deep space exploration.  RTGs use the heat\nemitted from radioactive decay (as shown in Figure 2) and the cold of space to create the temperature difference\nnecessary for energy conversion. Arrays of multiple TE devices are used to generate sufficient electricity. The\ncombination of the reliability of TEs, the energy density of radioisotopes, and the necessity of isolated operation make\nTEs ideal for powering onboard electronics on long-term space missions. What is the difference between a thermocouple and a TE for power generation?\nAnswers\n1. zT is inversely proportional to thermal conductivity and proportional to electrical conductivity, operating\ntemperature, and the square of the Seebeck coefficient.\n2. In theory, TE efficiency is limited only by the thermodynamically imposed Carnot efficiency, but the interrelation of\nmaterial properties with respect to temperature and structure have limited TE efficiencies in practice.\n3. While both thermocouples and thermoelectrics rely on the Seebeck effect to convert heat to electricity,\nthermocouples create a characteristic voltage that is used to measure temperature and are not optimized for zT and\nefficiency.\nReferences\n1. Introduction\nMelt flow rate is widely used in polymer technology as a product specification since this value, \nwhich includes a statement of the load and temperature under which it is obtained, gives an indi-\ncation of the processing properties of the polymer [1-4]. The value of melt flow rate is expressed as \nthe mass of polymer melt extruded from a heated cylinder of an extrusion plastometer through its \nprecision bore orifice by its piston in a period of time, the standard units of the value being grams \nper ten minutes (g/10 min). Measurements are carried out in accordance with a protocol that is \ndescribed in ASTM D1238-23a, Standard Test Method for Melt Flow Rates of Thermoplastics by \nExtrusion Plastometer [5].\nHere the melt flow rate certification of Standard Reference Material (SRM) 1474c, a polyethylene \nresin, is described. SRM 1474c is the designated successor to SRM 1474b, which is the successor \nto SRM 1474a [6]. SRM 1474c is from the same source material as SRM 1474b.\nThe flow rate obtained with the extrusion plastometer is not a fundamental polymer property. It \nis an empirically defined parameter critically influenced by the physical properties and molecular \nstructure of the polymer and the conditions of measurement. In order that measurements are \nmeaningful and comparable across laboratories, measurements must be made in accord with a \nstandard procedure. For SRM 1474c, measurements are carried out following ASTM D1238-23a. \nWithin this standard, Procedure A at a temperature of 190 °C and a load of 2.16 kg was utilized.\n2. Material and Bottling\nThe base material, as reported by the supplier, is a linear polyethylene with narrow molar mass dis-\ntribution (MMD) ethylene-hexene copolymer resin. The density reported by the supplier is 0.948 \n(g/cm3). The material was procured in two 25 kg bags in April 2002. The material was received in \npellet form. The bag from which SRM 1474c was produced was kept sealed at The National Insti-\ntute of Standards and Technology (until 2025). While in storage, the material was maintained at \nroom temperature. The pellets were dry mixed, bottled and numbered 1 through 414. Fifteen of \nthese units were chosen by stratified random selection for homogeneity and certification studies, \nas described below.\nA unit of SRM 1474c consists of approximately 60 g of uncolored polyethylene pellets in an amber \nglass bottle.\n3. Instrumentation\nMelt flow measurements were performed with an extrusion plastometer. A common alternative \nname for an extrusion plastometer is a melt flow indexer, or melt indexer. Critical geometrical \nfeatures, dimensions and tolerences are described in ASTM D1238-23a.\n1\n\nNIST SP 260-267 \nMay 2026\n4. Calibrations, Tolerances and Cleaning\nTemperature, mass and geometrical tolerances are prescribed by ASTM D1238-23a and were fol-\nlowed herein. The temperature calibration of the extrusion plastometer cylinder was conducted \nby the instrument vendor, utilizing the method that is prescribed by ASTM D1238-23a, using a \nNIST traceable resistance temperature detector (RTD). Mass measurements of the piston, foot \nand load were performed via balances that were calibrated via NIST traceable procedures. The \ncombined mass was within the ASTM D1238-23a prescribed tolerance of 0.5 % of total mass, or \n0.01 kg. The diameter of the cylinder bore was determined by the instrument vendor - the re-\nsulting measurements were in compliance with the tolerance of this specification described in the \naforementioned ASTM method. Dimensional measurements of all dies and feet were performed \nutilizing a micrometer calibrated by NIST traceable procedures. All the above measurements and \ncalibrations were carried out within one year of the melt flow measurements. Prior to each mea-\nsurement, the dimension of the inner bore of the die was checked with a Go/No Go gauge, per \nASTM D1238-23a specifications with a micrometer traceable to NIST.\nRigorous cleaning of the bore was conducted after each measurement using cotton gun cloth. \nCleaning of the foot, die, piston was conducted via brass wire brush. Satisfactory cleaning of the \nbore and of the outside surfaces of the die were confirmed by dropping the die into the bore and \nchecking that it falls freely to the base of the bore. Cleanliness of the foot was ascertained visually \nand by confirmation of unhindered motion of the piston-foot assembly through the bore upon full \nmanual insertion and retraction.\nProper vertical extrusion bore alignment was confirmed on a daily basis, before any melt flow \nmeasurements were conducted, via a circular level that was mounted on the inserted piston rod, \nper ASTM D1238-23a specifications.\n5. Measurement Procedure\nFor each of the fifteen selected bottles, two measurements were carried out for a total of 30 \nmeasurements. Six measurements were made each day. For any given bottle, both measurements \nwere made on the same day. The sequence of numbered charges taken from the bottled samples \nfor extrusion was randomized according to a procedure described by Natrella [7].\nThis nested measurement approach (bottle nested within day) allows for the separate estimation \nof a day effect and bottle effect as described in the nested random effects model. Since the partic-\nular days and bottles sampled are not of direct interest, but rather represent a larger population \nfor which we are interested, a random effects model (vs. fixed effects) is appropriate.\nMeasurements were conducted between May 20 to 30, 2025.\nThe melt flow rate of SRM 1474c samples was determined by ASTM D1238-23a, Procedure A, \na manual procedure described in section 10. The melt flow rate was determined at (190.0) °C \nusing a load of (2.16)  kg , a standard condition for polyethylene (This test condition is sometimes \nabbreviated as 190/2.16). Following ASTM D1238-23a only the first timed \nextrudate was used in the final data analysis. Following each measurement, the piston, bore, foot, \nand die were cleaned as described previously. (National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD), NIST Technical \nNote (TN) NIST TN 2268r2. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2268r2. \nAuthor ORCID iDs \nDavid Holmberg: 0000-0002-1738-8190 \nThomas Roth: 0000-0002-9986-7784 \n \n\nNIST TN 2268r2 \nSeptember 2026 \n \ni \nAbstract \nThe Flexible Resource Controller (FRC) is a multiple-objective controller that manages \nresidential heat pumps (HP), electric domestic water heaters (DHW), electric vehicle (EV) \ncharging, and batteries. The first objective is to manage energy use to save customers money—\ncharging storage and EVs when electricity prices are low and avoiding energy use (or \ndischarging the battery) when prices are high, while maintaining thermal comfort. A second \nobjective is to implement reactive power control at the battery inverter based on local voltage \nlevels (Volt-VAr) to minimize voltage excursions outside of acceptable limits. \nThe FRC has been developed for use in transactive energy co-simulations using the GridLAB-D \ndistribution grid simulator to study the impact of price-responsive controls on voltage and \nother building and grid metrics. It takes as inputs the house thermal properties, weather, and \nelectricity price data, and generates control variables (e.g., hot water temperature setpoint, \nbattery real and reactive power settings) that are sent to the GridLAB-D simulation engine \nduring its execution. The FRC makes use of hourly day-ahead prices (DAP) in addition to \noptional adjustment of control parameters in response to 5 min real-time prices (RTP). \nAlternatively, the FRC can adjust control parameters based on a congestion dynamic price (CDP) \ngenerated using service transformer power flows. Finally, the FRC can work in a pass-through \nmode, taking power levels for each device from the transactive energy market (TEM) and \npassing those on to GridLAB-D.  \nThe FRC currently implements simple patterns that shift power usage based on prices. The FRC \nHP controller implements precooling prior to the evening price peak and a raised house \nsetpoint temperature during the price peak while maintaining thermal comfort. The DHW \ncontroller lowers the tank setpoint after noon to reduce heating on peak while still providing \nhot water. The EV is charged at the lowest priced intervals within the owner’s scheduled \ncharging sessions. The storage battery is set to charge at night when rates are lowest and then \ndischarge during price peaks. Battery inverter Volt-VAr voltage control is implemented \nindependently of price response, operating at all hours of the day when activated.  \nThis document describes the control algorithms that were implemented in the Java \nprogramming language and provides an overview of a co-simulation that connects the \ncontroller to a GridLAB D distribution grid simulation. \nKeywords \nCongestion dynamic price; distributed energy resource; device controller; dynamic price; \nflexibility; price response; voltage control; Volt-VAr. \n  \n\nNIST TN 2268r2 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. Introduction \nThe Flexible Resource Controller (FRC) was developed in the context of transactive energy (TE) \nsimulation studies to understand the effect of different TE approaches (different markets, \ndynamic price tariffs, and controllers) on customer economics, customer comfort, and grid \npower quality. Power quality metrics include voltage volatility and acceptable voltage levels as \nwell as power factor, losses, and transformer loadings. The FRC was developed to study the \nimpact of price-responsive flexibility on distribution voltage and the value of voltage-responsive \nreactive power control (inverter Volt-VAr) relative to other voltage-control measures. The best \nsources of price-responsive flexibility include the largest loads in the house, electric heating and \ncooling equipment (e.g., electric heat pump) and electric water heater, in addition to an EV or \nstationary battery [1]. Each of these devices has thermal storage (i.e., building thermal mass) or \nelectrical storage (battery) to enable load shifting. \nEvery house in the R4-12.47-1 test grid model (the same GridLAB-D model used in [2]) has a \nheat pump, electric water heater, and stationary battery, and some have an EV (represented as \ncharge-only batteries). The capacities of the HPs and DHWs vary from house to house, as do the \nthermal properties of each house. The FRC manages the HP and the DHW in each house to \nmaximize customer financial savings while staying within allowable comfort/performance \nboundaries. The battery is managed for energy arbitrage—charging during low price times and \ndischarging during high price times. The purpose of the Volt-VAr control is to use inverter-based \nreactive power control to move voltage closer to the nominal 120 V level.  \nIn previous experiments where devices responded to 5 min wholesale market real-time prices \n(RTP), the resulting power flow and voltage were volatile, due to synchronized response to \nprice changes [2]. The FRC avoids this for the HP by adjusting the cooling load profile to precool \n(store energy in house thermal mass) and then raise temperature on peak; this profile is \ndifferent for each house according to its thermal constants. For the DHW and battery, some \nrandomization across houses is used to avoid synchronized response. The randomization may \nbe similar to what occurs when different controllers are present with different control logic, \nresponding in slightly different ways to the same price signal.  \nThe FRC controls primarily respond to the wholesale market hourly day-ahead prices (DAP). \nBased on previous research [2], response to DAP allows planning for storage use (including load \nshifting) and avoids the larger power swings that occur when all devices react to a volatile RTP \nsignal. On the other hand, the FRC also has logic that, if enabled, causes the controller to avoid \nusing power during RTP price spikes, as may be applicable to a tariff where part of a customer’s \nenergy use is paid at the RTP while a baseline amount is paid at DAP. In addition, the FRC can \ngenerate and respond to a congestion dynamic price (CDP) which is adjusted based on local \ntransformer congestion. In the case of raised CDP, devices may shift load to reduce cost to the \ncustomer. \nThe Volt-VAr control has been implemented to reduce the voltage range of fluctuations on the \ngrid and reduce the count of voltage excursions outside of ANSI C84.1 Range A limits [3]. As \n\nNIST TN 2268r2 \nSeptember 2026 \n2 \nvoltage levels rise, inverter reactive power consumption increases to lower voltage. Likewise, as \nvoltage drops, reactive power injection increases to raise voltage.  \nThe TEM pass-through mode enables a local market to determine prices and resulting load \nprofile. The TEM runs separately from the FRC as a day-ahead market. The TEM is used to \nbalance load across the day in order to minimize prices and maximize device flexibility, shifting \nEV and battery charging to the lowest cost intervals while still providing the power requested \nduring the charging windows. The final result is a power profile (hourly load or generation) for \neach hour of the coming day,

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Compton Effect\nThe Compton effect (also called Compton scattering) is the result of a high-energy photon colliding with a target, which\nreleases loosely bound electrons from the outer shell of the atom or molecule. The scattered radiation experiences a\nwavelength shift that cannot be explained in terms of classical wave theory, thus lending support to Einstein's photon\ntheory. The effect was first demonstrated in 1923 by Arthur Holly Compton (for which he received a 1927 Nobel Prize).\nThe effect is important because it demonstrates that light cannot be explained purely as a wave phenomenon. Thomson\nscattering, the classical theory of an electromagnetic wave scattered by charged particles, cannot explain low intensity\nshift in wavelength. Classically, light of sufficient intensity for the electric field to accelerate a charged particle to a\nrelativistic speed will cause radiation-pressure recoil and an associated Doppler shift of the scattered light, but the\neffect would become arbitrarily small at sufficiently low light intensities regardless of wavelength. Light must behave\nas if it consists of particles in order to explain the low-intensity Compton scattering. Compton's experiment convinced\nphysicists that light can behave as a stream of particles whose energy is proportional to the frequency.\nThe experiment\nA schematic diagram of the apparatus used by Compton is shown in the Figure below. A graphite target was\nbombarded with monochromatic x-rays and the wavelength of the scattered radiation was measured with a rotating\ncrystal spectrometer. The intensity was determined by a movable ionization chamber that generated a current\nproportional to the x-ray intensity. Compton measured the dependence of scattered x-ray intensity on wavelength at\nthree different scattering angles of 45  90  ,and 135\nFigure  The experimental intensity vs. wavelength plots observed by Compton for the above three scattering angles\n(See Fig. below) show two peaks, one at the wavelength  of the incident x-rays and the other at a longer wavelength\n.\nPhysics\nCompton effect is the decrease in energy (increase in wavelength) of an X-ray or gamma ray photon, when it interacts\nwith matter. Because of the change in photon energy, it is an inelastic scattering process. Inverse Compton scattering\nalso exists, where the photon gains energy (decreasing in wavelength) upon interaction with matter. Compton used a\ncombination of three fundamental formulas representing the various aspects of classical and modern physics,\ncombining them to describe the quantum behavior of light:\n1. Light as a particle, as noted in the photoelectric effect\n2. Relativistic dynamics: special theory of relativity\n3. Trigonometry: law of cosines\nWe can think of the photon as losing an amount of energy in the collision that is the same as the kinetic energy (KE)\ngained by the electron, although actually separate photons are involved. Closure: If A and B are two elements in G, then A☼B is also in G.\n2. Associativity: For all elements in G, (A☼B) ☼C==A☼ (B☼C).\n3. Identity: There is an identity element I such that I☼A=A☼I=A for \nevery element A in G.\n4. Inverse: There is an inverse or reciprocal of each element. \nTherefore, the set must contain an element B=inv(A) such \nthat A☼inv(A)=inv(A) ☼A=I for each element of G.\n\n3.012 Fundamentals of Materials Science: Bonding - Nicola Marzari (MIT, Fall 2005)\nExamples\n• Integer numbers, and addition\n• Integer numbers, and multiplication\n• Real numbers, and multiplication\n• Rotations around an axis by 360/n \n\nFigure 17.3\nImage of mirror planes in a water molecule removed for copyright reasons.\nSee Engel, T., and  P. [{"suffix": "", "text": "A practical guide to hydrogel working curves for bioprinting \nRion J. Wendland1*, Thomas J. Kolibaba1, Kristan S. Worthington2, Jason P. Killgore1* \n1. Applied Chemicals and Materials Division, National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, Boulder, CO USA \n2. Roy J. Carver Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA \n \n* Corresponding Authors: RJW: rion.wendland@nist.gov, JPK: jason.killgore@nist.gov  \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n\nAbstract: \nThe working curve is a widely implemented, but presently not standardized, method of assessing \nresin printability for photopolymer additive manufacturing technologies. While the working \ncurve has been studied and refined for plastic resins, application to hydrogel materials used in \nbioprinting has been limited. Hydrogels present measurement challenges due to their decreased \nsolids content, compliant nature, and significant swelling. Here, adapting lessons learned from \ninterlaboratory studies on plastic working curves, we assess various techniques for hydrogel \nworking curve measurements. Notably, across several formulations with various molecular \nweights and solids content, hydrogels exhibit near ideal log-linear behavior consistent with the \nJacobs model when measured appropriately. However, certain measurement modalities (such as \ncontact-based and rheological) can indicate Jacobs-like behavior, but with systematic errors in \nthe cure depth compared to non-contact optical methods. Overall, this work highlights the \nchallenges when conducting hydrogel working curve measurements and provides several \nconsiderations to help further develop and standardize measurements across 3D bioprinting \napplications. \n \n \n \nKeywords: \nHydrogels; working curve; Jacobs equation; photopolymerization; 3D printing \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n \n\n1. Introduction: \nThe use of photopolymer additive manufacturing (PAM) is widely established in the \nbiomedical field, with applications including tissue engineered cell scaffolds, pharmaceutical \ndelivery platforms, and microfluidic organ-on-a-chip devices [1-5]. Specifically, vat \nphotopolymerization, which includes stereolithography and digital light processing systems, \nenables the creation of complex parts and structures in a fast and reproducible manner. Given the \ngrowth and impact of bioprinting on the healthcare system, it is imperative to develop \nmeasurement techniques to compare bioprinting materials accurately and reproducibly across \nlaboratories and research groups.  \nIn vat photopolymerization, an established measurement of photopolymer resin \nprintability is the working curve. A common model used to understand the working curve is the \nJacobs model. This model defines a relationship between Beer-Lambert light absorption and the \ncritical exposure of light Ec necessary for liquid-to-solid polymerization [6]:  \n𝐶𝑑 = 𝐷𝑝ln⁡ (𝐸0\n𝐸𝑐\n) \nHere, Cd is the cure depth or thickness of a sample and E0 is the incident radiant light exposure. \nWhen cure depth as a function of incident radiant exposure is determined experimentally, a log-\nlinear plot produces slope Dp (light penetration depth: where light intensity attenuates to 1/e ≈ 37 \n%) and x-intercept Ec (Figure 1). While historically E0 is referred to as a “dose” rather than \n“radiant exposure”, a “dose” is not consistent with the SI unit system. Here, we use “radiant \nexposure” or “exposure” to refer to the area-normalized optical energy input into the system[7]. \nIdeally, measuring a resin’s working curve can enable users to determine suitable printing \nparameters (e.g., light intensity, cure time, layer thickness) for specific resins. Practically, these \nvalues can also be used as a quality control metric across resin batches, as well as an estimation \nof a resin’s z-resolution and throughput capabilities. \n  \nFigure 1. Example schematic of a working curve experiment. A) Photopolymer formulations are \nirradiated for discrete exposure durations in isolated areas of a methacrylate-functionalized glass slide and \n\n\nthe resulting cure depths are measured. B) Cure depths are plotted against radiant exposure on a log-linear \nplot: Dp is the slope of the regression while Ec is the x-intercept. \n \nIn the field of plastic PAM (i.e. PAM wherein plastic or elastomeric materials are \nprinted), the working curve has been the focus of many studies related to new measurement \ntechniques [8-10], assumptions of the Jacobs equation [11-14], or characterizations of new \nphotopolymer resins [15-18]. Despite the importance of the working curve, this measurement has \nyet to be standardized. For example, a recent interlaboratory study highlighted the variation of \nworking curve measurements across laboratories, with up to a 7-fold and 70-fold difference in \nreported Dp and Ec values, respectively [19]. Importantly, some of this variation can be attributed \nto spectral variability of commercial printers, most notably broadband light sources and variable \nexposure across the resin vat [20]. As such, the use of a well characterized and reproducible light \nsource is vital for standardized working curve measurements. This is clearly demonstrated in the \nmost recent interlaboratory study on plastic working curves, which made use of a standardized \nand well characterized LED light engine. This protocol resulted in significant improvements to \nthe variations in Dp from 7-fold down to 1.6-fold and Ec from 70-fold down to 2.1-fold [21]. \nThe rapid adoption of vat photopolymerization for bioprinting has accelerated the need \nfor robust hydrogel characterization methods. Bioprinting typically uses hydrogel resins for their \nadvantageous properties such as biodegradability, biocompatibility, and close approximation of \nnatural tissue mechanics [22-24]. These hydrogel precursor materials can be synthetic (e.g., \npolyethylene glycol, polyacrylamide, polycaprolactone) or natural (e.g., gelatin, silk, hyaluronic \nacid) which each come with corresponding advantages and disadvantages [25, 26]. The working \ncurve measurement could provide a means of comparing resins properties and print-relevant \nparameters between different materials, batches, or laboratories. Additionally, the magnitude of \nDp and Ec can provide important insights to bioprinting with live cells. For example, many live \ncell printing applications look to minimize the total energy exposure per layer to mitigate \npotentially harmful effects to the cells. Resins with low Ec would be prime candidates for live \ncell printing, as less energy exposure is needed to polymerize the layer. Likewise, high Dp resins \nwould potentially minimize the overall radiant exposure to the cells but may negatively impact \nthe achievable resolution of the printed structure. Regardless of material, implementing working \ncurves on hydrogels requires rethinking of the cure depth (thickness) measurement due the low \nstiffness samples (kPa to MPa) that could be easily deformed or damaged by typical contact-\nbased thickness measurement tools like handheld micrometers [27-29]. As an alternative, some \ngroups have used non-contact methods such as microscopy or photorheology to measure working \ncurve behavior on a variety of photopolymer materials [10, 19, 30, 31]. However, there remains a \ngap in understanding and quantifying how different measurement methods influence hydrogel \nworking curves and Jacobs parameters.  \nHere, we present a guide to practical considerations for measuring working curves on \nhydrogel systems. We use a model acrylate polymer, polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA), at \nvarious molecular weights and concentrations to compare how different cure depth measurement \ntechniques influence hydrogel working curve fit parameters. For all measurement techniques, we \n\nuse an identical light source to ensure that true comparisons can be made between methods. \nImportantly, we show that working curve measurements of photopolymer hydrogels cured with a \nwell-calibrated, narrowband LED light source produce the log-linear working curve relationship \npredicted from the Jacobs model. However, working curves and the extracted Ec and Dp \nparameters are strongly dependent on the measurement method. Contact methods substantially \ncompress soft samples, resulting in an underestimation of cure depth which effects the Dp and Ec \nvalues extracted from the Jacobs model fits. On the other hand, optical methods do not \nsubstantially deform samples but require appropriate contrast and analysis techniques to \naccurately determine cure depth. Gap-dependent photorheology is also investigated as a \ncandidate measurement technique, but the resultant cure profiles do not predictably correlate to \neither the contact or optical methods. Overall, the results presented here can be applied to all \nhydrogel photopolymer 3D printing applications, helping to further develop and standardize \nworking curve measurements across the field. \n \n2. Materials and Methods: \nCertain commercial equipment, instruments, or materials are identified in this paper to specify \nthe experimental procedure adequately. Such identification is not intended to imply \nrecommendation or endorsement by NIST. \n2.1 Materials \nPolyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA, Mw = 700 Da and Mw = 575 Da) and tartrazine were \npurchased from Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). PEGDA (Mw = 3400 Da) was purchased \nfrom Thermofisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). The photoinitiator lithium phenyl-2,4,6-\ntrimethylbenzoylphosphinate (LAP) was purchased from Colorado Photopolymer Solutions a \nsubsidiary of Arkema (King of Prussia, PA, USA). All chemicals were used as received.  \n2.2 Hydrogel Formulations \nThree water-based hydrogel formulations were used for experimentation. A “stiff” hydrogel \nconsisted of 40 % by mass PEGDA 700 in deionized water, while two “soft” hydrogels consisted \nof 10 % by mass PEGDA 700 or 20 % by mass PEGDA 3400 in deionized water. These \nformulations were chosen as a generalized subset of hydrogels, including differences in both \nmolecular weight and PEGDA concentrations. For comparing working curve parameters, three \nadditional hydrogel formulations were used: 20 % by mass PEGDA 700, 10 % by mass PEGDA \n575, and 25 % by mass PEGDA 575, all in deionized water. All formulations contained \nphotoinitiator LAP at 1 % by mass and photoabsorber tartrazine at 0.1 % by mass. Formulations \nwere stored protected from light prior to use. All measurements were performed with samples \npolymerized from the same batch of a given resin, and resins were refrigerated (4 °C) and kept in \nthe dark when not in use. \n \n \n\n2.3 Light Source \nTo photopolymerize the hydrogel samples for working curve measurements, a collimated LED \n(Solis-405C LED, Thorlabs; Newton, NJ) light source with a 2.5 mm aperture was used. Light \nwas filtered using a 1.9 nm bandpass filter centered at 405 nm (Figure S1). The LED drive \ncurrent was 370 mA, which resulted in an irradiance of 8.0 mW cm-2, as measured using an \nintegrating sphere photodiode power meter (S142C, Thorlabs). \n2.4 Hydrogel Fabrication \nFor working curve generation (except photorheology), hydrogel resins were polymerized onto \nglass slides functionalized with 3-(trimethoxysilyl) propyl methacrylate (Automate Scientific; \nBerkeley, CA, USA), using 1.6 mm thick silicone isolators (Grace Biolabs; Bend, OR) to ensure \nsufficient resin volume greater than any achieved cure depth (max cure depth was less than 400 \nµm in this study). After curing, samples were measured for cure depth within one hour using a \nvariety of techniques. \n2.5 Cure Depth Measurements \nTo measure the cure depth of hydrogel samples and generate a working curve, six different \nanalytical techniques were used: \n2.5.1 Handheld Micrometer (HHM) \nA f

Azaroff, L.V., Introduction to Solids, McGraw-Hill, 1960. \n2. Wert, C.A., and Thomson, R.M., Physics of Solids, McGraw-Hill, 1970. \n3. Nuffield, E.W., X-Ray Diffraction Methods, Wiley, 1966. \n4. HISTORICAL INTRODUCTION \nX-rays were discovered during the summer of 1895 by Wilhelm Röntgen at the \nUniversity of Würtzburg (Germany). Röntgen was interested in the cathode rays \n(beams of electrons) developed in discharge tubes, but it is not clear exactly which \naspects of cathode rays he intended to study. By chance he noticed that a fluorescent \nscreen (ZnS + Mn++) lying on a table some distance from the discharge tube emitted a \nflash of light each time an electrical discharge was passed through the tube. Realizing \nthat he had come upon something completely new, he devoted his energies to \ninvestigating the properties of the unknown ray “X” which produced this effect. The \nannouncement of this discovery appeared in December 1895 as a concise ten page \npublication. \nThe announcement of the discovery of X-rays was received with great interest by the \npublic. Röntgen himself prepared the first photographs of the bones in a living hand, \nand use of the radiation was quickly adopted in medicine. In the succeeding fifteen \nyears, however, very few fundamental insights were gained into the nature of \n1\n\n\nLN–5\nX-radiation. There was some indication that the rays were waves, but the evidence was \nnot clear-cut and could be interpreted in several ways. Then, at the University of \nMunich in 1912, Max von Laue performed one of the most significant experiments of \nmodern physics. At his suggestion, Paul Knipping (who had just completed a doctoral \nthesis with Röntgen) and Walter Friedrich (a newly appointed assistant to Sommerfeld) \ndirected a beam of X-rays at a crystal of copper sulfate and attempted to record the \nscattered beams on a photographic plate. The first experiment was unsuccessful. The \nresult of a second experiment was successful. They observed the presence of spots \nproduced by diffracted X-ray beams grouped around a larger central spot where the \nincident X-ray beam struck the film. This experiment demonstrated conclusively that \nX-radiation consisted of waves and, further, that the crystals were composed of atoms \narranged on a space lattice. \n2. THE “FINE STRUCTURE” OF CHARACTERISTIC X-RAYS \nIt is customary to consider the characteristic X-ray spectral lines as discrete lines (K α, \nKβ, Lα, Lβ, etc.). In reality, they are not discrete since the electron shells involved in the \nassociated electron transitions have energy sublevels (s, p, d orbitals). These sublevels \ngive rise to a “fine structure” insofar as the Kα lines are doublets composed of Kα1 and \nKα2 lines. Similarly, Lα, Lβ, etc., exhibit a fine structure. \nThese considerations suggest that X-ray spectra contain information concerning the \nenergetics of electronic states. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Rinse-Free Deposition of Molecular Layer-by-Layer (mLbL) Polyamide Reverse Osmosis Membranes\n\nIn Preparation for: Journal of Membrane Science Letters\nMarch 4th, 2025\n\nSamarpan Deb Majumder1, Christopher M. Stafford2*, and Xitong Liu1*\n\nDepartment of Civil & Environmental Engineering, the George Washington University, 800 22nd St NW, Washington D.C., Washington, D.C., 20052, United States\nMaterials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD, 20899, United States\n\n*Corresponding authors: xitongliu@gwu.edu\nchris.stafford@nist.gov\n\nAbstract\nThe molecular layer-by-layer (mLbL) deposition technique enables the fabrication of polyamide-based reverse osmosis membranes with low surface roughness and tunable membrane thickness, but scale-up of the process is challenged by the necessity for rinsing away unreacted monomers after each deposition step. By sensible tuning of monomer concentrations during deposition, we can eliminate the rinsing steps while still producing polyamide membranes with comparable thickness and surface properties. This approach markedly shortens fabrication time and improves reagent efficiency. By measuring the growth rate of the polyamide membrane as a function of deposition cycles and monomer concentration, we demonstrate that we can deliver a more targeted quantity of monomer to the growing film surface while maintaining a linear growth rate profile. Desalination tests reveal that mLbL membranes produced at the lowest monomer concentration (membrane thickness of ≈20 nm) achieved 99.9 % salt rejection within 4 h, while maintaining a flux of 0.9 L m⁻² h⁻¹ bar⁻¹, indicating that the crosslink density of the membrane remains high. This modified mLbL approach significantly reduces membrane fabrication time without compromising performance, offering a path towards scalable production of polyamide-based membranes with controlled thickness and low roughness while prioritizing both time and resource efficiency.\nKeywords: molecular layer-by-layer (mLbL), polyamide, reverse osmosis membrane, rinse free, desalination, membrane fabrication\n\nGraphical abstract:\n\n1. Introduction\nThin film composite polyamide membranes, first developed by Cadotte and colleagues in the late 1970s, are the basis for modern commercial reverse osmosis (RO) membranes (Cadotte et al., 1980). These membranes are created through interfacial polymerization (IP) involving a trifunctional acid chloride (e.g., trimesoyl chloride, TMC, dissolved in an organic solvent) and a difunctional amine (e.g., m-phenylenediamine, MPD, dissolved in water) on a porous support (Li et al., 2021). While IP membranes excel in water permeability and salt rejection, their high surface roughness and uneven distribution of polar groups contribute to scaling/fouling of the membrane and render structure-property relationships elusive (Al Mayyahi, 2018; Ismail et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2012; Tarboush et al., 2009). To address these issues, a process termed molecular layer-by-layer (mLbL) deposition was developed (Chan et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2012), which produces membranes with tunable film thickness, greatly reduced surface roughness, and controllable surface chemistry (Stafford et al., 2022), thus affording fundamental insights into the relationship between membrane chemistry/morphology and separation performance (Gu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023).\nThe mLbL process involves sequential deposition of monomer solutions and rinse solvents on a surface. In one cycle, the first half of the cycle includes deposition of TMC immediately followed by rinsing with an organic solvent such as toluene. On the second half of the cycle, MPD deposition is followed by another organic solvent rinse such as acetone or tetrahydrofuran. The average deposition rate of mLbL is approximately 0.4 nm per cycle. For example, for a target membrane thickness of 30 nm, 75 cycles would be required (Chan et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2012; Mulhearn et al., 2021), where each cycle is comprised of 2 deposition steps and 2 rinse steps (300 individual steps in total). The rinse step is crucial to prevent uncontrolled polymerization, similar to how a sweep gas in vapor-phase atomic layer deposition (ALD) processes removes unreacted reactants from the deposition surface (Maydannik et al., 2011). Despite the necessity of the rinse steps, it creates an exceptional obstacle for scaling up the mLbL process for industrial scale membrane manufacturing both in terms of excessive chemical/solvent use and time consumption. For example, to make a film of 20 nm thickness, the mLbL process consumes 80 mL of rinse solvents and takes around 2 h to complete 50 cycles of polyamide deposition on the substrate (thickness ≈ 20 nm). The rinse steps constitute around 80 % of the total time. An open question remains: is it possible to conduct mLbL deposition in the absence of rinse steps? In other words, can we deliver just enough monomer to the surface to result in the addition of a single molecular layer? If successful, would removing the rinse steps affect the morphology of the surfaces and the separation performance of the resulting RO membrane?\nRecently, dual-layer slot coating (DSC) and 3D printing have been introduced as innovative methods for scalable membrane fabrication of RO membranes from TMC and MPD, and we take inspiration from these approaches to improve the molecular layer-by-layer (mLbL) process. The DSC technique, as demonstrated by Park and his colleagues, confines interfacial polymerization within a controlled volume, enabling the synthesis of ultra-thin polyamide layers with minimal surface roughness (Park et al., 2017). This streamlined approach achieves precise, thin films around 15 nm, with enhanced permeability and selectivity. These developments corroborate the findings of Mulhearn et al., who identified 15 nm as an optimal thickness for balancing salt rejection with water permeance in desalination applications (Mulhearn et al., 2021). Similarly, the electrospray-based 3D printing technique delivers monomers in controlled doses, ensuring precise deposition and minimizing excess monomer delivery, thereby eliminating the need for traditional rinse steps to remove unreacted material (Chowdhury et al., 2018). Inspired by these advancements, we have adapted our mLbL process to eliminate rinse steps, drawing on similar principles to move mLbL closer to large-scale manufacturing.\nIn this study, we report on a rinse-free mLbL method (Fig. 1) enabled by decreasing solution concentration and volume, thereby effectively controlling polymer deposition on the surface and minimizing the presence of unreacted monomer after each cycle. The fabricated membranes exhibit tunable thickness (≈20 nm), low surface roughness, and high cross-linking density, comparable to mLbL membranes. Desalination tests reveal that the rinse-free mLbL membrane achieves a comparable NaCl rejection to a commercial brackish water membrane, exceeding 99 %. However, the mLbL membranes reaches a steady state more rapidly due presumably to their exceptional network structure, which results in a denser and more uniform selective layer. In contrast, commercial interfacial polymerization (IP)-based membranes exhibit a more heterogeneous structure with a ridge-and-valley morphology, requiring longer equilibration times to achieve stable transport properties​(Mulhearn et al., 2021).  The intent of this study is not to outperform existing commercial membranes but rather to investigate the potential of the mLbL concept for scalable manufacturing and integration with commercial production lines. Additionally, the rinse-free method is also in line with the broader goals of green chemistry, including waste prevention, reduced chemical use, and improved energy efficiency. \n\nFig.1. (a) Schematic representation of the modified layer-by-layer (mLbL) process and film thickness measurement. (b) Process for transferring the mLbL polyamide film from the substrate to a porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN) support for performance testing with poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) (PSS) as a release layer.\n\n\n\n2. Results and Discussion\n2.1. Film thickness for half-cycle depositions\nControlling the amount of monomer delivered and available for reaction is crucial for achieving the desired film growth and resulting properties (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Park et al., 2017). Fig.2. displays the relationship between solution concentration and film thickness, with measurements for the two different monomers, TMC and MPD. The original mLbL process utilized solution concentrations (wB) of 1 %, and the growth rate per TMC/MPD cycle was shown to be ≈0.4 nm / cycle, or 0.2 nm / half cycle. As seen in Fig 2, a half cycle deposition of wB = 1 % TMC or MPD delivered ≈30 nm of monomer to the surface (150× excess), which must be subsequently removed during a singular rinse step in the traditional mLbL deposition process. Subsequent publications on mLbL deposition empirically reduced the concentration of monomers to wB = 0.4 %, which still delivers a 50× excess of monomers to the growing film surface. To eliminate the rinse step in the mLbL process, we propose to lower the excess monomer even further. For the lowest concentration (wB = 0.01 %), a half cycle deposition yielded a monomer film thickness of (2 to 3) nm, which may be sufficient to confine the reaction zone and lead to controlled film growth in the absence of rinse steps. It should be noted that the TMC half cycle thickness is consistently greater than the MPD half cycle thickness.\n\nFig.2. Film thickness per half-cycle, which consists of a single deposition step of monomer (TMC or MPD) on the surface, without any rinsing step. Samples were prepared in triplicate for five different solution concentrations (% by mass fraction in toluene) of each monomer. The error bars represent one standard deviation of the data (n = 3).\n2.2. Film thickness as a function of deposition cycles\nMulhearn et al. concluded that an mLbL membrane having a thickness of 15 nm exhibited the ideal balance between flux and salt rejection (Mulhearn et al., 2021). Inspired by this, we tracked the mLbL growth rate for different solution concentrations with no rinse steps between each monomer deposition step. In these experiments, we measured the film thickness via ellipsometry for the as-cast membranes as well as after rinsing the films with deionized water (DI), as subsequent experiments will require exposure of the mLbL film to water (floating the polyamide film off the substrate and transferring to a porous PAN membrane, as well as performance testing). The DI water rinse should inform us whether there are unreacted monomers trapped in the membrane, which would be removed during our film transfer process. The aim of this study was to achieve a 20 nm film thickness at different concentrations without the need for intermediate rinse steps. Higher solution concentrations (wB = 0.4 % and wB = 1 %) lead to visibly inhomogeneous films (white particulates, high surface roughness, scattered light) and thus were excluded from this section of the study.\nAs shown in Fig. 3, analysis of monomer deposition across different concentrations exhibited a clear trend in how monomer concentration affects the control over the polyamide film thickness. At higher concentrations, such as wB = 0.1%, the deposition thickness per cycle started off relatively high and fluctuated more significantly, indicating less controlled and more excessive growth. In contrast, at wB = 0.05% and especially at wB = 0.01%, the deposition per cycle was more gradual and consistent, allowing for finer control over film thickness. For example, at wB = 0.01%, the polymer growth per deposition cycle was around 0.9 ± 0.1 nm whereas at wB = 0.05% and wB = 0.1%, the growth rate was around 1.5 ± 0.2 nm and 3.8 ± 0.9 nm, respectively (post-water rinse). Understanding the development \nof these deleterious stresses is necessary for improving predictive \nmodels and engineering design. Here, we present a suite of \nmetrologies and methodologies, including advanced thermal \nanalysis, rheological ch aracterization, shrinkage, and evolved \nstress measurements, to link residual stress development  with \nfundamental material properties in a commercial liquid \nencapsulant.  \nKeywords—liquid encapsulant, cure kinetics, rheology, cure \nshrinkage, residual stress \nI. INTRODUCTION \nSemiconductor packaging materials  are typically \nthermosetting polymer formulations with multiple components. \nIn these materials, residual stress es develop during the curing \nprocess and are closely linked with the reaction kinetics, liquid-\nto-solid transition, and cure-induced shrinkage [1]. Residual \nstresses continue to evolve in the cured material in response to \nhygrothermal conditions during service [2]. Characterizing these \nbehaviors is often challenging due to the complex formulations \nused in the semiconductor industry. However, understanding the \ndevelopment of residual stresses is necessary to inform \npredictive models and thus improve the engineering design and \nmanufacturing productivity of semiconductor assemblies. \nHere, we present a suite of advanced metrologies and \nmethodologies to measure and analyze the fundamental material \nproperties of a commercial liquid encapsulant. Thermal analysis \nis used to measure and accurately model the cure kinetics  for \ncomplex mechanisms. Rheological measurements supplement \nthe cure kinetics study and are used to identify the liquid-to-solid \ntransition during curing.  Thin film curvature measurements \ndemonstrate that this transition accurately predicts the  \ndevelopment of residual stress caused by the observed cure-\ninduced shrinkage. Stress measurements on the post -cured \nmaterial further reveal the effect of hygrothermal conditions on \nthe mechanical response. Taken together, this metrology suite \nties fundamental to part -scale measurements for a holistic \nunderstanding of the evolution of residual stresses during curing \nand in service, an essential step for improving predictive models.    \nII. Differential Scanning Calorimetry for Cure Kinetics \nDifferential scanning calorimetry (DSC) is widely used \nwithin the semiconductor community to investigate  the cure \nkinetics of  electronic packaging materials  [5], [7]–[9]. Prior \nwork by Tao et al.  [7] outlines several best practices for DSC \nmeasurements on epoxy molding compounds, which we \nimplement to study the liquid encapsulant. All measurements \nare performed using a DSC equipped with a refrigerated \ncooling system under nitrogen  purge gas . About 10 mg to \n15 mg of uncured encapsulant samples are sealed in 40 µL \nhermetic pans for measurement. The heat flow (𝑄̇ ) is measured \nas a function of temperature (T) by heating samples from -40 °C \nto 300 °C at constant heating rates b = (0.5, 1, 5, and 10 ) \n°C min-1. The standard uncertainties for temperature and heat \nflow are approximately ±  1 % and ±  3 %, respectively. The \ndegree of cure or conversion as a function of temperature , \nα(𝑇) = ∫ 𝑄̇ 𝑑𝑇/\tβ\t∆𝐻! , is calculated by integrating the \nexothermic reaction peaks starting from a temperature below \nthe onset of the reaction, dividing by the total heat of reaction \n(∆HT), and normalizing by the heating rate. The conversion rate \nis given by dα/dt. To replicate the recommended curing \nschedule, we perform an isothermal DSC test at 100 °C for 60 \nmin, followed by a second isothermal test at 165 °C for 60 min. \nModel-based kinetics analysis and simulation are performed \nusing a commercial  software following ICTAC \nrecommendations for the analysis of multi-step kinetics [10].  \nB. Rheometry for Liquid-Solid Transition \nRheometry is a versatile technique for measuring the time-\nevolving material properties of various materials, including  \nviscoelastic liquid encapsulants. Using a rotational rheometer, \nwe measure the viscoelastic storage (G') and loss (G\") moduli \nof the uncured encapsulant by deforming a small sample \nbetween two 8-mm disposable aluminum parallel plates  \naccording to a user -defined oscillating profile of strain \namplitude (g) and angular frequency (w). The instrument has a \nminimum resolvable torque of ±  0.05 μN m and angle of \n± 0.04 μrad. The storage and loss moduli represent the elastic \nand dissipative behavior, respectively, and arise due to the \nstress-strain phase lag inherent to viscoelastic materials. We \nidentify the critical strain below which the viscoelastic moduli \nare strain-independent, i.e., the linear viscoelastic region [11], \nby conducting amplitude sweep experiments where g is varied \nfrom 0.1 % strain to 100 % strain at isothermal temperatures up \nto 100 °C. The critical strain is temperature-dependent, with the \nlowest value (g » 0.3 % strain) occurring at 100 °C. Therefore, \nwe maintain the strain amplitude well below this critical value \nin consecutive experiments to measure the linear viscoelastic \nmoduli.  \nTo investigate the temperature evolution of the moduli \nduring the first heating ramp, we heat a sample from nominally \n40 °C to 100 °C at 5 °C min-1, hold at 100 °C for 5 min, then \ncool back down to 40 °C at 5 °C min-1. Therefore, we use a nascent approach called \noptimally windowed chirps (OWCh), which involves applying \na frequency -varying deformation profile to obtain \nmeasurements at significantly faster acquisition times \ncompared to the classical single -frequency method [12]. The \nOWCh parameters can be designed to apply much lower strain \namplitudes than rapid 'multiwave' methods  [13], allowing for \nmeasurements well below the critical strain. We measure the \ntime evolution of the moduli at 100 °C by continuously \napplying a modulated deformation profile, where g << 0.3 % \nstrain and w is varied from 0.9 rad s-1 to 25.2 rad s-1. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Evaluating Contaminant Effects and Blend Ratios on the Alkaline Hydrolysis of Polyester Textile Streams\nCharlotte M. Wentz1, Maxwell D. Mevorah1,2, Allison Carranza1,3, McKenzie L. Coughlin1, Amy Engelbrecht-Wiggans4†, Thomas P. Forbes1, Zois Tsinas5,1, Amanda L. Forster*1 \n1 Material Measurement Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, Maryland 20899, United States. \n2 Chemistry and Biochemistry Department, University of Maryland College Park, MD 20742. \n3 Chemistry and Biochemistry Department, West Virginia University, VA, 26506.\n4 Mechanical Engineering Department, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, NY, 14623.\n5 Theiss Research, La Jolla, California 92037, United States \n† Deceased April 5, 2025\n*Corresponding author: amanda.forster@nist.gov (240)-586-2650\n\nKeywords. Chemical recycling, textiles, cotton reuse, hydrolysis, waste management, post-consumer\nSynopsis. This study demonstrates a mild alkaline hydrolysis method to recover valuable components, including cotton and terephthalic acid, from mixed textile waste containing polyester blends, highlighting the potential for chemical recycling of discarded textiles.\nAbstract. The increasing amounts of discarded textiles represent a potentially valuable resource that could be reclaimed, for example, by chemical techniques. This work underscores the significance of utilizing chemical recycling techniques for multi-component fabrics under mild reaction conditions to investigate reusability of recovered components. We present a method for recovery of cotton, elastane, and nylon from polyester blends through mild alkaline hydrolysis, supported with a phase-transfer catalyst. To juxtapose the impact of these various fibers on the depolymerization of the polyester component, into terephthalic acid (TPA), consistent reaction conditions were maintained. The average TPA yield (by mass) was 93.9 % ± 2.8 % for pre-consumer materials and 89.5 % ± 3.1 % for post-consumer materials. This comparative analysis provides insights into factors contributing to the observed decrease in TPA yield. Inimitable to this study, analysis of the reuse potential of recovered cotton via tensile strength was performed. The average cotton recovery (by mass) was 95.9 % ± 0.8 %. Comprehensive material characterization of all recovered components was performed. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the potential contamination of TPA, quality of recollected fibers, and what components of a mixed textile stream act as potential “disruptors” to recyclability.  \nIntroduction. Recent studies of consumer waste has shown that the volume of textiles being discarded in the U.S. is growing, and there is increasing interest in reclaiming this material.1  The complex nature of textile waste, encompassing a diverse range of fibers from natural to synthetic, and the prevalence of blended fabrics all present challenges when reclaiming textile waste.1,2 Mechanical recycling, while cost-effective, exhibits limitations when processing multi-fiber blends, particularly those containing elastomeric fibers, and yields low-value products.3–7 Less than 1 % of textiles are recycled back to fibers.8,9 Chemical recycling offers a promising alternative for maximizing resource recovery.10,11 \nPreviously studies have explored polyester fiber depolymerization into reusable monomers like terephthalic acid (TPA) and bishydroxyethyl terephthalate (BHET) (see Table S1 for an abbreviation glossary).12–15 Common depolymerization methods include glycolysis 3,16–18 and hydrolysis.19–24 Dissolution, effective for fiber separation but does not facilitate depolymerization, is not considered here. Existing studies have encountered challenges, including the degradation of other synthetic fibers and cotton, resulting in the need for additional purification procedures, limiting reuse potential.20,25 Chemical recycling systems preferentially utilize pre-consumer textile waste (e.g., excess cuts, unused textiles) to minimize issues related to variable content (known textile construct, avoids dyes, additives, etc.). The majority of textile waste, however, is post-consumer materials, which are only beginning to be investigated in chemical recycling studies. \nThis study investigates the depolymerization of polyester-based textile blends into TPA utilizing a mild alkaline hydrolysis, such as polycotton (P:C) and elastane blends. The compare-contrast design of this investigation between well-known textile blends and unknown post-consumer textiles enables hypotheses regarding conditions (dyes, additives, fiber types, blend percentage, inaccurate labels, or elastomeric fiber constructs) that affect the reuse potential of recovered fibers and TPA. Our findings show an average TPA yield (by mass) of 93.9 % ± 2.8 % for pre-consumer materials and 89.5 % ± 3.1 % for post-consumer materials. Since resource collection of recycled cotton holds the highest potential for fiber-to-fiber recycling, key parameters for evaluating the suitability for re-spinning include microstructural changes, fiber length, and tensile strength.26 Others have studied parameters important to the reuse of collected cotton,5,18-21 but solid recollected fibers (excluding cotton) post-reaction are vastly overlooked. This study thoroughly examines reclaimed cotton for all these parameters for reuse, including the often-overlooked tensile strength. Given cotton’s resource-intensive nature27 and increasing demand, recycled cotton fibers hold precedence for being a focus for fiber recollection.28 Currently, only 1 % of the cotton market comprises recycled cotton, primarily from mechanical recycling of pre-consumer fabrics.27 This research offers a deeper understanding of the potential contamination in both TPA and recollected fibers, specifically identifying textile stream components that act as potential “disruptors” to recyclability.   \nMaterials and Methods: This work utilizes alkaline hydrolysis with phase-transfer catalysis (PTC) to enhance TPA yield19 across a 4 h reaction, ensuring 100 % yield. We maintain consistent reaction parameters, 10 wt% KOH, 0.2 wt% benzyltributylammonium chloride (BTBAC) at 90 °C, across all material types. Figure 1 illustrates this approach and shows the materials pre- and post-reaction. Various polyester (P) blends were laboratory-made with known pre-consumer fibers, including cotton (C), elastane (L), and nylon (N), to contrast post-consumer samples (Table S2). Specifically, lab-made blends 100:0, 75:25, 50:50, and 25:75 P:C were created. Other pre-consumer woven textile blends investigated include 88:12 P:L, 92:8 C:L, and lab-made blends of 80:20, 50:50, 25:75 P:(N:L). Post-consumer comparisons utilized a 52:48 P:C T-shirt and a 0:100 P:C pair of pants. Lastly, buttons or zippers, often composed of commodity plastics, are considered disruptors29 thus a post-consumer zipper was tested. Figure 1. For TPA, trace contaminants from dyes, additives, or other textile components were identified with Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR), Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR (Mid-IR)), Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA), and Pyrolysis Gas Chromatography Mass Spectrometry (Py-GC-MS) (see SI for instrument specifications). Collected solid fibers (C, N, L) were analyzed utilizing all the above, plus Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIR). For cotton fibers, quality was assessed by the mass recovery, surface chemistry changes (FTIR), degradation temperature changes (TGA), and fiber strength through tensile testing. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was also employed for thermal property analysis. \nResults and Discussion Pre-Consumer Blends\n1.0 Polycotton (P:C) Blends. We performed workshops and discussions with chemical recycling industry partners, where we identified their scaling challenges.29,30 Many chemical recyclers and sorters of textiles emphasized that their recycling systems primarily accept polyester fibers (> 80 %) and are reluctant to accept other synthetic or elastomeric fibers. This led to inquiries about mixed feedstocks such as: cotton fibers could hinder the depolymerization of polyester, other fiber types might degrade and contaminate recovered small molecules, current systems prioritize maximizing small molecules yields due to an established market for recycled TPA but limited infrastructure for recycled cotton, and polyester content below 80 % may be unreliable and contain other materials of interest that impede recycling or make cost-extraction unprofitable. These feedstock limitations could hinder the development of more inclusive textile recycling systems.29,30 \nSpecific TPA yields for each material class are shown in Figure 1b. In short, all P:C blends had an average TPA yield (by mass) of 95.0 % ± 1.6 %, with an average percent recovery of the unreacted solid cotton fibers of 95.9 % ± 0.6 %. Figure 2c shows materials before and after reaction, including recollected TPA and solid fibers. No notable difference in TPA or cotton yield was observed with changes in P:C blend ratio. Collected TPA identity is confirmed via FTIR, Figure 2a, with spectra closely matching commercially available TPA. TGA revealed that the recovered TPA exhibited a similar thermal degradation profile to distributor TPA, with a characteristic lower degradation temperature than the parent polyester fibers, Figure 2b. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Density of States\n1.1 Introduction\nThe density of states (DOS) is essentially the number of different states at a particular energy level that electrons are\nallowed to occupy, i.e. the number of electron states per unit volume per unit energy. Bulk properties such as specific\nheat, paramagnetic susceptibility, and other transport phenomena of conductive solids depend on this function. DOS\ncalculations allow one to determine the general distribution of states as a function of energy and can also determine the\nspacing between energy bands in semi-conductors .\n1.2 Density of States for Waves\nBefore we get involved in the derivation of the DOS of electrons in a material, it may be easier to first consider just an\nelastic wave propagating through a solid.
