Petersen,\n3 Elina Ghimire, Charlie A. Lindberg, Julia G. Murphy, Kexin Li, Steven J. Sibener, Aaron M. Forster,\n4 and Stuart J. Rowan*\nCite This: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsmacrolett.5c00829\n Read Online\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\n5 ABSTRACT: The addition of hard fillers to polymeric networks\n6 allows for enhancement of mechanical properties, generally at the\n7 expense of extensibility. In the case of filled elastomers (such as\n8 tires), the hard particles cause damage to the underlying network\n9 when strained, resulting in severe mechanical hysteresis in cyclic\n10 loading experiments (the Mullins effect). As such, dynamic networks,\n11 which are able to heal damage through exchange reactions, are a\n12 promising candidate for composite matrices. This work investigates\n13 the influence of tunable dynamic bonds at the surface of silica\n14 particles in the presence of a fixed, complementary dynamic network\n15 matrix. The surface chemistry, composed of benzalcyanoacetamide\n16 Michael acceptors, undergoes room temperature, catalyst-free\n17 dynamic exchange with thiols with equilibrium constants (Keq)\n18 that can be manipulated by the electronic nature of the acceptor. Increasing the Keq of the particle surface relative to the dynamic\n19 matrix was found to promote the overall reinforcement of the composites, while also influencing the phase separation behavior of the\n20 matrix. Critically, tensile experiments reveal that ambient dynamic exchange allows for the recovery of network damage as a function\n21 of waiting time between loading cycles.\n22\nC\nomposites, particularly in a polymer context, are useful\n23 for a variety of practical applications by allowing for the\n24 reinforcement of otherwise weak elastomers and networks with\n25 hard fillers.1−4 However, the filler species can also cause\n26 damage to the underlying network, leading to high toughness\n27 at the cost of reversibility.5 This mechanical hysteresis, which is\n28 common in filled rubbers, occurs in part because of poor\n29 compatibility between matrix and filler, leading to a buildup of\n30 stress.6−8 Additionally, higher filler loading can lead to the\n31 aggregation of particles and processing issues.9 Furthermore, to\n32 effectively dissipate stress and improve composite viability the\n33 filler must have appropriate compatibility with the underlying\n34 matrix.10 To that end, it is known that covalent bonding of the\n35 filler to the matrix improves the mechanical properties of\n36 composites.11−14\n37 Dynamic covalent networks (DCNs), which incorporate\n38 dynamic covalent chemistries15,16 such as transesterifica-\n39 tions,17,18 boronic esters,19,20 and disulfides21,22 into cross-\n40 linked networks, give access to self-healing,23,24 reprocess-\n41 ability,25,26 adhesion,27−29 and reconfigurable shape-memory\n42 properties.30−32 Such DCNs have been explored in a wide\n43 array of applications ranging from drug-delivery systems33,34 to\n44 smart/adaptive materials.35,36 However, because these materi-\n45 als can suffer from poor mechanical properties37,38 and long-\n46 term aging,39 research has been directed at studying the\n47 addition of rigid fillers such as silica particles,40 carbon fibers,41\n48and graphene42 to combat these issues. Polymeric materials are\n49known to concentrate stress at an interface when there is a\n50difference in mechanical moduli between components, which\n51remains an ongoing challenge.43−45\n52Dynamic covalent composite networks (DCCNs) are\n53attractive as their adaptive behavior can allow for improved\n54interfacial adhesion between the filler and matrix, as well as\n55enhance reprocessability. In addition, the self-healing ability of\n56DCCNs provides a potential route to repair stress-induced\n57damage in the composite. To that end, recent efforts have been\n58aimed at minimizing premature composite failure by\n59incorporating surface-modified fillers into DCNs where the\n60interface is capable of dissipating stress.46−48 For example,\n61studies by Bowman and co-workers have shown that dynamic\n62bonding of the particle to the underlying network has proven\n63effective to mitigate stress at an interface and improve overall\n64mechanical properties.49−51 The majority of such studies use\n65the same chemistry between the filler and the matrix,52,53\nReceived: December 18, 2025\nRevised: January 30, 2026\nAccepted: February 2, 2026\nLetterpubs.acs.org/macroletters\n© XXXX The Authors. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Exploration of dynamic mechanical analysis for studying degraded \npolymers: dynamic mechanical changes after ultraviolet exposure \nHsiu-Chin Huang a, b*, Donald Hunston a, Lipiin Sung c \na Research Associate, Engineering Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, \nGaithersburg, MD, 20899, USA \nb Department of Chemistry, Krieger School of Arts and Sciences, Johns Hopkins University \nc Materials and Structural Systems Division, Engineering Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, Gaithersburg, MD, 20899, USA \n \n* Corresponding author. E-mail address: hsiuchin.huang@nist.gov (H. Huang) \n \nABSTRACT \nMany techniques have been used to investigate the changes in the mechanical properties of \npolymers induced by photodegradation. In general, the observation of clear variations in bulk \nproperties relies on destructive testing methods. This indicates the difficulties associated with \ndistinguishing the effects of varying degradation levels using less-destructive approaches. This \nstudy employed dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) as a less-destructive approach by applying \na very low strain amplitude and narrowing the scanned temperature range. The temperature \nsweep with multi-frequency scans was limited from the glassy state to the lower portion of the \nglass transition. This approach was designed to minimize modification to the internal molecular \nstructure of the samples while still capturing discernible changes in mechanical behavior. An \namorphous polyester film was used with varying ultraviolet (UV) exposure. Different degrees of \ndegradation were carried out on the polyester using NIST SPHERE (Simulated Photodegradation \nvia High Energy Radiant Exposure). After exposure, samples were stored in an ambient \nenvironment for different durations. The DMA results showed the exposed polyester had higher \nstiffness and less sensitivity to a high-frequency oscillatory strain relative to the unexposed \npolyester. Furthermore, the continuous chemical conversion of unstable intermediates to final \nphotoproducts occurring in the samples after UV exposure was revealed. The chemical property \nwas characterized using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The impact of these \nchemical changes was effectively monitored using DMA by showing dynamic changes in the \nbulk mechanical properties of the samples during post-exposure storage. The dynamic \nmechanical changes facilitated the evaluation of the effects of varying degrees of degradation \nand the differences in internal structure between the exposed samples. This study demonstrated \nthe potential of utilizing DMA to assess polymer degradation, including in severely degraded \npolyester samples, in a less destructive manner compared to test-to-failure methods. \n \n1. Introduction \n\nPolymer photodegradation causes chain cleavage and involves complex chemical reactions that \neventually alter the original chemical structures and produce a decline in the mechanical \nproperties of materials, like impact resistance and toughness. There are many techniques for \ncharacterizing the mechanical properties of degraded polymers. Some focus on the changes \noccurring at the material’s surface, such as nanoindentation [1–3], atomic force microscopy \n(AFM) [4,5], and scratch testing [6,7], as the surface is expected to experience the most severe \nultraviolet (UV) damage. These techniques assess localized degradation without compromising \nthe material’s integrity. However, surface roughness and high material heterogeneities may cause \ninconsistent results, and the localized measurements sometimes do not represent the bulk \nmechanical properties.  \n \nFor evaluating the bulk properties of photodegraded polymers, tensile testing is widely used \n[1,3,7–11]. In this paper, the term tensile testing will refer to an experiment where the sample is \nloaded at room temperature and at a constant displacement rate until failure. The performance of \nUV-degraded samples is typically assessed based on the ultimate tensile strength [1,7–9], the \nelongation at break [3,7–9,11], and the toughness [1], although the entire load-deformation \nprofile is recorded during testing. Young’s modulus and changes in strength within the elastic \nregion are not sensitive indicators of degradation; they exhibit little variation even after \nprolonged exposure. This suggests that plastic deformation to failure is necessary for researchers \nto observe the brittle behavior of degraded polymers. Elastic deformation alone is insufficient to \nfully understand the impact of varying degradation levels on their bulk mechanical properties. \n \nDynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) is another method for measuring the bulk mechanical \nproperties of polymers. Unlike tensile testing, the photodegraded polymer samples are subjected \nto small-amplitude strains, avoiding failure [12]. However, to reveal changes in their properties, \nDMA usually involves scanning across a broad temperature range encompassing the glass \ntransition and rubbery plateau regions, thereby inducing large-scale molecular motions \n[3,4,8,13,14]. The molecular-level structural changes serve a comparable function to \nmacroscopic deformation in tensile testing when assessing the effects of UV exposure. The \nreliance on destructive measurements in both techniques highlights the challenge of detecting \ndistinct variations in bulk properties through less-destructive approaches.  \n \nThis study aimed to explore the feasibility of utilizing DMA as a less-destructive approach for \nevaluating the effects of different degrees of degradation through measurements conducted at a \nvery small strain amplitude and within a narrow temperature range. The material selected for this \nstudy is an amorphous polyester. The maximum temperature applied was restricted to 80 °C, \nthereby limiting the measurement to the lower half of the glass transition region. This approach \nwas designed to minimize molecular chain mobility and reduce structural alterations within the \ntested polymer samples. In this study, the polyester underwent varying exposure periods in an \naccelerated weathering device of NIST 0.5 m SPHERE (Simulated Photodegradation via High \nEnergy Radiant Exposure). Before DMA measurements, these UV-exposed polyester samples \nwere processed by a post-exposure treatment; they were stored in an ambient environment for \ndifferent durations. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy in an attenuated total reflection \n\nmode (ATR-FTIR) was used to characterize the chemical changes after UV exposure. These \nchemical and mechanical results were analyzed to understand the impact of dynamic chemical \nconversions occurring during the post-exposure treatment and the influence of UV exposure time \non the bulk mechanical properties of the polyester. \n \n2. Experimental section \n2.1. Materials \nThe material used in this study was an amorphous polyester film (500 μm) provided by the \nEastman Company¹ and stored under standard laboratory conditions prior to use. ATR-FTIR and \ndifferential scanning calorimeters (DSC) were used to identify the chemical composition and \nconfirm that the films were amorphous. The polyester film was compared to a known \npolyethylene terephthalate (PET) with 30% crystallinity, and their IR spectra were shown in \nFigure S1, which is found in the supplementary information. The ester carbonyl peak of the \namorphous polyester film is at 1713 cm−1, and the peaks related to the crystalline structures of \nPET (1470 cm−1, 1340 cm−1, 1120 cm−1, 968 cm−1, and 847 cm−1 [15,16]) are not observed in \nthe polyester. Moreover, there is no endothermic peak related to the loss of crystalline structure \nshown on the DSC heating curves of the pristine polyester in Figure S1. Consequently, the \npolyester was confirmed to be an amorphous polymer with a similar chemical structure to PET. \n \n2.2. Sample preparation and accelerated weathering \nThe polyester film was cut using dies into dog-bone-shaped specimens 65 mm long and 10 mm \nwide with a 3.2 mm wide neck and 25.4 mm gauge length for tensile test according to ASTM \nstandard D638 (Type V specimen [17]) and rectangle-shaped strips of 5.5 mm ± 0.1 mm wide for \nDMA. For the exposure process, the specimens were mounted on a Teflon sheet in a sample \nholder, in which a maximum of 15 strips could be aligned in parallel and exposed evenly under \nUV radiation. The samples were UV treated on only one side (length × width). The front-side \nsurface faces the UV light source and is the exclusive surface exposed to UV radiation, whereas \nthe back-side surface faces the Teflon sheet. Details for the sample holder and the layout of the \nenvironmental chambers for UV exposure can be found in the previous publication [11]. \n \nAccelerated weathering was conducted in the NIST 2 m SPHERE for the tensile test specimens \nand in the NIST 0.5 m SPHERE for the DMA specimens. A 20 d exposure with full-intensity UV \nradiation in the 2 m SPHERE equals one year of sunlight exposure in South Florida [18]. The 0.5 \nm SPHERE is still in development; it possesses the same functional capabilities as the 2 m \nSPHERE while delivering higher irradiance. Detailed information on the 2 m SPHERE has been \nreported elsewhere [9,11,19].  \n \nFull-intensity UV light at 295 nm to 400 nm wavelength range (≈ 160 W/m² and ≈ 518 W/m² \nfor the 2 m and 0.5 m SPHEREs, respectively) was used for both tensile test samples and DMA \nsamples. The tensile test samples were exposed at 50 °C, under a dry condition (≈ 0 % relative \nhumidity (RH)), and with various exposure times. The longest period was 8 d; the accumulated \nUV dose is around 111 MJ/m². The DMA samples were exposed at 50 °C, under (5 ± 1) % RH, \nwith three major periods (accumulated dose)—6 d and 20 h (≈ 306 MJ/m²), 11 d and 20.5 h (≈ \n\n531 MJ/m²), and 24 d and 12 h (≈ 1097 MJ/m²)—as well as a longest period of 36 d (≈ 1611 \nMJ/m²). To simplify the days, this paper used 7d, 12d, and 25d to describe the three major \nperiods. After being exposed for the designated period, the DMA samples were removed from \nthe chambers and stored under the same conditions as the unexposed polyester. They were kept \nin plastic Petri dishes covered with aluminum foil to avoid light before measurements. The \nstorage was considered a post-exposure treatment. The storage durations included 0 d, 1 d, 8 d, \nand 17 d and were simplified as 0d, 1d, 8d, and 17d in this study. If it is \nequal, then the trial wavefunction must coincide with the ground state eigenfunction of the \nSchrödinger equation, and the expectation value of the energy will obviously be the ground \nstate eigenvalue. \nThe variational principle has both practical and conceptual consequences; e.g. it \nallows us to find good approximate solutions to problems we would not be able to solve \nexactly if formulated as a differential equation. It also allows us to study most many-electron \nproblems using trial wavefunctions that are simple  linear combinations of atomic orbitals. It \nactually provides a justification for the concept of “hybridization” of atomic orbitals, and allows \nto explore ground and excited states of molecules and solids as simple linear combinations of \natomic orbitals (LCAO for molecules, “tight-binding” for solids). \nFor this problem we’ll go back to the hydrogen atom, and will consider a trial \nwavefunction Ψ= C exp (−αr ) ; different values of α  will correspond to different shapes of α \nΨ  (i.e. different decays towards large r). α can be considered a “tunable handle” that allows α \nus to explore all possible wavefunctions in a class (here, that of simple decaying exponentials \nas a function of the polar coordinate r). Closure: If A and B are two elements in G, then A☼B is also in G.\n2. Associativity: For all elements in G, (A☼B) ☼C==A☼ (B☼C).\n3. Identity: There is an identity element I such that I☼A=A☼I=A for \nevery element A in G.\n4. Inverse: There is an inverse or reciprocal of each element. \nTherefore, the set must contain an element B=inv(A) such \nthat A☼inv(A)=inv(A) ☼A=I for each element of G.\n\n3.012 Fundamentals of Materials Science: Bonding - Nicola Marzari (MIT, Fall 2005)\nExamples\n• Integer numbers, and addition\n• Integer numbers, and multiplication\n• Real numbers, and multiplication\n• Rotations around an axis by 360/n \n\nFigure 17.3\nImage of mirror planes in a water molecule removed for copyright reasons.\nSee Engel, T., and  P. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Depth Profiling Chemical Changes in Chemically Amplified Resists for EUV Lithography\nDaniel F. Sunday,1 Peter Dudenas,1 Priyanka Ketkar,1 Julia Murphy,1 Cherno Jaye,2 R. Joseph Kline,1 Gurpreet Singh,3 Eungnak Han,3 Lauren Doyle,3 Florian Gstrein3  \nMaterials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg MD, 20899\nMaterials Measurement Science Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg MD, 20899 \nIntel, Hillsboro, OR, USA\n\nAbstract\n Photoresist patterning for semiconductor manufacturing is encountering new challenges with the move to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, driven by smaller pitches, thinner resists and fewer photons. Obtaining information about the nanoscale distribution of chemical changes in the resist will provide key information to optimize processing and resist development. Soft X-rays provide sensitivity to chemical functional groups at key atomic absorption edges, including carbon, oxygen and fluorine. By conducting specular reflectivity measurements at these energies, we can track the chemical depth profiles in a resist. This process is demonstrated by characterizing the optical constant profiles, which are proportional to the concentration of chemical bonds in a film at soft X-ray energies, of an EUV resist coated on a cross-linked polystyrene (CLPS) mat. The resist was exposed to blanket exposures with different doses and measured at different stages of the process, including post-exposure but before the bake, after the post-exposure bake, and after development. Segregation of resist components was observed in the as-coated case films, with a fluorinated component aggregating at the film surface. Stratification of the chemical changes that occur in the film is observed after exposure, but before the bake. The magnitude of this stratification is dose dependent. After a post-exposure bake the stratification is no longer observed and the optical constant profile is uniform with the exception of the fluorinated components. These results are complemented by near edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy obtained with an imaging microscope. Finally, we also examine the CLPS mat before and after the process, and observe evidence for chemical changes in the CLPS, with the possibility of residual resist components residing in the film after development.  \n\nKeywords: Photoresist, Metrology, Reflectivity, Soft X-rays, Directed Self-Assembly\n\nIntroduction\nThe implementation of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography has resulted in new challenges for photoresists.1,2 Chemically amplified resists (CARs) are still the state of the art for high volume manufacturing, but the multicomponent nature of CARs is leading to new concerns about how the compositional heterogeneity can impact resist performance.3,4 CARs typically consist of at least three components, a polymer with a labile group that can be altered during exposure to switch the solubility, a photoacid generator (PAG) which catalyzes the chemical change, and a quencher which neutralizes the acid, thereby limiting its diffusion. Differences in interactions parameters and surface energies between each of these components will result in non-uniform component distributions in both the lateral and vertical directions.5 EUV patterning will produce smaller pitches  with thinner resists due to the reduced depth of focus increasing the role that compositional heterogeneity plays in resist performance. Due to a combination of limited material absorbance and flux from EUV sources, the combination of these materials’ stochastics with the photon stochastics means that pattern roughness driven will be a key issue going forward.6 Furthermore, thinner resist stacks means that interface effects will become increasingly important and understanding resist-underlayer interactions will be key to optimizing patterning processes. Characterizing these interactions can be challenging, as it requires sensitivity to changes in nanoscale chemical distributions.7 \nIn this study resonant soft X-ray reflectivity (RSoXR) will be used to characterize changes in the optical constant depth profiles of a CAR at different stages in the patterning process and relate those results to the changing chemical depth profiles of the components in the film. Reflectivity measurements will be complemented by near edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy, which provides important information about the chemical changes at the films surface. The target system will consist of a CAR on a cross-linked polymer mat (CLPS), where understanding interactions between the resist and CLPS are important for optimizing directed self-assembly (DSA), with DSA considered as a complementary process flow to EUV lithography.8,9 \nBecause photoresists are complex blends many different characterization techniques are used to investigate how exposure and processing results in changes to the chemical structure. Infrared spectroscopy (IR) is highly effective for understanding changes in certain chemical bonds but has limited resolution to interrogate how those chemistries are spatially distributed. Increasingly IR is being used in-situ in order to carefully study the effects of oxygen or moisture on resist performance, particularly for metal oxide resists.10 Time of flight (TOF) secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) has also become an important tool; TOF-SIMS offers exceptional sensitivity to low concentrations of components in a depth profiling modality, although achieving sub 10 nm resolution is still challenging. There are also variations on the technique which provide insight into the lateral distributions of components based on analysis of the statistics from multiple impacts from nano-projectiles.11–14 \nSoft X-ray based measurements provide additional tools to broaden the existing toolbox. Soft X-rays border the EUV spectrum and contain absorption edges for many of the key resist components, including the K-edges for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine. The carbon spectra in particular contains fine features where the absorption peaks for different functional groups are shifted to different energies and are clearly differentiable in the spectra.15 The magnitude of the absorption peak for a given functional group will be proportional to the concentration of that functional group. As a result changing soft X-ray energies in a measurement allows you to probe both the type of chemistry in the system and also the concentration of specific functional groups. This is often measured by collecting a NEXAFS spectra; this can be done by exposing the beam to X-rays at either the magic angle (55° from the surface), where the spectra are sensitive to the composition, or at multiple incident angles in order to provide sensitivity to both composition and molecular orientation.16 There are several modes in which NEXAFS measurements can be conducted,  including measuring electron yield  and measuring the transmission through a sample. Electron yield modes are surface sensitive, reaching a depth of only a few nm, with some control over the depth sensitivity being achievable when biasing the detector voltage to reject lower energy electrons in partial electron yield (PEY) mode. Transmission absorption measurements provide sensitivity to the bulk of the film, but because of the high absorbance of soft X-rays need to be conducted on either a free-standing film, which can be challenging to prepare, or on a thin membrane. NEXAFS has been used to examine resists in the past, characterizing both surface segregation of individual components and monitoring changes in chemical bonds after exposure and development.17–19  A challenge for photoresist research is that soft X-rays have the potential to alter the samples being measured. The development of a novel soft X-ray microscope called the Large Area Rapid Imaging Analytical Tool (LARIAT) provides a route for low dose measurements of photoresists, where concerns about altering the photoresist due to exposure to soft X-rays can be significantly alleviated.20  \nA different mode for utilizing soft X-rays is RSoXR, where specular reflectivity measurements are conducted at a series of different incident angles for a given energy near an absorption edge. This measurement is a variant of standard hard X-ray reflectivity, where fitting the reflectivity curve enables determination of the electron density profile, which can be related back to composition. Uniquely relating electron densities to composition is difficult for organic materials as there is often little differentiation between the electron density of different components in an organic material. Conducting reflectivity measurements at energies near an absorption edge provides a means to combine the nanometer scale spatial resolution of X-ray reflectivity measurements with the sensitivity to specific chemical bonds depending on the chosen X-ray energy. With an appropriate set of references to understand how changing concentrations impact the optical constants for a given material, this depth profile can be directly converted to a concentration profile of components in a film, or even a distribution of functional groups.21,22 This approach has been demonstrated to investigate the interface roughness between high-χ block copolymers (BCPs),23 the distribution of components with complex architectures,24 the additives in BCPs,21,25 and the molecular orientation in thin films.26–28 \nThe underlayer examined in this study is an CLPS mat, which is used as part of the guiding pattern for DSA. The DSA of BCPs has been explored as a patterning technique that takes advantage of the information chemically imprinted in the block copolymer (pitch and interface roughness) via the choice of polymer chemistry and molecular weight.29,30 Prior to the integration of EUV patterning, DSA was primarily explored as a density multiplication technique with the goal of a 3x or 4x reduction in the patterned pitch.31–33 Now that EUV patterning can produce patterns commensurate with the periodicity of BCPs, DSA is being considered as a roughness remediation technique, where a rough pattern can be made with the EUV tool, and the BCP “heals” the roughness.34,35 This technique has the potential to significantly reduce the dose required from the EUV tool, resulting in a significant increase in throughput at the costly EUV patterning step. The BCP needs to have nearly equivalent surface energies between the two blocks at the target annealing temperature, and the patterned surface needs to have different affinities for the two components.36 When patterning with polystyrene-b-poly(methyl methacrylate) (PS-b-PMMA), the most common polymer explored for DSA, the process typically uses an CLPS mat, which has a greater affinity for polystyrene, and a neutral brush backfilling the region between the CLPS stripes.33 For density multiplication, the neutrality of the backfilled brush is a key feature to ensure vertical orientation of the BCP throughout the pattern.37,38 However, for roughness remediation the optimal pattern structure in terms of the brush chemistry and composition has not been fully explored. In this study we examine whether any of the components from the resist will diffuse into the CLPS, which would potentially alter the CLPS surface energy and could lead to buried defects in the film. \nMaterials and Methods\nCrosslinkable polystyrene was spin coated to achieve ~6nm film and baked under nitrogen environment at 250 °C degree for 30 min. Chemically amplified resists were exposed using a custom EUV flood-exposure metrology cluster tool. The coated wafers were loaded into a vacuum chamber where an array of sites 1 cm in diameter were exposed with 13.5nm light at the desired doses. Once removed from the chamber, post processing steps were completed.\n\nFigure 1: Samples were prepa

[{"suffix": "", "text": "1 RheologyandMicrostructuralBehaviorofSemidiluteSuspensions\n2 ofSemiflexibleRodsacrossFiveDecades ofShearRate\n3 PaulF.Salipante,* SteveKuei,RyanP.Murphy,JeffreyA.Fagan,ChristopherM.Sims,\n4 KatieM.Weigandt,andStevenD.Hudson*\nCiteThis: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.macromol.4c02675\n ReadOnline\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations\n5 ABSTRACT: Rod-like particles are efficient rheology modifiers and are\n6 commonly found in a variety of biological and industrially relevant\n7 suspensions, from biofilaments to worm-like surfactant micelles. These\n8 suspensions display strong shear-thinning behavior, and ongoing efforts\n9 aim to understand the microstructural changes of these fluids: how they\n10 depend upon the properties of the suspended particles and how these\n11 changes manifest in the resulting rheology. With suspensions of fd\n12 bacteriophage as a model monodisperse rod system, we use capillary\n13 microrheometry and flow birefringence to determine rheological\n14 behavior across nearly six decades of shear rate up to 6× 105 s−1, at various semidilute concentrations. A single, and surprisingly\n15 large, primary fitting parameter accounting for the characteristic distance of hydrodynamic interactions is consistent with viscosity\n16 data up to very high shear rates. These results may prompt other work to understand the mechanics of these interactions.\n17 ■INTRODUCTION\n18 The flow behavior and stability of complex fluids in shear are\n19 commonly studied; this is particularly true of suspensions of\n20 long filaments due to their ability to efficiently viscosify. Strong\n21 shear thinning, and in some cases flow instabilities, have been\n22 observed in filamentous suspensions, for example, of rigid\n23 filaments such as actin,1 semiflexible polymers,2,3 and materials\n24 with transitory fibrous and sometimes branched structures.4\n25 There are ongoing efforts to understand how microstructure\n26 drives bulk flow dynamics.\n27 In the simplest abstractions to theoretically describe their\n28 rheological behavior, these filaments can be treated as either\n29 coiled (when flexible) or rod-like (when stiff). The focus of\n30 this work is rod-like filaments. At rest, rod-like fluids have clear\n31 equilibrium phase transitions as a function of rod concen-\n32 tration.5 However, when subjected to flow, the rod orientations\n33 are affected, which leads to shifts to higher concentrations in\n34 the dilute, semidilute, and concentrated transition regimes and\n35 introduces the possibility of a mechanical origin of\n36 transition.6−10 These microstructural changes produce strong\n37 non-Newtonian rheological behavior and can potentially\n38 generate dynamical instabilities, such as shear bands.11\n39 Theoretical approaches begin with Jeffery’s calculations for\n40 the equations of motion of dilute ellipsoids in shear flow.12 In\n41 higher concentration suspensions, two realms of interparticle\n42 interactions, excluded volume and hydrodynamics, have been\n43 explored. The direct excluded-volume interactions limit the\n44 diffusive motion and decrease the effective diffusivity.\n45 Calculating the effects of these two types of interactions has\n46mainly been a separate line of research. Furthermore, it has\n47been argued that hydrodynamic interactions may be neglected\n48when the rods are long and thin.13 It will nevertheless be\n49necessary in this report to use both of these interactions\n50together.\n51Concerning colloidal Brownian suspensions,7,8 the Fokker−\n52Planck equation describes the competition between shear and\n53rotational diffusion coefficient through an orientational\n54distribution function (ODF). As rod concentration is increased\n55to reach the semidilute regime, however, neighboring rods can\n56hinder each other’s rotational freedom, leading to the need to\n57include a pair-correlation function to properly describe the\n58relationships between the structure and dynamics. Lang et al.14\n59compared two promising theoretical calculations for rigid-rod\n60fluids with measurements from rheology with small-angle\n61neutron scattering (rheoSANS). Assuming a pair-correlation\n62function that is independent of shear rate, Lang et al.14 use this\n63ODF to derive a relationship between the microscopic\n64orientational ordering tensor and macroscopic measurables\n65such as the zero-shear viscosity η0 and the onset of shear\n66thinning. It outlines critical challenges and \nopportunities related to polymer -based “soft” materials in \nadvanced semiconductor packaging, with emphasis on polymer \nscience, measurement science (metrology), and the strategic \ndevelopment of Research-Grade Test Materials (RGTMs).  These \nefforts, led by the NIST CHIPS team, aim to advance the \nfundamental understanding of structure –property–processing \nrelationships, promote standardized guidelines and innovative \nmethods for material characterization, and accelerate the \ndevelopment, qualification, and adoption of next -generation \npackaging materials.  The Perspective also distills key insights \nfrom the panel discussion with industry experts, emphasizing the \nneed for close collaboration among materials scientists, process \nengineers, and metrology experts to enable a holistic strategy, \nfurther highlighting the importance of cross -sector partnerships \namong industry, academia, and government to address pressing \nchallenges in packaging materials and processes. \n \nIndex Terms — Advanced semiconductor packaging, c ure \nkinetics, heterogeneous integration (HI), metrology, m oisture \n \nThis work was supported in part by the National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, U.S. Department of Commerce, under Award  \n# 70NANB24H283. INTRODUCTION \nOLYMERIC materials—soft, versatile compounds \ncomposed of long, flexible, and repeating molecular \nchains—have been used in semiconductor packaging \nfor decades.  Since the early 1960s, polymeric packaging \nmaterials have primarily served a straightforward function: \nmechanically encapsulating chips and securely attaching them \nto circuit boards [1].  Historically, polymer -related challenges, \nsuch as coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch and \nmoisture absorption (the so- called “popcorning” effect [2]), \nwere primarily associated with mechanical reliability concerns \nrather than directly affecting device performance.  Many of \nthe polymeric materials introduced decades ago, including \nepoxies, silicones, and polyimides, remain remarkably similar \nto those still widely used today.  They continue to fulfill \ncritical roles such as encapsulants, underfills, molding \ncompounds, adhesives, thermal interface materials (TIMs), \nand substrate dielectric layers ( Fig. 1 ), providing essential \nelectrical insulation, mechanical support, and environmental \nprotection for advanced packages [3, 4]. \nToday, the semiconductor industry is undergoing a \ntransformative shift towards heterogeneous integration \n(HI) [5] to overcome the limitations of traditional transistor \nscaling and achieve enhanced performance, miniaturization, \nand cost efficiency.  Over the next decade, emerging \ntechnologies—including 5G/6G wireless networks, artificial \nintelligence (AI), and high -performance computing (HPC), \nwill rely heavily on advanced packaging enabled by HI [6].  \nAs packaging architectures evolve into increasingly intricate \n3D structures with finer feature sizes, smaller gap heights, \nflexible chiplets, and diverse materials interfaces, the demands \non polymeric materials have become significantly more \nstringent.  A broad spectrum of properties —including \nmechanical, thermal, electrical, and chemical —must now be \nsimultaneously optimized.  For instance, the transition from \nrigid chips to flexible electronic systems demands polymers \nwith enhanced flexibility, toughness, and long- term fatigue \nresistance [7].  Likewise, 5G/6G applications require precise  \nP \n\n2 \n> REPLACE THIS LINE WITH YOUR MANUSCRIPT ID NUMBER (DOUBLE -CLICK HERE TO EDIT) < \n \n \nFig. 1. Polymer-based materials used in advanced packaging. \n(a) An overmolded flip chip package. (b) A lidded flip chip \npackage. \n \ncontrol over dielectric properties to minimize transmission \nloss and maintain signal integrity in high -frequency operating \nenvironments [8, 9].  Furthermore, integrating a wide range of \nmaterials into complex 3D multi- chip structures presents \nsignificant challenges in materials selection, process \noptimization, and interconnect reliability [10]. \nThese evolving requirements underscore the need to re -\nexamine legacy packaging resins and develop high-performance \npolymer-based materials tailored for next -generation \ntechnologies [11].  Modern formulations often involve multiple \nresins, multifunctional additives, and inorganic fillers, \nsignificantly increasing the complexity of material design and \nmanufacturing.  This is further compounded by the industry’s \nheavy reliance on overseas material suppliers [12], limited \ntransparency into material composition and performance data, \nand inadequate characterization standards and metrology \nmethods, all of which create additional hurdles in materials \ndevelopment and implementation.  At the same time, \nlongstanding challenges—such as thermomechanical reliability \nconcerns intrinsic to polymer behavior—persist and are further \namplified in the context of HI. \nAddressing these multifaceted challenges requires a robust \nand integrated materials science framework underpinned by \nadvanced and precise metrology techniques [13].  This \nPerspective explores key challenges and opportunities related \nto polymer -based materials in advanced semiconductor \npackaging, with a focus on polymer science fundamentals, \nmeasurement science (metrology), and the strategic \nimplementation of Research -Grade Test Materials (RGTMs).  \nThese components are essential for deepening the fundamental \nunderstanding of structure -property-processing relationships \nin complex polymer formulations, promoting standardized \nguidelines and innovative methods for material \ncharacterization, and accelerating the development, \nqualification, and adoption of next -generation packaging \nmaterials. \nII. POLYMER-BASED MATERIALS IN ADVANCED PACKAGING \nGiven the diverse roles and growing functional demands of \npolymer-based materials in advanced packaging applications, \ncareful optimization of their chemical composition, \nmechanical properties, thermal stability, and dielectric \nperformance is essential.  In this section, we briefly revisit key \nprinciples in polymer science —spanning both polymer \nphysics and chemistry—that lay the groundwork for \nunderstanding structure -property-processing relationships in \nthese materials. \nThe glass transition temperature ( Tg) is often reported as a \nsingle value in material datasheets —but the underlying \nphysics is far more complex and intriguing [14].  As Nobel \nLaureate P. W. Anderson famously remarked, the glass \ntransition is “perhaps the deepest and most interesting \nunsolved problem in solid -state physics [15].”  T g marks the \ntemperature range over which a crosslinked polymer gradually \ntransitions from a rigid, glassy state to a soft, rubbery state, \ndictating the material’s physical and mechanical properties, \nprocessing conditions, and application temperature limits [16].   \nHowever, the glass transition as measured in the laboratory \nis not a thermodynamically defined phase change; rather, it is \na kinetic phenomenon that arises from the dramatic slowdown \nof molecular motions as the material cools and falls out of \nequilibrium [14, 16, 17].  As such, T g depends on the intrinsic \npolymer structure as well as external factors such as timescale \n(rate or frequency), thermal history (how the glass is formed), \nand measurement method (i.e., the property being probed).  \nThe value of T g increases by approximately (3 to 5)  °C for \nevery order -of-magnitude increase in cooling rate [17, 18] .  \nFurthermore, Tg can shift under real -world operating \nenvironments—through mechanisms such as physical \naging [19], stress relaxation, and moisture ingress, which alter \nthe polymer relaxation dynamics and effectively modify its \nglass transition behavior. \nThe glass transition has many manifestations, including \nchanges in heat capacity, specific volume, modulus, viscosity, \nand dielectric constant.  Each manifestation is measured by a \ndifferent technique.  Thus, in practice, T g can vary \nsignificantly depending on how it is measured— differential \nscanning calorimetry (DSC), dynamic mechanical analysis \n(DMA), rheometry, thermomechanical analysis (TMA), \ndilatometry, or dielectric analysis (DEA) each detect different \nproperty changes [20].  For example, Tg values from DMA \nloss tangent peaks can be (15 to 20)  °C higher than those \nmeasured by dilatometry on cooling at 1 °C/min—a \ndiscrepancy that can lead to substantial error when predicting \nrate-dependent processes  [21]. Subscripts refer to which \ncomponent (e.g., “Zn” or “A”) is being described. Superscripts (e.g., “g” or “s”) refer to \nthe phase. Some superscripts include a naught (e.g., “o, g”), which means that the \ncomponent in that phase is at a specific reference state (typically P = 1 atm, and the \ntemperature of interest) as opposed to at any given pressure. You don’t need to know the \nbook’s notation, but if you want to, and if recitation didn’t clear it up, then please see me. \nHad trouble understanding the Gibbs energies that are unique for each state. Okay, I \nthink this was referring to the initial state and final state in the mixing problem. I \ncompared this process to subtracting product and reactant formation free energies in a \nchemical reaction process. Since molar Gibbs energy is the same as chemical potential, \nthe Gibbs energy of the two states is the sum of µA in the solution and µB in the solution \n(final state), versus µA in its pure state and µB in its pure state (intitial, separated state). \nAs you saw in problem 2, chemical potential of the same component in its pure state \nversus in a solution are not equal. Hope that helps. \nHow do we know what expressions like (dF/dT)V = -S are?  For first derivatives, it comes \nright from your state function expressions. On the one hand, dF = -SdT - PdV. On the \nother hand, dF(T, V) = (δF/δT)V dT + (δF/δV)T dV (I’m using deltas instead of dels so I \ndon’t have to go into equation editor; yes, sometimes I’m lazy). You just compare those \ntwo expressions, so make sure you have them in your notes for an exam. For the second \nderivatives, you have to do a little more work, but basically they will come out to either \nan expression using heat capacity or one using compressibility, and you can learn and \nnote down those two patterns. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Ferroelectricity\nFerroelectricity is a property observed in certain materials characterized by the presence of a spontaneous electric\npolarization without the presence of an electric field, much like how ferromagnetism is characterized by a spontaneous,\npermanent magnetic field. A subclass of piezoelectric and pyroelectric materials, ferroelectric materials are\nnoncentrosymmetric crystals, where some atoms in the unit cell are misplaced to create a permanent electric dipole due\nto the imbalances observed in the distribution of electric charge. Barium titanate (BaTiO ), a common ferroelectric\nmaterial with the perovskite crystal structure, portrays this property by displacing the titanium ion at body center\n0.05Å along the +b direction and the oxygen atoms 0.08Å in the -b direction, creating a slight dipole moment (figure 1).\nThis displacement, coupled with the relatively small size of the Ti  ion, makes it difficult for the titanium ion to bond\nwith all of the oxygen ions.\nFigure : : Crystal structure of barium titanate below its Curie temperature. Green circles represent Ba2+ ions, blue\ncircles O2- ions, and the red circle represents the Ti4+ ion.\nCrystal Structure and Material Preparation\nFerroelectricity is a displacive phenomenon where ions within the unit cell are placed asymmetrically, creating dipole\nmoments. These asymmetries may form in two different ways, either displacively or by order-disorder. Ferroelectrics\nwith the perovskite crystal structure, like barium titanate (BaTiO ) and lead titanate (PbTiO ), are commonly\ndisplacive-type ferroelectrics, where at temperatures below the Curie temperature, ions are displaced slightly from\nequilibrium to create an asymmetry in the electron population densities, which leads to the permanent dipole moment.\nIn order-disorder ferroelectrics, like NaNO , the dipoles are present at all temperatures, but are randomly oriented\nabove the Curie temperature. The dipoles align after the temperature is brought below the threshold.\nFigure : a & 2b: Representations of the polar axes of a ferromagnetic material before (left) and after (right) heat\ntreatment under an applied field.\nWhile the individual unit cells of a ferroelectric material possess their own dipole moment, without the presence of an\nexternal electric field these moments do not align with each other to produce any long-range symmetry (figure 2a).\nWithin individual grains the polar axes are aligned but across the bulk of the sample there is no net polarization. At\nsufficiently high temperatures for the grains to break down, and in the presence of an electric field, the polar axes may\nrealign to match the field. If the material is cooled under this field, the polar axes remain aligned, thus forming a\nsubstance that has an observable, spontaneous electric dipole (figure 2b). In the case of barium titanate, the titanium ion\nis displaced in the direction of the electric field and the oxygen ions displaced against it, creating the dipole. With\nsubsequent inputs of alternating electric fields, the dipoles realign by shifting the titanium ion to the other side of the\nunit cell.\n3\n4+\n3 3\n3\n9/30/26, 2:10 PM Ferroelectricity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Ferroelectricity 1/3\n\nProperties\nFerroelectricity is characterized by the presence of a spontaneous electric dipole while not exposed to an external\nelectric field, much like how ferromagnetism is characterized by a spontaneous magnetic dipole. Above a certain\ntemperature, called the Curie temperature (T ), ferroelectric materials lose this polarization and behave like\nparamagnetic or diamagnetic materials. At the Curie temperature, the energy within the crystal allows the ions to\narrange themselves in a stable equilibrium, eliminating the polarization caused by the displacement of one or more\nions.\nFigure : : The hysteretic relationship between applied electric field and ferroelectric polarization. At the origin, the\nferroelectric material is unpolarized and in a zero field. Applying a positive E-field polarizes it positively until its\npolarity changes linearly with applied field. Applying the reverse field does not unpolarize the ferroelectric until it\nreaches a certain magnitude, where the left-side of the loop reaches P=0. (source: commons.wikimedia.org)\nThe change in polarity of ferroelectrics with an applied electric field is observed to follow a simple hysteresis loop\n(figure 3). If the crystal structure of a ferroelectric has been broken down in high heat and not in the presence of an\nelectric field., it is unpolarized as seen in the origin of figure 2. With an applied field, the polarization quickly\napproaches a point where the polarization is linearly proportional to the applied electric field. If an opposite electric\nfield is applied, the polarity does not change significantly until the field reaches a relatively large magnitude, and the\npolarity of the ferroelectric reverses and levels off. This loop can be repeated numerous times to alter the polarity of the\nferroelectric, often to the order of 10 cycles depending on the material.\nThe polarization of ferroelectrics is a non-volatile property once the polarization is set. External electric fields are\nunable to change the polarization direction unless the magnitude of the field reaches the required threshold, and\nmagnetic fields have negligible effects on the electronic polarization observed.\nApplications\nMany application of ferroelectric materials utilize the polarization reversal, or switching effect, that the materials\nexperience when exposed to powerful electric fields. This switching effect is utilized in digital memory applications, as\nreversing the polarity of the material allows for the creation of 0 and 1 bits in computing. As the polarization of\nferroelectrics is nonvolatile and does not require extra input to remain polarized, ferroelectrics possess an advantage\nover traditional semiconductors when it comes to digital storage. Dielectric random access memory (DRAM) in a\ncomputer relies on electricity to maintain its storage, and unexpected shutdowns or power outages cause loss of\ninformation, allowing the short-term memory modules in computer to behave like back-up long-term memory banks.\nThis property also makes ferroelectrics ideal for electronic access cards, like keycards or transit cards, as their polarized\nstates are not disrupted by magnetic fields and do not decay over time. The ability to maintain its polarization without\noutside input also means ferroelectric random access memory (FeRAM) only requires energy when it is read or written,\nwhile DRAM requires a constant energy input to maintain the information stored. The energy-saving possibilities of\nFeRAM are therefor highly researched and a leading reason for the development of more efficient FeRAM assemblies.\nThe hysteretic behavior of the polarization of ferroelectrics also makes them very good candidates for alternatives to\ndielectrics in capacitors. As the polarization of ferroelectrics can reach very high levels, as well as the possibility of\ntuning the strength of the dipole according to the strength of the input electric field. As dielectric capacitors cannot be\ntuned like ferroelectric capacitors, the latter are capable of being made much smaller in comparison to the former.\nQuestions\n1. At T>T , a certain ferroelectric material displays no ferroelectric properties, and through sensitive imaging\ntechniques, it is determined that the material displays a perfect perovskite crystal structure. When T<T , imaging\nreveals that the ions within the crystal have shifted slightly and no longer indicate a perfect perovskite crystal, as the\nions at body-center have shifted slightly towards individual sides of the unit cells. What kind of ferroelectric phase\ntransformation is observed in this material?\n2. You have grown a BaTiO  crystal and apply an electric field to it in order to produce a net dipole. However, when\nyou try to measure the moment there is nothing to be seen. Assuming that your measurement equipment is working\nproperly, what might be the issue with your sample and how might you go about fixing it?\n3. A brand new ferroelectric has just recently been discovered and you are tasked with determining its viability as a\nnew material to make FeRAM out of. You develop a prototype device and subject it to conditions (rate of electric\nCurie\n16 \nC\nC\n3\n9/30/26, 2:10 PM Ferroelectricity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Ferroelectricity 2/3\n\ninput, temperature) that RAM modules often experience in computers. The ferroelectric holds up well in tests in the\nbeginning, but loses all ability to store information as tests continue. What might be happening to the ferroelectric in\nthese tests to eliminate the polarizability of the FeRAM module?\nAnswers\n1. This is indicative of a displacive phase transformation.\n2. The grains within the sample may not have their polar axes aligned, so attempts to polarize it are not effective.\nIncreasing the temperature, exposing the substance to an electric field, and then cooling it while in the field will\nalign the polar axes to a certain degree, allowing them to produce a net electric dipole moment.\n3. Ferroelectrics can be polarized while they are operating at temperatures below their Curie temperature, where the\nions within the material have enough energy to combine and form symmetric crystals. As the test continues, the\ntemperature increases past the ferroelectric's Curie temperature and can no longer be polarized.\nReferences\n1. Damjanovic, D. (2006). [{"suffix": "", "text": "Effect of Ionic Liquids on the Structure of Ionomer Inks\nTyler B. Martin* and Kimber Stamm Masias*\nCite This: Macromolecules 2025, 58, 8288−8294\n ReadOnline\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: This study investigates the impactof ionic liquids (ILs) on the structure\nand performance of catalyst inks used in proton exchange membrane fuel cells\n(PEMFCs). Using contrast variation small-angle neutron scattering (CV-SANS), we\nelucidate the structural interactions between ionomers, Pt/C catalyst particles, and ILs.\nThe analysis reveals that IL composition significantly influences the arrangement of\nionomersandtheirinteractionswithotherinkcomponents.Inparticular,oneoftheILs\n([BMIM][C4]) exhibited stronger associations with both ionomer and catalyst\nparticles, resulting in reduced availability of platinum catalytic sites and lower PEMFC\nperformance. These findings demonstrate the structural origins of electrochemical\nperformance variations, providing insights into the design of improved ionic liquid formulations for enhanced fuel cell efficiency.\n■INTRODUCTION\nProton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFC) convert\nchemicalenergyfromthereactionofH2 andO2 intoelectricity,\npresenting a low emission route to a carbon neutral energy\nsource. A major component of a PEMFC is the membrane\nelectrodeassembly(MEA)whichconsistsofgasdiffusionlayers,\ncatalyst layers, and the polymer electrolyte membrane. While\nreducingtheunitcostbyreplacingtheplatinum(Pt)catalystisa\nlargeandongoingfocusofresearchers,otherchallengespersist.\nEfficiency of PEMFCs is hampered by energy losses at the\ncathode during the oxygen reduction reaction,1 opening the\ndoor to investigation of non-Pt catalysts,2 shape-controlled\ncatalysts,3 alternative ionomers for proton transport,4 and\nimproving the triple phase boundary between carbon, Pt, and\nionomer.\nSearching for ever-better performance, researchers have\ninvestigated the inclusion of ionic liquids (ILs) in the ionomer\ncomplexwiththeaimofimprovingtheefficiencyofO2 diffusion\nthrough the polymer by modifying the ionomer-Pt catalyst\ninterface.5−8 Severalinvestigationshaveshowntheinclusionof\nILsimprovestheO2 transportkineticsaswellastheaccessibility\nofPtcatalystsites.Severalelectrochemicaloriginsforthechange\nin performance can be proposed, including changes in\nhydrophobicity that impact proton transport or variations in\ntheO2 transportkinetics.Structuraloriginsfortheperformance\nimprovement, such as changes in the association between the\nionomer side chain thiol groups and the Pt catalyst, are also\nplausible.Theseexplanationshavebeenconsideredinthedried\ncatalyst layer of the MEA but theimpact of including the ionic\nliquidintothecatalystinkusedtocreatetheMEAhavenotbeen\nexplored.\nInordertofabricateafunctionalMEA,allcomponentsofthe\nMEAaremixedandsuspendedinacatalystinkusingwaterand\nalcohol as solvents. The structure and eventual function of the\nMEAisdirectlyimpactedbythepropertiesoftheink,including\nthe coating of the ionomer onto the carbon-supported Pt\ncatalyst (Pt/C) and the subsequent aggregation of the catalyst\nparticles themselves. Identifying the impact of the ILs on the\nordering and aggregation of the ink components will allow a\nbetter understanding of the structural rearrangements of the\nrealized MEA thatmodify itselectrochemical performance.\nMeasuring the arrangement of the catalyst ink components\nusing traditional techniques, such as small-angle scattering, is\nchallenging.Thecontrastandfractalassemblyofthecarbonand\nPt components of the ink dominate the signals of both small-\nangle X-ray and neutron scattering (SAXS and SANS,\nrespectively). Even attempting to leverage simple contrast\nmatching techniquesinSANSfails duetothestrongscattering\nand neutronSLDof thecarbonand Pt.\nTo overcome this, previous studies have used contrast\nvariation SANS (CV-SANS) to study the catalyst layer inks\n(without ionic liquids).9−12 Using CV-SANS, these authors\nwereabletoidentifythestructuralarrangementoftheionomers\nintheirinks,despiterawSANSintensitybeingdominatedbythe\nPt/C. The CV-SANS approach takes the SANS pattern of a\nmaterial measured at several contrast conditions and decom-\nposes the scattering into individual component scattering\nfunctions. This allows for the understanding of not only the\noverall solution structure of the ink, but also the relative\narrangement of the individual components (e.g., IL, ionomer,\nPt/C).\nIn this study, we use CV-SANS to determine the impact of\nmultipleionicliquidsonthestructureofaliquidphasecatalyst\nReceived: March 14, 2025\nRevised: July 17, 2025\nAccepted: July 17, 2025\nPublished: July 28, 2025\nArticlepubs.acs.org/Macromolecules\n© 2025 The Authors. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Electron-Hole Recombination\nRecombination is the mechanism that is utilized by extrinsic semiconductors to equilibrate excess charge carriers\nthrough the bringing together and annihilation of oppositely charged carriers. Specifically the annihilation of positively\ncharged holes and negatively charged impurity or free electrons. Recombination results in the release of energy, this\nenergy stems from the act of electrons jumping down from the conduction band in order to recombine with holes\ngenerated in the valence band. The energy released can be in the form of photons or thermal lattice vibrations known as\nphonons. The resultant energy strength and type are determined by material characteristic band gap energy and the\npresence of defects within a material that can act as traps for charge carrier movement. Understanding the distinction\nand controlling the dominating recombination mechanisms for materials is highly important for the optimization of\nsemiconductor devices such as solar cells and light emitting diodes.\nIntroduction\nWhen a free electron inhabits the conduction band, it exists in a meta-stable state. Therefore to compensate for the\nunfavorable energy state the electron will move into an empty state, characterized as an electron hole. The movement\nof the electron into the empty state can occur in one or more steps through the band gap. The difference in energies\nbetween the meta-stable and the final state of the electron is then released so to allow the electron to occupy its final\nstate. The process of electron and hole annihilation is known as recombination. If the energy released through\nrecombination is in the form of a photon, the process is known as radiative-recombination and is most common for\nelectrons moving fully from the conduction to the valence band. Non-radiative recombination is often the result of\nmaterial defects and intermediate energy levels in the band gap. Non-radiative recombination can be categorized as\neither Auger or defect level driven recombination.\nFigure : A simplistic comparison of electron paths during a) radiative \"band to band\" recombination and non-radiative\nb) Shockley-Read-Hall c) Auger recombination. Black circles represent meta-stable electrons in the conduction band\nwhile gray squares represent electron holes in the conduction band. E  is an arbitrary energy level introduced into the\nband gap that acts as recombination center.\nRadiative Recombination\nRadiative recombination is the mechanism responsible for photoemission in semiconductor light emitting diodes and is\nmainly associated with band to band recombination as a result of the high energy differences associated with a\ncomplete band gap transition. Direct band to band recombination is only possible in materials with extremely low\ndefect concentrations due to the fact that strain fields in the crystal structure will alter atomic interaction distances and\nstrengths. This difference is directly related to electron interaction density in the material which, according to the band\ntheory of semiconductors, will alter the band structure of the material. Direct band gap Extrinsic semiconductors, like\nGaAs, are manufactured to have little to no crystalline defects so to prevent the creation of defect levels within the band\ngap.\nWhen radiative recombination occurs, the photon emitted has a characteristic energy similar to the band gap of the\nmaterial and therefore will have a very weak interaction with the material. Therefore allowing for photons emitted\nwithin the sample through radiative recombination events to escape.\nNon-Radiative Recombination\nWhen intermediate energy levels are introduced into the band gap of a material through defects in the crystal structure,\ncharge carriers have the possibility of becoming trapped, thus making recombination extremely less favorable. When\nan electron or a hole is captured in an energy level close to the conduction or valence bands respectively, it is said that\nthe carrier is trapped. The probabilities for electron occupation and hole occupation are represented by equations one\nand two respectively. For an electron trap, the energy required for an electron to occupy that energy state is\nsignificantly higher than the chance for a hole to occupy said state (Eqn.3).\nRC\n9/30/26, 2:04 PM Electron-Hole Recombination - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Electron-Hole_Reco… 1/3\n\nThe converse is true for a hole trap (Eqn.4).\nAs a result of this disparity in occupation of a state, specific to one type of charge carrier, the trapped carrier will not be\nable to recombine and eventually return to the initial state. A high concentration of carrier traps will result in the\nreduction in carrier mobility and in turn a reduction in recombination rate.\nFigure 2. An extremely simplistic visualization of the respective charge carrier traps and their locations in the band\ndiagram of an extrinsic semiconductor. Electrons are represented by the black circles and the electron holes are\nrepresented by the gray squares.\nEnergy levels present within the band gap with energies that are located more equidistant from both the valence and\nconduction bands are known as recombination centers. After a carrier is captured by a recombination center there is a\nfinite probability that a carrier of opposite charge will also be capable of occupying the same energy state, therefore\nresulting an an electron-hole pair annihilation. This form of recombination is known as Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) or\ndefect level recombination. The resultant intermediate step results in a lower energy difference between the starting\nand ending energies of the electron and in turn a smaller energy released during recombination. This energy is often in\nthe form of thermal vibrations known as phonons, which are then absorbed into the material which results in heating.\nThis heating occurs at the defect sites within the material and can be extremely detrimental to device efficiency due to\nthe fact that electron mobility decreases with phonon concentration and that heat energy can result in growth of\nstrained areas within the material.\nFigure 3. A simple visual comparison between traps and a SRH recombination center with respect to both holes and\nelectrons. Holes are represented by (H+) and electrons are shown by (e-).\nAuger recombination requires the interaction of three carriers. when an electron and a hole interact and recombine the\nenergy is not transferred into heat energy or thermal vibrations. Instead the energy is transferred into an electron\nwithin the conduction band, which is then promoted to an energy higher in the conduction band. This electron then\nreleases energy in the form of thermal vibrations as it returns to the lowest possible state within the conduction band.\nFor this reason Auger recombination is highly detrimental to the efficiency of extrinsic semiconductor LED's with high\nconcentrations of electron donor atoms. Additionally, the concentration of Auger recombination events increases with\nan increase in input energy intensity as a result an increased electron concentration in the conduction band.\nGallium Nitride LED's\nGallium nitride (GaN) is a direct band gap binary III/V semiconductor that is commonly used for bright light emitting\ndiodes. It is also commonly used for solar cells in military and space applications as a result of its low sensitivity to\nionizing radiation. GaN has a wide band gap of 3.4 eV which allows for the emission of violet light [3]. This violet\n9/30/26, 2:04 PM Electron-Hole Recombination - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Electron-Hole_Reco… 2/3\n\nemission is used in Blu-Ray players to read disks. Gallium nitride LEDs can be manufactured to produce light with\ncolors ranging from the low end of visible up to ultraviolet. This is done by altering the concentrations and types of\ndopant atoms.\nPure GaN is highly crystalline with a wurtzite crystal structure. When dopant atoms are added to make the\nsemiconductor either p-type (addition of magnesium) or n-type(addition of Si or oxygen), the material exhibits a high\ndislocation density. This high dislocation density, on the order of ten billion defects per square centimeter introduced\ntensile stresses making the semiconductors brittle and inefficient [4]. The inefficiency stemmed from a high number of\nnon-radiative recombination centers where strain fields absorbed energy and released it as phonons into the material.\nThe addition of buffer layers when depositing the GaN using molecular beam epitaxy at low temperatures allowed for\nthe relaxation of the stresses and in turn a high performance LED. The ability to alter the size of the band gap for GaN\nwhile maintaining a low defect density led to the commercialization of light emmiting diodes of multiple colors and\nintensities. All as a result of reducing the number of defects and in turn the number of non-radiative recombination\nzones.\nQuestions\n1. Thin film crystalline GaN LEDs are grown on insulating substrates so to prevent current leakage, often there is a\nhigh lattice mismatch between the film and the substrate so intermediate layers are grown to reduce the amount of\nstress dislocations in the film. Why is the replication of defects in semiconductor thin films undesirable?\n2. A solar cell made of a heavily dosed silicon based semiconductor with no observed defects begins to experience a\nreduction in efficiency. What could be a potential cause for this reduced efficiency, and what is one practical\nsolution to this problem?\n3. An orange colored LED is dipped in liquid nitrogen and then illuminated, a change to green, a smaller wavelength\nof light, was seen. Given that no defects were introduced, what is happening to the band to band recombination?\nAnswers\n1. Dislocations and other defects in the crystal structure of a extrinsic semiconductor like GaN will alter the band\nstructure and possibly introduce non-radiative recombination centers, thus decreasing the LED efficiency and\noutput.\n2. Materials with high concentrations of electrons in the conduction band are subject to Auger recombination\nregardless of defect presence. either choosing a different material with a lower electron donor concentration or by\nreducing the energy input you will lower the probability for Auger recombination and in turn increase efficiency of\nthe solar cell.\n3. The electron interaction in the material is changing and in this case, results in the increased size of the band gap.\nTherefore the electrons have a higher difference in initial and final states, thus creating higher energy photons.\nReferences\n1.
