Rieland,* Yamil Simón-Manso,* Adam Zuber, Anthony P. Kotula, Kalman B. Migler,\nWilliam E. Wallace, and Kathryn L. Beers\nCite This: ACS Polym. Au 2026, 6, 1134−1146\n Read Online\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: Quantitative chemical characterization of postcon-\nsumer plastics is challenging because of the large number of\npolymer chemistries and additives used in formulating plastic\nproducts. Plasticizers are an important family of additives used to\nlower the glass transition temperature and enhance flexibility in\npolymer formulations. However, their identification and quantifi-\ncation are difficult in recycling and end-of-life processes. This study\ncritically assesses two analytical techniques for their suitability in\nplasticizer identification: mass spectrometry (high resolution,\nselectivity, and sensitivity) and time-gated Raman spectroscopy\n(nondestructive, quicker, and minimal sample preparation). Here,\nwe generate searchable libraries for the identification of 91\ncommon plasticizers using these two techniques, along with the\ndevelopment of reliable tools to measure their spectral similarity. We then analyze the reliability of identifications based on time-\ngated Raman and/or liquid chromatography−mass spectrometry with atmospheric pressure chemical ionization, explicitly\nhighlighting the advantages and disadvantages of each technique for a given plasticizer chemical family. We have applied these tools\nto identify and quantify plasticizers in a NIST Standard Reference Material (SRM 2860, Phthalates in Polyvinyl Chloride).\nKEYWORDS: chemometrics, plasticizers,polymers, time-gatedRaman spectroscopy,mass spectrometry\n1. INTRODUCTION\nPlastics are highly complex and variable materials, with one\nreport identifying over 10,000 unique chemical substances\n(e.g., monomers, additives, process aids) actively used in\nplastics production.1 This complexity compounds when\nconsidering the recovery, separation, and reprocessing of\npostconsumer plastics and the characterization of degraded\nmaterials in mismanaged plastics. Characterization of plastic\ncomposition is relevant for sortation during recycling, quality\nassurance, and understanding plastics leaked into the environ-\nment. Several analytical techniques are used for assessing\nplastic composition such as near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy\nand mass spectrometry (MS). NIR is commonly used to\nidentify polymer type during recycling processes. However, in\nvibrational spectroscopy techniques, like NIR, the presence of\nplastic additives can result in crowded, overlapping spectral\nfeatures that can be difficult to deconvolute and can hinder\npolymer identification. Certain additives, like pigments, can\nalso undergo competing phenomena during spectroscopy, such\nas fluorescence and adsorption, which can overwhelm the\ndesired signal and/or limit outgoing light via scattering and\nemission processes. MS is commonly employed for more\ngranularchemicalcompositionassessment,particularlyofsmall\nmolecules and additives. 2,3 When identifying polymer\ncomposition in environmentally recovered plastics, a suite of\ntechniques including Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform\ninfrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, and thermal analysis are often\nused in tandem to overcome challenges in identification as a\nresult of degradation and fluorescent pigments.4−6 There is a\nneed for approaches that enable accurate plastic composition\ncharacterization at higher-throughput and lower cost.7\nAparticularchallengeisalackofaccessiblespectraldatathat\nadequately addresses the needs of industry and researchers.\nAgnostic of analytical technique, there tend to be two types of\nopen databases: (1) pure components (e.g., homopolymer,\nplasticizers, pigments, etc.)8−10 and (2) postconsumer and\nfound objects (e.g., marine debris, lab-weathered samples,\nReceived: March 27, 2026\nRevised: June 18, 2026\nAccepted: June 22, 2026\nPublished: July 13, 2026\nArticlepubs.acs.org/polymerau\nNot subjecttoU.S.Copyright. Published\n2026 by American Chemical Society\n1134\nhttps://doi.org/10.1021/acspolymersau.6c00065\nACS Polym. Au 2026, 6, 1134−1146\nThis article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0\nDownloaded from pubs.​acs.​org/​apaccd/​article-pdf/​6/​4/​1134/​65895791/​acspolymersau.​6c00065.​pdf by NATL INST OF STANDARDS & TECHNOLOGY user on 25 September 2026\n\n\nassorted postconsumer packaging, etc.).11−15 While both types\nof databases have their uses, pure-component spectral libraries\noffer greater opportunities for characterization beyond bulk-\npolymer identification. However, currently there is limited\navailability of high-quality, pure-component databases that\ncater to polymer-relevant additives and chemicals of concern,\nhindering the advancement of chemometric and nontargeted\nanalysis for polymeric systems. The limited availability of such\ncentralized databases contributes to duplication of effort,\nconsuming research time and resources. We also note that\ngenerating clean and reproducible spectra of “pure” homopol-\nymers presents more of a challenge than small molecule\ncompounds due to their inherent structural diversity (e.g.,\nmolecular mass, dispersity, crystallinity) and the necessity of\nadding stabilizers and other additives during synthesis. Beyond\nmolecular structure, other aspects of polymer samples can\nsignificantly impact spectral features depending on the\nanalytical technique applied.16−18 For example, in vibrational\nspectroscopy, measurements are sensitive to surface properties\nthat impact interactions with incident light such as form factor\n(nurdle, powder, fragment, fiber, foam) and surface roughness.\nThis paper will first compare the emerging technique of\ntime-gated Raman spectroscopy with the more established\nhyphenated liquid chromatography− mass spectrometry with\natmospheric pressure chemical ionization (particularly LC-\nAPCI-timsTOF MS/MS) for plastic composition analysis and\ntheir potential for analyzing plasticizers in plastics. Next, a\nstudy of two parallel libraries of 91 common plasticizers\napplying both techniques will be described and the results\ndiscussed. Finally, we applied these tools to identify plasticizers\ninaNISTStandardReference Material(SRM2860,Phthalates\nin Polyvinyl Chloride) and provided a perspective on the\nadvantages and disadvantages of each technique and their\ncombined usage.\n2. BACKGROUND\n2.1. Time-Gated Raman Spectroscopy\nRaman spectroscopy (RS) is a vibrational spectroscopy\ntechnique that measures the energy of inelastically scattered\nphotons resulting from monochromatic incident light inducing\na change in the virtual energy states of sample molecules (e.g.,\nrotational, vibrational, and electronic energy states). For a\nsample to be Raman-active, it must be able to undergo a\nchange in electric-dipole polarization. This contrasts with\ninfrared (IR) spectroscopy, which depends on a change in the\nelectric dipole moment. Therefore, molecules that are strongly\nRaman active are often weak in IR and vice versa. Due to this\ndistinction, Raman spectroscopy excels in the measurement of\nmolecular features such as electronically neutral bonds (e.g.,\nC−C, C−H, C�C) and aromatic rings which are common in\npolymer and plasticizer structures.\nHerein, we demonstrate time-gated Raman Spectroscopy\n(TGRS)19 as an advanced analytical technique that shows\npromise in characterizing samples with moderate fluores-\ncence.20 TGRS is a time-resolved method that captures the\nevolution of spectral signal over several nanoseconds. In\nprinciple, this allows the temporal deconvolution of the near-\ninstantaneous Raman scattering from the longer time-scale\nfluorescence emission, where lifetimes can differ by up to 2\norders of magnitude. By using a pulsed laser and carefully\ncontrolling the delay and width of the detection gate, TGRS\ncan significantly suppress fluorescence, ambient light, and even\nthermal emission, yielding a much clearer Raman spectrum\nwith an improved signal-to-noise ratio.\nTGRS offers significant advantages for analyzing plasticizers\nand polymers, especially in challenging real-world scenarios,\nsuch as the fluorescence suppression in pigmented and\nweathered plastics.20 TGRS greatly improves our ability to\nidentify polymers and their additives in the presence of\nmoderate fluorescence, which is often difficult with conven-\ntional Raman techniques. Common black pigments such as\ngraphite and sulfur black cause significant interference to\nRaman spectroscopy through the competing effects of\nfluorescence21 and strong absorbance of the incident light.\nWe have observed moderate success in characterizing such\nsamples using TGRS (unpublished). On the other hand,\nRaman spectroscopy is inherently highly specific, providing\nunique “fingerprints” for different polymers and their blends.\nTGRS is valuable for identifying and characterizing recovered\nplastics from various environments (e.g., marine litter) and has\nexciting potential for industrial applications such as quality\nassessment, recycling sortation, and characterization of\nenvironmental samples.\nAnintrinsiclimitationofvibrationalspectroscopytechniques\nis the handling of complex chemical mixtures. In principle, the\nRaman spectra of a sample should be a linear combination of\ntheindividualcomponentspectraweightedwithconsiderations\ntoward the relative amount of each component, Raman\nscattering cross-section,22,23 and impacts from chemical\ninteractions (e.g., van der Waals, π−π stacking) that may\nshift or suppress bands. Various chemometric methods are\nused to effectively deconvolute the spectra of simple\nmixtures.22,24 However, challenges remain for deconvoluting\nmore complex systems that may have several component\nspecies as well as fluorescence contributions. In the following\ndiscussion, we differentiate between RS as a class of techniques\nand TGRS to distinguish aspects of the results that are unique\nto the capabilities of TGRS compared to results that may\nfeasibly be replicated on a continuous wave Raman instrument.\n2.2. Mass Spectrometry\nMass spectrometry (MS) is a powerful analytical technique\nused to identify and quantify molecules on the basis of the\nmass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of their ions.25 Its application to\nplasticizers and polymer additives has revolutionized our\nunderstanding of these materials, offering detailed insights into\ntheir composition, structure, degradation, and loadings.26 At its\ncore, MS involves three main steps: (1) ionization: the sample\nmolecules are converted into charged ions. This is a crucial\nstep as it determines which types of molecules can be analyzed\nand the nature of the resulting fragments. (2) Mass analysis:\nthe ions are separated based on theirm/z ratio. Different mass\nanalyzers (e.g., quadrupole, time-of-flight (TOF), ion traps,\nFourier transform ion cyclotron resonance (FT-ICR)) achieve\nthis separation through varying electric and/or magnetic fields.\n(3) Detection: Separated ions are converted into a measurable\nsignal by detectors such as electron multipliers, Faraday cups,\nor scintillation detectors, and their abundances are recorded,\ngeneratingamassspectrumdepictingionabundanceversusm/\nz. In addition, the mass analyzers may include multistage ion\nseparation known as tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS or\nMSn), which involves multiple, sequential stages of ion\nisolation, fragmentation of mass-selected ions in a buffer gas,\nand analysis to improve structural identification and reduce\ninterference. These mass spectra provide a unique “fingerprint”\nACS Polymers Au pubs.acs.org/polymerau Article\nhttps://doi.org/10.1021/acspolymersau.6c00065\nACS Polym. Au 202

[{"suffix": "", "text": "1 \n \nMacroSimGNN: Efficient and Accurate Prediction of Macromolecule \nPairwise Similarity via Graph Neural Network \n \nJiale Shi1,2, Runzhong Wang1, Nathan J. Rebello1, Jiarui Lu1,3, Bradley D. Olsen1*, Debra J. \nAudus2* \n \n1. Department of Chemical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, \nMassachusetts 02139, United States \n2. Materials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, \nGaithersburg, Maryland 20899, United States \n3. Department of Computer Science, Wellesley College, Wellesley, Massachusetts 02482, \nUnited States \n \n*Correspondence: email: bdolsen@mit.edu and debra.audus@nist.gov \n \nAbstract \nEfficient and accurate prediction of macromolecule pairwise similarity is essential for developing \ndatabase search engines and is useful for machine learning based predictive tools . Existing \nmethods for calculating macromolecular similarity suffer from significant drawbacks. Graph edit \ndistance is accurate but computationally expensive, and graph kernel methods are computationally \nefficient but inaccurate. This study introduces a graph neural network model, MacroSimGNN, \nwhich significantly improves computational efficiency while maintaining high accuracy on \nmacromolecule pairwise similarity. Furthermore, this approach enables feature embeddings based \non macromolecular similarities to a set of landmark molecules, enhancing both unsupervised and \nsupervised learning tasks. This method represents  a significant advancement in macromolecular \ncheminformatics, paving the way for the development of advanced search engines and data-driven \ndesign of macromolecules. \n \nIntroduction \nMacromolecules are both ubiquitous and indispensable. 1, 2 Biological macromolecules, such as \nglycans,3, 4 proteins5-7 and nucleic acids,8-10 are essential for life, serving as catalysts for survival \nand growth functions , while  synthetic macromolecules find extensive use in fields such as \ntextiles,11 water purification,12, 13 energy,14 transportation,15 construction,16 and biotechnology.17 \nMacromolecule similarity offers insights into quantitative structure -property relationships18, 19 as \nsimilar macromolecules are more likely to have similar properties. Similarity is also essential for \nefficient search algorithms for macromolecule databases  by enabling ranking of targets .20-26 \nFurthermore, macromolecul ar similarity either forms the basis or enhances machine learning \ntechniques, including clustering, classification, and regression for predicting properties and \ndiscovering new macromolecular materials. 19, 27-44 Based on chemical intuition and experience, \n\n \n2 \n \nsimilar polymers or macromolecules are more likely to exhibit similar properties, and require \nsimilar synthetic strategies. When experimental researchers aim to design new polymers or \nestimate their physical properties, pairwise similarity searches can be useful for identifying \npreviously synthesized polymers that resemble the target structures. This can assist in synthesis \nplanning and provide a simple, rough estimate of the physical and chemical properties of the new \npolymers. \n \nWhile sequence matching algorithms 45, 46 can be used for similarity calculations in simple linear \nmacromolecules, many complex macromolecules have non-linear topologies.4, 47-50 To address this, \nboth atomistic and coarse -grained graph representations 51-53 were developed for macromolecule \nsimilarity calculation s. However, the graph similarity calculations between atomistic graph \nrepresentations of macromolecules are computationally expensive and impractical due to the high \nnumber of atoms compared to small molecules. Consequently, coarse -grained graph \nrepresentations47, 54, 55  were utilized, where nodes represent monomers and edges represent \nconnections between monomers. Two main approaches have been used to calculate pairwise \nsimilarity in these coarse -grained representations: graph edit distance  (GED)47, 54, 55  and graph \nkernels.47, 56-59 GED measures the minimum operation costs to transform one graph to another .60 \nHowever, GED is a nondeterministic polynomial-time hardness (NP-hard) problem. Even with \ncoarse-grained representations, computing the exact GED remains costly,47, 54, 55, 61, 62 limiting its \nuse in scale -up or time -sensitive applications. Graph kernel methods  map graphs to a high -\ndimension space and measure similarity between graphs using inner products in that space. Graph \nkernels often provide an approximation of graph similarity rather than an exact measure since the \nmapping processing and inner production operation can lose small but important structural \ndifferences between graphs. Therefore, graph kernel methods offer improved efficiency but often \nsuffer from reduced accuracy.47, 56-59 Several recent advances in deep learning demonstrated that \ndeep neural networks have the potential to learn graph matching-related tasks, leading to state-of-\nthe-art matching accuracy while also benefits from the efficiency.62-64 \n  \nBai et al.62 proposed the SimGNN framework which is a graph neural network approach designed \nfor rapid and accurate computation of small molecule pairwise graph similarity. In SimGNN, 62 \neach small molecule is represented as a chemical compound graph, with nodes representing atoms \nand embedded using one-hot encoding. Applying SimGNN to the atomistic graph representations \nof macromolecules is impractical because obtaining a dataset with the exact GEDs between \natomistic graph representations of macromolecules, which have a large number of atoms within a \nreasonable timeframe is unrealistic. On the other hand, in the coarse-grained graph representations \nof macromolecules, nodes represent monomers or linkage groups, and one-hot encoding cannot \naccurately quantify the chemical differences between these nodes nor can it handle the infinite \nnumber of possible monomers. Therefore, the direct application of SimGNN to the coarse-grained \ngraph representations of macromolecules reduces the chemical resolution for macromolecule \nsimilarity calculation. \n\n \n3 \n \n \nBuilding on the work of SimGNN 62, this study introduces MacroSimGNN, an extension tailored \nfor macromolecule coarse -grained graph representation pairwise similarity predictions. \nMacroSimGNN uses Morgan Fingerprints for node embedding s to handle the infinite variety of \nnodes in the coarse -grained graph representations of macromolecules , accurately quantify the \ndifferences between nodes which represent monomers or linkage groups and allow extrapolation \nto unseen nodes . MacroSimGNN aims to overcome the significant drawbacks 47, 54-59 of existing \napproaches by enhancing computational efficiency while preserving high accuracy.  Furthermore, \nMacroSimGNN achieves zero -shot predictions on the new macromolecule dataset with high \naccuracy and performs effective transfer learning to improve predictions using only a small amount \nof data from the new dataset  while SimGNN is not able to do these due to the one -hot encoding \nlimitation. MacroSimGNN is then applied along with landmark distance embedding65, 66 for both \nunsupervised and supervised learning tasks.  This work has potential applications in \nmacromolecule search, as well as quantitative design tools for macromolecules. \n \nMethods \nMacroSimGNN \nAs shown in Figure 1a, in the coarse-grained graph representations of macromolecules, each node \nis a monomer or linkage group. In real-world scenarios, macromolecules are not formed directly \nfrom atoms in a single step; instead, they are synthesized through the polymerization of monomers. \nCompared to atomistic graphs, coarse-grained graphs clearly distinguish the monomers, providing \nan accurate reflection of the chemical information. Additionally, the choice of coarse -grained \ngraphs enables the calculation of the GED between the macromolecules in a reasonable time frame, \nwhich is not possible if a condensed atomistic graph representation67, 68 is used.62 The embedding \nof each node (monomer or linkage group) is achieved via a  Morgan fingerprint (radius = 3, nBits \n= 128, useChirality=True).47 This choice is the same setting in Mohapatra et al.47 Edges represent \nconnections between monomers or linkage groups without chemical specificity or directionality in \norder to align with the frameworks of MacroSimGNN and SimGNN,62 which do not include edge-\nspecific information. \nAs illustrated in Figure 1b, the methodology of MacroSimGNN comprises four stages, mirroring \nthose of SimGNN but with modifications to accommodate macromolecular complexities. Stage 1 \ninludes graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for node -level embedding s. Nodes are initially \nembedded using Morgan molecular fingerprints,47 where 𝑢𝑖,𝑛\n0 ∈ ℝ𝐷 is a 128 dimension vector for \nnode 𝑛 of graph 𝑔𝑖 which has 𝑁 nodes, differentiating this initial stage from SimGNN 62 which \nuses one-hot encoding. The graph convolution operation generates the node embeddings for a set \nof nodes in graph 𝑔𝑖, 𝑈𝑖 ∈ ℝ𝑁×𝐷, where the n-th row, 𝑢𝑖,𝑛 ∈ ℝ𝐷 is the embedding of node 𝑛 after \ngraph convolution operation. Stage 2 is  graph-level embedding, where an embedding vector for \neach graph (ℎ𝑖) is generated by aggregating the input node embeddings (𝑈𝑖). The node weights are \n\n \n4 \n \ndependent on the similarity matric and are learned and optimized during the training process. Stage \n2 is for the neural tensor network used in Stage 3; it is not used for the pairwise node comparison \nin Stage 3.  Stage 3 is  graph-graph interactions including the neural tensor network 62, 69 and the \npairwise node comparison .62 The neural tensor network models the relationship between two \ngraph-level embeddings.  \n𝑝(ℎ𝑖, ℎ𝑗) = 𝑓 (ℎ𝑖\n𝑇𝑊[1:𝐾]ℎ𝑗 + 𝑉 [ℎ𝑖\nℎ𝑗\n] + 𝑏) (1) \nWhere 𝑊[1:𝐾] ∈ ℝ𝐷×𝐷×𝐾 is a weight tensor, [] denotes the concatenation operation, 𝑉 ∈ ℝ𝐾×2𝐷 is \na weight vector, 𝑏  ∈ ℝ𝐾  is a bias vector and 𝑓 ( ∙ ) is a ReLU  activation function. 𝐾  is a \nhyperparameter that defines the dimension of the graph-level interaction scores 𝑝(ℎ𝑖, ℎ𝑗). \nHowever, if only the neural tensor network was used, the node-level information such as the node \nfeature distribution and graph size may be lost by the graph -level embedding.62 The differences \nbetween two graphs lie in small substructures and are usually hard to reflect  in graph-level \nembedding. To overcome this limitation, the pairwise node -level interaction score is obtained by \n𝑆 = 𝑈𝑖𝑈𝑗\n𝑇, through matrix multiplication. Next, a normalized histogram feature vector 𝑞(hist (𝑆)) \nis created and concatenated with the graph -level interaction scores 𝑝(ℎ𝑖, ℎ𝑗). Stage 4 is a fully \nconnected neural network which predicts the similarity score, 𝑠̂(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) between graphs 𝑔𝑖 and 𝑔𝑗. \n𝑠̂(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) is compared against the ground-truth similarity score 𝑠(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) using the following mean \nsquared error loss function: \n𝐿𝑜𝑠𝑠 = 1\n|𝒟| ∑ (𝑠̂(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) −  𝑠(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗))\n2\n(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝑠̂(𝑔𝑖,𝑔𝑗).\n (2) \nWhere 𝒟 is the set of training graph pairs.  \nDuring training, no explicit symmetry constraint is imposed on the MacroSimGNN framework. \nInstead, the model learns physical symmetry from the inherently symmetric training data, where \nthe ground truth of 𝑠(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) and 𝑠(𝑔𝑗, 𝑔𝑖) are both used for training MacroSimGNN. As a result, \nthe predicted values of 𝑠̂(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) and 𝑠̂(𝑔𝑗, 𝑔𝑖) are very close, though slightly different due to the \nregression nature of the task. For predictions on testing datasets, a symmetry -enforced prediction \nstrategy is implemented to ensure strictly symmetric results and improve prediction accuracy. This \nsymmetry strategy uses the average value  (𝑠̂(𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗) + 𝑠̂(𝑔𝑗, 𝑔𝑖)) /2 as the final similarity score \nprediction for the graph pair (𝑔𝑖, 𝑔𝑗). [{"suffix": "", "text": "Nanoscale mapping of composition \nand orientation in electrospun \npolymeric nanofibers loaded with \ncarbon atomic wires\nSimone Melesi1, Devon S. Jakob2, Jeremy F. Schultz2, Adam J. Biacchi2, Piotr Pińkowski3, \nBartłomiej Pigulski3, Chiara Castiglioni4, Chiara Bertarelli4, Sławomir Szafert3,  \nCarlo S. Casari1 & Andrea Centrone2\nThis study yields a comprehensive nanoscale investigation of the composition and molecular \norientation of electrospun poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) nanofibers containing halogen-\nterminated carbon atomic wires (CAWs), a finite-length analog of the carbyne construct. This is \naccomplished by conducting light-polarization-dependent experiments with advanced techniques such \nas atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR), optical photothermal infrared microscopy \n(O-PTIR), and hyperspectral photoluminescence (PL) microscopy. In PMMA nanofibers, AFM-IR \nreveals a remarkable, homogeneous uniaxial orientation of PMMA chains along the fiber axis, down \nto the ≈ 20 nm scale. Semi-quantitative analysis of IR dichroic ratios indicates a nearly orthogonal \nalignment ( ψ avg ≈ 79◦ ) of the C = O dipole with respect to the nearly all-trans planar polymer \nbackbone, consistent with expectations of the electrospinning process and in agreement with prior \nmodeling of polymer chain dynamics. Congruous AFM-IR, O-PTIR, and hyperspectral PL data show that \nincorporation of CAWs into the PMMA nanofibers results in a peculiar compositional heterogeneity, \nwith alternating 3 μm to 4 μm long PMMA-rich and CAW-rich regions across the fiber length. Notably, \nhyperspectral PL data reveal that CAWs preferentially align along the fiber axis, with sparse, 1.5 μm \nto 3 μm long domains displaying locally reduced or enhanced molecular orientation. We envision that \nthe widely applicable approach used here will foster engineering of anisotropic nanostructures with \nadvanced functionalities and complex compositions, laying the groundwork for future applications in \nnanoelectronics, photonics, and energy storage that demand anisotropic molecular orientation and \ncomposition.\nKeywords Carbyne, Electrospinning, Orientation, AFM-IR, O-PTIR, Hyperspectral Photoluminescence\nCarbynes are infinitely long, one-dimensional chains of sp-hybridized carbon atoms 1,2. They attract growing \ninterest thanks to mechanical, electrical, and optical properties that have been predicted to outperform those \nof graphene, carbon nanotubes, and other carbon nanostructures 3–10. Carbon atomic wires (CAWs), the \nfinite-length experimental realization of the carbyne construct (Fig. S1), have shown promise as additives in \nadvanced nanocomposite materials11 and as active elements in field effect transistors, organic electronics, and \nsupercapacitors12–14.\nThe one-atom-diameter structure of CAWs is strongly anisotropic. For example, first-principles calculations \npredict record-breaking stiffness along the carbynes’ chain axis 3,11. Similarly, optical properties such as \nabsorption15,16, photoluminescence 15,17, dielectric function 18, first-order hyperpolarizability 19, and transport \nproperties, e.g., current and electron density3,20, are also anisotropic and considerably enhanced along the chain \naxis. However, the engineering of devices and composites harnessing such directionally outstanding properties \n1Micro and Nanostructured Materials Laboratory — NanoLab, Department of Energy, Politecnico di \nMilano, Via Lambruschini 8, Milano 20156, Italy. 2Nanoscale Device Characterization Division, Physical \nMeasurement Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, Maryland 20899, \nUSA. 3Faculty of Chemistry, University of Wrocław, 14F. Joliot-Curie, Wroclaw 50–383, Poland. 4Department \nof Chemistry, Materials and Chemical Engineering “Giulio Natta”, Politecnico di Milano, Milano, Italy. email:  \nslawomir.szafert@uwr.edu.pl; carlo.casari@polimi.it; andrea.centrone@nist.gov\nOPEN\nScientific Reports |        (2026) 16:16247 1| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-46988-8\nwww.nature.com/scientificreports\n\n\nrequires new methods for assessing and controlling the alignment of CAWs. Thus far, only a few studies have \nreported aligned CAWs. For example, CAWs stabilized by gold clusters were aligned with an applied electric \nfield21,22 or by gravity15, while hydrogen-terminated CAWs were aligned within a polyvinyl alcohol (PV A) matrix \nby uniaxial stretching16,17. Recently, electrospinning has been proposed as an alternative strategy to incorporate \nCAWs within poly(methyl methacrylate) - PMMA nanofibers23. Since electrospinning produces nanofibers24–27 \nby ejecting a polymeric solution from a needle under high bias, the polymeric chains experience intense stretching \nforces that induce molecular alignment 28–31. Commonly, a suitable substrate collector (e.g., rotating drum, \nwheel-like bobbin, split electrode, etc27–33, is employed to obtain nanofibers with a high degree of macroscopic \ngeometrical alignment. While the alignment of polymeric macromolecules has been extensively investigated \nat a macroscopic scale (i.e. averaging the orientation of many fibers) these effects are largely unexplored at the \nsingle or intra-fiber levels and not yet reported for CAWs in polymeric fibers. Although a certain degree of \norientation of polymer chains within an electrospun nanofiber should be expected, the orientation of short, \nadditive, molecules like the 4-carbon-long molecules studied here, in such fiber composites is neither expected \nnor has been reported previously. Given CAWs’ finite length, understanding their physical aggregation within \na host medium, like the fibers in our samples, is critically important to establish percolative paths of electronic \ntransport38 or to exploit anisotropic effects in hetero-terminated dipolar or push-pull carbon wires23.\nHere, a suite of high spatial resolution spectroscopic techniques, such as atomic force microscopy infrared \nspectroscopy (AFM-IR)32–35 and hyperspectral photoluminescence (PL) microscopy36,37 are used to determine \nthe composition and orientation heterogeneity of PMMA nanofibers containing halogen-terminated CAWs38,39. \nThe AFM-IR technique, also known as photothermal induced resonance (PTIR), combines the chemical \nspecificity of IR spectroscopy with the spatial resolution of atomic force microscopy (AFM), enabling IR \nanalysis at the ≈ 10 nm scale 38; i.e., much smaller than the optical diffraction limit. Spectra obtained with \nAFM-IR/PTIR are typically characterized by undistorted, absorptive profiles39,40 which are congruous with the \nspectra in far-field IR databases, leading to a steadily growing number of applications encompassing material \nscience41–44, photovoltaics45,46, medicine47–52, geology53,54, and art conservation55,56 among others. Recent PTIR \nexperiments with wide-bandwidth optomechanical AFM probes 57–59 also enabled quantitative measurement \nof the thermal properties of materials at the nanoscale. Moreover, control over the polarization of light used in \nAFM-IR measurements has proven useful in the study of anisotropic materials, enabling direct study of their \nmolecular orientation60,61. We note that AFM-IR is one of several nanoscale IR techniques, including scattering-\ntype scanning near-filed microscopy (s-SNOM) 35, peak-force tapping IR (PFIR) 62 and photoinduced force \nmicroscopy (PiFM)63. Details on operating principles and applications are available in recent reviews32–35,64.\nThe rapid analysis of hyperspectral PL microscopy based on high-throughput imaging filters has also enabled \nbroad applications in material science 36, and photovoltaics37 and has been shown to complement AFM-IR for \nphotoluminescent samples36.\nIn this study, AFM-IR experiments with polarized light reveal remarkable uniaxial intra-fiber orientation of \npolymeric chains in PMMA nanofibers along the fiber direction that is homogeneous at the ≈ 20 nm scale. In \ncontrast, AFM-IR data obtained on CAW-loaded PMMA nanofibers show chemical heterogeneity with CAWs \nenrichment in regions with locally larger fiber diameters. These results are corroborated at the ≈ 500 nm scale \nusing the optical photothermal infrared technique (O-PTIR) 65. However, the AFM-IR and O-PTIR signal \nintensities are insufficient to estimate the local orientation of CAW-rich regions. Remarkably, complementary \npolarized hyperspectral PL data clearly show that CAW molecules are primarily oriented with their molecular \nchain axis parallel to the fiber axis at the ≈ 500 nm scale, demonstrating that electrospinning-induced forces \npromote alignment of CAW molecules within nanofibers. Therefore, although the short (four sp-hybridized \ncarbon atoms long) CAWs employed here differ from the ideal (i.e. infinite length) carbyne model, they can \nbe engineered to exhibit anisotropic properties, highlighting the effectiveness of electrospinning for producing \nanisotropic nanocomposites.\nIn summary, the advanced characterization described in this work provides a detailed, spatially resolved \npicture of the internal structure and organization of nanocomposite systems. Such structural information \nencompasses the orientation of polymer chains, phase separation and spatial distribution of constituents, and \nthe alignment of domains within individual nanostructures. Although this proof-of-principle-investigation \nfocuses on the structural and molecular characterization of our samples, we believe that the wide applicability \nof our approach will foster future engineering efforts for realizing anisotropic nanostructures with advanced \nfunctionalities and complex compositions.\nExperimental section\nPoly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) with M w = 996k and high-performance liquid chromatography grade (≥ \n99.7%) N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were used as received. Halogenated CAWs (referred to as C 4I) were \nsynthesized following a previously reported procedure66–68. The chemical structure of C4I is shown in Fig.S1.\nPMMA and PMMA/C4I nanofibers were produced by electrospinning a PMMA 6% g/g mass fraction (0.6 M, \nbased on the monomer molecular mass) solution in DMF and a 6% mass fraction solution of PMMA in DMF \nwith the addition of C 4I (0.36 M), respectively23. Briefly, PMMA was stirred in DMF at 60 °C until completely \ndissolved (≈ 5 h). After cooling down to room temperature, the C4I powder was added to the polymeric solution \nand stirred for 3 h until a homogeneous solution was obtained. Electrospinning was performed in a horizontal \nconfiguration by loading the feed solution in a 2.5 mL syringe with a 22-gauge needle and using an infusion \npump. Aligned nanofibers were obtained by electrospinning the solutions for 5 s onto Si substrates (P-doped \nwith low IR absorption) mounted on a rotating drum (1200 min− 1) with a needle-to-collector distance of 20 cm \nby applying 12 kV (DC) to the needle and using 0.2 mL/h rate. A schematic representation of the electrospinning \nsetup is reported in the Fig. S2. After DMF evaporation via electrospinning deposition and considering the \nScientific Reports |        (2026) 16:16247 2| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-46988-8\nwww.nature.com/scientificreports/\n\ninitial concentrations of the constituents in the solution, the nominal mass fraction of C4I within the nanofibers \nis expected to be 62.5%.\nThe diameter distribution of the fibers and their relative orientation were determined from images obtained \nusing a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) and an image processing software by analyzing \napproximately 100 fibers. FE-SEM images on as-prepared (uncoated) samples were acquired in low-current \nmode, using an acceleration voltage of 5  kV , a vacuum pressure in the sample chamber of ≈ 0.5  Pa, and \nmagnifications ranging from 10000x to 100000x.\nAFM-IR experiments were obtained using

Water trapped within a heated \ninterior region of concrete was used as an idealized system to determine the thermodynamic \nconditions of water that subsequently would lead to potential occurrence of a BLEVE event. The \nthermodynamic states that favor BLEVE was identified and delineated in the P–T phase \ndiagram of water and was shown to be highly constrained to narrow ranges of temperature and \nthe amount of water trapped (fill density) in the heated region. \nKeywords \nConcrete; fire; spalling; superheated liquid; thermodynamics. \n\nNIST TN 2385 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. Introduction \nWhen concrete is exposed to a fire, thermal energy from the fire is transported from the \nexposed concrete surface to the concrete interior. As the concrete interior is heated, its \ntemperature increases, causing the free water (moisture) in the concrete starts to evaporate, \nand the resulting water vapor diffuses towards the heated concrete surface where it is further \nheated and towards the unheated interior regions where it condenses and fills the pores within \nthe concrete. When the interior temperature is high enough, the dehydration of chemically \nbound water also occurs and generates more water vapor. As this heating process continues, a \nsudden and at times violent ejection of pieces of surface layers of the heated concrete, termed \nspalling, could occur. The propensity for spalling depends on many parameters including how \nthe concrete is heated (heating rate), concrete strength and constituents, how concrete is \ncured, and other factors. Majority of research literature has indicated that spalling results from \na highly coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical coupled process occurring in concrete exposed to \nhigh temperatures (e.g., fires). Many excellent review articles on various theories and \nhypotheses that had been used to partially explain the mechanisms of concrete spalling can be \nfound in the literature [1–7]. \nOne of the hypotheses on spalling was attributed to Ichikawa [8], who in passing suggested that \nthe spalling of concrete had been the result of a BLEVE (boiling liquid expanding vapor \nexplosion) event1. In this study, superheated liquid theory is used to re-examine Ichikawa’s \nBLEVE hypothesis. Specifically, this study only seeks to answer the question: What are the \nthermodynamic conditions of the water trapped in a continuously heated interior region of \nconcrete that would potentially trigger a BLEVE event? An idealization is made in the \nthermodynamic analysis in that there is an interior region of concrete where water is initially \ntrapped. In other words, the amount of water (either liquid, vapor, or liquid-vapor) in the \nheated region is fixed and is treated as a closed system. How the water is generated, \ntransported, and eventually accumulated in the region within the heated concrete is not the \nfocus of this study. \n \n1 The AIChE Center for Chemical Process Safety defines BLEVE as “A type of rapid phase transition in which a liquid contained above its \natmospheric boiling point is rapidly depressurized, causing a nearly instantaneous transition from liquid to vapor with a corresponding energy \nrelease.” https://www.aiche.org/ccps/resources/glossary \n\nNIST TN 2385 \nSeptember 2026 \n2 \n2. A superheated liquid is a meta-stable liquid that exists at \ntemperatures beyond its saturation boiling point at the same pressure. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Report: U.S.-EU Virtual Workshop on Plastics Recycling Standards and \nDefinitions to Support Transatlantic Trade \n \nOctober 31, 2024 \nAuthors: Noah Last1 and Laure Baillargeon2 \n1 National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States Department of Commerce \n2 Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs, European Commission \nExecutive Summary \nThis report was written following a virtual government-to-stakeholder event hosted on October 1, 2024 \nby the U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC)’s Plastics Recycling Workstream of Working Group 1: \nTechnology Standards, with representatives from the United States (U.S.) Government and European \nUnion’s (EU’s) European Commission (EC). The event brought together stakeholders from the U.S. and EU \nwith expertise in the plastic industry, plastic recycling industry, plastic recycling standards, and \ntransatlantic trade to answer the question Which plastics recycling standards and definitions matter the \nmost for EU-U.S. trade? This report summarizes the feedback received from stakeholders and provides a \nhigh-level analysis of the priorities raised by EU and U.S. stakeholders. The consensus was that more \nmulti-stakeholder dialogues should be prioritized moving forward, such as workshops like this one, \nworking groups, and official collaborations like that between the Association of Plastics Recyclers (APR) \nin the U.S. and RecyClass in the EU. These engagements may focus on themes from this workshop, such \nas food-contact material for packaging, recycled content and recycled material quality, substances of \nconcern, and chain of custody. These engagements should consider including stakeholders from U.S. and \nEU governments; the private sector; and standards organizations like ANSI, ASTM, and CEN. A list of \nrelevant existing standards, standards under development, and needed standards was also developed. \nThe U.S.-EU TTC supported the organization of this event. The TTC aims to promote U.S. and EU \ncompetitiveness and prosperity and the spread of market-oriented values by increasing transatlantic \ntrade and investment in products and services of emerging technology, strengthening our technological \nand industrial leadership, boosting innovation, and protecting and promoting critical and emerging \ntechnologies and infrastructure. \n \n  \n\nBackground \nThe U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC) was established in June 2021 to support cooperation \nbetween the United States (U.S.) and the European Union (EU) on trade, technology, and economic \npolicy. It serves as a platform to address challenges related to global trade, emerging technologies, and \nsupply chain security while promoting shared values and strengthening transatlantic economic ties. The \nTTC established 10 Working Groups (WGs) chaired by relevant U.S. and European Commission (EC) \nagencies. WG 1 – Technology Standards was tasked with developing approaches for coordinating in \ncritical and emerging standards and is led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) \nand the International Trade Administration (ITA) for the U.S. and the Directorate General for Internal \nMarket, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (DG GROW) and the Directorate-General for \nCommunications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CONNECT) for the EU. WG 1 operates through \nseveral workstreams on different topics, including the Plastics Recycling Workstream. \nWG 1’s Plastic Recycling Workstream (referred to moving forward as the Workstream) is led by a \nrepresentative from NIST and DG GROW and was tasked with identifying 1) which standards exist to \nsupport the trade of recycled plastics and products containing recycled plastics between the U.S. and EU \nand 2) where there is a need to create new standards or better align existing standards. The Workstream \nhas been meeting since February 2024 with leadership from one U.S. and one EU standards \ndevelopment organization: ASTM International’s plastics committee (D20) and CEN-CENELEC’s plastic \nrecycling committee (CEN/TC 249), respectively. \nThe Workstream assessed the standards landscape in the U.S. and EU and concluded that there is a lack \nof alignment around standards and terminology, including around topics such as recyclates, resin types, \nand post-consumer waste. It also identified three focus areas for future work: \n1. Terminology, \n2. Design for recycling, and \n3. Upcoming EU circular economy regulations. \nThe Workstream realized that input from experts in plastic recycling standards, terminology, and \ntransatlantic trade would be necessary to create this alignment. Therefore, they organized a virtual U.S.-\nEU Workshop on Plastics Recycling Standards and Definitions on October 1, 2024. Industry, nonprofit, \nand government stakeholders from the U.S. and EU were invited to apply to participate, with applicants \nchosen based on their background first in plastic recycling trade and standards, then in plastics recycling \nbroadly.  \nWorkshop structure \nFifty-nine people (48 from the private sector, 11 from the U.S. and EU governments) were convened for \nthe 2.25-hour workshop. Sophie Mueller, Head of the Standardisation Unit for DG GROW (EU), and \nAnthony Quinn, Team Lead – Standards for the ITA (U.S.), gave opening remarks. Then representatives \nfrom ASTM International’s plastics committee (D20) and CEN-CENELEC’s plastic recycling committee \n(CEN/TC 249) introduced the motivation for the workshop and the workshop’s guiding question: Which \nplastics recycling standards and definitions matter the most for EU-U.S. trade? Private-sector participants \nentered breakout rooms of six people, with an even split between U.S. and EU representatives \n(government participants were excluded from the breakout rooms), to answer four questions: \n\n1. Which plastic recycling definitions have the most impact on trade between the U.S. and EU? Are \nthere potential issues? \n2. Which plastic recycling standards have the most impact on trade between the U.S. and EU? Are \nthere potential issues? \n3. Which sectors or sub-sectors are most relevant to this discussion? (e.g., plastic materials, \nproducts, packaging) \n4. What steps can be taken to create further alignment between the U.S. and EU? \nParticipants reconvened for a whole-group discussion on their responses. \nEase of trade \nParticipants rated the ease of trading recycled plastics between the EU and U.S., on average, at 5.6 on a \nscale of 10 (with 1 being impossible and 10 being very easy with no issues), and the ease of trading \nplastic products with recycled content at 6.1 (6.3 from the EU to the U.S. and 5.9 from the U.S. to the \nEU), suggesting that market operators encounter some issues when trading these items across the \nAtlantic. \nWhen asked what mattered the most to ensure easy EU-U.S. trade of plastic materials, products or \npackaging, a majority of participants mentioned the need for aligned definitions, rules, and regulations \n(9 votes), particularly regarding food contact material regulations (6 votes). Another cluster of ideas (3 \nvotes) was around the need for ensuring traceability for recycled materials, including in trade data. \nThemes \nSix themes emerged from the discussions on potential trade barriers due to differing regulations, \nstandards or definitions between the EU and the US, suggesting a need for alignment to facilitate trade. \nThis report only presents these themes and summarizes the workshop’s discussion surrounding them. \nWhile more context on the policy, research, standards, and market landscapes will be needed to \novercome the trade barriers discussed surrounding these themes, this context is outside the scope of \nthis report. \nRecycled content and chain of custody: Definitions (e.g., definitions of recyclate and post-consumer, \npost-industrial, and pre-consumer wastes), calculation methods (e.g., mass balance and its various \nattribution models), and traceability (i.e., chain of custody) of recycled content were among the most \nfrequently mentioned topics, with participants suggesting a strong perceived need for alignment. Some \nparticipants also mentioned the importance of ensuring a common language and traceability on recycled \ncontent in transatlantic trade, including through documentation or certificates.  \nFood packaging. A number of sectors were presented as relevant to the workshop’s theme: medical, \nautomotive, batteries, electrical and electronic equipment (EEE), building and construction, agriculture, \nand textiles. However, the most-discussed sector was packaging, especially food-grade packaging. The \nU.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) have different \nrequirements for food-grade packaging, leading to different specifications for selling this packaging in the \nU.S. and EU. Packaging producers in the workshop and their representatives expressed uncertainty \naround how to be compliant with FDA and EFSA rules, with a perceived need for further alignment of \nrules between the EU and the U.S.  \n\nRecycled material quality. Several participants suggested that better standards are needed to harmonize \nrecycled plastic and feedstock qualities. Bale specifications exist in the U.S. under the Recycled Materials \nAssociation (ReMa, formerly the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries) and quality grades for sorted \nplastic wastes are being developed in CEN. A number of testing methods for recycled plastics also exist \nthrough ASTM and CEN, but better visibility around these standards and alignment may be needed to \novercome the challenges expressed during the workshop. Several stakeholders expressed a need to align \non recyclability standards. Design-for-recycling guidelines are being developed by CEN and APR, including \nfor plastic packaging and automotive plastics. \nSubstances of concern. Compliance with U.S. and EU regulations around substances of concern—e.g., \nPFAS, micro- and nanoplastics—was a challenge identified by workshop stakeholders. The EU’s \nRegistration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) regulation includes a list of \nthese materials for the EU. It was also suggested that companies importing products containing \nchemically recycled plastics (plastics recycled via chemical recycling) into the U.S. struggle to comply with \nthe EPA’s Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA); once the material stops being waste and starts being a \nfeedstock again, detailed compositional information on the feedstock is needed to ensure compliance \nwith the TSCA. \nMarket development. One goal of eliminating trade barriers for recycled plastics and the products \ncontaining them between the U.S. and EU is to support the development of the plastic recycling industry. \nWorkshop participants hoped that establishing common policy agendas between the nations could \nsupport the recycling economic model. Participants also asserted that one challenge to both market \ndevelopment and policy alignment between the nations is that the U.S. lacks national targets for \nrecycled plastics, while the EU does have specific targets. This lack of targets 1) may be inhibiting the \ndevelopment of the plastic recycling market, both upstream and downstream, and 2) stifles alignment \nopportunities between the U.S. and EU. Regarding the latter, national targets could create more points of \ncontact through which the nations can align.  \nCollaborations. Workshop participants suggested that creating better alignment between the U.S. and \nEU to support the trade of recycled plastics and products containing them will require collaborations \nbetween several groups. For example, an online repository listing U.S., EU, and other international \nstandards was proposed; this could be sponsored by U.S. and EU government agencies, or by CEN and \n

[{"suffix": "", "text": "The Role of Humidity in Enhancing CO2 Capture Efficiency in Polyethyleneimine Thin Films\n\nJohn R. Hoffman, Avery E. Baumann, Christopher M. Stafford\n\nMaterials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD, 20899, United States\n\n*To whom correspondence should be addressed: chris.stafford@nist.gov\n\n\nAbstract\n\nAmine impregnated sorbents have been extensively studied for direct air capture (DAC) of CO2 in both dry and humid conditions. In a dry environment, CO2 capture follows a carbamate formation mechanism. Amine efficiency can be improved by allowing more amine sites to participate in the reaction. Introducing water vapor helps break up internal hydrogen bonding within the amine-based polymer, which increases both the polymer mobility and accessibility of amine sites. In this work, we evaluate the influence of humidity on the CO2 capture in polyethyleneimine (PEI) thin films using tandem quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) and polarization modulation infrared reflection-absorption spectroscopy (PM-IRRAS). We show that tandem QCM/PM-IRRAS enables more accurate CO2 uptake measurements, as the combined techniques can separate individual mass changes due to CO2 and H2O sorption. CO2 adsorption capacity and amine efficiency were evaluated for a 10 nm and 100 nm film at varied temperatures, humidities, and CO2 concentrations. We find that water sorption greatly enhances CO2 uptake when the capture is limited by diffusional resistance (at higher CO2 concentration and in 100 nm films) but has less influence in conditions where CO2 availability is limiting uptake (at lower CO2 concentration and in 10 nm films). Thus, we argue that humidity does improve capture, but not at all conditions. Our approach enhances the understanding of H2O-assisted sorption of CO2 in PEI across a range of conditions while also presenting a measurement strategy to apply to, and hopefully optimize, component uptake in materials of interest to the CO2 capture community.\n\nKeywords: CO2 adsorption, Amine efficiency, QCM, PM-IRRAS, Humidity, Diffusion \n\nHighlights: \nTandem QCM/PM-IRRAS distinguishes component uptake by PEI from mixed H2O/CO2 feeds \nH2O enhances CO2 capture only when uptake is limited by diffusional resistance\n40% RH sufficiently plasticizes PEI to achieve thickness-independent capture 5% CO2\nEffect of humidity on CO2 uptake is less apparent for ultrathin PEI films (10 nm)\n\n\n\n\n\n1. Introduction\n\nDirect air capture (DAC) of CO2 from the atmosphere is one of many approaches being proposed to reduce the global impact of climate change, a necessary feat in order to achieve net-zero emission targets.[1] DAC is a negative emission technology that can balance CO2 emissions that arise from sectors difficult to decarbonize, as well as reduce the impact of legacy emissions.[2] Supported polymeric amines are promising candidates for DAC, with many supports and amine structures demonstrated in the literature.[3–5] Amine incorporation is often achieved via physical impregnation of polyethyleneimine (PEI) or through grafting of amino silanes within mesoporous silica supports.[6,7] There are a multitude of factors controlling CO2 capture within these amine-containing materials. During capture, CO2 must first diffuse from the environment into the bulk material and then further diffuse within the material to specific amine sites.[8] Reactions at amine sites result in carbamate formation,[9] which requires interactions between one CO2 molecule and two amines when performed in a dry environment.[10] As the distance CO2 must diffuse within the amine layer increases, the overall amine efficiency decreases as it becomes more difficult for CO2 to reach all available amine sites or for CO2 molecules to find two closely neighboring amine groups for reaction.[11,12] This has been shown in literature examples in coned-shaped porous structures[13] as well as in work previously done in our group which examined the capture process in a planar geometry.[14] \n\nIncreasing capacity and amine efficiency (the amount of CO2 captured per amine site) is critical for more wide-spread deployment of DAC materials. Previously, we evaluated CO2 capture in PEI using a planar or thin film geometry, which allows for precise control of certain design parameters, such as amine coating thickness, that are difficult to tune when studying 3-dimensional sorbent particles. Varying the film thickness of the polymeric amine is analogous to varying amine loadings in porous supports[15] while providing a defined CO2 diffusional path length as compared to sorbent particles. Our results showed a dependence of capture capacity and amine efficiency on film thickness.[14] Films of >50 nm thickness displayed higher capacity but lower amine efficiency than films <50 nm. In the thick film regime, we argued that capture was limited by amine site availability as deeper lying amine sites do not react with CO2 as they are potentially unreachable. Thinner films <50 nm, are not limited by amine availability but rather by CO2 availability. For this reason, thinner films achieve higher amine efficiency but a lower capture capacity due to the overall decrease in amine sites.\n\nThere are also transient effects which influence the CO2 transport in PEI films. The diffusion of CO2 into the amine sorbent has multiple impacts on the dynamics of the polymer, which in turn can influence capture capacity. CO2 is well known for its ability to plasticize polymers and break up hydrogen bonding between the polymer chains, which can increase the diffusion coefficient of gases within PEI. However, the coordination of two amines per one CO2 molecule results in an ionic crosslinking effect that decreases the dynamics of the PEI chains.[16] This crosslinking effect may inhibit the ability of CO2 to diffuse freely through the material. A detailed understanding of the CO2 transport in PEI films requires understanding the complicated interplay between these two connected systems.\n\nWater, in a similar manner as CO2, can also plasticize PEI by interrupting the hydrogen bonding between polymer chains.[16–18] It is proposed that CO2 can diffuse more readily through a humidity-swollen material, allowing access to deeper lying amine sites.  Higher mobility amine sites allow for better coordination between amines and CO2 molecules throughout the film thickness.[19] Water also alters the reaction mechanism, through enhanced zwitterion stabilization and hydronium carbamate/carbamic acid formation.[20,21]  While two amines are needed to stabilize the carbamate product in dry conditions, only one amine is necessary in humid conditions due to additional proton donation from water during hydronium carbamate formation.[20] This increases the maximum potential amine efficiency from 0.5 to 1.[22] It is also possible to form bicarbonate, but this has been shown to be energetically unfavorable compared to the formation of hydronium carbamate and carbamic acid in a humid environment.[23] The formation of bicarbonate has predominately been observed in low amine density sorbents, such as grafted amines,[24] while high amine density polymers, including PEI, remain dominated by carbamate formation. In addition to the benefits that humidity plays in CO2 capture, there are also concerns regarding the stability of amine materials, through humidity-assisted oxidative degradation reactions.[25] Since humidity is ubiquitous in the atmosphere,[18] proper evaluation of CO2 capture at DAC conditions necessitates its inclusion.\n\nMeasuring CO2 capture in humid environments is difficult due to the competing adsorption of both species into the material.[26] Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) coupled to an outlet gas analyzer is one commonly used technique, in which the mass of sorbent material and outlet CO2 concentration are measured through the adsorption/desorption process.[27,28] Evaluating CO2 capture in a humid environment typically follows a  pre-humidification step in which the sorbent is exposed to humidity prior to CO2.[29,30] This allows for the determination of the H2O sorption capacity and then the CO2 capture capacity when switching to a humidified CO2 feed. This process is limited in evaluating the co-adsorption of both species, as both species contribute to the total adsorbed mass during exposure and are non-distinguishable.\n\nA more accurate analysis requires the ability to distinguish the adsorption of each species individually during adsorption. Previous work from our group investigated dry CO2 capture using a tandem quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) and polarization modulation infrared reflection-absorption spectroscopy (PM-IRRAS) platform.[14] As we will show here, this experimental tool is capable of distinguishing the individual contributions of CO2 and H2O to the total sorbed mass.[16] When using QCM alone, the total uptake mass is measured, which includes both chemisorbed CO2 and physisorbed H2O. Distinguishing the relative uptake of these two components is possible through Fourier Transform infrared (FTIR) spectral analysis via PM-IRRAS, in which specific water and carbamate peak heights can be correlated to corresponding mass gain of each component during capture.\n\nThis work furthers our understanding of the role of humidity on the CO2 capture of PEI thin films. Film thicknesses of 10 nm and 100 nm were evaluated as they represent the two thickness regimes limited by either CO2 availability or amine accessibility, respectfully, from previous studies under dry sorption conditions.[14] CO2 capture capacity and amine efficiency are evaluated as a function of temperature, humidity level, and CO2 concentration. These conditions were chosen to fully assess the impact on capture capacity and determine the role that humidity has in potentially improving DAC processes.\n\n\n2. Materials and Methods\n\nCertain equipment, instruments, software, or materials are identified in this paper in order to specify the experimental procedure adequately. Such identification is not intended to imply recommendation or endorsement of any product or service by NIST, nor is it intended to imply that the materials or equipment identified are necessarily the best available for the purpose.\n\nTandem quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) and polarization modulation-infrared reflection-adsorption spectroscopy (PM-IRRAS) measurements were performed using a custom QCM cell (AWSensors, Valencia, Spain) mounted within the PM-IRRAS accessory of a Nicolet iS50 infrared (IR) spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA) as detailed in previous work.[14] \n\nMeasurements were made using standard 1 in (25.4 mm) diameter gold coated AT-cut quartz QCM substrates (AWSensors) with a resonant frequency of 5 MHz. The gold coated crystals provide the necessary IR reflective surface for PM-IRRAS measurements. The QCM crystals were cleaned by sonicating for 10 min in acetone and 10 min in isopropanol. The crystals were then dried using nitrogen and exposed to UV-ozone (UVO, Model 42, Jelight Company, Inc, Irvine, CA) for 20 min prior to testing. QCM measurements were performed with the clean crystal at all tested temperatures to obtain the baseline frequency values of each crystal. \n\nHyperbranched polyethyleneimine (PEI), (molecular mass = 25 kDa, Sigma-Aldrich) was dissolved in ethanol at mass fractions of 0.25 % and 2 % and spin coated onto the clean QCM crystals to produce films of desired thickness. PEI films of 10 nm and 100 nm thickness were prepared and confirmed using a M-2000XI variable angle spectroscopic ellipsometer (J.A. Woollam Co., Inc., Lincoln, NE). The coated crystals were placed within the QCM cell and heated to 60 C under 750 standard cubic centimeters per minute (SCCM) N2 flow to remove any adsorbed CO2 and water prior to measurements. \nThermodynamic driving forces: Writing a fundamental equation \nWhat goes into internal energy? \n•\t When we introduced the concept of work, we stated that every form of work can be thought of as a \ngeneralized thermodynamic force acting to create some generalized ‘displacement’ in the system. Why not U = U(T,V)? The answer will unfortuna tely not be clear until we \nintroduce the second law.  The second law dictates that certain thermodynamic functions will reach \nextrema (maximima or minima) when the system is at equilibrium- e.g. the entropy will be maximized at \nequilibrium. When U and S are written as function of S,V and U,V respectively, they are said to be written \nin terms of their natural variables. State functions of natural variables have extremum principles at \nequilibrium (they will be maximized or minimized at equilibrium).  In other words, the reason we write U as \na function of S and V is that it is the most useful form to write internal energy equations for most \nproblems- we can use this equation for internal energy to calculate equilibrium properties. \nGeneralized expression for the internal energy: internal energy of open systems \n•\t The first law expression above only applies to very simple thermodynamic systems- which have can \nundergo only hydrostatic work and have no transport or chemical transformation of components.  \nExtending our first law expression is straightforward for any thermodynamic case where other forms of \nwork are important. We have seen how to make calculations of these quantities from measurable \nquantities.  However, in these calculations we have been limited to analyzing processes whose \nspontaneous behavior we take as a given - we have not yet made predictions of what processes will \noccur. We have quantified thermody namic properties at a first-order phase transition, but we have not yet \nprovided the tools to predict where a phase transition will happen in P,T,V space. Carey: 0000-0002-8741-258X \nBenjamin Johnsson: 0009-0008-8513-0483 \nContact Information \nStephanie S Watson, Ph.D. \nstephanie.watson@nist.gov \n\nNIST TN 2382 \nSeptember 2026 \ni \nAbstract \nPyrrhotite in concrete aggregate can lead to severe cracking due to expansion reactions. \nMost research has focused on screening methods and mix designs that lower the permeability of \nnew structures. However, there is a need to evaluate the feasibility of mitigation techniques for \nexisting structures containing pyrrhotite aggregate but have not yet shown signs of deterioration. \nEfforts at NIST have focused on evaluating the potential of concrete sealants, which can reduce \nor entirely eliminate the ingress of water and air into the concrete. Since pyrrhotite requires both \noxygen and water to react, one or both component ’s concentrations can be reduced to delay \npyrrhotite oxidation for some amount of time. One methodology being vetted for characterizing \nthe performance of  mitigating sealants is air permeability  test. This report details efforts to \nvalidate changes made to a commercially available air permeameter to better facilitate NIST’s \nneeds. This validation testing was generally conducted in two parts. Part 1 focused on validating \nas-received equipment for use with 152.4 mm (6-inch) diameter concrete cores, which is the size \nthe commercially available set -up is made to test. Part 2 focused on validating retrofitting the \nequipment to test 101.6 mm (4-inch) diameter cores, the common diameter used for laboratory \nand field-cast concrete specimens.  \n \nKeywords \nAir Permeability; Concrete; Pyrrhotite; RILEM-Cembureau Permeability \n\nNIST TN 2382 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. These properties include thermal, electrical,\nmagnetic, and optical properties . The shape is derived from the periodicity and symmetry of the crystalline lattice\nand energy bands . For the Fermi surface all points in reciprocal space at which \\(E=E_f\\). In different dimensions\nthere are different representations which include:\n1D: represented by a pair of points\n2D: represented by a line (which could be a closed loop)\n3D: represented by a surface (which could be a closed surface)\nBelow is a depiction of the Fermi surface and Fermi sphere.\nFigure  Fermi surface and Fermi sphere\nThe ground state of N free electrons is constructed by occupying all one electron levels  with energies\nWhere  is determined by requiring the total number of one electron levels with energies less than  to be equal to the\ntotal number of electrons. When the lowest of these are filled by a specified number of electrons, two quite distinct\ntypes of configuration can occur:\nA certain number of bands may be completely filled, all others remaining empty. The band gap is determined\nby the difference between the highest occupied energy level and the lowest occupied energy level.\nA number of bands may be partially filled. When this occurs, the energy of the highest occupied level, the\nFermi energy, lies within the energy range of one or more bands. For each partially filled band there will be a\nsurface in k-space separating the occupied from the unoccupied levels. The set of all such surfaces is known as\nthe Fermi surface. The parts of the Fermi surface arising from the individual partially filled bands are known\nas branches of the Fermi surface .\nThus the Fermi surface is a constant energy surface in k-space, just as the more familiar equipotentials of electrostatic\ntheory are constant energy surfaces in real space . The Fermi surface is also independent of temperature, when there\nis an increase in temperature only a small amount of electrons are excited and thus they move from the inside to the\noutside surface. The value of the Fermi Energy is determined by the electron concentration. So higher the Fermi level\nthe higher the . [{"suffix": "", "text": "Ladder Operators\nMathematically, a ladder operator is defined as an operator which, when applied to a state, creates a new state with a\nraised or lowered eigenvalue . Their utility in quantum mechanics follows from their ability to describe the energy\nspectrum and associated wavefunctions in a more manageable way, without solving differential equations. We will\ndiscuss the most prominent example of the use of these operators; the quantum harmonic oscillator. Their use does not\nend there, however, as the mathematics of ladder operators can easily be extended to more complicated problems,\nincluding angular momentum and many body problems. In the latter case, the operators serve as creation and\nannihilation operators; adding or subtracting to the number of particles in a given state.\nQuantum Harmonic Oscillator\nThis diagram shows the energy levels and wavefuntions for the harmonic oscillator potential. HISTORICAL INTRODUCTION \nX-rays were discovered during the summer of 1895 by Wilhelm Röntgen at the \nUniversity of Würtzburg (Germany). Röntgen was interested in the cathode rays \n(beams of electrons) developed in discharge tubes, but it is not clear exactly which \naspects of cathode rays he intended to study. By chance he noticed that a fluorescent \nscreen (ZnS + Mn++) lying on a table some distance from the discharge tube emitted a \nflash of light each time an electrical discharge was passed through the tube. Realizing \nthat he had come upon something completely new, he devoted his energies to \ninvestigating the properties of the unknown ray “X” which produced this effect. The \nannouncement of this discovery appeared in December 1895 as a concise ten page \npublication. \nThe announcement of the discovery of X-rays was received with great interest by the \npublic. Röntgen himself prepared the first photographs of the bones in a living hand, \nand use of the radiation was quickly adopted in medicine. In the succeeding fifteen \nyears, however, very few fundamental insights were gained into the nature of \n1\n\n\nLN–5\nX-radiation. There was some indication that the rays were waves, but the evidence was \nnot clear-cut and could be interpreted in several ways. Then, at the University of \nMunich in 1912, Max von Laue performed one of the most significant experiments of \nmodern physics. At his suggestion, Paul Knipping (who had just completed a doctoral \nthesis with Röntgen) and Walter Friedrich (a newly appointed assistant to Sommerfeld) \ndirected a beam of X-rays at a crystal of copper sulfate and attempted to record the \nscattered beams on a photographic plate. The first experiment was unsuccessful. The \nresult of a second experiment was successful. They observed the presence of spots \nproduced by diffracted X-ray beams grouped around a larger central spot where the \nincident X-ray beam struck the film. This experiment demonstrated conclusively that \nX-radiation consisted of waves and, further, that the crystals were composed of atoms \narranged on a space lattice. \n2. THE “FINE STRUCTURE” OF CHARACTERISTIC X-RAYS \nIt is customary to consider the characteristic X-ray spectral lines as discrete lines (K α, \nKβ, Lα, Lβ, etc.). In reality, they are not discrete since the electron shells involved in the \nassociated electron transitions have energy sublevels (s, p, d orbitals). These sublevels \ngive rise to a “fine structure” insofar as the Kα lines are doublets composed of Kα1 and \nKα2 lines. Similarly, Lα, Lβ, etc., exhibit a fine structure. \nThese considerations suggest that X-ray spectra contain information concerning the \nenergetics of electronic states. Obviously, analysis of X-rays emitted from a target of \nunknown composition can be used for a quantitative chemical analysis. As such it is very valuable to be able to construct a\nphase diagram and know how to use it to predict behaviour of materials.\nThe main theory behind phase diagrams is based around the latent heat\nthat is evolved when a mixture is cooled, and changes phase. This means\nthat by plotting graphs of temperature against time for a variety of\ndifferent compositions, it should be possible to see at what temperatures\nthe different phases form.\nIt is relatively easy to produce a rough binary phase diagram, as will be\nshown later in the package, but although it is quick to take readings for\nthe top part of a phase diagram, it takes longer, and hence more\nsensitive equipment to monitor the changes that take place when a solid\nchanges phase. A typical simple binary phase diagram is as follows:\nWhere L stands for liquid, and A and B are the two components and α\nand β are two solid phases rich in A and B respectively. The blue lines\nrepresent the liquidus and solidus lines, which are relatively simple to\nmeasure. The red lines involve a solid-to-solid transition, and so require\nmuch more sensitive equipment.\nHowever, there is also a lot of thermodynamic theory behind phase\ndiagrams, which allows more problematic or more complex systems to\n10/1/26, 12:27 PM Phase Diagrams and Solidification (all content)\nhttps://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/phase-diagrams/printall.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com 2/44\n\nbe predicted, and this can lead to faster creation of phase diagrams, as it\ncan take a long time to pick up all the stable phases in experiments, and\nthere is not always the time available for such practical work.\nA crucial point to remember is that a phase diagram should always\ndisplay the equilibrium phases, and so with cooler temperatures, these\nare hard to attain due to kinetic problems. Even at higher temperatures,\nthere may be problems of having enough time for the solid to fully\nequilibrate as the system is cooling.\nThermodynamics: Basic terms\nInternal Energy, U\nThe internal energy of a system is the sum of the potential energy and\nthe kinetic energy. For many applications it is necessary to consider a\nsmall change in the internal energy, dU, of a system.\ndU = dq + dw = CdT - PdV\ndq = the heat supplied to a system\ndw = the work performed on the system\nC = heat capacity\ndT = change in temperature\nP = pressure\ndV = change in volume\nAt constant volume,\ndU = C dT\nEnthalpy, H\nEnthalpy is the constant pressure version of the internal energy.\nEnthalpy,\nH = U + PV.\nTherefore, for small changes in enthalpy,\ndH = dU + PdV + VdP.\nAt constant pressure,\ndH = C dT.\nEntropy, S\nEntropy is a measure of the disorder of a system. In terms of molecular\ndisorder, the entropy consists of the configurational disorder (the\narrangement of different atoms over identical sites) and the thermal\nvibrations of the atoms about their mean positions. A change in entropy\nis defined as,\nV\nP\n10/1/26, 12:27 PM Phase Diagrams and Solidification (all content)\nhttps://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/phase-diagrams/printall.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com 3/44\n\nFor reversible changes, i.e. changes under equilibrium conditions,\ndq = TdS\nFor natural changes, i.e. under non-equilibrium conditions,\ndq < TdS\nGibbs free energy, G\nThe Gibbs free energy can be used to define the equilibrium state of a\nsystem. It considers only the properties of the system and not the\nproperties of its surroundings. It can be thought of as the energy which\nis available in the system to do useful work.\nFree energy, G, is defined as,\nG = H - TS = U + PV - TS\nFor small changes,\ndG = dH - TdS - SdT = VdP - SdT + (dq - TdS)\nFor changes occurring at constant pressure and temperature,\ndG = dq - TdS\nTherefore, dG = 0 for reversible (equilibrium) changes, and dG < 0 for\nnon-reversible changes.\nFrom this it is clear that G tends to a minimum at equilibrium.\nThe Helmholtz free energy, F, is sometimes used instead of G, and is the\nequivalent of G for changes at constant volume. It is defined as,\nF = U - TS\nThermodynamics of Solutions\nConsider a mechanical mixture of two phases, A and B. If this is then\ntransformed into a single solution phase with A and B atoms distributed\nrandomly over the atomic sites, then there will be,\nAn enthalpy change associated with interactions between the A and\nB atoms, ΔH\nAn entropy change, ΔS , associated with the random mixing of the\natoms\nA free energy of mixing, ΔG  = ΔH  - TΔS\nAssume that the system consists of N atoms: x N of A and x N of B,\nwhere,\nx  = fraction of A atoms and x  = (1 - x ) = fraction of B atoms\ndS ≥ dq\nT\nmix\nmix\nmix mix mix\nA B\nA B A\n10/1/26, 12:27 PM Phase Diagrams and Solidification (all content)\nhttps://www.doitpoms.ac.uk/tlplib/phase-diagrams/printall.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com 4/44\n\nEnthalpy of mixing\nIn calculating ΔH  it is assumed that only the potential energy term\nundergoes any significant change during mixing. This change arises from\nthe interactions between nearest-neighbour atoms. Consider an alloy\nconsisting of atoms A and B. If the atoms prefer like neighbours, A atoms\nwill tend to cluster and likewise B atoms, so a greater number of A-A and\nB-B bonds will form. If the atoms prefer unlike neighbours a greater\nnumber of A-B bonds will form. If there is no preference A and B atoms\nwill be randomly distributed.\nLet w  be the interaction energy between A - A nearest neighbours, w\nthat for B - B nearest neighbours and w  that for A - B nearest\nneighbours.\nAll of these energies are negative, as the zero in potential energy is for\ninfinite separation between atoms.\nLet each atom of A and B have co-ordination number z.\nTherefore, the total number of nearest-neighbour pairs is Nz/2.\nProbability of A - A neighbours = x\nProbability of B - B neighbours = x\nProbability of A - B neighbours = 2x x\nFor a solid solution the total interaction energy is,\nH  - U  = Nz/2 (x  w  + x  w  + 2x x  w )\nFor pure A, H  = (Nz/2)w\nFor pure B, H  = (Nz/2)w\nHence the enthalpy of mixing is given by,\nΔH  = H  - (x H  + x H ) = (Nz/2)x x  (2w  - w  - w )\nWe can define an interaction parameter\nW = (Nz/2)(2w  - w  - w )\nTherefore,\nΔH  = Wx x\nIf A-A and B-B interactions are energetically more favourable than A-B\ninteractions then W > 0.
