[{"suffix": "", "text": "Compressed Qubit Noise Spectroscopy:\nPiecewise-Linear Modeling and Rademacher Measurements\nKaixin Huang,1, 2,∗ Demitry Farfurnik,3, 4 Dror Baron,3 and Yi-Kai Liu2, 5\n1Joint Quantum Institute (JQI), NIST/University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA\n2Joint Center for Quantum Information and Computer Science (QuICS),\nNIST/University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742, USA\n3Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering,\nNorth Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, 27695, USA\n4Department of Physics, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, 27695, USA\n5Applied and Computational Mathematics Division,\nNational Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Gaithersburg, MD 20899, USA\n(Dated: September 29, 2026)\nRandom pulse sequences are a powerful method for qubit noise spectroscopy, enabling efficient\nreconstruction of sparse noise spectra. Here, we advance this method in two complementary di-\nrections. First, we extend the method using a regularizer based on the total generalized variation\n(TGV) norm, in order to reconstruct a larger class of noise spectra, namely piecewise-linear noise\nspectra, which more realistically model many physical systems. We show through numerical simula-\ntions that the new method resolves finer spectral features, while maintaining an order-of-magnitude\nspeedup over conventional approaches to noise spectroscopy. Second, we simplify the experimental\nimplementation of the method, by introducing Rademacher measurements for reconstructing sparse\nnoise spectra. These measurements use pseudorandom pulse sequences that can be generated in\nreal time from a short random seed, reducing experimental complexity without compromising re-\nconstruction accuracy. Together, these developments broaden the reach of random pulse sequences\nfor accurate and efficient noise characterization in realistic quantum systems.\nI. I NTRODUCTION\nCharacterizing the spectral properties of environmen-\ntal noise is essential for understanding and mitigating\ndecoherence in quantum systems. In particular, the accu-\nrate reconstruction of the noise spectral density,S(ω), in-\nforms both noise-resilient control protocols and error mit-\nigation strategies in quantum technologies [1–3]. Dynam-\nical decoupling (DD) techniques enable indirect access\ntoS(ω) by modulating a system’s sensitivity to environ-\nmental fluctuations via tailored control sequences. How-\never, conventional methods of DD often rely on coarse\nfrequency resolution or assumptions of spectral smooth-\nness, limiting their effectiveness in resolving structured\nand non-smooth features [4–8].\nTo improve the resolution and resource efficiency of\nnoise spectroscopy, compressed sensing (CS) has emerged\nas a powerful framework for spectral reconstruction in\nquantum noise spectroscopy, particularly when the spec-\ntrum possesses sparse structure in a suitable representa-\ntion [9, 10]. Recent work has introduced random pulse se-\nquences as a tool for the direct measurement of arbitrary\nlinear functionals ofS(ω), enabling the CS reconstruction\nof sharp spectral peaks with fewer measurements [11].\nWhile this approach is effective for perfectly sparse\nspectra, it leaves two key challenges unresolved: can this\nmethod be applied to a larger class of noise spectra that\nare not perfectly sparse? And can the practical difficulty\n∗ kxhuang@umd.edu\nof applying the desired random pulse sequences in an ex-\nperiment be reduced? This paper addresses both of these\nchallenges separately.\nA. A Larger Class of Noise Spectra\nMany realistic noise processes, including charge and\nmagnetic noise in solid-state qubits, exhibit more com-\nplicated spectral features rather than sparse peaks rep-\nresented by simple delta functions [12, 13]. For example,\nthe spectra of quantum dot systems often combine nar-\nrow resonances with broad, slowly varying backgrounds.\nThis motivates the need for models that retain sparsity\nwhile capturing richer structures. Piecewise-linear, and\nmore generally piecewise-polynomial, functions provide\nsuch a representation.\nIn this work, we develop a CS protocol for reconstruct-\ning piecewise-linear noise spectra by enforcing sparsity\non the second derivativeS′′(ω). Specifically, we apply an\nL1-norm regularization onS′′(ω), which promotes recon-\nstructions that are globally continuous but exhibit sparse\ncurvatures. This approach aligns with recent advances\nin total generalized variation (TGV) [14–16] and higher-\norder sparse regularization techniques for inverse prob-\nlems [17, 18]. It can also be viewed as an extension of\nwell-known work on compressed sensing in the context\nof medical imaging, for piecewise-constant images in two\ndimensions, based on regularization using the total vari-\nation (TV) norm [19–22].\nOur method extends this to the problem of compressed\nsensing of a piecewise-linear function using TGV regu-\n\n2\nlarization, in one dimension. This particular setting ap-\npears to be more challenging from a theoretical perspec-\ntive, and beyond the scope of the above works. Nonethe-\nless, our numerical simulations on simulated spectra with\nvarying degrees of piecewise-linearity demonstrate high-\nfidelity reconstructions.\nB. Simpler Pulse Sequences\nNext, we consider the experimental implementation of\nrandom pulse sequences, which can be resource-intensive.\nIn particular, previous work proposed the use of random\npulse sequences with complex, long-range correlations,\nwhich are difficult to generate in real time. Instead, the\nentire pulse sequence typically had to be generated “of-\nfline,” using a desktop computer, then transferred to an\narbitrary waveform generator (AWG), before being ap-\nplied to a physical qubit. The loading and storage of a\ngreat number of different pulse sequences creates a bot-\ntleneck in experiments.\nTo address this bottleneck, we introduce a simplified\nvariant of the method, using uncorrelated random pulses,\nwhich we call Rademacher measurements. These pulse\nsequences are easier to generate in real time, using a short\nrandom seed and a high-quality pseudorandom number\ngenerator [23], so that the entire pulse sequence never has\nto be stored in memory. This opens up the possibility\nof generating the random pulse sequences “on the fly”\nusing a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), without\nany need for an AWG.\nIn this scheme, the total evolution time is divided into\nequal segments indexed by m = 1, 2,...,M, each time\nsegment is assigned a Rademacher random variable Um\n(i.e., an independent random variable that takes on the\nvalues 1 and−1 with equal probability), and rotation\nπ-pulses are applied to the qubit whenever Um+1̸=Um.\nAt first glance, it may seem that these pulse sequences\nconsist of nothing more than white noise, and thus can\nonly measure a single degree of freedom of the environ-\nment of the qubit. We get around this difficulty by using\na simple trick: we perform many measurements using\nthe same realization of the random variablesUm (i.e., by\nrunning a pseudorandom number generator many times\nusing the same seed). This lets us measure the signal\nassociated with the fluctuations in a single realization of\nthe pulse sequence. By repeating this measurement with\ndifferent fluctuations, we collect enough information to\nfully characterize the environment of the qubit.\nDespite their simplicity, we show via theory and simu-\nlations that Rademacher measurements retain the same\ncompressed-sensing efficiency as Fourier-based random\npulses [11], while substantially reducing experimental\ncomplexity. Interestingly, these Rademacher measure-\nments are similar in spirit to Gaussian measurements in\ncompressed sensing, which are well-studied [24, 25]. But\nour Rademacher measurements have an unusual feature,\nwhich is different from these older works on compressed\nsensing: our measurements depend quadratically (rather\nthan linearly) on the random variables Um, as shown\nin Eq. (14). For this reason, our recovery guarantee\nfor Rademacher measurements relies on more recently-\ndeveloped techniques, involving the recovery of struc-\ntured low-rank matrices [26, 27].\nC. Application to Quantum Dots\nFinally, we extend our investigation to realistic phys-\nical systems, focusing on the noise spectra of self-\nassembled quantum dots [13]. We demonstrate the ef-\nficiency of the TGV-based CS method, combine it with\nthe Rademacher measurements technique, and demon-\nstrate its potential for rapidly reconstructing realistic\nnoise spectra. We also explore modifications of the pro-\ntocol that further reduce the number of control pulses\nwithout significant loss in reconstruction accuracy. These\nresults broaden the applicability of random-pulse-based\nnoise spectroscopy and improve its practicality for near-\nterm quantum devices.\nThe remainder of the paper is organized as follows.\nThe basic model and background are introduced in\nSec. II. The two main techniques of the paper are de-\nveloped in detail in Secs. III and IV. We explore appli-\ncations of our techniques on realistic systems in Sec. V.\nWe conclude with a summary and a discussion of open\nproblems in Sec. VI.\nII. N OISE SPECTROSCOPY MODEL\nWe consider a single qubit (“the system”) subject to\npure dephasing due to coupling with a classical fluctuat-\ning environment. The Hamiltonian is given by\nˆH(t) = ˆH0 + ˆHV (t) = [Ω +V (t)]σz, (1)\nwhere ˆH0 = Ωσz is the system Hamiltonian, and ˆHV (t) =\nV (t)σz describes the coupling of the spin qubit to a\nstochastic noise process V (t) from the bath (e.g., fluc-\ntuations of a magnetic field). The noise spectrum S(ω)\nis defined as the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation\nfunctiong(t−t′) =⟨V (t)V (t′)⟩V , where⟨·⟩V denotes the\naverage with respect to the ensemble ofV (t) [28, 29]. We\nfurther assume that the noise spectrum is band-limited,\ni.e., S(ω) = 0 for|ω|>ωc, where ωc is a high-frequency\ncutoff [30, 31].\nTo estimate the spectrum S(ω), we employ the filter\nfunction formalism [32], which applies control pulses to\nchange the frequency domain susceptibility of the qubit\nto noise. A control sequence can be associated with a\nfilter function,F (ω), that characterizes the qubit’s spec-\ntral response. For a qubit initialized and measured in the\n|+⟩ = 1√\n2(|0⟩ +|1⟩) state, the survival probability over\n\n3\nevolution time T can be approximated as\nP (T )≈ 1\n2 + 1\n2 exp\n\u0012\n−\nZ ωc\n−ωc\ndωS(ω)F (ω)\n\u0013\n. (2)\nThe decay exponent, χ(T ) =\nR\ndωS(ω)F (ω), quantifies\nthe extent to which the noise spectrum overlaps with the\ncontrol’s frequency response. Note that F (ω) depend\nimplicitly on the evolution time T .\nEquation (2) provides a pathway for estimating the\nspectrum of a noisy environment via linear inversion.\nWe apply a set of m control sequences on the system,\nthen measure the corresponding survival probabilitiesPk,\nk = 1,...,K. For each k, one obtains estimates of\nχk =− log(2Pk−1). To make the inversion tractable, we\ndiscretize the frequency axis at N points{ωn}, leading\nto the approximation\nχk =\nNX\nn=1\nFk(ωn)S(ωn) +ϵk. (3)\nHereϵk represents the error in thek-th measurement. In\nmatrix form, Eq. (3) becomes\nχ = FS +ϵ, (4)\nwhereχ∈ RK contains the measured decay exponents,\nF∈ RK×N encodes the filter functions, and S∈ RN rep-\nresents the discretized noise spectrum. The estimation\nof S then reduces to solving a linear regression problem.\nA common way to solve this problem is to apply the\nCarr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) pulse sequence with\nevenly spaced rotation π pulses, whose filter function is\napproximately the Dirac δ-function. One can then solve\nEq. (4) via nonnegative least squares (NNLS) or other\ndeconvolution methods [11]. Intuitively, each CPMG se-\nquence captures a narrow range of the spectrum, and\none needs to apply many sequences to cover all frequency\nranges. As a result, the numb

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Survey of agricultural plastic waste in the American Midwest: usage and disposal\n\nJulie M. Rielanda, Christina Goreb, Kalman B. Miglera, Kathryn L. Beersc*\nEmails: Julie.rieland@nist.gov, Christina.gore@nist.gov, Kalman.migler@nist.gov, Kathryn.beers@nist.gov \n\naMaterials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, United States of America\n\nbApplied Economics Office, Engineering Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, United States of America\n\ncMaterials Measurement Lab, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, United States of America\n\n*Corresponding Author\n\nHighlights:\n\nBurning of APW is common in the sample group, at 83 % participation\nIdentified a negative correlation between recycling and landfilling participation \n61 % of farmers were not aware of APW recycling programs within reasonable access\nFilm type plastics accounted for the highest volume of farming waste\n\nAbstract\n\nAn estimated 2.7 % of US plastics are made for agricultural applications in forms such as films, jugs, fence posts, and hoses. However, there is limited data on rates of use, and more importantly on fate at end of life. We first present a comprehensive global literature review, capturing agriculture plastic waste (APW) disposal practices over the past 25 years. As an initial step in improving understanding, a survey (N = 73) was conducted in the American Midwest focused on farming along the Kansas and Missouri border to better understand APW generation, disposal behaviors, and perceived barriers to participation in recycling programs. We found that rates of APW burning are high in our sample, with 83 % of respondents burning some of their waste, resulting in an annual burn rate of around 55 % by mass. This is the highest rate of APW burning observed in the global literature in the last 5 years. We also identified a statistically significant inverse relationship between recycling and landfilling participation highlighting transportation requirements as a significant barrier to participation. Low overall participation in managed waste disposal activities suggests there is a substantial need for creative and cost-effective ways to facilitate responsible management of APW.\n\n\n\n\nIntroduction\n\nAgriculture plastic waste \n\nPlastic agricultural materials are cheap and offer many functional benefits, which has led to their mass adoption at all scales of agriculture.  For example, the use of plastic mulch can reduce agrochemical and irrigation needs, provide protection against soil-borne plant diseases, and extend the growing season (Goldberger et al., 2019). In livestock agriculture, light-weight plastic films called silage or bale wrap are used to wrap harvested grasses to facilitate beneficial fermentation while reducing instances of crop loss and cattle sickness due to fungi and mold (Levitan et al., 2005; Schettini et al., 2022). It is estimated that about 2.7 % of total US plastic demand is used for agriculture applications, or roughly 1.56 billion kg based on 2025 estimates (Malarkey & Babbitt, 2022). However, there is increasing interest in understanding the impacts of plastic on the environment, including soil quality, particularly as a result of how it is managed after use. . Managing agricultural plastic waste (APW) is challenging and highly dependent on the available infrastructure and management programs in each farming community. Currently, a spectrum of methods is deployed ranging from highly accessible methods like burning and dumping, technical solutions like using biodegradable alternatives, and infrastructurally demanding activities such as sanitary landfill, recycling, and waste to energy incineration (WTEI).  Given the scale and distribution of the various management practices, there is an opportunity to optimize the handling of APW for safe, efficient, economical, and effective outcomes. Understanding the context of APW decisions is a first step to facilitating these improved management outcomes. \n\nThere are few studies of APW usage and disposal rates, especially for the US, where the selling, usage, and disposal of agricultural plastics are conducted by various private enterprises. However, concerns regarding the adequate disposal of APW have been described in the literature since the 1970s (Ayer and Hogan, 1977; Mihai and Grozavu, 2019; Mihai and Taherzadeh, 2017). Rural communities often experience stark gaps in access to municipal waste services such as sanitary landfilling and recycling compared to their urban neighbors (Keske et al., 2018; Musella et al., 2019; Park et al., 2013). This is likely tied to smaller, low-density populations that limit revenue for infrastructure and municipal programs. Many such communities are unable to offer residents conveniences like curbside waste and recycling pickup, instead requiring them to transport waste to collection sites or directly to landfills and pay disposal fees (Environmental Research & Education Foundation, 2023; Mihai and Taherzadeh, 2017). It has been speculated that these inconveniences and costs may disincentivize participation in managed waste disposal activities (Khan et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2023). Further, there is evidence that people will often opt for the most expedient APW disposal method (e.g., burning, dumping, or burying) in the absence of accessible, convenient, and cost-effective options (Cleanfarms, 2021; Clemon et al., 2022). This is a problem because discarded plastics can be hazardous to wildlife and shed microplastics through UV-degradation and abrasion or incomplete combustion via open-burning. Although microplastics remain a challenging environmental problem even with managed disposal options such as landfilling (Lodh et al., 2025), mechanical recycling (Suzuki et al., 2024), and waste to energy incineration (Zhang et al., 24).\n\nAPW disposal terminology\n\nThe comparison of data across geography and time is complicated by inconsistent use of terminology, especially with respect to the non-descriptive usage of terms such as landfill, incineration, and recycling. The lack of precise and descriptive language makes it difficult to compare and catalog the impact of material flows documented in the literature.  For instance, the generic term landfill has been used ambiguously to refer to both sanitary landfill, an engineered and regulated form of waste disposal, as well as informal/illegal dumps, which may pose an acute hazard to groundwater and local communities (Madon et al., 2019; Morita et al., 2021, Lodh et al., 2025). The term incineration has been broadly used to refer to open-burning, municipal trash incineration, and waste-to-energy incineration (WtEI) (Kim et al., 2023); and recycling has been used to refer to any combination of mechanical recycling, chemical recycling, pyrolysis, and WtEI (Mayanti and Helo, 2022; Plastics Recyclers Europe, 2023; Takeya, 2009). For the purpose of this study, landfilling will refer to the use of a managed sanitary landfill,  dumping will refer to the disposal of solid waste outside of a sanitary landfill, burning will refer to open-burning, and recovery will refer to the act of recovering post-industrial/consumer plastics for reuse purposes not limited to mechanical recycling, chemical recycling (including to monomer, pyrolysis oil, and stock chemicals), and WtEI. In the context of the survey literature and our survey instrument, ‘recycling’ is understood to be applied interchangeably with ‘recovery’ focusing on the farmers’ acts of preparing, accumulating, and conveying APW materials for future repurposing off-farm regardless of specific recovery method.\n\nOpen-buring of APW\n\nLiterature documenting APW disposal methods show a wide spectrum of APW disposal behaviors including managed (landfill, municipal incineration, and recovery) and unmanaged disposal (burning, dumping, plowing into soil, etc.,) methods. Of the unmanaged disposal methods, burning is the most popular. It was recently estimated that 57 % of all global plastic waste is open-burned (Cottom et al., 2024). The popularity of open-burning has been attributed to its lack of cost, effective volume reduction, and limited knowledge among citizens regarding the extent of associated hazards (Cottom et al., 2024; Pathak et al., 2023). Further, while policies against the burning of plastic waste are common, there is often poor compliance that has been attributed to perceived benefits of trash burning and weak enforcement of the bans (Cottom et al., 2024; Pathak et al., 2023). \n\nThe open-burning of plastics is a problem because it results in incomplete combustion of plastic, leading to a wide range of emission products, both particle and gaseous associated with the bulk plastic and its added constituents (e.g., plasticizers, flame retardants) (Velis and Cook, 2021). Many of the products from the burning of plastic are toxic and carcinogenic, and there are further concerns regarding the health and environmental impacts of burning residual agrochemicals that can be present on APW (Gullett et al., 2012).\n\nThe United States Midwest Farming Region\n\nThe current study examines farming practices in the US Midwest in the context of current activities in the literature regarding APW disposal. The Midwest region includes a large portion of the central US, although there is some contention over the inclusion of certain states. In its most inclusive form, the Midwest stretches down from Canada to Kansas in the south, and east from Ohio to Nebraska in the west (Map available in Figure S3). The Midwest is one of the most productive agriculture regions in the world accounting for 1.4 million km2 of farmland, producing 90 % of corn and 83 % of soybeans in the US as well as 42 % of US animals and animal products including cattle, chicken, and hogs (Pryor and Barthelmie, 2013; Agamerica lending, 2021). Despite the scope and volume of farming performed in the region, there is limited aggregate data regarding the associated utilization and disposal of agricultural plastic. To date, we could find only one study that aimed to characterize APW in the Midwest, and it narrowly addresses pesticide containers used on farms in Nebraska (Reed et al., 2001). The US does not currently distinguish organic and inorganic farm waste in the counts of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and due to many of the farms in the region being small (< 1 km2), independent holdings, substantial amounts of non-biomass farm waste (e.g., APW) ends up in municipal landfills or burned on the farm (Sarpong et al., 2024). While there have been studies that assess similar farming activities in the UK and Canada (King et al., 2023; Muise et al., 2016), due to the unique waste infrastructure, culture, and governance structures of the US, there is a pressing need to characterize APW generation and disposal in this region. \n\nThrough this study, we assessed farmers’ plastic usage, APW disposal habits, and perceptions around sustainable APW disposal behaviors. This was carried out through a quantitative online survey distributed at a farm show in Pittsburg, Kansas May 17-19, 2024, and via email circulation closing on June 30th, 2024. Our aim was to collect information on the usage and disposal of plastic materials used on Midwestern farms, with the goal of increasing understanding of these understudied practices.\n\nMaterials and Methods\n\nLiterature Review Methods\n\nA literature review was performed using Web of Science (WoS)‡ and Google Scholar (GS)‡. The WoS keyword string was (((agriculture** AND plastic AND waste) AND survey) NOT GIS)). The websites and reports of international APW recycling programs were also included in the scope of the literature review using the support of the Google in-browser translation tool as necessary. [{"suffix": "", "text": "The Structure and Morphology of Single-\nComponent Oligomeric RNA Delivery Vectors\nDerived from Amphiphilic Charge-Altering\nReleasable Transporters\nPaul Joshua Hurst, Yuan Jia, Summer Ramsay-Burrough, Rebecca L. McClellan, Joshua T. Arens,\nSamuel R. Khasnavis, Trevor J. Del Castillo, Mahmoud M. AbdElwakil, Michael J. Lueckheide,\nVivek M. Prabhu, and Robert M. Waymouth*\nCite This: ACS Nano 2025, 19, 38954−38969\n Read Online\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: Advances in nucleic acid delivery have inspired\nefforts to mimic the function of natural viruses through the\ndevelopment of self-assemblies capable of gene delivery. RNA\nassemblies based on amphiphilic polymers are emerging as\nalternatives to lipid nanoparticles, but the factors that govern\nthe self-assembly of RNA with polymeric amphiphiles are\npoorly understood. Here, we describe the structure of\ncoacervate nanoparticle assemblies derived from RNA and\nsynthetic cationic polymer amphiphiles based on Charge\nAltering Releasable Transporters (CARTs). CARTs are effective gene delivery agents derived from block copolymer\namphiphiles. Cryogenic electron microscopy and tomography (CryoEM, CryoET), small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) and\nsmall-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) reveal that the self-assembly of RNA with low molar mass (≤10,000 g/mol) CART\namphiphiles generates nanoparticles with disordered bicontinuous internal morphologies composed of interpenetrating lipid\nand aqueous coacervate domains. Systematic variation of the cationic and lipophilic blocks in low molar mass CART\namphiphiles demonstrates that both the internal domain spacings (6 to 8 nm) and the order of the resulting bicontinuous\nCART-RNA assemblies depend on the CART chemical structure and the oligonucleotide cargo (mRNA vs siRNA). Notably,\nthe presence of RNA drives the formation of bicontinuous morphologies. In contrast, CART/RNA assemblies with higher\nmolar mass (≥28,000 g/mol) CART amphiphiles fail to generate bicontinuous assemblies, instead yielding aggregates\ncomposed of particles approximately 10 to 20 nm in diameter. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Vol.:(0123456789)\nChromatographia (2025) 88:801–805 \nhttps://doi.org/10.1007/s10337-025-04438-z\nBRIEF REPORT\nAbsolute Molar Mass Determination in Mixed Solvents. 3. Accuracy \nof ∂n/∂c Values Obtained by Assuming 100% SEC Mass Recovery\nAndré M. Striegel1\nReceived: 24 July 2025 / Revised: 27 August 2025 / Accepted: 3 September 2025 / Published online: 9 September 2025 \nThis is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2025\nAbstract\nAccurate values of the specific refractive index increment (∂n/∂c) are essential to the accurate determination of molar mass \naverages, distributions, and related macromolecular parameters by, among others, size-based separations with online static \nlight scattering and differential refractive index (DRI) detection. Examined here is the 100% mass recovery method of cal-\nculating the ∂n/∂c of dilute macromolecular solutions, when employing mixed solvents in a size-based separation (e.g., size-\nexclusion chromatography or SEC) with DRI detection. This method has been used successfully in the past for determining \nthe ∂n/∂c of various polyelectrolytes. It is quicker, generally simpler, and less sample-intensive than its offline, batch-mode \nDRI counterpart. Whether or not the 100% mass recovery method allows for the necessary solvent equilibration within the \nimmediate vicinity of the polymer chain during a chromatographic run, so as to allow for accurate determination of ∂n /∂c \nin SEC/DRI experiments, is evaluated here. This is done using a set of three narrow-dispersity linear polystyrene standards \ncovering a 40-fold range in molar mass, dissolved in a 25:75 mix of tetrahydrofuran and N ,N-dimethyl formamide. Results \nare compared to those previously obtained by the batch-mode method and from calculations involving the accurately known \nmolar masses of the polymers and refractive indices of the solvents. The 100% mass recovery method of obtaining ∂n /∂c \nvalues, while of great help for determining the ∂n/∂c of, e.g., polyelectrolytes, does not appear able to overcome the obstacle \nof preferential solvation when analyzing macromolecules in a mix of non-isorefractive solvents with dissimilar second virial \ncoefficients.\nKeywords Size-exclusion chromatography · Specific refractive index increment · 100% mass recovery method · Absolute \nmolar mass · Preferential solvation\nIntroduction\nAccurate determination of macromolecular molar mass (M) \naverages and distributions is crucial to evaluating novel syn-\nthetic procedures, as well as to optimizing the processing \nand end-use properties of materials [1]. Most M determina-\ntions are performed using size-based separation methods, \nmost commonly size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) but \nalso hydrodynamic chromatography (HDC) and flow field-\nflow fractionation (flow FFF) techniques [2–4]. In combina-\ntion with these, the most accurate means of determining M \nis generally through the use of online static light scattering \ndetection, most commonly multi-angle static light scatter -\ning (MALS) in combination with concentration-sensitive \ndetection such as differential refractometry (DRI) [1 , 5]. A \ncrucial value in static light scattering and DRI calculations \nis the specific refractive index increment (∂n/∂c) of the ana-\nlyte solution. This value corresponds to the change in the \nrefractive index of a dilute analyte solution as a function \nof analyte concentration, at a given solvent, temperature, \nand wavelength of incident light. The accuracy with which \nthe ∂n/∂c is known directly translates into the accuracy of \ncalculated M and related values. As such, an error of E % in \n∂n/∂c will translate into an error of E  % in weight-average \nmolar mass (M w), when the latter is determined by SEC/\nDisclaimer Commercial products are identified to specify the \nexperimental procedure adequately. Such identification does not \nimply endorsement or recommendation by the National Institute \nof Standards and Technology, nor does it imply that the materials \nidentified are necessarily the best available for the purpose.\n * André M. Striegel \n andre.striegel@nist.gov\n1 Chemical Sciences Division, National Institute of Standards \nand Technology (NIST), 100 Bureau Drive, MS 8390, \nGaithersburg, MD 20899-8390, USA\n\n802 A. M. Striegel \nMALS/DRI. Additionally, most size-based experiments are \nconducted in neat solvents or in solvents with only a mod-\nest amount of additive (e.g., salts). While the use of mixed \nsolvents is common in interaction polymer chromatography \nmethods (e.g., gradient polymer elution chromatography \n[6]), which have traditionally employed evaporative mass \ndetectors, this is not the case in size-based methods [7]. The \nlatter is due to the widespread use of differential detectors \nin size-based methods and to the propensity for preferential \nsolvation of macromolecules in mixed solvents. Preferential \nsolvation refers to the greater “affinity” of the macromol-\necule toward one solvent over the other in a mix, as initially \ndemonstrated by the classic work of H. Kneebone Tompkins \nin 1896 [8]. When employing differential detection methods \nsuch as MALS or DRI, preferential solvation translates into \nthe solvent baseline no longer accurately representing the \nsolvent contribution to the peak height of chromatographic \n(or fractographic, henceforth implied) slices.\nRecent work toward the determination of accurate M \naverages and distributions by SEC/MALS/DRI in mixed sol-\nvents has shown that it is possible to obtain accurate values \nunder certain conditions. These conditions include the use \nof an isorefractive solvent pair, and also, the use of a near-\nisovirial solvent pair, i.e., when using solvents which, at the \nexperimental conditions, possess either identical refractive \nindices and/or which allow for dilute polymer solutions with \nsimilar second virial coefficients. (The second virial coef-\nficient serves to provide a quantitative measure of analyte \nsolvation at a particular set of solvent/temperature condi-\ntions). Details, requirements, and caveats in each case can \nbe found in references [ 9, 10]. Also examined in reference \n[10] was the amount of preferential solvation undergone by \npolystyrene (PS) in a 25:75 mix of tetrahydrofuran (THF) \nand N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF), two solvents which \nare neither isorefractive nor near-isovirial. Employing poly-\nstyrene standards with accurately determined M  averages \nand distributions and ∂n/∂c values obtained by offline, batch-\nmode DRI (otherwise considered a benchmark method of \ndetermining ∂n /∂c), it was shown that these ∂n /∂c values \nwere biased due to preferential solvation. Moreover, it was \nshown that in the 25:75 THF:DMF mix, the solvent ratio in \nthe immediate vicinity of the macromolecules examined was \nactually 75:25 THF:DMF, due to the greater affinity of PS \ntoward THF over DMF. This resulted in errors in calculated \nM, of up to 1 ×  105 g  mol−1 for PS with M = 8 ×  105 g  mol−1.\nAnother method for determining the ∂ n/∂c of a dilute \nmacromolecular solution at a particular set of experimental \nconditions (wavelength, temperature, and solvent composi-\ntion) is to assume that the concentration of the solution has \nbeen determined accurately and that 100% of the injected \npolymer has eluted from the SEC column (or appropriate \nseparation device) and is contained within the integration \nlimits and baseline of the DRI peak (it is also assumed that \nthe calibration constant of the DRI detector is accurately \nknown). This is generally referred to as the “100% mass \nrecovery method” of determining ∂n/∂c, or sometimes as the \n“∂n/∂c from peak method” [11] and has been employed to \ndetermine this parameter for dilute polyelectrolyte solutions. \nWhen studying polyelectrolytes, it is often assumed that the \nchromatographic column acts as a type of dialysis chamber \nso that, over the course of thousands of theoretical plates, \nequilibration occurs within the solvated region of the macro-\nmolecule [12]. The method is generally quicker, less sample-\nintensive, and easier to perform than its offline, batch-mode \nDRI counterpart and has found to yield, in a great many \ncases, ∂n /∂c values almost identical to those obtained by \noffline, batch-mode DRI with sample dialysis and other \nappropriate procedures [12– 15]. Given the method’s suc-\ncess for polyelectrolytes, it can naturally be asked whether \nthe same type of equilibration during a chromatographic run \noccurs when analyzing a neutral macromolecule in a mix \nof two solvents so that, at the end of the run, the effects \nof preferential solvation are obviated within the immediate \nvicinity of the polymer chain. Because the accuracy of the \n100% mass recovery option was not evaluated in [10], it is \ndone here, for the three narrow-dispersity linear PS stand-\nards previously analyzed, in a 25:75 THF:DMF mix and \ncovering a 40-fold range in M.\nExperimental\nThe SEC/MALS/DRI; absolute refractive index (aRI); and \noffline, batch-mode DRI ∂n /∂c methods; along with the PS \nstandards and the solvents employed; have all been described \nin detail in [10]. As such, only the 100% mass recovery \nmethod is described here.\nThe determination of ∂ n/∂c by the 100% mass recovery \nmethod employed the same experimental runs as did the \nSEC/MALS/DRI determinations of the M  averages and \nmolar mass distributions (MMDs) of the PS standards. For \nall analyses, concentrations were well below the critical \noverlap concentration c *. The calibration constant of the \nDRI was determined by the instrument manufacturer using \na series of NaCl solutions, the ∂n/∂c of which is well known \n(0.1740 mL   g−1 in water at 25 °C at a vacuum wavelength \nλ0 of 658 nm). The aRI of the 25:75 THF:DMF mix was \n1.4224, measured using the aRI capability of the same DRI \nas employed in the SEC experiments, at the same experi-\nmental conditions (λ 0 = 658 nm, temperature = (25.0 ± 0.1) \n°C). At these conditions, the ∂n /∂c of PS as determined by \noffline, batch-mode DRI experiments was (0.168 ± 0.001) \n mL−1 g (note a typo in Table 1 of reference [10], where the \nunits of ∂n/∂c are incorrectly stated in the table footnote as \nbeing mg  mL−1).\n\n803\nAbsolute Molar Mass Determination in Mixed Solvents. 3. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Full-field strain reveals relaxation behaviors of main-chain liquid\ncrystal elastomers in the polydomain-monodomain transition\nJ Van Blitterswyk 1,2, A.K. Landauer 1*, T.D. Nguyen 2*, C.M. Yakacki 3, A.M. Forster 1*\n1Material Measurement Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, 100 Bureau\nDr., Gaithersburg, 20899, MD, USA.\n2Department of Mechanical Engineering, The Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, USA.\n3Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Colorado Denver, Denver, CO, USA.\n*Corresponding author(s). E-mail(s): alexander.landauer@nist.gov; vicky.nguyen@jhu.edu;\naaron.forster@nist.gov;\nAbstract\nBackground:Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are polymers with nematic ordering that exhibit unique mechan-\nical behaviors attributed to the interplay of network stretching and mesogen reorientation under loading. These\ncompeting viscoelastic mechanisms can lead to complex and heterogeneous local deformation response when\nexposed to an external stimulus such as light, thermal gradients, or applied stress.Objective:This study devel-\noped stereo digital image correlation (stereo-DIC) measurements and analyses of strain fields in polydomain\nLCE specimens undergoing the polydomain-monodomain (P-M) transition to reveal deformation mechanisms.\nMethods:Two macro-scale deformation modes probed the material response: quasi-static uniaxial extension\nand stepped stress-relaxation. Stereo-DIC tracked the full-field surface strain. A bespoke technique was developed\nconsisting of a clustering algorithm to identify coherent strain clusters in the strain field at the maximum stress\nof the step loading and a stretched exponential model fit to the time-evolving strain response of the clusters and\nfitting to the stress relaxation response. This technique quantified differences in the viscoelasticity of the domains\ninvolved in the P-M transition.Results:Strain maps during the hold period showed that strain heterogeneity\nincreased with time. Strain in the majority of clusters either increased asymptotically or decreased asymptoti-\ncally with time, leading to increasing strain heterogeneity. The characteristic relaxation times varied between the\nclusters and were different from the that of the macroscopic stress response.Conclusion:A new technique for\nquantifying surface strain clustering is available. Initial findings on LCEs suggest that the kinematics of viscous\nmesogen rotation depends on the local strain state.\nKeywords:liquid crystal elastomers, digital image correlation, full-field measurements, polydomain-monodomain\ntransition, polymers, soft elasticity, viscoelasticity, stress relaxation, machine learning, clustering\n1\n\n1 Introduction\nLiquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are cross-linked poly-\nmer networks composed of flexible segments and\nanisotropic, rigid molecules, referred to as mesogens.\nMesogens form well-ordered domains with spatially-\nvarying orientations giving rise to features of both\ncrystalline and rubbery materials [1]. Moreover, the\nmechanical properties can be tailored by synthesizing\nthe networks with the mesogens in an isotropic state\nprior to cross-linking to give rise to a polydomain net-\nwork, or with the mesogens aligned to give long-range\norder in a monodomain. The coupling between the liq-\nuid crystal (LC) order and the rubbery matrix gives rise\nto a phenomenon known as soft elasticity, where strain\nmay increase without a proportional increase in stress\nin the global response of the polymer system [2]. The\nmobility of the mesogens allows them to rotate rela-\ntive to the surrounding cross-linked network and align\nalong the direction of maximum principal strain. Meso-\ngen rotation accommodates large strains at zero stress\n(soft elasticity) or with little increase in stress (semi-\nsoft elasticity). Under uniaxial stretching, this process\noccurs over a range of strains creating an extended\nplateau in the stress-strain response of the macro-scale\nmaterial. Once mesogens are aligned in a monodomain,\nthe material stiffens and behaves like a traditional\ncross-linked network [3–6]. This process is often termed\nthe polydomain-monodomain (P-M) transition. The fea-\ntures of the stress-strain response and P-M transition\ndepend strongly on orientation of the network during\nsynthesis [5, 7–9], temperature [4, 6, 10–12], and loading\nrate [1, 13–15].\nThe soft-elastic phenomenon of LCEs is attractive for\nimpact mitigation applications as a reversible energy dis-\nsipation mechanism [16, 17]. The relationship between\nmesogen order and applied stress with resultant changes\nin bulk mechanical properties has been studied exten-\nsively in the equilibrium regime [3–5, 8, 9, 13–15, 18–20],\nbut there have been far fewer studies on non-equilibrium\nfeatures, such as the slow stress relaxation [3, 6, 13, 18,\n21]. Stress relaxation experiments have shown that the\nbehavior of LCEs is complicated by the interaction of\ndomain rotation and polymer chain relaxation mecha-\nnisms [5, 6, 13, 15, 21] and depends on many factors\nincluding the applied strain amplitude, synthesis history,\nmesogen order, network topology, and chemical struc-\nture, e.g., side-chain vs. main chain [13, 18, 22], strain\nrate [23], and loading condition [20]. In general, the\nrelaxation behavior can be characterized by two domain\ntime constants associated with fast and slow power-law\nrelaxation, where the fast relaxation domain is gener-\nally related to direction changes in the nematic domains\nand the slow domain relates to network entanglements\n[13, 15]. Specifically, Ohzonoet al.[21] showed that\nthe hysteretic and relaxation behavior of LCEs depends\nstrongly on the chemistry and strain history and is sen-\nsitive to local energy barriers due to the interaction\nof mesogens. Using stress-relaxation experiments at dif-\nferent levels of applied strain, Clarke & Terentjev [13]\nshowed that the relaxation slows towards the onset of\nthe P-M transition due to the elastic restraint on relax-\nation by neighboring domains as rotation first begins.\nA similar behavior was observed for side-chain LCEs\nin [18] where the relaxation time for isotropic poly-\ndomain nematic elastomers (PNEs) was considerably\nlonger than nematic PNEs where the memory effect of\nthe nematic synthesis acts to restore the original align-\nment more rapidly. These mechanisms may be used to\ninform designs for impact mitigation.\nAs a result of the sensitivity to local energy barri-\ners caused by constraints from neighboring mesogenic\ngroups and network structure, one would expect the\nrelaxation response to be heterogeneous and complex\nthroughout the P-M transition. This has been shown\nin many equilibrium studies where the deformation can\nbecome heterogeneous under uniaxial monotonic load-\ning [6, 13–15, 21, 24, 25]. This heterogeneity in the local\nmaterial response complicates the matter of using global\nstress and extension measurements for material model-\ning as this represents the aggregate response of many\ncomplex interactions. Therefore, the purpose of this\nwork was to develop a full-field deformation measure-\nment analysis that quantifies and uncovers the spatial\nand temporal heterogeneity of the relaxation across the\nPM transition in LCEs. To do so, we use incremen-\ntal stress relaxation experiments to perturb the system\nfrom equilibrium at different levels of global strain to\ninform the kinematics of competing mechanisms (poly-\nmer stretching versus mesogen rotation) during relax-\nation. We also apply a clustering algorithm to the rich\nspatial strain measurements to quantify the variation in\nlocal relaxation responses across the gauge region. To\nthe authors knowledge, this is one of a limited number\nof studies to use full-field measurements to characterize\nthe response of LCEs [14, 24, 26] to mechanical stretch-\ning, and the first to leverage this for investigation of the\nstress relaxation response.\n2 Materials and methods\n2.1 Materials\nPentaerythritol tetrakis(3-mercaptopropionate)\n(PETMP), 2,2’-(Ethylenedioxy) diethanethiol\n(EDDET), 2,6 Di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol\n(inhibitor), triethylamine (TEA), Phenylbis(2,4,6-\ntrimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide (PPO), and\ntoluene were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St.\nLouis, MO, USA) 1. 2-Methyl-1,4-phenylenebis(4-(3-\n(acryloyloxy)propoxy)benzoate) (trade name RM 257)\nwas purchased from Matrix Scientific (Columbia, SC,\nUSA). [{"suffix": "", "text": "Resistivity\nResistivity is the material property that pertains to how difficult it is for electrical current to flow through said material.\nMaterials with high resistivity are known as insulators while materials with low resistivity are known as conductors.\nSpanning from 10  Ωm to 10  Ωm (see Figure ), resistivity possess the largest range of values for any physical\nproperty. Resistivity is essential in many material applications including resistors in electrical circuits, dielectrics,\nresistive heating, and superconducting.\nFigure :  Regimes of materials according to resistivity.\nIntroduction\nThe fundamental relationship that explores a materials opposition to electron flow was first derived in 1826 by Georg\nOhm, a German physicist and mathematician. Ohm's Law is represented by the following equation:\nwhere\nV [Volts: J/C] is the voltage applied to the material,\nI [Amperes: C/s] is the electrical current flow, and\nR [ohms: V/A] is the resistance of the material specimen.\nIt is important to note that resistance is dependent on the specific geometry of a material specimen as seen in Figure 2.\nFigure  Material specimen dimensions that relate resistance to resistivity.\nTo represent the electrical resistivity as an intrinsic material property, the voltage must be divided by the length L at\nwhich it is applied to and the current must be divided by the area A it flows through to produce an electric field  and\ncurrent density J respectively. This translation to electric field and current density yields the following equation for\nresistivity:\nwhere  is the resistivity of a material . When comparing materials, it is common to invert the value of resistivity to\nmake conductivity  [Siemens] which can easily be used to rank materials on the basis of how well each conducts\nelectrons. Due to the significant temperature dependence on resistivity and conductivity, a material's resistiveness\nmeasured at room temperature [20°C].\nAs mentioned above, materials are broken into three essential regimes: insulators, semiconductors, and metals. The\nmanifestation of resistivity in conducting materials, metals and semiconductors, can be fully realized by evaluating the\nbehavior of electrons at the quantum mechanical level.\nResistivity of Pure Metals\nMetals are structured by a lattice of atoms that are metallically bonded to one another. The sea of delocalized electrons\nfound in metallic bonding is created by having a high density of states (i.e. electrons) at the Fermi level which are easily\nexcited into the conduction band. From this bonding, electrons a can be thought of as free electrons moving through the\nmetal matrix. As the electron flows, it will interact with individual atoms, causing scattering events, which decrease the\neffectiveness of electrons at traversing the metal. The mobility of the electrons play an important role in quantifying the\nresistivity of a metal as seen in the following equation:\n-8 20\nRunaway argument for \\eatSpaces?\n9/30/26, 2:11 PM Resistivity - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Resistivity 1/4\n\nwhere e is the charge of an electron,  Fermi velocity of a conduction electron, τ is the relaxation time between\nscattering events, and  is the population density of electrons at the Fermi energy. Additionally, it is seen that the\npopulation density of electrons at the Fermi level is taken in to account as opposed to the total number of valance\nelectrons, which explains the exceptionally low resistivity of silver, copper and gold.\nTemperature Dependence\nThe equation above shows that the resistivity of a metal is inversely proportionally to the relaxation time. This means\nthe number of scattering events plays a substantial role in the resistivity of a metal. A large contributor to the number\nof scattering events iin a metal is the thermal vibrations of each atom in the lattice. As the temperature of a material\nincreases, each atom beings to oscillate about its central position, increasing the probability that an electron would\ncollide with it. With\npolycrystalline metals, there will be a number of sources of defects in the microstructure including Grain boundaries,\ndislocations, and vacancies. Along with defects, impurities in a metal can host a scattering site. In 1864 Augustus\nMatthiessen, a British chemist and physicist, was the first to incorporate all of these aspects into the resistivity of a\nmetal. Matthiessen's Rule is as follows:\nwhere  is the resistivity due to temperature,  is the resistivity due to impurities and  is the the resistivity due\nto defects. While temperature, defects, and impurities do in fact contribute to resistivity, some deviation from the\nsimple summation postulated by Matthiessen has been reported for specific metals.\nResistivity of Alloys\nFrom Matthiessen's Rule it was seen that the resistivity of a metal was influenced by the impurities present. This\nportion of the resistivity begins to have a significant contribution when metals are alloyed together. An alloy can be\nviewed as a metal with a large number of impurities, meaning there is a great deal more scattering sites to increase the\nresidual resistivity of the metal. The result of this increase is a translation of the plot in Figure  upward. At varying\ncompositions of a simple binary alloy, the resistivity of the system is a linear interpolation of the resistivity of each pure\nmetal. If the system exhibits an energetically favorable phase transition that results in a more ordered structure than\nthat of the solute atoms in solution, a drop in resistivity at that composition will be observed. (30 points total)  The Thermodynamics of nanoparticle -based cancer therapy .  Recently, \na novel anti-cancer therapy has been developed at Rice University, based on the design of \nnanomaterials that become rapidly superheated in response to illumination with laser light.  \nThe therapy is illustrated  below: Amorphous silica nanoparticles with diameters of ~100 nm \nare coated with a very thin (~10 nm thick) shell of gold. Landauer3\n(0000-0003-2863-039X)1, Cecelia Vederman (0009-0009-5343-1545)1,3, and Amanda L.4\nForster (0000-0001-7397-4429)1,*\n5\n1National Institute of Standards and Technology, Material Measurement Laboratory, 100 Bureau Drive,6\nGaithersburg, MD 208997\n2Georgetown University, Institute for Soft Matter Synthesis and Metrology, 3700 O St NW, Washington, DC 200578\n3Montgomery College, 20200 Observation Drive, Germantown, MD 208769\n*Corresponding authors: Katarina Goodge (katarina.goodge@nist.gov) and Amanda Forster10\n(amanda.forster@nist.gov)11\nABSTRACT12\nNear infrared (NIR) spectroscopy is a rapid, non-invasive technique often used for chemical bond structure identification,\nmaking it a prime candidate for feedstock identification and validation for industrial processes involving polymers. It has rapidly\ngained popularity in the textile industry; however, the availability of high-quality, known provenance NIR data for textile fibers\nand fabrics is limited. Applying NIR to answer questions such as fiber classification or polymer blend identification typically\nrequires the use of models or algorithms. The underpinning data for these models is typically in proprietary libraries or self-built\ndatabases; thus, benchmarking model performance across the industry is challenging. Here, a new dataset is presented to\naddress this challenge. The dataset contains data on textile specimens for applications including fiber content classification,\nsystems and software development, and validation of textile sorting systems. The data repository includes directories for\nbenchtop NIR spectral data, handheld NIR spectral data, and fabric-scale microscopy images.\n13\nBackground & Summary14\nChemical composition can be determined by a number of techniques such as Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy,15\nNear-Infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and Mass16\nSpectrometry(MS).NIRspectroscopyisanoninvasive,nondestructive,rapid,in-lineopticalmaterialcharacterizationtechnique17\nused in many industries, such as pharmaceuticals or plastics production. NIR sensors are often favored for high-throughput18\nindustrial applications because of their non-contact modality, which makes them easy to integrate into fully automated19\nsystems1. NIR has also previously been used in fiber identification2–6 for historical garments7, forensic applications8,9, quality20\ncontrol10–14, and emerging fields such as textile recycling15–20, demonstrating its versatility in characterizing textile materials.21\nIn a recent workshop geared towards reclaiming and reshoring textile production to the United States,21 participants highlighted22\nidentification of fiber type using NIR for feedstock validation to be a challenge and a barrier to scale up of this nascent industry.23\nStudies using NIR data often focus on building and testing models to perform certain actions, such as classification and24\nquantification of fiber identity. Many of these models are based on machine learning (ML) algorithms, which typically require25\nextensivedatainputsandarelimitedbytheavailabilityandqualityoftheinputdata. Todate, librariesofNIRspectrafortextiles26\nhave limited scope, may be inaccessible due to the use of proprietary information, or are otherwise not broadly available to27\nthe community. Datasets that are more broadly usable by the community follow open data guidelines such as the Findable,28\nAccessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) data principles22. Thus, to streamline modeling efforts, data needs to be29\ncollected and released in a high-quality, well-validated, open-source, and accessible manner to provide the underpinnings of30\nthese models and to compare model results.31\nA standard test method for fiber identification via NIR does not currently exist, further complicating efforts at comparison.32\nThe American Association of Textile Chemists and Colorists (AATCC) Test Method 2023 describes Fourier transform mid-IR33\nspectroscopy, and ASTM Standard E1790-0024 describes NIR spectroscopy as a general methodology. With the diverse34\nspectral ranges of assorted spectrometers combined with the varied quality and form factor of fabric samples, it is difficult35\nto meaningfully compare different model results found in literature. Using one well-validated dataset as a basis for model36\ncomparison enables performance benchmarking and meaningful cross-comparison.37\n\nARTICLE IN PRESS\nARTICLE IN PRESS\n800 1000 1200 1400 1600 1800 2000 2200 2400\nAbsorbance\n[a.u.]\nWavelength [nm]\nBenchtop Handheld\nNIR\nNIR\nFTIR\n▬ Cotton\n▬ Polyester\nHandheld\nBenchtop\n(a)\n(b)\nFigure 1.Data collection for fabric specimens. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Exploration of dynamic mechanical analysis for studying degraded \npolymers: dynamic mechanical changes after ultraviolet exposure \nHsiu-Chin Huang a, b*, Donald Hunston a, Lipiin Sung c \na Research Associate, Engineering Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, \nGaithersburg, MD, 20899, USA \nb Department of Chemistry, Krieger School of Arts and Sciences, Johns Hopkins University \nc Materials and Structural Systems Division, Engineering Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, Gaithersburg, MD, 20899, USA \n \n* Corresponding author. E-mail address: hsiuchin.huang@nist.gov (H. Huang) \n \nABSTRACT \nMany techniques have been used to investigate the changes in the mechanical properties of \npolymers induced by photodegradation. In general, the observation of clear variations in bulk \nproperties relies on destructive testing methods. This indicates the difficulties associated with \ndistinguishing the effects of varying degradation levels using less-destructive approaches. This \nstudy employed dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) as a less-destructive approach by applying \na very low strain amplitude and narrowing the scanned temperature range. The temperature \nsweep with multi-frequency scans was limited from the glassy state to the lower portion of the \nglass transition. This approach was designed to minimize modification to the internal molecular \nstructure of the samples while still capturing discernible changes in mechanical behavior. An \namorphous polyester film was used with varying ultraviolet (UV) exposure. Different degrees of \ndegradation were carried out on the polyester using NIST SPHERE (Simulated Photodegradation \nvia High Energy Radiant Exposure). After exposure, samples were stored in an ambient \nenvironment for different durations. The DMA results showed the exposed polyester had higher \nstiffness and less sensitivity to a high-frequency oscillatory strain relative to the unexposed \npolyester. Furthermore, the continuous chemical conversion of unstable intermediates to final \nphotoproducts occurring in the samples after UV exposure was revealed. The chemical property \nwas characterized using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The impact of these \nchemical changes was effectively monitored using DMA by showing dynamic changes in the \nbulk mechanical properties of the samples during post-exposure storage. The dynamic \nmechanical changes facilitated the evaluation of the effects of varying degrees of degradation \nand the differences in internal structure between the exposed samples. This study demonstrated \nthe potential of utilizing DMA to assess polymer degradation, including in severely degraded \npolyester samples, in a less destructive manner compared to test-to-failure methods. \n \n1. Introduction \n\nPolymer photodegradation causes chain cleavage and involves complex chemical reactions that \neventually alter the original chemical structures and produce a decline in the mechanical \nproperties of materials, like impact resistance and toughness. There are many techniques for \ncharacterizing the mechanical properties of degraded polymers. Some focus on the changes \noccurring at the material’s surface, such as nanoindentation [1–3], atomic force microscopy \n(AFM) [4,5], and scratch testing [6,7], as the surface is expected to experience the most severe \nultraviolet (UV) damage. These techniques assess localized degradation without compromising \nthe material’s integrity. However, surface roughness and high material heterogeneities may cause \ninconsistent results, and the localized measurements sometimes do not represent the bulk \nmechanical properties.  \n \nFor evaluating the bulk properties of photodegraded polymers, tensile testing is widely used \n[1,3,7–11]. In this paper, the term tensile testing will refer to an experiment where the sample is \nloaded at room temperature and at a constant displacement rate until failure. The performance of \nUV-degraded samples is typically assessed based on the ultimate tensile strength [1,7–9], the \nelongation at break [3,7–9,11], and the toughness [1], although the entire load-deformation \nprofile is recorded during testing. Young’s modulus and changes in strength within the elastic \nregion are not sensitive indicators of degradation; they exhibit little variation even after \nprolonged exposure. This suggests that plastic deformation to failure is necessary for researchers \nto observe the brittle behavior of degraded polymers. Elastic deformation alone is insufficient to \nfully understand the impact of varying degradation levels on their bulk mechanical properties. \n \nDynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) is another method for measuring the bulk mechanical \nproperties of polymers. Unlike tensile testing, the photodegraded polymer samples are subjected \nto small-amplitude strains, avoiding failure [12]. However, to reveal changes in their properties, \nDMA usually involves scanning across a broad temperature range encompassing the glass \ntransition and rubbery plateau regions, thereby inducing large-scale molecular motions \n[3,4,8,13,14]. The molecular-level structural changes serve a comparable function to \nmacroscopic deformation in tensile testing when assessing the effects of UV exposure. The \nreliance on destructive measurements in both techniques highlights the challenge of detecting \ndistinct variations in bulk properties through less-destructive approaches.  \n \nThis study aimed to explore the feasibility of utilizing DMA as a less-destructive approach for \nevaluating the effects of different degrees of degradation through measurements conducted at a \nvery small strain amplitude and within a narrow temperature range. The material selected for this \nstudy is an amorphous polyester. The maximum temperature applied was restricted to 80 °C, \nthereby limiting the measurement to the lower half of the glass transition region. This approach \nwas designed to minimize molecular chain mobility and reduce structural alterations within the \ntested polymer samples. In this study, the polyester underwent varying exposure periods in an \naccelerated weathering device of NIST 0.5 m SPHERE (Simulated Photodegradation via High \nEnergy Radiant Exposure). Before DMA measurements, these UV-exposed polyester samples \nwere processed by a post-exposure treatment; they were stored in an ambient environment for \ndifferent durations. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy in an attenuated total reflection \n\nmode (ATR-FTIR) was used to characterize the chemical changes after UV exposure. These \nchemical and mechanical results were analyzed to understand the impact of dynamic chemical \nconversions occurring during the post-exposure treatment and the influence of UV exposure time \non the bulk mechanical properties of the polyester. \n \n2. Experimental section \n2.1. Materials \nThe material used in this study was an amorphous polyester film (500 μm) provided by the \nEastman Company¹ and stored under standard laboratory conditions prior to use. ATR-FTIR and \ndifferential scanning calorimeters (DSC) were used to identify the chemical composition and \nconfirm that the films were amorphous. The polyester film was compared to a known \npolyethylene terephthalate (PET) with 30% crystallinity, and their IR spectra were shown in \nFigure S1, which is found in the supplementary information. The ester carbonyl peak of the \namorphous polyester film is at 1713 cm−1, and the peaks related to the crystalline structures of \nPET (1470 cm−1, 1340 cm−1, 1120 cm−1, 968 cm−1, and 847 cm−1 [15,16]) are not observed in \nthe polyester. Moreover, there is no endothermic peak related to the loss of crystalline structure \nshown on the DSC heating curves of the pristine polyester in Figure S1. Consequently, the \npolyester was confirmed to be an amorphous polymer with a similar chemical structure to PET. \n \n2.2. Sample preparation and accelerated weathering \nThe polyester film was cut using dies into dog-bone-shaped specimens 65 mm long and 10 mm \nwide with a 3.2 mm wide neck and 25.4 mm gauge length for tensile test according to ASTM \nstandard D638 (Type V specimen [17]) and rectangle-shaped strips of 5.5 mm ± 0.1 mm wide for \nDMA. For the exposure process, the specimens were mounted on a Teflon sheet in a sample \nholder, in which a maximum of 15 strips could be aligned in parallel and exposed evenly under \nUV radiation. The samples were UV treated on only one side (length × width). The front-side \nsurface faces the UV light source and is the exclusive surface exposed to UV radiation, whereas \nthe back-side surface faces the Teflon sheet. Details for the sample holder and the layout of the \nenvironmental chambers for UV exposure can be found in the previous publication [11]. \n \nAccelerated weathering was conducted in the NIST 2 m SPHERE for the tensile test specimens \nand in the NIST 0.5 m SPHERE for the DMA specimens. A 20 d exposure with full-intensity UV \nradiation in the 2 m SPHERE equals one year of sunlight exposure in South Florida [18]. The 0.5 \nm SPHERE is still in development; it possesses the same functional capabilities as the 2 m \nSPHERE while delivering higher irradiance. Detailed information on the 2 m SPHERE has been \nreported elsewhere [9,11,19].  \n \nFull-intensity UV light at 295 nm to 400 nm wavelength range (≈ 160 W/m² and ≈ 518 W/m² \nfor the 2 m and 0.5 m SPHEREs, respectively) was used for both tensile test samples and DMA \nsamples. The tensile test samples were exposed at 50 °C, under a dry condition (≈ 0 % relative \nhumidity (RH)), and with various exposure times. The longest period was 8 d; the accumulated \nUV dose is around 111 MJ/m². The DMA samples were exposed at 50 °C, under (5 ± 1) % RH, \nwith three major periods (accumulated dose)—6 d and 20 h (≈ 306 MJ/m²), 11 d and 20.5 h (≈ \n\n531 MJ/m²), and 24 d and 12 h (≈ 1097 MJ/m²)—as well as a longest period of 36 d (≈ 1611 \nMJ/m²). To simplify the days, this paper used 7d, 12d, and 25d to describe the three major \nperiods. After being exposed for the designated period, the DMA samples were removed from \nthe chambers and stored under the same conditions as the unexposed polyester. They were kept \nin plastic Petri dishes covered with aluminum foil to avoid light before measurements. The \nstorage was considered a post-exposure treatment. The storage durations included 0 d, 1 d, 8 d, \nand 17 d and were simplified as 0d, 1d, 8d, and 17d in this study. Here, 0d means the samples \nwere measured on the same day of sample removal. \n \nThe workflow chart in Figure 1 summarizes the whole experimental process. In Process 1, the \npolyester specimens have not been weathered and are referred to as unexposed polyester in this \nwork. After the weathering process in the SPHERE, the exposed samples for the DMA \nmeasurements are listed in Process 3. Here, 7d(17d) represents the samples weathered for 6 d \nand 20 h and measured on the 17th d of storage. The same notation applies to the other samples in \na similar manner. All chemical characterizations were conducted before measurements for \nmechanical and thermal properties. \n  \n \nFigure 1. Workflow chart of this study. \n \n2.3. Mechanical characterization \n2.3.1 Tensile testing \nTensile tests used the polyester dog-bone-shaped specimens and were performed at room \ntemperature on an MTS Criterion 45 test machine (MTS Systems Corporation, Eden Prairie, \nMN, USA)¹ based on ASTM standard D638-14 [17]. The gauge length was set at 25.4 mm, in \ncontrast to the 7.6 mm gauge length specified in ASTM D638-14. The 25.4 mm gauge length \nincludes a small section of the neck at each end. This introduces a small error in calculating the \nabsolute value of the properties, but the interest here is the differences produced by exposure. \nSince the error is the same for all specimens,

It all started with Black Body radiation when scientist attempted to explain the curve\nof frequency (or wavelength) vs intensity. Max Planck was first to explain the behavior in 1900 , but no one accepted\nit; as there is no explanation for assuming energy corresponding to particular wavelength quantized rather than\ncontinuous.
