[{"suffix": "", "text": "Depth Profiling Chemical Changes in Chemically Amplified Resists for EUV Lithography\nDaniel F. Sunday,1 Peter Dudenas,1 Priyanka Ketkar,1 Julia Murphy,1 Cherno Jaye,2 R. Joseph Kline,1 Gurpreet Singh,3 Eungnak Han,3 Lauren Doyle,3 Florian Gstrein3  \nMaterials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg MD, 20899\nMaterials Measurement Science Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg MD, 20899 \nIntel, Hillsboro, OR, USA\n\nAbstract\n Photoresist patterning for semiconductor manufacturing is encountering new challenges with the move to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, driven by smaller pitches, thinner resists and fewer photons. Obtaining information about the nanoscale distribution of chemical changes in the resist will provide key information to optimize processing and resist development. Soft X-rays provide sensitivity to chemical functional groups at key atomic absorption edges, including carbon, oxygen and fluorine. By conducting specular reflectivity measurements at these energies, we can track the chemical depth profiles in a resist. This process is demonstrated by characterizing the optical constant profiles, which are proportional to the concentration of chemical bonds in a film at soft X-ray energies, of an EUV resist coated on a cross-linked polystyrene (CLPS) mat. The resist was exposed to blanket exposures with different doses and measured at different stages of the process, including post-exposure but before the bake, after the post-exposure bake, and after development. Segregation of resist components was observed in the as-coated case films, with a fluorinated component aggregating at the film surface. Stratification of the chemical changes that occur in the film is observed after exposure, but before the bake. The magnitude of this stratification is dose dependent. After a post-exposure bake the stratification is no longer observed and the optical constant profile is uniform with the exception of the fluorinated components. These results are complemented by near edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy obtained with an imaging microscope. Finally, we also examine the CLPS mat before and after the process, and observe evidence for chemical changes in the CLPS, with the possibility of residual resist components residing in the film after development.  \n\nKeywords: Photoresist, Metrology, Reflectivity, Soft X-rays, Directed Self-Assembly\n\nIntroduction\nThe implementation of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography has resulted in new challenges for photoresists.1,2 Chemically amplified resists (CARs) are still the state of the art for high volume manufacturing, but the multicomponent nature of CARs is leading to new concerns about how the compositional heterogeneity can impact resist performance.3,4 CARs typically consist of at least three components, a polymer with a labile group that can be altered during exposure to switch the solubility, a photoacid generator (PAG) which catalyzes the chemical change, and a quencher which neutralizes the acid, thereby limiting its diffusion. Differences in interactions parameters and surface energies between each of these components will result in non-uniform component distributions in both the lateral and vertical directions.5 EUV patterning will produce smaller pitches  with thinner resists due to the reduced depth of focus increasing the role that compositional heterogeneity plays in resist performance. Due to a combination of limited material absorbance and flux from EUV sources, the combination of these materials’ stochastics with the photon stochastics means that pattern roughness driven will be a key issue going forward.6 Furthermore, thinner resist stacks means that interface effects will become increasingly important and understanding resist-underlayer interactions will be key to optimizing patterning processes. Characterizing these interactions can be challenging, as it requires sensitivity to changes in nanoscale chemical distributions.7 \nIn this study resonant soft X-ray reflectivity (RSoXR) will be used to characterize changes in the optical constant depth profiles of a CAR at different stages in the patterning process and relate those results to the changing chemical depth profiles of the components in the film. Reflectivity measurements will be complemented by near edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy, which provides important information about the chemical changes at the films surface. The target system will consist of a CAR on a cross-linked polymer mat (CLPS), where understanding interactions between the resist and CLPS are important for optimizing directed self-assembly (DSA), with DSA considered as a complementary process flow to EUV lithography.8,9 \nBecause photoresists are complex blends many different characterization techniques are used to investigate how exposure and processing results in changes to the chemical structure. Infrared spectroscopy (IR) is highly effective for understanding changes in certain chemical bonds but has limited resolution to interrogate how those chemistries are spatially distributed. Increasingly IR is being used in-situ in order to carefully study the effects of oxygen or moisture on resist performance, particularly for metal oxide resists.10 Time of flight (TOF) secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) has also become an important tool; TOF-SIMS offers exceptional sensitivity to low concentrations of components in a depth profiling modality, although achieving sub 10 nm resolution is still challenging. There are also variations on the technique which provide insight into the lateral distributions of components based on analysis of the statistics from multiple impacts from nano-projectiles.11–14 \nSoft X-ray based measurements provide additional tools to broaden the existing toolbox. Soft X-rays border the EUV spectrum and contain absorption edges for many of the key resist components, including the K-edges for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine. The carbon spectra in particular contains fine features where the absorption peaks for different functional groups are shifted to different energies and are clearly differentiable in the spectra.15 The magnitude of the absorption peak for a given functional group will be proportional to the concentration of that functional group. As a result changing soft X-ray energies in a measurement allows you to probe both the type of chemistry in the system and also the concentration of specific functional groups. This is often measured by collecting a NEXAFS spectra; this can be done by exposing the beam to X-rays at either the magic angle (55° from the surface), where the spectra are sensitive to the composition, or at multiple incident angles in order to provide sensitivity to both composition and molecular orientation.16 There are several modes in which NEXAFS measurements can be conducted,  including measuring electron yield  and measuring the transmission through a sample. Electron yield modes are surface sensitive, reaching a depth of only a few nm, with some control over the depth sensitivity being achievable when biasing the detector voltage to reject lower energy electrons in partial electron yield (PEY) mode. Transmission absorption measurements provide sensitivity to the bulk of the film, but because of the high absorbance of soft X-rays need to be conducted on either a free-standing film, which can be challenging to prepare, or on a thin membrane. NEXAFS has been used to examine resists in the past, characterizing both surface segregation of individual components and monitoring changes in chemical bonds after exposure and development.17–19  A challenge for photoresist research is that soft X-rays have the potential to alter the samples being measured. The development of a novel soft X-ray microscope called the Large Area Rapid Imaging Analytical Tool (LARIAT) provides a route for low dose measurements of photoresists, where concerns about altering the photoresist due to exposure to soft X-rays can be significantly alleviated.20  \nA different mode for utilizing soft X-rays is RSoXR, where specular reflectivity measurements are conducted at a series of different incident angles for a given energy near an absorption edge. This measurement is a variant of standard hard X-ray reflectivity, where fitting the reflectivity curve enables determination of the electron density profile, which can be related back to composition. Uniquely relating electron densities to composition is difficult for organic materials as there is often little differentiation between the electron density of different components in an organic material. Conducting reflectivity measurements at energies near an absorption edge provides a means to combine the nanometer scale spatial resolution of X-ray reflectivity measurements with the sensitivity to specific chemical bonds depending on the chosen X-ray energy. With an appropriate set of references to understand how changing concentrations impact the optical constants for a given material, this depth profile can be directly converted to a concentration profile of components in a film, or even a distribution of functional groups.21,22 This approach has been demonstrated to investigate the interface roughness between high-χ block copolymers (BCPs),23 the distribution of components with complex architectures,24 the additives in BCPs,21,25 and the molecular orientation in thin films.26–28 \nThe underlayer examined in this study is an CLPS mat, which is used as part of the guiding pattern for DSA. The DSA of BCPs has been explored as a patterning technique that takes advantage of the information chemically imprinted in the block copolymer (pitch and interface roughness) via the choice of polymer chemistry and molecular weight.29,30 Prior to the integration of EUV patterning, DSA was primarily explored as a density multiplication technique with the goal of a 3x or 4x reduction in the patterned pitch.31–33 Now that EUV patterning can produce patterns commensurate with the periodicity of BCPs, DSA is being considered as a roughness remediation technique, where a rough pattern can be made with the EUV tool, and the BCP “heals” the roughness.34,35 This technique has the potential to significantly reduce the dose required from the EUV tool, resulting in a significant increase in throughput at the costly EUV patterning step. The BCP needs to have nearly equivalent surface energies between the two blocks at the target annealing temperature, and the patterned surface needs to have different affinities for the two components.36 When patterning with polystyrene-b-poly(methyl methacrylate) (PS-b-PMMA), the most common polymer explored for DSA, the process typically uses an CLPS mat, which has a greater affinity for polystyrene, and a neutral brush backfilling the region between the CLPS stripes.33 For density multiplication, the neutrality of the backfilled brush is a key feature to ensure vertical orientation of the BCP throughout the pattern.37,38 However, for roughness remediation the optimal pattern structure in terms of the brush chemistry and composition has not been fully explored. In this study we examine whether any of the components from the resist will diffuse into the CLPS, which would potentially alter the CLPS surface energy and could lead to buried defects in the film. \nMaterials and Methods\nCrosslinkable polystyrene was spin coated to achieve ~6nm film and baked under nitrogen environment at 250 °C degree for 30 min. Chemically amplified resists were exposed using a custom EUV flood-exposure metrology cluster tool. The coated wafers were loaded into a vacuum chamber where an array of sites 1 cm in diameter were exposed with 13.5nm light at the desired doses. Once removed from the chamber, post processing steps were completed.\n\nFigure 1: Samples were prepa

Cox \nToby Considine \nThis publication is available free of charge from: \nhttps://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2387\n\n\n \nNIST Technical Note  \nNIST TN 2387 \n \nApplying Retail Markets and \nTransactive Resources for Grid \nFlexibility           \n \nDavid Holmberg \nBuilding Energy and Environment Division  \nEngineering Laboratory  \n \nWilliam T. Cox \nCox Software Architects \n \nToby Considine \nTC9 \n \nThis publication is available free of charge from:  \nhttps://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2387 \nSeptember 2026 \n \n \n \n \n \nU.S. Department of Commerce  \nHoward Lutnick, Secretary \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology  \nArvind Raman, NIST Director and Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology\n\n\nNIST TN 2387 \nSeptember 2026 \n \n \nCertain equipment, instruments, software, or materials, commercial or non-commercial, are identified in this \npaper in order to specify the experimental procedure adequately. Such identification does not imply \nrecommendation or endorsement of any product or service by NIST, nor does it imply that the materials or \nequipment identified are necessarily the best available for the purp ose.  \nNIST Technical Series Policies \nCopyright, Use, and Licensing Statements \nNIST Technical Series Publication Identifier Syntax \nPublication History \nApproved by the NIST Editorial Review Board on 2026-09-28 \n \n \nHow to Cite this NIST Technical Series Publication \nHolmberg D, Cox W, Considine T (2026) Applying Retail Markets and Transactive Resources for Grid Flexibility .  \n(National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD), NIST Technical Note (TN) NIST TN 2387. \nhttps://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.TN.2387. \nAuthor ORCID iDs \nDavid Holmberg: 0000-0002-1738-8190 \n \n\nNIST TN 2387 \nSeptember 2026 \ni \nAbstract \nThe electric grid faces strain driven by rapidly growing loads (e.g., data centers, onshoring of \nindustry), retiring dispatchable generation, and increasing intermittent alternative energy \nsources. Traditional utility mechanisms for managing customer resources, such as demand \nresponse (DR), do not provide 24/7 localized balancing. Large flexible loads such as data centers \ncannot allow direct outside dispatch control, which leaves utilities without an effective way to \nuse edge flexibility. Local markets enable continuous and efficient integration of flexibility. \nCommon Transactive Services (CTS) specifies an open messaging protocol for local energy \nmarkets at the feeder, neighborhood, campus, and building levels. Based on standard financial \nmarket semantics, CTS enables interoperable participation of edge devices, microgrids, and \nfacility systems. \nLocal markets solve distribution grid problems through local resource coordination while \nkeeping customer information private. CTS markets can help to address: (1) distribution grid \ninfrastructure, voltage, and reliability challenges, (2) dynamic trading of data centers’ own \nenergy generation and storage, (3) siting for storage and generation using local market history \nfor improved investment decisions, and (4) adding market capability to a device, microgrid, or \nfacility using CTS standard interactions and data structures. \nThis technical note discusses grid challenges, the value of local markets, and the role of CTS. It \nthen reviews next steps for deployment, regulator support, and technical work. It also provides \nexamples of how CTS can be applied and reviews key CTS semantics. \nKeywords \nCommon Transactive Services; Flexibility; Local Markets; Market Agent; Transactive Energy; \nTransactive Resources. \n  \n\nNIST TN 2387 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. Introduction \n Current Challenges for Integration of Customer Flexibility \nThe electric grid is facing a narrowing margin of control. It was built for yesterday’s load peaks, \nand yet we are adding large loads (data centers, industry) while retiring dispatchable \ngeneration and adding intermittent energy sources. Adverse weather or localized failures stress \nthe grid. Distributed energy resources (DER)—solar photovoltaics (PV), electric vehicles (EV), \nand batteries—offer flexibility that could stabilize the grid if it could be used effectively.  \nUtilities, governments, and edge users are adding storage, expanding demand response (DR) \nflexibility, adding generation, revising interconnection rules, and deploying microgrids. These \ntools help, but distribution problems remain: voltage fluctuations, overloaded transformers, \nand the difficulty of coordinating behind-the-meter (BTM) loads and generation.  Utilities lack \npractical mechanisms to manage these problems while maintaining grid stability; on the other \nhand, large facilities lack effective ways to offer their flexibility to others.  \nUtilities commonly use DER management systems (DERMS) [1]. A DERMS system interacts both \nindirectly with DER via DR programs and directly controls some equipment to maintain grid \nstability. DR enables use of customer device flexibility as a bulk capacity resource. Additionally, \na utility may use dynamic prices to access DER flexibility [2]. However, system-wide DR events \n(or prices) cannot mitigate distribution-level voltage and transformer overload problems. Local \nelectricity markets not only reduce peak flows but enable local resource sharing for improved \nvoltage stability and reduced transformer loading while improving local resilience. \nData centers and industrial facilities that require gigawatts of power may install on-site \ngeneration to guarantee their own resilience and to skip long interconnection queues [3]. \nInternal business processes determine their willingness to export or consume across the day. \nUtilities want visibility and direct control access to that behind-the-meter (BTM) plant, but \nthese large facilities will not allow outside dispatch. To the utility, the site remains a black box. \nBut in a local market context, the need for local energy supply is communicated via tendered \nprices. If local prices reward a change the facility can accept, the customer can buy or sell \nwithout opening the box to outside control. \nWholesale markets prefer large generators that can deliver power when needed. Effective Load \nCarrying Capability (ELCC) 1 accredits capacity on that model. A data center or factory that \nserves its own work first scores poorly on ELCC because the metric cannot see availability that \nmoves with internal processes. ELCC describes the black box from outside. It does not describe \nwhat the facility will do if a local market pays for a specific interval. A market allows the facility \nto enter on its own terms, not via centralized dispatch of the plant. \nGrid operators have tried to achieve load flexibility through demand response, paying \ncustomers to reduce load at peak times. Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) have grown as a popular \n \n1 A measurement of a resource’s ability to produce energy when the grid most likely faces electricity shortfalls. In PJM, this applies to the \ncapacity market, not to the day-ahead or real-time energy markets. \n\nNIST TN 2387 \nSeptember 2026 \n2 \napproach to manage customer resources to meet wholesale or utility capacity shortfalls. That \nmodel takes customer flexibility and fits it into a bulk capacity resource. The Federal Energy \nRegulatory Commission (FERC) Order No. 2222 follows this same wholesale-aggregation path. \nOn the positive side, DR, VPP, and dynamic tariffs achieve some flexibility. They fit the present \ngrid framework and build some DER integration skills. However, they do not provide 24/7 \nbalancing down in the distribution system or maximize DER resource flexibility.  \n The Value of Local Energy Markets \nMarkets are the proven mechanism to balance supply and demand over time. Wholesale \nelectricity markets have demonstrated this at regional scale for decades. Local markets \noperating continuously at the feeder, neighborhood, campus, or building level, can perform the \nsame function with finer geographic and temporal granularity. \nLocal markets can fill troughs, reduce peaks, coordinate flexible load and storage, and reduce \nthe need for additional supply and distribution infrastructure [4]. In doing so, they create clear \ninvestment signals for distributed storage and generation exactly where it is most valuable.  \nCoordinating equipment owned by many actors, each with private information and priorities, \nposes a knowledge problem, identified by Hayek [5]. A customer’s DER serves that customer \nfirst. A central controller cannot know the customer’s changing schedule and priorities. Even \nfeeder-level VPP depends on centralized management and pre-negotiated dispatch availability. \nWhile feeder-level focus helps to defer infrastructure upgrades [6], it still depends on central \nobservation and control. Markets coordinate dispersed knowledge through prices,

As the commercial space sector grows, this “ take-make-use-\ndispose” paradigm is increasingly challenged by the economic  and operational realities of long -\nduration space activity.  This report captures key themes from the 2025 Building an In -Space \nCircular Economy seminar series, convened by the Department of Commerce Office of Space \nCommerce and the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The seminars examined the \ntechnical, regulatory, and economic requirements needed to support a transition toward circular \nspace operations. Major themes include the need for streamlined regulations alongside \ngovernment procurement strategies that establish dependable demand , clarification of salvage \nrights and ownership transfer pathways, and the development of standards to support servicing, \nrefueling, reuse, recycling, and data exchange. Additionally, the report highlights the importance \nof orbital infrastructure, including servicing hubs, modular platforms, recycling architectures, \nlogistics networks, and energy systems, as well as the critical role of materials science and \nmanufacturing innovation. Key c oncepts such as design for circularity, materials passports, \nfeedstock processing, and in-space manufacturing are identified as enabling tools for extending \nthe value of space assets. The multidisciplinary nature of the participants, presentations, and \ndiscussions highlighted that building an in -space circular economy will require coordina tion \namong policy, finance, technology, and standards organizations. \nKeywords \nCircular space economy ; design for circularity; in-situ resource utilization; in-space \nmanufacturing; in -space recycling; in -space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing ; \ninteroperability; interoperability standards; modularity; orbital infrastructure; space policy; \nspace resource utilization; space sustainability; standards. \n \n\nNIST SP 1500-39 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \nExecutive Summary ................................ ................................ ................................ ............................ 1 \n1. Although commercial launch services have reduced \ntransportation costs, delivering mass to orbit remains expensive and logistically challenging. As \ncommercialization of the space industry continues to expand, the traditional single mission, \nlinear operational model is increasingly challenged. Historically, spacecraft are designed, \nlaunched, operated, and then deorbited or moved to graveyard orbits. However, a n in -space \ncircular economy model could reduce dependence on terrestrial resupply by extending asset \nlifetimes and enabling the inspection, servicing, repair, reuse, repurposing, recycling, and \nremanufacturing of materials and systems already in space. \nThe 2025 Building an In -Space Circular Economy seminar series, convened by the U.S. \nDepartment of Commerce Office of Space Commerce and the National Institute of Standards and \nTechnology, brought together representatives from government, industry, academia , and \nnonprofit organizations.  Each seminar attracted more than 300 registered attendees, roughly \nhalf of whom represented industry . Participants examined the technical, regulatory, economic, \ninfrastructure, and standards -related conditions needed to transition towards  circular space \noperations. A central finding was that circularity requires many elements to work together. It \ndepends on coordinated circular design practices, clear ownership pathways, and strong market \ndemand. Additionally, it needs physical and digital infrastructure, financing m echanisms, and \ntrusted operational standards. \nCircularity must begin during the design of space systems. Future assets developed with \ndefined pathways for servicing, repair, and upgrades  are essential. Modular components, \nstandardized interfaces, accessible attachment points, reduced material complexity, and digital \nrecords such as ‘materials passports’ are needed to make future servicing and recovery feasible. \nWithout these provisions, assets remain difficult or uneconomical to repair, repurpose, or \nrecycle. This perpetuates the traditional linear operating model. \nPolicy and regulatory uncertainty remain a significant barrier. Circular a ctivities such as \ninspection, servicing, and debris capture do not fit cleanly within regulatory systems originally \ndeveloped for launch, reentry, remote sensing, and spectrum use. Companies face overlapping \njurisdictions, uncertain authorization pathways, and unpredictable timelines. Seminar \nparticipants identified the need to clarify salvage permission, ownership transfer, custody, \noperational control, and liability b efore defunct assets or debris can legally become inputs for \nreuse or recycle. \nSeminar participants emphasized that government demand is essential for establishing early \nmarkets. Circular space infrastructure requires substantial upfront investment before

Explain your choice of true/false (in 1 or 2 brief sentences), and if\nnecessary, show an equation that supports your statement.\n i. A first-order phase transition can be identified by a discontinuous increase in\nthe value of several variables of a system at the transition temperature,\nincluding volume, heat capacity, enthalpy, and entropy.\nFalse.  First-order phase transitions are characterized by a discontinuity in each of these functions;\nhowever, the heat capacity may jump to a higher or lower value after the phase transition (e.g.,\ntransformation from a liquid to a gas), and volume also is not constrained to jump to a higher value\n(e.g. ice has a larger molar volume than liquid water).\n ii. If the entropy change of a first-order phase transformation at constant\npressure ΔStrans is positive for stability, then the enthalpy of transformation\nΔHtrans must also be positive.\nTrue.  At a first-order phase transition at constant pressure, the enthalpy change and entropy\nchange are related to one another by \n€ \nΔHtrans=dqrev,trans=TtransΔStrans.  Since the absolute temperature\nmust be positive, the sign of the enthalpy and entropy changes must be the same.\n iii. Minimizing the Helmholtz free energy of the system + its surroundings under\nconditions of constant temperature and volume to determine the equilibrium\nstate is equivalent to maximizing the entropy of the universe, in obedience to\nthe second law.\nFalse.  Minimizing the free energy of the system alone at constant temperature and volume is\nequivalent to maximizing the entropy of the universe in a spontaneous process.\n iv. The entropy of materials decreases as temperature decreases, but if a hot\nliquid is placed in thermal contact with a cold reservoir, the liquid will\nspontaneously cool to the temperature of the reservoir, and this spontaneous\nprocess will not violate the second law.\nTrue.  Though the entropy of the material will be decreased in this process, the entropy of the\nsurroundings will substantially increase in the process of accepting heat from the system (heat must\nleave the system in this process).  Thus the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) will\nincrease.\n\n3.012 Quiz 2 2 of 4 10/27/04\n v. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Brillouin Zones\nHistory\nThe concept of a Brillouin zone was first developed by Léon Brillouin (1889-1969), a French physicist. During his work\non the propagation of electron waves in a crystal lattice, he introduced the concept of Brillouin zone in 1930.\nQuantum mechanical perturbations techniques by Brillouin and by Eugene Wigner resulted in what is known as the\nBrillouin-Wigner formula.  He also made contributions to quantum mechanics, radio wave propagation in the\natmosphere, solid state physics, and information theory. He also studied the propagation of monochromatic light\nwaves and their interaction with acoustic waves, i.e., scattering of light with a frequency change, which became known\nas Brillouin scattering.\nBrillouin Zones\nA Brillouin zone is defined as a Wigner-Seitz primitive cell in the reciprocal lattice. The first Brillouin zone is the\nsmallest volume entirely enclosed by planes that are the perpendicular bisectors of the reciprocal lattice vectors drawn\nfrom the origin. The concept of Brillouin zone is particularly important in the consideration of the electronic structure\nof solids. There are also second, third, etc., Brillouin zones, corresponding to a sequence of disjoint regions (all with the\nsame volume) at increasing distances from the origin, but these are used more rarely. As a result, the first Brillouin\nzone is often called simply the Brillouin zone. (In general, the n-th Brillouin zone consist of the set of points that can be\nreached from the origin by crossing n − 1 Bragg planes.) \nThe region in k-space (here an imaginary plane whose rectangular coordinates are kx and ky) that low-k electrons can\noccupy without being diffracted is called first Brillouin Zone, shown in Figure        . The second Brillouin zone is also\nShown; it contains electrons with  values from  to  for electrons moving in the ±x and ±y directions, with the\npossible range of k values narrowing as the diagonal directions are approached.\nFigure  The first and second Brillouin zones of a two-dimensional square lattice\nFurther Brillouin zones can be constructed in the same manner. These symmetry operations are usually denoted as point\noperations, since they leave at least one point of the lattice invariant, which is not the case for translations. The set of all\npoint operations for a particular crystal structure forms a group which is denoted as point group. The point group of\nthe diamond structure has 48 symmetry elements which are reflected in the symmetry of the first BZ. A quick\nexamination (see Figure ) shows that the BZ is invariant under various rotations, for example 90  rotations about the\n,  and  axes and under reflections through certain planes.\nThe point symmetries of the crystal structure are mirrored in the crystal potential, and hence in the one-particle\nHamiltonian used for band structure calculations. Two important consequences for the electron band structure arise:\nWave functions can be expressed in such a form that they have definite transformation properties under symmetry\noperations of the crystal. Certain matrix elements of operators can be shown to vanish and selection rules can be\ndeduced, when classifying the wave functions according to their symmetry.\nThe energy bands possess the full point symmetry of the point group of the crystal. The symmetries can be exploited\nto restrict the band structure calculation to a fraction of only 1/48th of the first BZ. Yang: 0000-0003-2024-0899 \nContact Information \njiann.yang@nist.gov  \n\nNIST TN 2385 \nSeptember 2026 \ni \nAbstract \nThe BLEVE (boiling liquid expanding vapor explosion) hypothesis on fire-induced spalling of \nconcrete was examined using superheated liquid theory. Water trapped within a heated \ninterior region of concrete was used as an idealized system to determine the thermodynamic \nconditions of water that subsequently would lead to potential occurrence of a BLEVE event. The \nthermodynamic states that favor BLEVE was identified and delineated in the P–T phase \ndiagram of water and was shown to be highly constrained to narrow ranges of temperature and \nthe amount of water trapped (fill density) in the heated region. \nKeywords \nConcrete; fire; spalling; superheated liquid; thermodynamics. \n\nNIST TN 2385 \nSeptember 2026 \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. Introduction \nWhen concrete is exposed to a fire, thermal energy from the fire is transported from the \nexposed concrete surface to the concrete interior. As the concrete interior is heated, its \ntemperature increases, causing the free water (moisture) in the concrete starts to evaporate, \nand the resulting water vapor diffuses towards the heated concrete surface where it is further \nheated and towards the unheated interior regions where it condenses and fills the pores within \nthe concrete. When the interior temperature is high enough, the dehydration of chemically \nbound water also occurs and generates more water vapor. As this heating process continues, a \nsudden and at times violent ejection of pieces of surface layers of the heated concrete, termed \nspalling, could occur. The propensity for spalling depends on many parameters including how \nthe concrete is heated (heating rate), concrete strength and constituents, how concrete is \ncured, and other factors. Majority of research literature has indicated that spalling results from \na highly coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical coupled process occurring in concrete exposed to \nhigh temperatures (e.g., fires). Many excellent review articles on various theories and \nhypotheses that had been used to partially explain the mechanisms of concrete spalling can be \nfound in the literature [1–7]. \nOne of the hypotheses on spalling was attributed to Ichikawa [8], who in passing suggested that \nthe spalling of concrete had been the result of a BLEVE (boiling liquid expanding vapor \nexplosion) event1. In this study, superheated liquid theory is used to re-examine Ichikawa’s \nBLEVE hypothesis. Specifically, this study only seeks to answer the question: What are the \nthermodynamic conditions of the water trapped in a continuously heated interior region of \nconcrete that would potentially trigger a BLEVE event? An idealization is made in the \nthermodynamic analysis in that there is an interior region of concrete where water is initially \ntrapped. In other words, the amount of water (either liquid, vapor, or liquid-vapor) in the \nheated region is fixed and is treated as a closed system. How the water is generated, \ntransported, and eventually accumulated in the region within the heated concrete is not the \nfocus of this study. \n \n1 The AIChE Center for Chemical Process Safety defines BLEVE as “A type of rapid phase transition in which a liquid contained above its \natmospheric boiling point is rapidly depressurized, causing a nearly instantaneous transition from liquid to vapor with a corresponding energy \nrelease.” https://www.aiche.org/ccps/resources/glossary \n\nNIST TN 2385 \nSeptember 2026 \n2 \n2. Thermodynamic Limit of superheat \nIn a series of seminal papers by Reid [9–14], he postulated that superheated liquid theory could \nbe used to explain BLEVE. A superheated liquid is a meta-stable liquid that exists at \ntemperatures beyond its saturation boiling point at the same pressure. These liquids are meta-\nstable with respect to small thermodynamic perturbations. \nFrom the classical thermodynamic stability theory [15], the metastable state is defined on a P–\nV phase diagram as \n \n,\n0\nTn\nP\nV\n¶ =¶  (1) \nwhere P, V, T, and n are pressure, volume, absolute temperature, and amount of substance, \nrespectively. If an equation of state (EOS) for the fluid of interest is available, the \nthermodynamic limit of superheat (Tsl), defined as the temperature at which Eq. (1) is satisfied, \ncan be calculated. \nNote that one can also estimate the limit of superheat based on kinetic theory models [16]. \nSince the thermodynamic limit of superheat is based on intrinsic thermodynamic stability \ncriteria, it is a theoretical limit. Therefore, limits of superheat calculated using kinetic theory \nmodels are lower than their thermodynamic counterparts [9,16]. \nFor the present discussion, it suffices to use the thermodynamic limits of superheat to explain \nthe potential occurrence of BLEVE since they can be easily calculated using an EOS. The Peng-\nRobinson EOS [17] was used to obtain the thermodynamic limit of superheat of water as a \nfunction of pressure. If the perturbation is sufficiently large, superheated liquids will partially vaporize \nand form a final, more stable state, usually consisting of vapor and residual liquid Reid [14]. In \nthe context of fire-induced spalling, isothermal depressurization is the likely scenario. \n\nNIST TN 2385 \nSeptember 2026 \n5 \n3. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Journal of Polymer Science, 2026; 0:1–11\nhttps://doi.org/10.1002/pola.70283\n1\nJournal of Polymer Science\n SPECIAL ISSUE  Special Issue in Celebration of Prof. Sindee Simon's 65th Birthday\nRESEARCH ARTICLE\nPredicting Cure Evolution and Thermal Endurance of \na Highly Filled Epoxy Underfill for Advanced Packaging\nRyan Giang1,2  |  Ran Tao1,3  |  Elena Moukhina4  |  Amanda L. Forster1  |  Tae Joon Cho1  |  Polette J. Centellas1  |  \nStian K. Romberg1,5  |  Zois Tsinas1,6  |  Christopher L. Soles1\n1Material Measurement Laboratory, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, Maryland, USA | 2Department of Chemical and Nano \nEngineering, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, California, USA | 3Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, North Carolina \nState University, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA | 4NETZSCH-  Gerätebau GmbH, Selb, Germany | 5Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, \nUniversity of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA | 6Theiss Research, La Jolla, California, USA\nCorrespondence:  Ran Tao (ran.tao@nist.gov )\nReceived:  11 May 2026 | Revised:  19 July 2026 | Accepted:  20 July 2026\nKeywords: advanced electronic packaging | cure kinetics | differential scanning calorimetry | diffusion-  controlled reaction | epoxy underfill | \nisoconversional analysis | thermal endurance | thermogravimetric analysis | vitrification\nABSTRACT\nEpoxy underfill materials are critical to advanced semiconductor packaging by enhancing mechanical integrity, redistributing \nthermomechanical stresses, and improving solder-  joint reliability in flip-  chip and other fine-  pitch interconnect architectures. \nTheir performance is strongly influenced by cure evolution during processing and thermal stability during service, making \nquantitative evaluation important for process optimization and long-  term reliability assessment. The cure kinetics and thermal \ndegradation behavior of a highly-  filled epoxy underfill were investigated using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), ther -\nmogravimetric analysis (TGA), and diffusion-  incorporated kinetic modeling. Isoconversional analysis showed that the apparent \nactivation energy varied with conversion and increased sharply at high conversion, indicating multi-  step cure behavior and dif -\nfusion control. A two-  step modified Kamal–Sourour model incorporating diffusion control in the second step improved predic -\ntion of conversion after vitrification and was used to predict cure evolution under a designed oven cure schedule, which achieved \nnearly complete cure. Cryomilling improved TGA reproducibility without causing detectable chemical changes. Analysis follow -\ning the ASTM E1641/E1877 protocols revealed a strong temperature dependence of estimated thermal endurance based on a 5% \nmass- loss criterion under nitrogen. Together, the results provide a quantitative framework for predicting cure evolution under \npractical thermal schedules, evaluating late-  stage diffusion effects, and estimating degradation-  based thermal endurance for \nhighly- filled industrial thermosets.\n1   |   Introduction\nEpoxy underfill materials are widely used in advanced elec -\ntronic packaging to improve mechanical integrity, redistribute \nthermomechanical stresses, and enhance solder-  joint reliabil -\nity. They are used as encapsulants that fill the gap between the \nsemiconductor die and the substrate, particularly in flip-  chip \nand other fine-  pitch interconnect architectures [ 1]. By encap -\nsulating the interconnect region, underfill helps protect solder \njoints from fatigue, cracking, delamination, and environmental \ndamage during service. Their performance depends not only on \nthe final epoxy network structure after processing [ 2], but also \non the cure path itself, since the evolution of conversion, glass \ntransition temperature, and residual stresses [ 3, 4] during pro -\ncessing can strongly influence long-  term reliability [5]. A quan-\ntitative understanding of cure evolution is important for both \nfundamental insight and industrial practice, supporting process \noptimization and materials qualification [ 6]. For commercial \n© 2026 Wiley Periodicals LLC.\nAll rights reserved, including rights for text and data mining and training of artificial intelligence technologies or similar technologies.\n\n\n2 Journal of Polymer Science, 2026\nunderfill formulations used at industry scale, the combined \neffects of multi-  step cure behavior arising from complex resin \nchemistry and high inorganic filler loading make it difficult to \npredict cure completion using simplified kinetic descriptions \ncommonly employed in industry practice [7–10].\nKinetic analysis of thermoset curing is commonly performed \nusing model- free and model- based approaches. Isoconversional \nmethods are useful for assessing changes in activation energy \nand thus whether a single-  step kinetic description is appropri -\nate, whereas model-  based approaches can be used to describe \nthe full reaction path [ 11]. For many epoxy systems, however, \nthe apparent activation energy varies with conversion [ 12–14], \nindicating that multiple reaction steps may be involved [ 15]. \nFurthermore, at high conversion, vitrification reduces molecu -\nlar mobility and diffusion limitations increasingly suppress the \nreaction rate [16, 17]. Under these conditions, purely chemically \ncontrolled models may adequately describe the early and inter -\nmediate stages of cure but often fail to capture the late-  stage \nregime. A kinetic description that accounts for both multi-  step \ncure behavior and diffusion limitations is therefore needed to \npredict cure evolution across all cure stages relevant to practical \nprocessing conditions.\nIn addition to cure kinetics, thermal stability is also an import -\nant consideration for underfill materials used in demanding ser-\nvice environments. For example, electronic components in an \nautomotive engine compartment experience an ambient service \ntemperature of around 150°C, and operating temperatures can \nrange from 175°C to 200°C [ 18]. Thermal degradation behavior \nof epoxy underfill is influenced by its chemical composition, in -\ncluding both the polymer network and inorganic filler content. \nDynamic thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) [ 19] performed at \nmultiple heating rates, together with ASTM E1641 and ASTM \nE1877 methods [ 20, 21], provides a practical route for estimat -\ning apparent activation energy from degradation-  based kinetic \nanalysis and for assessing temperature-  dependent thermal en -\ndurance [ 22]. For highly filled thermosets, reproducible TGA \nmeasurements require consistent sample preparation because \nheat and mass transfer during decomposition are sensitive to \nsample geometry [ 20]. Establishing a reproducible method for \nthermal degradation analysis is therefore essential for obtaining \nmeaningful kinetic parameters and lifetime predictions.\nThe cure kinetics and thermal degradation behavior of a highly \nfilled epoxy underfill have been investigated using dynamic \ndifferential scanning calorimetry (DSC), dynamic TGA, and ki -\nnetic modeling. Model-  free analysis was first used to evaluate \nthe conversion dependence of the apparent activation energy, \nand a two-  step modified Kamal–Sourour model with diffusion \ncontrol was then used to describe cure evolution and predict \nconversion under a practical oven cure schedule. To evaluate \nthermal stability, cured samples were cryomilled to improve \nTGA reproducibility, and the dynamic TGA data were analyzed \nusing ASTM E1641 and ASTM E1877 to estimate the apparent \nactivation energy and temperature-  dependent thermal endur -\nance. Together, these results provide a quantitative framework \nfor linking cure schedule design, diffusion-  incorporated cure \nkinetics modeling, and degradation-  based lifetime assessment \nfor highly filled epoxy underfill systems used in advanced pack -\naging applications.\n2   |   Experimental\n2.1   |   Materials\nA commercial epoxy underfill, Loctite ECCOBOND UF 1173, \nwas purchased from Henkel Corporation.1 It is a one- part, silica- \nfilled, epoxy-  based thermosetting resin system widely used in \nindustrial processes for flip-  chip and fine- pitch device encapsu-\nlation. The liquid underfill material was shipped on dry ice from \nthe manufacturer and stored at −40°C upon receipt prior to use.\n2.2   |   DSC Measurements\nA TA Instruments Discovery DSC 2500 differential scanning \ncalorimeter with an RCS 90 intracooler maintained at − 90°C \nand nitrogen purge gas was used to study the cure kinetics of \nthe commercial underfill. The masses of DSC samples ranged \nfrom 10 to 20 mg. After removal from the − 40°C freezer, the \nliquid underfill was allowed to equilibrate to room temperature \nfor 10 min before being loaded into 40 μL hermetic aluminum \npans and sealed for measurement. The DSC temperature was \ncalibrated using indium, tin, and lead at 10 K min−1, and the heat \nflow was calibrated with indium. The standard uncertainties for \ntemperature and heat flow are estimated to be ±1% and ±3%, \nrespectively.\nFor dynamic DSC experiments, the uncured samples were \nheated from 30°C to 300°C at constant heating rates of 0.6, 1, \n3, 5, 10, and 20°C min−1. The samples were then quenched to \n−30°C at a rate of approximately 50°C min−1 after the first heat -\ning scan, and a second heating scan up to 300°C at 10°C min−1 \nwas performed to measure the cured material Tg and any resid -\nual heat. To measure the Tg of the uncured material, a broader \ntemperature range, from − 90°C to 300°C, was used for the first \nheating scan.\n2.3   |   Preparation and Processing of Cured Epoxy \nUnderfill\nThe uncured liquid material was deposited onto a glass substrate \nlaminated with a fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) protec -\ntive film with an aluminum support backing. It was then placed \nin a forced-  air oven (Cascade TEK model TFO-  3) and cured \nusing a two-  step schedule: first at 150°C for 30 min, followed \nby 185°C for 30 min. A thermocouple was directly attached to \nthe surface of the glass substrate to monitor the substrate tem -\nperature, and the temperature data were recorded every 100 ms \nthroughout the thermal curing process. The oven was allowed \nto equilibrate to room temperature before retrieving the cured \nsamples.\nThe cured samples were removed from the glass substrate and \ncut into approximately 50 mm2 pieces (1–2 mm thick) using a \nrazor blade. The pieces were then weighed to obtain a total mass \nof approximately 4 g. Cryogenic milling (cryomilling) was per -\nformed using a Retsch CryoMill equipped with a stainless-  steel \ngrinding jar with a 25 mm diameter milling ball continuously \ncooled with liquid nitrogen from an autofill system to main -\ntain a cryogenic temperature of − 196°C. [{"suffix": "", "text": "1 \n \n \nStructure-Property Relationships for Biodegradability in Copolyesters  \nAuthors: Katharina A. Fransen 1, Julia Casey1, Gabrielle Godbille-Cardona1, Natalie Mamrol2, \nJiale Shi1, Alex Zappi1, Jignesh S. Mahajan1, Jiarui Lu3, Debra J. Audus4, and Bradley D. Olsen1* \n*Corresponding Author \n \n1Department of Chemical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA \n2Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge , MA 02139, \nUSA \n3Department of Computer Science, Wellesley College, Wellesley, MA 02481, USA \n4Materials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, \nUSA \n*Corresponding Author \nBradley D. Olsen \nMassachusetts Institute of Technology, Room 66-558A \n77 Massachusetts Ave.  \nCambridge, MA 02139 \nPhone: 617-715-4548 \nEmail:  bdolsen@mit.edu \n \nAbstract: With growing concerns about increasing plastic pollution, interest in biodegradable \npolymers, particularly polyesters, continues to grow. Copolymerization is an important molecular \nhandle to tune properties to achieve material performance and biodegradat ion simultaneously.  \nTo better understand the structure -property relationships that govern biodegradability, a 300 -\nmember copolymer library was synthesized and tested using a high -throughput clear -zone \nbiodegradation assay; testing shows over 80  % of the copolymer library is biodegradable even \nthough only 50 % of the homopolymers from which they are derived are degradable. Repeat units \nwith longer carbon backbones decreased biodegradability, though copolymers showed \nbiodegradability at all average repeat unit lengths examined. For both homopolymers and \ncopolymers, oxygen substitution of backbone carbons was established as a lever to improve \nbiodegradability. A novel chemical similarity -informed embedding that considers polymer \nchemical structure and composition was developed and implemented for the simultaneous \n\n2 \n \nquantitative structure-property relationship modeling of homopolymers and copolymers. Random \nforest models could simultaneously capture homopolymer and copolymer behavior with 78 % and \n95 % accuracy, respectively; however, models trained only on homopolymer data could not \npredict copolymer biodegradability. Unlike random forest models, linear models were not able to \ncapture both homopolymer and copolymer biodegradability.  \nMain Text: \nIntroduction: \n Biodegradable polyesters present a promising end -of-life solution for materials that often \nsuffer accidental environmental release, are targets for industrial degradation, 1-4 or shed \nmicroplastics into the environment through daily use and wear. 2 Polyesters are a promising \nmaterial class for the development of biodegradable polymers as they contain ester bonds \ncapable of undergoing both chemical degradation and biodegradation.5-6  Additionally, polyesters \nsuch as poly(3 -hydroxybutyrate) and poly(3 -hydroxyvalerate) have been synthesized and \nleveraged as energy sources by microbes, providing naturally occurring microbes capable of \nbiodegrading polyesters.7-8 Studies on the biodegradability of polyesters have focused on small \n(< 10) sets of polymers,9-12 examining the effect of isolated chemical structure effects such as side \nchains or repeat unit length, 13 or developing biodegradable polymers for a specific application \nsuch as packaging,10 fibers,14 or medicine.15-16 As the need for sustainable polymer development \ngrows,17 an understanding of how material structure affects biodegradation and the development \nof predictive biodegradability models becomes increasingly critical to address the accumulation \nof polymers and microplastics in the environment.2, 18-19  \n At the same time, different intended applications require materials with varying \nmechanical, optical, thermal, and transport properties. 20-21 Copolymerization presents a \ndemonstrated route to achieve tuned material properties without sacrificing all of the benefits from \nthe original material selection. For example, terephthalic acid, ethylene glycol, and \ncyclohexanedimethanol are often copolymer ized to obtain polyethylene terephthalate glycol \n\n3 \n \n(PETG) for applications such as 3D printing. 22-23 Moving towards greener materials, lactone \ncopolymers, including copolymerization of lactide and its stereoisomers, have been used to tune \nphysical properties beyond those available among homopolymers.11, 24-25 In addition, terephthalic \nacid, adipic acid, and butanediol are copolymerized to form polybutylene adipate terephthalate  \n(PBAT), a quickly growing competitor to polylactic acid with improved flexibility and toughness , \nwhich presents a promising tunable and biodegradable route towards polymer waste \nmanagement.12, 26-27  \n Despite the importance of biodegradability for the development of these sustainable and \ngreen materials, the systematic design of biodegradable polymers remains a major challenge.  \nCriteria for biodegradability under various degradation conditions have been set forth by agencies \nsuch as the American Society for Testing and Materials ( ASTM) and the International \nOrganization for Standardization ( ISO), including standards for anerobic environments, aerobic \nenvironments accelerated by high temperatures, marine environments, and industrial \ncomposting.28-32 The standardized tests provide valuable information for end -of-life fate \ndetermination in their targeted environments, but their required testing timeframes (30 -180 \ndays)28-33 and variability in the microbial consortia between individual tests and test types present \nchallenges for the use of these tests when comparing the biodegradability and compostability of \npolymers. While biodegradable and compostable are often used interch angeably for polymers,34 \nin this work biodegradability is used to refer to the ability of materials to degrade under ambient \nmicrobial action34 and compostability is interpreted as defined in ASTM D6400 and establishes a \nmaterial as certifiable by the Biodegradable Products Institute in the United States.33  \n Accelerated biodegradation testing methods have been identified as a key challenge in \nbiodegradable polymer development 35 as timeframes 28-29, 31 -32 associated with standard test \nmethods hinder their use as primary screening tools. Several accelerated biodegradation \nstrategies have been developed , which enable testing for polymer biodegradation within 30 \ndays.36-39 Recently, the accelerated clear -zone biodegradation test 39 was adapted for high -\n\n4 \n \nthroughput. This test leverage d a Paucimonas lemoignei (P. lemoignei) colony to degrade \npolymer particulates, providing control over the microbial action governing the degradation and \nguaranteeing replicability. P. lemoignei contains 7 known polyester depolymerases  which are \nexcreted extracellularly.7, 40-41 Automation of the visual degradation data collection and processing \nsupported the simultaneous testing of 100 -200 polymers in two weeks. The high -throughput \naccelerated clear -zone biodegradation test has enabl ed the testing of a poly ester and \npolycarbonate library with over 600 members, the identification of important trends for \nbiodegradability in the tested polymers, and the development of polyester biodegradation \nstructure-property relationships using machine learning.42 \n Quantitative structure -property relationship (QSPR) modeling to predict polymer \nproperties promises to help researchers navigate increasingly large design spaces to find optimal \npolymer designs. Polymer property prediction using machine learning has been demonstrated43-\n46 but continues to face challenges across data generation and curation, polymer featurization \nand fingerprinting, and model selection and training. 47 Dataset sizes, especially experimental \ndatasets, are expensive to generate and limited in size even when produced through high -\nthroughput experimentation. 47 Polymers also present unique challenges for representation as \nthey are comprised of stochastic chemical structures which most chemical representations, \ndeveloped for small molecules,46, 48 are not designed to capture. Although strides have been made \nin capturing the stochasticity of polymers in a singular representation such as BigSMILES, 49-50  \nfingerprint embedding methods for polymer machine learning remain challenging due to not only \nthe stochastic nature of the polymer but topological variability and variable monomer compositions \nin copolymers. 47 Advances in applying fingerprinting strategies remain limited to polymers with \none or two monomers51 or rely on additional machine learning models to generate embeddings.52 \nAs a result, monomers, repeat units, or ring repeat units 53-54 are often used as a basis for small \nmolecule chemical fingerprinting algorithms to generate the polymer representations. Copolymers \nface additional representation challenges due to their variable local monomer sequences which \n\n5 \n \nare not captured by monomer or repeat unit -based representation strategies. One proposed \nsolution to address this challenge has been summing monomer fingerprint vectors in proportion \nto the monomer composition, 51 but such strategies do not capture functional group connections \nbetween monomers or their relative abundances in the polymer, and a significant need for \nadditional polymer representations remains.  \n This work applied high-throughput experimentation and QSPR modeling in order to \ndevelop a deeper understanding of the impact of copolymerization on polymer biodegradability.   \nA 300-member copolymer library was synthesized and evaluated for biodegradability to augment \nan existing polyester and polycarbonate biodegradability dataset and identify the impact of \ncopolymerization of more than two monomers in AA/BB polycondensation. A novel chemical \nsimilarity-informed embedding incorporating polymer chemical structure and composition was \nintroduced and leveraged to develop predictive random forest and linear machine learning models \nfor polyester biodegradability, probing the transferability of homopolymer biodegradation data in \npredicting copolymer biodegradability.  \nExperimental Section:  \nPolymer Synthesis and Characterization \nMaterials: Monomers and catalysts were purchased from Sigma Aldrich, TCI America, and AK \nScientific and used as received. Polymers with a degree of \npolymerization less than 5 were resynthesized at higher temperatures, under higher vacuum, and \nwith longer reaction times to achieve higher molecular weights. \nThermodynamic driving forces: Writing a fundamental equation \nWhat goes into internal energy? \n•\t When we introduced the concept of work, we stated that every form of work can be thought of as a \ngeneralized thermodynamic force acting to create some generalized ‘displacement’ in the system.  In a \nsimilar way, we said that temperature can be thought of as a thermodynamic force that causes a ‘thermal \ndisplacement’ which is the change in entropy of the system: \n•\t The internal energy, which sums the contributions from these two terms, can be written as a perfect \ndifferential depending on S and V: \nThe ‘natural’ variables of state functions \no\t Why do we write U = U(S,V)? Why not U = U(T,V)? The answer will unfortuna tely not be clear until we \nintroduce the second law.  The second law dictates that certain thermodynamic functions will reach \nextrema (maximima or minima) when the system is at equilibrium- e.g. the entropy will be maximized at \nequilibrium. When U and S are written as function of S,V and U,V respectively, they are said to be written \nin terms of their natural variables. State functions of natural variables have extremum principles at \nequilibrium (they will be maximized or minimized at equilibrium).  In other words, the reason we write U as \na function of S and V is that it is the most useful form to write internal energy equations for most \nproblems- we can use this equation for internal energy to calculate equilibrium properties. \nGeneralized expression for the internal energy: internal energy of open systems \n•\t The first law expression above only applies to very simple thermodynamic systems- which have can \nundergo only hydrostatic work and have no transport or chemical transformation of components.  \nExtending our first law expression is straightforward for any thermodynamic case where other forms of \nwork are important. We have seen how to make calculations of these quantities from measurable \nquantities.  However, in these calculations we have been limited to analyzing processes whose \nspontaneous behavior we take as a given - we have not yet made predictions of what processes will \noccur. Okay, I \nthink this was referring to the initial state and final state in the mixing problem. I \ncompared this process to subtracting product and reactant formation free energies in a \nchemical reaction process. Since molar Gibbs energy is the same as chemical potential, \nthe Gibbs energy of the two states is the sum of µA in the solution and µB in the solution \n(final state), versus µA in its pure state and µB in its pure state (intitial, separated state). \nAs you saw in problem 2, chemical potential of the same component in its pure state \nversus in a solution are not equal. Hope that helps. \nHow do we know what expressions like (dF/dT)V = -S are?  For first derivatives, it comes \nright from your state function expressions. On the one hand, dF = -SdT - PdV. On the \nother hand, dF(T, V) = (δF/δT)V dT + (δF/δV)T dV (I’m using deltas instead of dels so I \ndon’t have to go into equation editor; yes, sometimes I’m lazy). You just compare those \ntwo expressions, so make sure you have them in your notes for an exam. For the second \nderivatives, you have to do a little more work, but basically they will come out to either \nan expression using heat capacity or one using compressibility, and you can learn and \nnote down those two patterns. As always, I’m available in OH and over email. \nlecture vote: 6 clear, 3 suggestive (mostly R1)\nproblems vote: 4 clear, 2 suggestive (mostly R2)\nmixed vote: 5\nnot mentioned: 9"}]

(2026) Data Collection Instrument: Evaluating \nMethodological Differences in Discrete Choice Experiments (National Institute of Standards and Technology, \nGaithersburg, MD), NIST Data Collection Instruments (DCI) NIST DCI 0 10. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.DCI.010 \n \nAuthor ORCID iDs \nXiatian Iogansen: 0000-0002-4851-1323 \nChristina Gore: 0000-0002-3586-6918  \nJoshua Kneifel: 0000-0002-3114-5531 \nJohn Paul Helveston: 0000-0002-2657-9191 \n\nNIST DCI 010 \nJuly 2026 \n \ni \nAbstract \nThis Data Collection Instrument (DCI) establishes a guideline and survey framework for \nquantifying consumer preferences and willingness-to-pay (WTP) for commodities that containing \nrecycled plastic. The instrument combines behavioral experience metrics, attitudinal scales, and a \nDiscrete Choice Experiment (DCE). The DCE employs a multi -dimensional split-sample design \nthat varies across three critical axes: (1) product context, contrasting low-cost discretionary items \n(phone cases) with high-cost functional goods (sneakers); (2) valuation methodology, comparing \nbaseline attribute -based valuations against information  treatment valuations; and (3) the \ninformation framing, which provides respondents with external data showing either a significant \ndecrease or increase in the energy required for production. By isolating the causal effect of \nsustainability disclosures through a within-subject \"information shock\" mechanism, this research \nestimates how stated preferences and WTP for attributes associated with recycled plastic products \nshift after information is provided. Beyond the expected empirical findings, this DCI provides a \nreproducible methodological blueprint for researchers and practitioners, enhancing the reliability \nof stated preference studies for emerging circular economy technologies.  Additionally, this DCI \ncontains a series of questions aimed at validating that the data is from human subjects rather than \nsynthetic data.  \n \nKeywords \ndiscrete choice experiment (DCE); conjoint analysis; recycled plastic; information treatment; \nwillingness-to-pay (WTP); consumer preferences \n\nNIST DCI 010 \nJuly 2026 \n \nii \nTable of Contents \n1. Introduction  \nThe accurate measurement of consumer preferences for novel product attributes is essential for \nboth market development and policy design, particularly for innovations like recycled plastics. \nSurvey methods collecting stated preference (SP) data are often u sed to evaluate the willingness \nto pay (WTP) in the absence of observational data for new products or product attributes that are \nnot currently on the market. A common survey method for eliciting WTP estimates for products \nis a discrete choice experiment (DCE), where the attribute levels of an item change and consumers \nanswer a series of questions where they select between a few alternative products (Contemporary \nGuidance for Stated Preference Studies, 2017; Louviere, 1988).  \nHowever, a methodological debate has emerged regarding the integration of information \ntreatments within DCEs and how these treatments may influence preference measurements \n(Haghani et al., 2021) , particularly in the context of hypothetical bias , the well -documented \ntendency for respondents to overstate their preferences or WTP in hypothetical settings compared \nto real-world behavior (Penn & Hu, 2018). Information treatments allow the treatment effect to be \ncalculated based on the change in behavior after the information is provided, rather than only \nrelying on the attribute variation between choices. This research addresses this methodological gap \nby directly comparing standard DCEs with information  treatment-enhanced DCEs using the \ncontent of recycled plastic used in a consumer product as a case study.  \nThe environmental context is significant: A global life cycle analysis of plastics shows that of the \n400 million tonnes of plastic produced worldwide in 2022, only about 9.5% was made from \nrecycled materials, with the remainder derived from virgin materials (Houssini et al., 2025). In the \nUnited States (US), while accounting for a high share of global production (19%) and consumption \n(21%) (Environment, 2018; Heller et al., 2020), the recycling rate for post-consumer plastic waste \nmay be as low as 5 % to 6 % ( Milbrandt et al. , 2022) . Studying consumer WTP for products \ncontaining recycled plastic is critical to capture the economic value of plastic waste and mitigate \npotential impacts of plastic waste . However, the drivers and barriers related to the demand for \nrecycled plastics are not thoroughly understood.   \nThis study aims to answer both contextual questions regarding the recycled plastics market and \nmethodological questions regarding survey design: \n● Contextual objectives \n○ Identify the demographics of current and prospective consumers of products \ncontaining recycled plastic (hereafter, “recycled plastic products”). \n○ Analyze how consumers trade off product attributes (e.g., price vs. % of recycled \ncontent) across different product categories like phone cases and sneakers. \n○ Quantify whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for products containing \nrecycled plastics compared to products with conventional \"virgin\" plastics. \n○ Evaluate how energy -related information provision and individual environmental \nknowledge impact WTP. \n● Methodological objectives \n\nNIST DCI 010 \nJuly 2026 \n \n2 \n○ Quantify differences in WTP estimates between standard DCEs and information-\ntreatment DCEs  \n○ Determine how the magnitude of the information treatment effect (e.g., specific \nenergy consumption) influences results. \n○ Assess how contextual factors, including product category (e.g., phone cases versus \nsneakers), information format (e.g., texts vs. videos), and device type for taking the \nsurvey (e.g., mobile vs. desktop), moderate the differences between methodological \napproaches. \nTo accomplish these objectives, this DCI outlines the development and implementation of a \nconjoint choice experiment survey designed to collect data from US consumers using a rigorous \nsplit-sample experimental approach with multiple treatment arms.  By building on established \nsurvey methodology literature, this approach seeks to isolate the specific effects of information \nprovision within the choice experiment framework, providing a robust mechanism for evaluating \nboth consumer preferences and the impact of survey design on economic valuation. \n\nNIST DCI 010 \nJuly 2026 \n \n3 \n2. Background \n2.1. Methodological Challenges in Stated Preference Research \nStated preference methods face persistent challenges regarding reliability and external validity \n(Lancsar & Swait, 2014; Louviere, 1988) . While these methods are invaluable for estimating \ndemand for novel products and attributes, questions remain about how study design choices \ninfluence results. Recent meta- analyses (Xie et al., 2022; Yeh & Hirsch, 2023)  have shown \nsignificant variability in WTP estimates across different studies examining the same attributes, \nsuggesting that methodological factors may play a substantial role in determining outcomes. A \nsystematic review (Kanya et al., 2019) suggests that hypothetical WTP was on average 3.2 times \ngreater than actual WTP. \nInformation provision represents a particularly challenging aspect of state preference ( SP) \nresearch. On one hand, providing contextual information ensures that participants have a baseline \nunderstanding of unfa

For the Fermi surface all points in reciprocal space at which \\(E=E_f\\). The band gap is determined\nby the difference between the highest occupied energy level and the lowest occupied energy level.\nA number of bands may be partially filled. When this occurs, the energy of the highest occupied level, the\nFermi energy, lies within the energy range of one or more bands. For each partially filled band there will be a\nsurface in k-space separating the occupied from the unoccupied levels. The set of all such surfaces is known as\nthe Fermi surface. Let’s now place a \nfourth and fifth B ion above and below the A ion in directions that are normal to the plane of \nthe triangle. Voila! Five-fold coordination!! One mole of an ideal gas is compressed reversibly from 5L to\n1 L at a constant pressure of 5 atm, and absorbs 2400 J of heat during this process.\na.
