[{"suffix": "", "text": "Contents lists available at ScienceDirect\nExtreme Mechanics Letters\njournal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/eml  \nBridging the impact response of polymers from the nanoscale to the \nmacroscale\nKyle R. Callahan a,b\n ,1, Katherine M. Evans c\n ,1, William F. Heard d\n , Santanu Kundu a,b\n ,∗,\nEdwin P. Chan c\n ,∗\na Center for Advanced Vehicular Systems, Mississippi State University, Starkville, 39759, MS, United  States\nb Dave C. Swalm School of Chemical Engineering, Mississippi State University, Starkville, 39762, MS, United  States\nc Materials Science and Engineering Division, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, 20899, MD, United  States\nd Geotechnical and Structure Laboratory, Engineer Research and Development Center, Vicksburg, 39180, MS, United  States\nA R T I C L E  I N F O\nKeywords:\nImpact performance\nPolymers\nMechanical properties\n A B S T R A C T\nImpact from a fast-moving object is a common event, but it can vary greatly in terms of scale, speed, and \nenergy depending on the specific case. Recently, it has been suggested that scaling analysis can be used to \nrelate the impact performance of materials at the nano- and microscale to their behavior at the macroscale, \nwhich is relevant for most applications. In this study, we explore the broad applicability of this approach by \nconducting micro- and macroprojectile impact tests on polymethyl methacrylate and polycarbonate films. By \napplying Buckingham 𝛱 dimensional analysis to all the impact test results, we demonstrate that the minimum \nperforation velocity is directly related to the geometric and material properties of each system across a broad \nrange of size and energy scales. Interestingly, we find that the failure stress of the polymer, a critical material \nproperty that defines perforation resistance, can be empirically determined based on the deformation of the \nspecific impact test.\n1. Introduction\nMost people do not need to worry about impact protection on a daily \nbasis. Automobile windshields are designed to protect against road \nhazards, such as pebbles and rocks that travel at velocities on the order \nof 20 m s−1 [1]. Aircraft and spacecraft can withstand projectiles such \nas debris or dust particles that impact these vehicles at significantly \nhigher velocities [2,3]. These examples illustrate the variability in \nimpact energies associated with the various impact events because of \ndifferent projectile sizes and velocities. Fig.  1 illustrates examples of a \nfew impact events demonstrating the broad range of impact energies \nand size-scale of the deformation.\nTraditionally, understanding the impact performance of a material \ninvolves studying it with a macroscale projectile impact test, with \nvarious projectile materials and sizes traveling up to 2000 m s−1, to \nidentify the critical velocity when perforation occurs [4,5]. However, \nthese tests are expensive, both in terms of the amount of material \nneeded and the time required to conduct them. To address these \nlimitations and facilitate the discovery of new materials, laser-induced \nprojectile impact testing (LIPIT) has been developed as an alternative \n∗ Corresponding authors.\nE-mail addresses: krc315@msstate.edu (K.R. Callahan), katherine.evans@nist.gov (K.M. Evans), william.f.heard@usace.army.mil (W.F. Heard), \nsantanukundu@che.msstate.edu (S. Kundu), edwin.chan@nist.gov (E.P. Chan).\n1 Contributed equally.\nmeans to study the impact performance of ultrathin materials. Here, \nmicroprojectiles impact ultrathin films with thicknesses, ℎ ≈ 50 nm  to \n1 μm , and impact velocities ranging from 𝑣𝑖 ≈ 100  m s−1 to 1000 m \ns−1 [6]. This combination of high-velocity impacts and ultrathin sample \nthickness has enabled the characterization of the impact performance \nof a variety of materials [7–15] at deformation rates from ≈106 s−1 to \n108 s−1. Since LIPIT characterizes a material’s impact performance at \nthe microscale, the critical question is whether the results translate to \nthe performance of the same material at the macroscale.\nRecent studies have addressed this impact performance question by \napplying various scaling analyses to connect either simulation to LIPIT \nresults [16] or LIPIT to macroscale impact tests [15]. Buckingham 𝛱\ntheory, which involves relating physically similar systems together by \narranging key variables into dimensionless quantities [17], has been \nutilized to connect the impact responses of polycarbonate (PC) from \nLIPIT to macroscale ballistic experiments [15]. A scaling relationship \nwas developed between the minimum perforation velocity (𝑉0) and \nvarious geometric (film thickness, projectile size) and materials prop-\nerties (failure stress of polymer, densities). The failure stress (𝜎f) of \nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.eml.2025.102331\nReceived 22 October 2024; Received in revised form 5 March 2025; Accepted 7 April 2025\nExtreme Mechanics Letters 77 (2025) 102331 \nAvailable online 18 April 2025 \n2352-4316/Published by Elsevier Ltd. \n\nK.R. Callahan et al.\nFig. 1. Examples of impact events in different materials across different energy and size scales. (a) Crater resulting from the collision of a meteorite with Earth [18]. (b) A cracked \nwindshield of a car [1]. (c) Damage resulting from the impact of debris on the space shuttle window [3]. (d) A microparticle embedded into a polycarbonate thin film, captured \nin a microballistic impact study.\nSource: Image adapted from [13].\nthe polymer, which scaled with both the projectile size and strain rate \nof the impact test, was shown to be an important material property \ndictating the impact performance of a material. However, questions re-\nmain over the general applicability of this approach and the underlying \nmechanisms that define it as impact performance is material-specific.\nIn this work, we address these questions by experimentally study-\ning the impact performance of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) and \npolycarbonate (PC) using both micro- and macroprojectile impact tests. \nSimilar to PC, PMMA is a glassy amorphous polymer. However, PMMA \ntypically exhibits more brittle mechanical behavior than PC during \nhigh-velocity impacts [4]. Thus, comparing these two polymers will \nallow us to gain insight into how a polymer’s material properties \ncontribute to its impact performance.\n2. Impact testing\n2.1. Microprojectile impact studies\nMicroscale ballistic impact experiments were conducted using LIPIT\n[13]. A schematic of the test is shown in Fig.  2a. In a typical test, a \nsilica microprojectile of radius 𝑎p = 10 μm  (microParticles GmbH) was \nlaunched via laser ablation from a launchpad comprised of a 20 cm \n× 40 cm glass coverslip substrate, with a 30 nm thick layer of gold, \nand a 30 μm , 40 μm , or 50 μm  layer of polydimethylsiloxane. The \nmicroprojectile then perforated the polymer thin film at an impact \nvelocity 𝑣𝑖 and exited the film at a residual velocity 𝑣𝑟. These velocities, \nmeasured via an ultrafast camera (Specialized Imaging Ltd, SIMD12) \nwith 20 ns exposure time per frame and an interframe time of 300 ns, \nare used to calculate the energy dissipation of the film during the \nimpact event based on a kinetic energy balance of an inelastic collision, \nas discussed below.\nPMMA with a number average molecular mass of 267 kg mol−1 and \npolydispersity index of 1.3 was obtained from Polymer Source, Inc. \nTo prepare PMMA thin films for the LIPIT studies, the polymer was \ndissolved in toluene, and heated to ≈90 ◦C for ≈48 h. This solution was \nfiltered using a 0.45 μm filter and then spin-coated at 157 rad/sec (1500 \nrpm) onto a clean silicon wafer substrate. The film thickness, measured \nusing an interferometer (LS-DT2, Filmetrics), was ℎ ≈ 367 nm. The \nfilms were then diced into 2 mm × 2 mm squares with a razor blade \nand floated off on a water bath. The diced PMMA films were picked \nup with transmission electron microscopy grids (PELCO, Tabbed 100 \nmesh, Nickel, Ted Pella, Inc.), dried by wicking with a wipe, and used \nfor the LIPIT measurements without additional processing. Additional \ndetails regarding the experimental setup for the LIPIT experiments for \nPC are located in Chen et al. [13]. We note that the LIPIT results for \nPC were obtained from a prior study [13].\n2.2. Macroprojectile impact studies\nMacroscale ballistic impact experiments were conducted using a \nstationary powder gun with a 1.27 cm internal diameter Mann bar-\nrel at the Engineer Research and Development Center (ERDC). Flat \nsheets (25.4 mm × 25.4 mm) of PMMA with average thicknesses (ℎ) \nof 1.4 mm, 2.8 mm, and 5.4 mm were used. PMMA (General Optix \nby Plaskolite) was purchased from Curbell Plastics. The sample was \nsecured to a frame by clamps before the experiment. To measure the \nimpact (𝑣𝑖) and residual velocity (𝑣𝑟) of the projectile, a Phantom TMX \n7510 camera was used to film the entire impact event at 180,000 \nframes per second. To study the effects of projectile properties on the \nimpact performance, projectiles with two different radii, 𝑎p = 2 .0 mm \nand 6.35 mm, were used. The 2.0 mm projectiles were either T4 2017 \naluminum (Al) with a density 𝜌p = 2790  kg m−3 or S2 Rockbit steel \n(St) with a density 𝜌p = 7790  kg m−3. The 6.35 mm projectiles were \nexclusively S2 Rockbit steel. Four-piece nylon sabots fit the various \nprojectiles to the internal diameter of the rifle barrel. A separator \nplate, placed downstream from the gun, intercepted the sabot pieces \nExtreme Mechanics Letters 77 (2025) 102331 \n2 \n\nK.R. Callahan et al.\nFig. 2. Saidi \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899, USA  \nE-mail: marek@nist.gov \n \n \nSummary: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) can segment novel, previously unseen objects from 2D images. This \ncapability is especially important in automated bin picking applications, where low-volume and high-variability scenarios are \ncommon. When prompted by a point, SAM outputs three masks with varying confidence scores. Prior research indicates that \nSAM's performance depends on the type of parts in a bin: for parts that are visually decomposable into subcomponents, \ncorrectly segmented masks are more often associated with a medium confidence score. Conversely, for parts that are not readily \nvisually decomposable into subcomponents, correct masks are typically associated with the highest confidence score. We \ninvestigated the transition from visually decomposable to non-decomposable part categories in simulation by using  \ncomputer-aided design (CAD) models with gradually altered geometric features. Differences in the dimensions of these \ngeometric features cause corresponding differences in grayscale images. We found that this transition occurs within a relatively \nnarrow range of feature modifications and image intensities. This demonstrates the strong sensitivity of SAM to the specific \ntypes of parts within a bin. Consequently, prior knowledge of a part's complexity can be leveraged to better tune the processing \nof SAM's output. \n \nKeywords: Foundation models, Segment anything model, Robotic bin picking. \n \n \n1. Introduction \n \nThe successful deployment of bin picking systems \nto automate manufacturing tasks, such as assembly or \nkitting, depends strongly on vision system \nperformance. The vision system must segment the \nacquired depth images to determine the six degree -of-\nfreedom (6DoF) pose of individual parts, enabling the \nintegrated robot to execute tasks successfully. \nAccurate instance segmentation of unorganized \npiles of manufacturing parts remains especially \nchallenging. While early segmentation algorithms \nrequired model retraining for different parts [1], the \nemergence of foundation models such as the Segment \nAnything Model (SAM) has made retraining for novel \nparts almost obsolete [2]. When prompted by a point \nin a query image or a bounding box, SAM outputs \nthree binary segmentation masks with distinct \nconfidence scores. \nContinued research on prompts has led to the \nadoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), which \nallow the use of text -based prompts to obtain \nsegmentation masks for specified objects [3 -5]. These \nnew Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) \ntechniques have yielded promising results for semantic \nsegmentation when tested on Common Objects in \nContext (COCO) -style databases [6]. However, \nextensive testing on images of industrial parts \nrandomly filling a bin still needs to be conducted. \nAnother kind of prompt in the form of a  \ncomputer-aided design (CAD) model was recently \nproposed [7]. It is especially useful for bin picking \napplications where CAD models of the parts filling the \nbins are usually available. A modified version of SAM \n(SAM3) [5] was trained on synthetic images cre ated \nwith the NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulator [8], which was \nused to build multi -object scenes utilizing CAD \nmodels from the ABC dataset of industrial parts [9]. It \nwas tested on two standard industrial benchmark \ndatasets, T -LESS and ITODD, which do not contain \nmany heavy clutter scenes typical of bin picking \napplications [10, 11]. \nCurrently, using point prompts in depth images \nremains the easiest way to obtain instance \nsegmentation masks. To maximize the efficiency of \nrobotic path planning, the vision system should \nprovide as many correct masks as possible, prompted \nfrom points scat tered across the entire image area. \nPrevious work demonstrated that SAM's performance \ndepends heavily on the type of parts in the bin [12]. For \nparts that are visually decomposable into \nsubcomponents (as in Fig. 1(a)), accurate masks from \nSAM’s multi-mask output were most often associated \nwith the medium (second -highest) confidence score. \nFor parts lacking obvious subcomponents (as in  \nFig. 1(b)), accurate masks typically correlated with the \nhighest confidence score. \n \n \n   \n(a)                         (b) \n \nFig. 1. Examples of two types of parts: a) visually \ndecomposable into subcomponents (drawn with different \ncolors); b) not readily decomposable into subcomponents. \n \n \nPreviously, the distinction between the two types \nof parts was based on subjective, unquantifiable \n\n\nXII International Conference on Sensors and Electronic Instrumentation Advances (SEIA' 2026)  \n30 September – 2 October 2026, Granada, Spain \n9 \nevaluation. In this study, a more objective metric is \nformulated. We systematically investigate how SAM's \nperformance shifts during the transition from one type \nof part to another by gradually altering the geometric \nfeatures of the part within a simulated bin. Our results \nsuggest that this transition occurs over a relatively \nnarrow range of geometric changes. Those changes \nresult in corresponding changes in the 8 -bit grayscale \nintensity of depth images. We found that two compact, \nadjacent regions on a depth  image whose intensities \ndiffer by less than 15 will most likely be segmented as \none region that stretches over both adjacent areas. \nThus, a part represented in a depth image as a patch \nwhere no compact subregions can be identified with \nintensity differences greater than ∆𝐼 =  15, should be \nclassified as non-decomposable part. \nPatches consisting of subregions with intensity \ndifferences much larger ( ∆𝐼 ≫ 15) correspond to \ndecomposable parts for which binary masks associated \nwith the medium score will be more accurate. Our \nresults reveal a specific range of differences in \ngeometric features, along with a corresponding range \nof intensities in a grayscale image , where no single \nstrategy (strongest vs. medium score mask) is \npreferred. In such mixed regions, to maximize the \nnumber of correctly segmented parts in a bin, masks \nassociated with both the strongest and medium \nconfidence scores may need to be analyzed. \nThus, prior knowledge of a part's dimensions and \nshape can be utilized to optimize the processing of \nSAM's output, thereby improving overall bin picking \nsystem performance. \n \n \n2. Simulation \n \nWe generated two types of grayscale images: one \nshowing a bin filled with screws, and the other \nshowing a mosaic of tiles with different intensities. \nThe first type yielded a realistic-looking pile of screws, \nbut to check SAM's performance, many images had to \nbe visually evaluated. The second type shows artificial \nscenes composed of geometric primitives for which a \nmetric gauging SAM's performance can be calculated \nby running autonomous image processing algorithms. \nAn 8-bit grayscale was used for all images, and binary \nmasks output by SAM associated with the largest \nconfidence score were analyzed. \n \n \n2.1. Distributed over entire volume.\nMicroscopic \nappearance\nThin lines Wide bands or broad lines\nLattice \norientation\nNo change in lattice orientation. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Report: U.S.-EU Virtual Workshop on Plastics Recycling Standards and \nDefinitions to Support Transatlantic Trade \n \nOctober 31, 2024 \nAuthors: Noah Last1 and Laure Baillargeon2 \n1 National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States Department of Commerce \n2 Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs, European Commission \nExecutive Summary \nThis report was written following a virtual government-to-stakeholder event hosted on October 1, 2024 \nby the U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC)’s Plastics Recycling Workstream of Working Group 1: \nTechnology Standards, with representatives from the United States (U.S.) Government and European \nUnion’s (EU’s) European Commission (EC). The event brought together stakeholders from the U.S. and EU \nwith expertise in the plastic industry, plastic recycling industry, plastic recycling standards, and \ntransatlantic trade to answer the question Which plastics recycling standards and definitions matter the \nmost for EU-U.S. trade? This report summarizes the feedback received from stakeholders and provides a \nhigh-level analysis of the priorities raised by EU and U.S. stakeholders. The consensus was that more \nmulti-stakeholder dialogues should be prioritized moving forward, such as workshops like this one, \nworking groups, and official collaborations like that between the Association of Plastics Recyclers (APR) \nin the U.S. and RecyClass in the EU. These engagements may focus on themes from this workshop, such \nas food-contact material for packaging, recycled content and recycled material quality, substances of \nconcern, and chain of custody. These engagements should consider including stakeholders from U.S. and \nEU governments; the private sector; and standards organizations like ANSI, ASTM, and CEN. A list of \nrelevant existing standards, standards under development, and needed standards was also developed. \nThe U.S.-EU TTC supported the organization of this event. The TTC aims to promote U.S. and EU \ncompetitiveness and prosperity and the spread of market-oriented values by increasing transatlantic \ntrade and investment in products and services of emerging technology, strengthening our technological \nand industrial leadership, boosting innovation, and protecting and promoting critical and emerging \ntechnologies and infrastructure. \n \n  \n\nBackground \nThe U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC) was established in June 2021 to support cooperation \nbetween the United States (U.S.) and the European Union (EU) on trade, technology, and economic \npolicy. It serves as a platform to address challenges related to global trade, emerging technologies, and \nsupply chain security while promoting shared values and strengthening transatlantic economic ties. The \nTTC established 10 Working Groups (WGs) chaired by relevant U.S. and European Commission (EC) \nagencies. WG 1 – Technology Standards was tasked with developing approaches for coordinating in \ncritical and emerging standards and is led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) \nand the International Trade Administration (ITA) for the U.S. and the Directorate General for Internal \nMarket, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (DG GROW) and the Directorate-General for \nCommunications Networks, Content and Technology (DG CONNECT) for the EU. WG 1 operates through \nseveral workstreams on different topics, including the Plastics Recycling Workstream. \nWG 1’s Plastic Recycling Workstream (referred to moving forward as the Workstream) is led by a \nrepresentative from NIST and DG GROW and was tasked with identifying 1) which standards exist to \nsupport the trade of recycled plastics and products containing recycled plastics between the U.S. and EU \nand 2) where there is a need to create new standards or better align existing standards. The Workstream \nhas been meeting since February 2024 with leadership from one U.S. and one EU standards \ndevelopment organization: ASTM International’s plastics committee (D20) and CEN-CENELEC’s plastic \nrecycling committee (CEN/TC 249), respectively. \nThe Workstream assessed the standards landscape in the U.S. and EU and concluded that there is a lack \nof alignment around standards and terminology, including around topics such as recyclates, resin types, \nand post-consumer waste. It also identified three focus areas for future work: \n1. Terminology, \n2. Design for recycling, and \n3. Upcoming EU circular economy regulations. \nThe Workstream realized that input from experts in plastic recycling standards, terminology, and \ntransatlantic trade would be necessary to create this alignment. Therefore, they organized a virtual U.S.-\nEU Workshop on Plastics Recycling Standards and Definitions on October 1, 2024. Industry, nonprofit, \nand government stakeholders from the U.S. and EU were invited to apply to participate, with applicants \nchosen based on their background first in plastic recycling trade and standards, then in plastics recycling \nbroadly.  \nWorkshop structure \nFifty-nine people (48 from the private sector, 11 from the U.S. and EU governments) were convened for \nthe 2.25-hour workshop. Sophie Mueller, Head of the Standardisation Unit for DG GROW (EU), and \nAnthony Quinn, Team Lead – Standards for the ITA (U.S.), gave opening remarks. Then representatives \nfrom ASTM International’s plastics committee (D20) and CEN-CENELEC’s plastic recycling committee \n(CEN/TC 249) introduced the motivation for the workshop and the workshop’s guiding question: Which \nplastics recycling standards and definitions matter the most for EU-U.S. trade? Private-sector participants \nentered breakout rooms of six people, with an even split between U.S. and EU representatives \n(government participants were excluded from the breakout rooms), to answer four questions: \n\n1. Which plastic recycling definitions have the most impact on trade between the U.S. and EU? Are \nthere potential issues? \n2. Which plastic recycling standards have the most impact on trade between the U.S. and EU? Are \nthere potential issues? \n3. Which sectors or sub-sectors are most relevant to this discussion? (e.g., plastic materials, \nproducts, packaging) \n4. What steps can be taken to create further alignment between the U.S. and EU? \nParticipants reconvened for a whole-group discussion on their responses. \nEase of trade \nParticipants rated the ease of trading recycled plastics between the EU and U.S., on average, at 5.6 on a \nscale of 10 (with 1 being impossible and 10 being very easy with no issues), and the ease of trading \nplastic products with recycled content at 6.1 (6.3 from the EU to the U.S. and 5.9 from the U.S. to the \nEU), suggesting that market operators encounter some issues when trading these items across the \nAtlantic. \nWhen asked what mattered the most to ensure easy EU-U.S. trade of plastic materials, products or \npackaging, a majority of participants mentioned the need for aligned definitions, rules, and regulations \n(9 votes), particularly regarding food contact material regulations (6 votes). Another cluster of ideas (3 \nvotes) was around the need for ensuring traceability for recycled materials, including in trade data. \nThemes \nSix themes emerged from the discussions on potential trade barriers due to differing regulations, \nstandards or definitions between the EU and the US, suggesting a need for alignment to facilitate trade. \nThis report only presents these themes and summarizes the workshop’s discussion surrounding them. \nWhile more context on the policy, research, standards, and market landscapes will be needed to \novercome the trade barriers discussed surrounding these themes, this context is outside the scope of \nthis report. \nRecycled content and chain of custody: Definitions (e.g., definitions of recyclate and post-consumer, \npost-industrial, and pre-consumer wastes), calculation methods (e.g., mass balance and its various \nattribution models), and traceability (i.e., chain of custody) of recycled content were among the most \nfrequently mentioned topics, with participants suggesting a strong perceived need for alignment. Some \nparticipants also mentioned the importance of ensuring a common language and traceability on recycled \ncontent in transatlantic trade, including through documentation or certificates.  \nFood packaging. A number of sectors were presented as relevant to the workshop’s theme: medical, \nautomotive, batteries, electrical and electronic equipment (EEE), building and construction, agriculture, \nand textiles. However, the most-discussed sector was packaging, especially food-grade packaging. The \nU.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) have different \nrequirements for food-grade packaging, leading to different specifications for selling this packaging in the \nU.S. and EU. Packaging producers in the workshop and their representatives expressed uncertainty \naround how to be compliant with FDA and EFSA rules, with a perceived need for further alignment of \nrules between the EU and the U.S.  \n\nRecycled material quality. Several participants suggested that better standards are needed to harmonize \nrecycled plastic and feedstock qualities. Bale specifications exist in the U.S. under the Recycled Materials \nAssociation (ReMa, formerly the Institute of Scrap Recycling Industries) and quality grades for sorted \nplastic wastes are being developed in CEN. A number of testing methods for recycled plastics also exist \nthrough ASTM and CEN, but better visibility around these standards and alignment may be needed to \novercome the challenges expressed during the workshop. Several stakeholders expressed a need to align \non recyclability standards. Design-for-recycling guidelines are being developed by CEN and APR, including \nfor plastic packaging and automotive plastics. \nSubstances of concern. Compliance with U.S. and EU regulations around substances of concern—e.g., \nPFAS, micro- and nanoplastics—was a challenge identified by workshop stakeholders. The EU’s \nRegistration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) regulation includes a list of \nthese materials for the EU. It was also suggested that companies importing products containing \nchemically recycled plastics (plastics recycled via chemical recycling) into the U.S. struggle to comply with \nthe EPA’s Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA); once the material stops being waste and starts being a \nfeedstock again, detailed compositional information on the feedstock is needed to ensure compliance \nwith the TSCA. \nMarket development. One goal of eliminating trade barriers for recycled plastics and the products \ncontaining them between the U.S. and EU is to support the development of the plastic recycling industry. \nWorkshop participants hoped that establishing common policy agendas between the nations could \nsupport the recycling economic model. Participants also asserted that one challenge to both market \ndevelopment and policy alignment between the nations is that the U.S. lacks national targets for \nrecycled plastics, while the EU does have specific targets. This lack of targets 1) may be inhibiting the \ndevelopment of the plastic recycling market, both upstream and downstream, and 2) stifles alignment \nopportunities between the U.S. and EU. Regarding the latter, national targets could create more points of \ncontact through which the nations can align.  \nCollaborations. Workshop participants suggested that creating better alignment between the U.S. and \nEU to support the trade of recycled plastics and products containing them will require collaborations \nbetween several groups. For example, an online repository listing U.S., EU, and other international \nstandards was proposed; this could be sponsored by U.S. and EU government agencies, or by CEN and \n

Inside the box are two A-B liquid solutions of different\ncomposition, separated by an internal partition that is diathermal and\nimpermeable to component B. The dividing wall has the property that its\ndisplacement (δV) and the flow of component A through it are coupled by the \nfollowing relation: δV = K δnA. \nWhat is the \nrelevant equilibrium extremum principle to apply for such a system? \nSince temperature and volume\nare both constant, the relevant \nequilibrium criterion is\nminimization of the Helmholtz \nfree energy: F (T, V, n). \na) Draw a picture of this system, indicating constant parameters.  \nb) What are the constraints on this system? \n2dn1 \nA = −dnA ; dV1 = dV2 \nxdV = KdnA ; ( dnB = 0)x \n\nc) Determine the equilibrium criterion for A in terms of its chemical potential\nand the pressure on each side of the box.\nConsider the total Helmholtz energy, and the energy on either side of the box.\n€ \ndF = −SdT − PdV +\ni\nC\n∑ µi\nj\nj\nP\n∑ dni\nj\n€ \ndF1 = −SdT − P1dV1 + µi\n1\ni\nC\n∑ dni\n1 = −P1dV1 + µA\n1 dnA\n1\ndF2 = −SdT − P2dV2 + µi\n2\ni\nC\n∑ dni\n2 = −P2dV2 + µA\n2 dnA\n2\nThe above made use of the fact that the dnB is equal to zero.  Now we substitute\nin our first two constraints immediately, followed by the third one:\n€ \ndFtot = dF1 + dF2 = −P1dV1 + P2dV1 + µA\n1 dnA\n1 − µA\n2 dnA\n1\n= −P1KdndnA\n1 A\n1 + P2KdnA\n1 + µA\n1 dnA\n1 − µA\n2 dnA\n1\n= dnA\n1 (K(P2 − P1) + µA\n1 − µA\n2 )\nFor a minimum, dF must be equal to zero, and this must be true independent of\nminor fluctuations in the composition of the two liquid mixtures.  Thus:\n€ \nµA\n1 − KP1 = µA\n2 dnA\n1 − KP2\nNote that if the partition did not have the magical quality of coupling volume and\ncomposition, the usual conditions for mechanical (equal pressures on either side)\nand chemical (equal chemical potentials on either side) equilibrium would hold."}]

[{"suffix": "", "text": "Solving the Ultraviolet Catastrophe\nIntroduction\nThis is a very interesting story which first time lead people to believe that energies (associated with waves) are\nquantized rather than continuous. It all started with Black Body radiation when scientist attempted to explain the curve\nof frequency (or wavelength) vs intensity. Max Planck was first to explain the behavior in 1900 , but no one accepted\nit; as there is no explanation for assuming energy corresponding to particular wavelength quantized rather than\ncontinuous. Instead Rayleigh-Jeans law which was proposed after Plack's law was accepted though it failed at low\nvalue of wavelength as it was based on the equipartition theorem of classical statistical mechanics. Planck's law was\naccepted only when Einstein applied quantization of energy to explain specific heat of materials at low temperature in\n1905. The term \"ultraviolet catastrophe\" was first used in 1911 by Paul Ehrenfest .\nBlack Body Radiation\nBlack Body\nA black body is an idealized object which absorbs and emits all frequencies. It refers to an object or system which\nabsorbs all radiation incident upon it and re-radiates energy which is characteristic of this radiating system only, not\ndependent upon the type of radiation which is incident upon it. The radiated energy can be considered to be produced\nby standing wave or resonant modes of the cavity which is radiating.\nExplaining Black Body Radiation\nClassical physics can be used to derive an equation which describes the intensity of blackbody radiation as a function of\nfrequency for a fixed temperature the result is known as the Rayleigh-Jeans law . Although the Rayleigh-Jeans law\nworks for higher wavelengths , it diverges as  become low in value; this divergence for high frequencies is called the\nultraviolet catastrophe.\nFigure  The ultraviolet catastrophe is the error at short wavelengths in the Rayleigh–Jeans law (depicted as \"classical\ntheory\" in the graph) for the energy emitted by an ideal black-body. The error, much more pronounced for short\nwavelengths, is the difference between the black curve (as classically predicted by the Rayleigh–Jeans law) and the blue\ncurve (the measured curve as predicted by Planck's law). from Wikipedia.\nThe radiated energy can be considered to be produced by standing wave or resonant modes of the cavity which is\nradiating.\nA single standing wave in stationary medium. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Impact ofSide-Chain Polarityand Symmetry on theStructureand\nPropertiesofAcyclic DioxythiophenePolymers\nJoshua M. Rinehart, Zhuang Xu, Ziming Wang, Anna M. Österholm, Lucas Q. Flagg, Lee J. Richter,\nChad R. Snyder, Ying Diao, and John R. Reynolds*\nCiteThis: Chem. Mater. 2025, 37, 4593−4606\n ReadOnline\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: Conformationallyflexibleside-chainsonconjugated\npolymers promote solution processability while significantly\nimpacting solution aggregation, solid-state ordering, and poly-\nmer−electrolyte interactions. These side-chains can strongly\ninfluence the repeat unit symmetry, polarity, steric bulk, and\nnoncovalent interactions that collectively dictate how polymer\nchains pack and assemble. Acyclic dioxythiophene polymers\n(PAcDOTs) are highly redox-active thiophene-based organic\nmixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs) where both the 3-\nand 4-positions of the thiophene ring are substituted by alkoxy\ngroups. In this study, we explore the solution and solid-state\nstructures of both symmetric (R1 = R2) and asymmetric (R1 ≠\nR2) PAcDOTs, where R1 and R2 are both either nonpolar or\namphiphilic, and we observe rich process-structure behavior. The combination of regio-symmetric and amphiphilic side-chains\nresults in a chiral, lyotropic phase in chloroform solutions that persists as a metastable state in thin films. Temperature-dependent\ngrazingincidenceX-rayscatteringandcross-polarizedopticalmicroscopyindicatethatPAcDOTswithregio-symmetriclinearside-\nchainscancrystallizeintohighlyorderedmorphologiesuponthermaltreatment.Finally,weshowthatside-chainpolarity,symmetry,\nand thermal annealing affect the electrochemical doping and dedoping processes.\n■INTRODUCTION\nPolythiophene and its derivatives have become foundational\nstructures in the field of conjugated polymers with the\nthiophene unit serving as a versatile building block for the\ndesign of new polymers with diverse structures and proper-\nties.1−3 Among these, poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) and\npoly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) have stood out\noverdecadesowingtotheirwidespreadavailabilityandproven\neffectiveness in various electronic and photovoltaic applica-\ntions. For example, P3HT and other poly(3-alkylthiophenes)\n(P3ATs)exhibitrespectableholemobility,makingthemprime\nmaterials for organic field effect transistors (OFETs) and\norganic photovoltaics.4−6 However, to optimize hole mobility,\nP3ATs must be made highly regioregular (RR), which\ncomplicatespolymersynthesisbyrequiringspecificconditions\nand catalysts that are not suitable for all thiophene\nderivatives.7,8\nThe material properties of P3HT are strongly correlated to\nthe degree of regioregularity, and consequently, sample-to-\nsample variations yield drastically different processing behav-\niors and material properties, ultimately yielding devices with\nprocessing-dependent properties.9−13 Head-to-tail regioregu-\nlarity produces P3ATs with the most planar backbones and\nlowest bandgaps compared to regiorandom or head-to-head\nregiochemistry.14 For large-scale synthesis and potential\ncommercialization, it is desirable to have polymers whose\nstructureandsubsequentpropertiesremainconsistentwithout\nthe need for highly controlled synthetic conditions to achieve\nhigh levels of regioregularity. This can be accomplished by\ndesigningmonomersandrepeatunitswithinherentsymmetry\nto ensure the formation of regio-symmetric repeat units.\nDesigning monomers with a C2 symmetry axis yields\nsymmetric repeat units, enabling simpler polymerization\nconditions for generating regio-symmetric polymers. Figure 1\nillustrates how symmetric monomers lead to regio-symmetric\nrepeat units because all coupling modes between thiophene\nunits�2,2′, 2,5′, 5,2′, and 5,5′�are equivalent. In contrast,\nasymmetric side-chain substitution, such as in P3ATs,\nintroduces chemically distinct regiochemical linkages (e.g.,\n2,2′ vs 2,5′ linkages), thereby disrupting regio-symmetry.15\nReceived: December 12, 2024\nRevised: June 3, 2025\nAccepted: June 4, 2025\nPublished: June 20, 2025\nArticlepubs.acs.org/cm\n© 2025 The Authors. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Predicting Properties from Near-Infrared Spectra with Machine\nLearning for Improved Polyolefin Differentiation\nShuaijun Li, Robert J. S. Ivancic, Bradley P. Sutliff, Derek Huang, Enrique Blázquez-Blázquez,\nTyler B. Martin, Kalman B. Migler, Debra J. Audus,* and Sara V. Orski*\nCite This: ACS Polym. Au 2026, 6, 246−255\n Read Online\nACCESS\n Metrics & More\n Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information\nABSTRACT: As the scale and variety of plastics produced continue to grow,\nplastics recycling will require innovative solutions. The industrial state-of-the-art\nsorting technology, near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, as currently used, cannot\neffectively differentiate polyolefins, the single largest class of polymers by volume.\nChemical similarity combined with architectural diversity in polyolefins stymies\nsubclass delineation, such as differentiating low-density polyethylene from high-\ndensity polyethylene, due to their spectral similarity and chemical overlap. To\naddress this challenge, we use machine learning (ML) to directly predict density,\ncrystallinity, and short-chain branching from NIR spectra, enabling property-based\nsorting for more effective recycling. After testing a variety of ML models, we find that partial least squares regression provides high\nprediction accuracy with model simplicity. Since the resulting model leverages the correlated intensities, we develop a method to\nenhance interpretability by identifying the most important wavenumbers for property prediction, which we then relate to known\npolyolefin CH3 NIR vibrational absorption bands. This approach provides a linkage between ML model predictions and the\nunderlying polyolefin chemistry and confirms that our models effectively capture spectrum−structure−property relationships in\npolyolefins, reinforcing the fundamental role of polymer chain structure in determining properties. These findings significantly\ncontribute to the understanding of polyolefin differentiation using NIR spectroscopy, which could inform future advancements in\nproperty-based sorting strategies for plastic recycling efficiency.\nKEYWORDS: machinelearning,near-infraredspectroscopy,propertyprediction,polyolefinsorting,plasticrecycling,modelinterpretability\n1. INTRODUCTION\nPolyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP) represent 42% of\nthe volume of all US plastics produced1 with wide use in\nautomotive parts, furniture, housewares, and packaging, and\nspecialty material applications, such as biomedical implants.2\nThe versatility of polyolefins arise from their wide range of\nmaterial properties, driven by interdependent structural\nparameters such as monomer and comonomer content,\nbranching content and type, molecular distributions (e.g.,\nbranching distributions, molecular mass distributions), and\nformulations (e.g., blends).3 Furthermore, polyolefin chain\nconformations are influenced by structural properties, material\nprocessing, and process history, which impact bulk properties\nsuch as density and crystallinity. Density is often used to grade\npolyolefins, and crystallinity contributes to the rigid, impact\nresistance (with high crystallinity) or the flexible character\n(more amorphous) of each semicrystalline polyolefin material.\nSeveral reviews in the literature have described the breadth of\ncommercial polyolefin grades available.4−7\nDespite their ubiquitous use, polyolefin recycling remains\nchallenging.8,9 TheAmericanSociety forTestingand Materials\n(ASTM) resin identification codes (RIC)10 only broadly\ncategorize polyolefins, which leads to heterogeneous bales. For\ninstance, Smith et al. analyzed 23 high-density polyethylene\n(HDPE) resins with RIC #2, revealing 56 characteristics that\nvaried significantly across samples when examined through\nFourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, differential\nscanning calorimetry (DSC), thermogravimetric analysis,\nrheology, color analysis, and mechanical testing.11 This high\nlevel of heterogeneity clearly illustrates why current sorting\npractices struggle to produce consistent, high-quality recycled\nstreams. Achieving maximum recycling and reprocessing rates\nrequires significant improvements in sorting accuracy and\nefficiency to minimize feedstock heterogeneity and incentivize\ngreater postconsumer resin incorporation. Therefore, there is a\ncritical need to develop more precise methods for identifying\nand sorting polyolefins based on their material properties.\nMachine learning (ML) has been increasingly applied to\npolymer property prediction and recycling, with recent reviews\noutlining key challenges and opportunities.12,13 Researchers\nhave explored various spectroscopy methods combined with\nReceived: September 16, 2025\nRevised: December 12, 2025\nAccepted: December 15, 2025\nPublished: January 29, 2026\nArticlepubs.acs.org/polymerau\n© 2026 The Authors. Published by\nAmerican Chemical Society\n246\nhttps://doi.org/10.1021/acspolymersau.5c00131\nACS Polym. Au 2026, 6, 246−255\nThis article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0\nDownloaded from pubs.​acs.​org/​apaccd/​article-pdf/​6/​1/​246/​64248227/​lg5c00131.​pdf by NATL INST OF STANDARDS & TECHNOLOGY user on 04 September 2026\n\n\nML, such as mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy, Raman\nspectroscopy, and hyperspectral imaging, among others14−17\nto predict polymer properties, to evaluate postconsumer\nrecyclate viability, and to characterize biomass and waste\nmaterial.11,18,19 For example, Tao presented a fast and effective\nmethod for characterizing biomass and waste using attenuated\ntotal reflectance (ATR) − FTIR spectroscopy and ML\nmodels,19 while Stavinski et al.14 and Zinchik et al.20 explored\nthe application of MIR spectroscopy combined with ML to\nimprove classification of postconsumer plastic waste. While\nthese spectroscopic techniques are attractive because they can\noffer richer chemical information and potentially higher\nresolution for material identification, they pose significant\nchallenges for industry applications due to low acquisition\nspeeds, background fluorescence, or high cost.15\nOne potential method for improving sorting is to leverage\nNIR spectroscopy. NIR spectroscopy has emerged as the\nindustrial state-of-the-art technique for medium to large\nvolume plastic waste sorting due to its rapid, nondestructive,\nand efficient identification capabilities between different\nfamilies of polymers such as polyethylene terephthalate,\nHDPE, and others categorized by the RIC.21,22 By more\naccurately identifying and separating these polymer types,\nrecyclers can streamline processing, reduce contamination, and\nultimately produce higher-quality recyclate suitable for reuse.\nHowever, distinguishing different members of the polyolefin\nfamily effectively using NIR alone remains challenging due to\noverlapping spectral features arising from their chemically\nsimilar structures.23 Researchers have explored various\nmethods to improve NIR sorting, addressing these challenges\nand enhancing its accuracy for polyolefin separation. Sato et al.\ninvestigated NIR spectra of PE samples, including HDPE, low-\ndensity polyethylene (LDPE), and linear low-density poly-\nethylene (LLDPE) to predict their physical properties such as\ndensity, crystallinity, and melting points.24 They used principal\ncomponent analysis (PCA)25 for differentiating PE subclasses\nand partial least squares regression (PLSR)26 to build\ncalibration models predicting the physical properties. They\nfound that the first three principal components (PCs)\naccounted for more than 97% of the variance in NIR\nintensities and that the three types of PEs can be classified\ninto three clusters considering the first and third PCs. They\nalso achieved correlation coefficients for predicting these three\nproperties and found that the spectral resolution is not critical\nin predicting accuracy. Bredacs et al. explored the use of\nvarious infrared (IR) spectroscopic techniques including ATR-\nFTIR, NIR, and dual-comb spectroscopy to predict density\nand melt flow rate of PE materials, with the goal of improving\nmechanical recycling of postconsumer PE products.27 Their\nresults showed that NIR could broadly classify PE materials by\ndensity. However, these studies were limited to PE samples,\nrelied on conventional chemometric methods and did not\nexploremodelinterpretation,leavingkeyspectralcontributions\nto property prediction largely unexplored. Furthermore, a\ncritical scientific gap remains as it is not only the predictions\nthat are required but also an understanding of which spectral\nregionsdrive those predictions. This is essential for insight and\ntrust in model generalization.\nIn our previous work, we investigated the correlation\nbetween NIR spectra and bulk properties of polyolefins via\ndimensionality reduction techniques.28 First, functional PCA29\nwas applied to NIR spectra of polyolefins, including PP, and\nseparation among various PE subclasses was successfully\nobserved. Then, to further explore the relationship between\nthe extracted spectral features and polymer properties, we\nidentified strong correlations between NIR spectral data of PE\nwith density, crystallinity, and short-chain branching (SCB).\nOur findings underscored the potential for NIR spectroscopy-\nbased sorting of polyolefins by material properties. However,\nthis study did not consider blends of polyolefins, nor did it\nmake quantitative property predictions, which is essential for\nfine-grained sortation. More recently, we further expanded the\nuse of ML based pipelines to optimize NIR data preprocessing\nand classification, achieving over 95% accuracy in differ-\nentiating polyolefins when considering existing class distinc-\ntions (HDPE,LDPE, LLDPE, PP).30 However, these advances\nprimarily address class distinctions but do not capture the\ncontinuous nature of polymer properties that influence\nrecyclability, highlighting the need for further development\ntoward high-value, property-based sorting.\nTo improve NIR-based polyolefin differentiation for refined\nsorting, in this work, we employed ML techniques to predict\nthe material properties of both nonblended and blended\npolyolefins, including density, crystallinity, and SCB from NIR\nspectra. These properties are critical for effective sorting of\npolyolefin waste as they directly influence the polymer’s\nmechanical and thermal behavior, which are essential for\ndetermining its suitability for various recycling processes and\nultimate end use. As detailed in the Methods section, we have\ncollected various types of polyolefins, including HDPE, LDPE,\nLLDPE, and PP. Additionally, we considered blends of HDPE\nand PP, as well as blends of HDPE and LDPE. After applying\nspectral preprocessing, we trained and tested a variety of\nsupervised ML models and found PLSR provides the simplest\nmodel with low prediction error. To interpret the ML\npredictions, we developed a method that identifies a small\nnumber of important wavenumbers contributing to each\npredictedpropertyandfoundthatkeyspectralregionsstrongly\ncorrelated with known polyolefin absorption bands associated\nwith polymer branching and chain-end structures. These\nspectra-chemistry linkages not only validated the robustness of\nour MLapproachbut also improvedour understandingof how\npolymer molecular structures influence macroscopic proper-\nties. Therefore, our findings lay the foundation for more\neffective recycling practices via property-based sorting, a\ncritical step toward achieving a circular plastics economy.\n2. METHODS\n2.1. Materials\nWe collected a total of 39 samples from diverse sources* including 10\ncommercial samples, 9 from the Hawaii Pacific University Polymer\nKit 1.0, and 4 PE Standard Reference Materials from the National\nInstitute of Standards and Technology (NIST): SRM 1473, 1474,\n1475, and 1476. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Controlling the Reaction Pathway to Tune Packaging \nEpoxy Properties  \nPolette Centellas  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \npolette.centellas@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0003-3248-3409 \nRan Tao  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nran.tao@nist.gov              \nORCID: 0000-0002-5208-7895 \nAndrew Korovich \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nandrew.korovich@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0003-3736-1523 \nAlexander K. Landauer  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nalexander.landauer@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0003-2863-039X \n \nAmanda Forster \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \namanda.forster@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0001-7397-4429 \nSiena Iavarone-Garza \nUniversity of Maryland \nCollege Park, MD, USA \nsiena.iavarone@gmail.com  \nDante Ribeiro \nPennsylvania State University \nUniversity Park, PA, USA \ndanterib01@gmail.com   \nHuong Giang Nguyen  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nhuong.nguyen@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0002-1052-7565 \n \n \nAbstract— Semiconductor packaging demands materials with \nsimultaneously tuned properties. We demonstrate that the \nthermoset processing pathway influences functional properties, \nincluding moisture, dielectric, and thermomechanical responses. \nUsing a model  epoxy system, our findings establish pathway \ncontrol as a lever to engineer thermoset performance for reliable \nsemiconductor packaging. \nKeywords—epoxy thermoset, thermal curing, moisture uptake, \ndielectric response, coefficient of thermal expansion \nI. INTRODUCTION \nThermoset polymers, such as epoxies,  are indispensable in \nsemiconductor packaging, serving as underfills, molding \ncompounds, dielectric layers, and adhesives. As packages \nbecome more complex (ex.  finer pitches, higher I/O counts, \nthinner components), these polymers are increasingly required \nto execute multiple functions concurrently. Beyond basic \nencapsulation and adhesion, they must provide environmental \nprotection from moisture and ionic contamination, minimize \nelectrical signal noise , and redistribute th ermomechanical \nstresses generated by the coefficient-of-thermal-expansion \nmismatch across dissimilar materials in the package stack -up \n[1, 2, 3]. Key material attributes, including moisture sorption, \ndielectric properties , and thermal expansion, must be \ndeliberately tuned to meet both process and lifetime \nrequirements. \nA central challenge is that these properties are not controlled \nsolely by formulation; they also depend strongly on how the \nnetwork is formed during curing. Thermoset epoxies are \ntypically processed from low -viscosity monomers into \ncrosslinked solids via thermally activated reactions. However, \nthe thermal history can steer the reaction through different \npathways, producing networks that are chemically similar yet  \nstructurally or topologically distinct. For example, curing above \nversus below the evolving glass transition temperature (Tg) can \nshift the system from a reaction-controlled regime to a diffusion-\nlimited regime as vitrification occurs, altering the effective \ndegree of conversion, crosslink density distribution, and degree \nof network heterogeneity  [4, 5] . These structural differences \ninfluence free volume, segmental mobility, and the population \nof polar groups , features that directly affect the kinetics and \nthermodynamics of moisture uptake, dielectric behavior, and \nthermomechanical performance under service -relevant \nhygrothermal conditions . It is important to realize that  \ncontrolling the reaction pathway provides a processing -based \nlever to tune epoxy performance without necessarily changing \nchemistry, enabling optimization strategies that are compatible \nwith manufacturing constraints. \nIn this work, we demonstrate and quantify how reaction \npathway control can be used to tailor packaging -relevant \nproperties. Using a model epoxy thermoset, we systematically \ninvestigate three distinct reaction pathways designed to span \ncuring scenarios rele vant to packaging process windows \n(including conditions that promote or avoid vitrification during \ncure). We then connect the pathway-dependent network \nformation to the (i) moisture sorption/desorption behavior, (ii) \ndielectric constant and loss , and (ii i) coefficient of thermal \nexpansion, establishing a structure –processing–property \nframework that helps explain why nominally similar cures can \nyield meaningfully different reliability-critical responses. This \napproach provides practical guidance for selecting cure \nschedules that balance moisture resistance, dielectric properties, \nand mechanical integrity for advanced semiconductor packaging \napplications. \nJan Obrzut  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \n jan.obrzut@nist.gov          \nORCID:  0000-0001-6667-9712 \nStian Romberg  \nUniversity of Tennessee \nKnoxville, TN, USA \n sromberg@utk.edu         \nORCID: 0000-0003-1026-2023 \nChristopher Soles  \nNational Intitute of Standards \nand Technology \nGaithersburg, MD, USA \nchristopher.soles@nist.gov \nORCID: 0000-0002-1963-6039 \n \nOfficial contribution of the National Institute of Standards and Technology; \nnot subject to copyright in the United States.  \nNational Institute of Standards and Technology Award # 70NANB24H283.  \n1680\n2026 IEEE 76th Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC)\nU.S. Government work not protected by U.S. copyright\nDOI 10.1109/ECTC51846.2026.00275\n2026 IEEE 76th Electronic Components and Technology Conference (ECTC) | USGov | DOI: 10.1109/ECTC51846.2026.00275\nAuthorized licensed use limited to: NIST Research Library & Museum. Downloaded on July 27,2026 at 14:46:47 UTC from IEEE Xplore.  Restrictions apply. \n\nII. EXPERIMENTAL \nA. Model Thermoset \nWe study a model thermoset system of bisphenol F \ndiglycidyl ether (DGEBF) epoxy resin and diethyl toluene \ndiamine (DETDA) curing agent. We select this chemistry for its \nindustrial relevance as DGEBF epoxy is a foundational \ncomponent of commercial underfill f ormulations [1, 2]. The \nresin components are individually degassed in a planetary mixer \nat a pressure of 100 mbar running at 2500 rpm for 5 min.  The \ncomponents are then combined at a stoichiometric ratio \n(2 equivalents DGEBF: 1 equivalent DETDA) and returned to \nthe mixer for a second degassing and mixing step under identical \nconditions. The resin is used for testing within a few days of \nmixing. When not in use, it is stored in a freezer maintained at \nca. 3 ° C to minimize background curing.       \nB. Reaction Pathways \nThe model thermoset is cured using three different reaction \npathways, i.e., cure schedules. Schedule A involves curing the \nmaterial for 8 h at 120 ° C. By maintaining the cure temperature \nbelow the glass transition temperature of the fully cured \nthermoset (Tg ~ 140 ° C [6, 7]), we expect the material to slowly \ntransition from its liquid state to a rubbery state to a glassy state \n(i.e., vitrify), resulting in a highly crosslinked network. \nSchedule B involves isothermal curing for 2 h at 150 ° C. Curing \nat a temperature above the  ultimate Tg will more quickly \ntransition the material from its liquid state to a rubbery state, \nwithout vitrifying [4]. Schedule C involves curing the material \nfor 1 h at 80 ° C followed by 2.5 h at 150 ° C. Multistep curing \nprofiles that combine low - and high -temperature steps are \ncommonly employed in composites manufacturing to minimize \nresidual stresses [5]. All samples are cured in a convection oven \nwith heating ramp rates of 5 ° C min-1 and allowed to slowly cool \nto room temperature before being removed.  \nIII. MATERIAL CHARACTERIZATION \nA. Conversion Prediction \nWe develop a cure kinetics model to predict the evolution of \nthe degree of conversion during thermal curing. First, we \nperform differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) dynamic \nheating scans on the uncured material from 40 ° C to 315 ° C at \nconstant heating rates of (1, 3, 5, 10, 20) ° C min-1. The standard \nuncertainties for temperature and heat flow are approximately \n± 1 % and ± 3 %, respectively. Then, we simultaneously fit the \nmeasured heat flow curves with a two-step reaction model using \na commercial kinetic analysis software [8, 9, 10]. The validity \nof the two-step model is supported by literature, which describes \nthe crosslinking of DGEBF with DETDA to first involve \nreaction with a primary amine to form a secondary amine, \nfollowed by a second reaction with the newly formed secondary \namine [11]. The cure kinetics model is then used to predict the \ndegree of conversion profile for each of the three reaction \npathways.   \nB. Moisture Transport Properties \nThe moisture transport properties of the cured samples are \nmeasured using an isothermal vapor sorption analyzer. Free -\nstanding films with an initial mass of ca. 13 mg and a thickness \nof ca. 120 µm are prepared for the experiments by sandwiching \na small amount of resin between two glass plates lined with \nfluoroethylene-propylene (FEP) adhesive to prevent the epoxy \nfrom bonding to the substrates. Glass coverslips are placed \naround the deposited resin (in between the glass plates) to \ncontrol the cured film thickness.  \nThe cured films are conditioned for 240 min at 110 ° C under \npure nitrogen flow, i.e., 0 % relative humidity (RH). The sample \nenvironment is then set to run at (40, 60, 80, and 0) % RH in a \nstepwise manner at an isothermal temperature of 30 ° C. The \nduration of each stage is 1200 min. Dry nitrogen is continuously \nmixed with a humid nitrogen flow to achieve the desired % RH. \nThe instrument has a ± 0.1 µg mass resolution and ± 1 % RH \ncontrol standard uncertainty. The mass change (M) is calculated \nrelative to the dry mass measured at the end of the conditioning \nstage (mdry) such that M(t) = [m(t) – mdry]\t/\tmdry. \nThe four sorption/desorption stages are simultaneously fit \nwith Fick’s one -dimensional diffusion model to extract the \noverall moisture diffusivity ( D) and the saturated moisture \ncontent (Msat) at each % RH stage [12], \n𝑀(𝑡) = 𝑀! + (𝑀\"#$ − 𝑀!) [{"suffix": "", "text": "Real and Reciprocal Crystal Lattices\nCrystal is a three dimensional periodic array of atoms. Crystal lattice is the geometrical pattern of the crystal, where all\nthe atom sites are represented by the geometrical points. There are two classes of crystal lattices. When all of the lattice\npoints are equivalent, it is called Bravais lattice. Otherwise, it is called non-Bravais lattice. The non-Bravais lattice may\nbe regarded as a combination of two or more interpenetrating Bravais lattices with fixed orientations relative to each\nother.\nThe crystal lattice can also be defined by three fundamental translation vectors: , , . When, \n, (n1, n2, n3 are arbitrary integers.), The whole crystal looks the same in every respect when viewed from  and .\nAdditionally, if any two points have the relation of  and , when a proper set of , ,  is chosen, , ,  are said\nto be the primitive vector, and they can form the primitive unit cell.\nPrimitive cell has the smallest volume. The volume of the nonprimitive unit cell is an integral multiple of the primitive\nunit cell. The choice of primitive unit cell is not unique, and there are many ways of forming a primitive unit cell. One\nway of choosing a unit cell is shown in Figure . The procedure is:\n1. draw lines to connect a given lattice points to all nearby lattice points;\n2. at the midpoint and normal to these lines, draw new lines or planes.\nThe smallest volume enclosed in this way is a primitive unit cell, and also called the Wigner-Seitz primitive cell.\nFigure  Procedure to create a Wigner-Seitz primitive cell.\n2. Fundamental types of crystal lattices\nBecause of the translational symmetry of the crystal lattice, the number of the types of the Bravais lattices can be\nreduced to 14, which can be further grouped into 7 crystal system: triclinic, monoclinic, orthorhombic, tetragonal, cubic,\nhexagonal, and the trigonal (rhombohedral). Figure  shows all of the Bravais lattice types.\nFigure  14 Bravais lattices and 7 crystal systems\nThese 14 lattice types can cover all possible Bravais lattices. All other lattices shape must be identical to one of the\nlattice types listed in Figure . For example, a base centered tetragonal is identical to a simple tetragonal cell by\nchoosing a proper unit cell. As shown in Figure , connect two base centered tetragonal lattices, and choose the shaded\narea as the new unit cell. It is found that the base centered tetragonal cell is identical to the simple tetragonal cell. It is\nmathematically proved that he lattice types listed in Figure  is a complete lattice type.\n9/30/26, 2:07 PM Real and Reciprocal Crystal Lattices - Engineering LibreTexts\nhttps://eng.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Materials_Science/Supplemental_Modules_(Materials_Science)/Electronic_Properties/Real_and_Reciproc… 1/4\n\nFigure :  Identify a base-centered tetragonal lattices to a simple tetragonal lattice. The blue area\nare the bases of the simple tetragonal lattice cell.\n3. Fundamental Types of Symmetry Properties\nCrystal lattices are periodic structures, they have one or more types of symmetry properties, such as inversion,\nreflection, rotation. Table  summarized the characteristic symmetry elements of the 7 crystal system.\nInversion: If the cell remains the same after the mathematical transformation performance of  and – , it has inversion\nsymmetry. All Bravais lattices have inversion symmetry.\nReflection: If the cell remains the same after a mirror reflection is performed on it, it has reflection symmetry.\nRotation axis: If the cell remains the same after it rotates around an axis with some angle, it has the rotation symmetry,\nand the axis is call n-fold, when the angle of rotation is .\nTable : Characteristic symmetry elements of the 7 crystal system\nCrystal system Reflection plane Rotation axis\nTriclinic None None\nMonoclinic 1 1 2-fold\nOrthorhombic None 3 2-fold\nTetragonal None 1 4-fold\nCubic 9 4 3-fold\nTrigonal None 1 3-fold\nHexagonal None 1 3-fold\nA non-Bravais lattice is the lattice with each site associated with a cluster of atoms called basis. Therefore the\ndescription of symmetry of a non-Bravais lattice includes the symmetry of the basis and the symmetry of the Bravais\nlattice on which this basis is imposed. The symmetry of the basis is called point-group symmetry. Because of the\nrequirements of translational symmetry for the lattice as a whole, there are totally 32 types of the point group\nsymmetry.\nAdditionally, the rotation symmetry of the basis is essentially the same as the rotation symmetry of the Bravais lattice,\nwhich has 14 types. Combination the rotation symmetry of the point groups with the translational symmetry, 72 space\ngroups are generated. As for the space groups involve symmetry elements such as screw axes, glide planes, etc., they\ncan not be the simple sum of point group and space group. With the consideration of this, 230 space groups are\nobtained.\n4. The workflow begins with controlled thawing of a \ncryopreserved NISTCHO vial (RM 8675), followed by post -thaw recovery and automated measurement of \nviable cell density and viability. Cells are expanded through a seed train and used to inoculate a single -use \nstirred-tank bioreactor at an initial viable cell density of approximately 0.5 × 106 1/mL. \nThe fed -batch culture is operated for 14 days at 37 °C with dissolved oxygen controlled at 40 %, pH \nmaintained between 6.9 and 7.1, and agitation initiated at 160 rpm. A 2:1 mixture of Advanced CHO Feed 1 \nand Cellvento 4Feed COMP is added on Days 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13. Glucose is supplemented to a target \nconcentration of 8 g/L, and antifoam is added according to a culture-age-dependent schedule. The culture is \nsampled throughout the run for cell concentration, viabilit y, cell diameter, pH, glucose, and other process \nmeasurements as applicable. \nThe bioreactor procedure was developed using the Eppendorf BioBLU 3c single-use bioreactor configuration \ndescribed in this publication. [{"suffix": "", "text": "Vol.:(0123456789)\nChromatographia (2025) 88:801–805 \nhttps://doi.org/10.1007/s10337-025-04438-z\nBRIEF REPORT\nAbsolute Molar Mass Determination in Mixed Solvents. 3. Accuracy \nof ∂n/∂c Values Obtained by Assuming 100% SEC Mass Recovery\nAndré M. Striegel1\nReceived: 24 July 2025 / Revised: 27 August 2025 / Accepted: 3 September 2025 / Published online: 9 September 2025 \nThis is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2025\nAbstract\nAccurate values of the specific refractive index increment (∂n/∂c) are essential to the accurate determination of molar mass \naverages, distributions, and related macromolecular parameters by, among others, size-based separations with online static \nlight scattering and differential refractive index (DRI) detection. Examined here is the 100% mass recovery method of cal-\nculating the ∂n/∂c of dilute macromolecular solutions, when employing mixed solvents in a size-based separation (e.g., size-\nexclusion chromatography or SEC) with DRI detection. This method has been used successfully in the past for determining \nthe ∂n/∂c of various polyelectrolytes. It is quicker, generally simpler, and less sample-intensive than its offline, batch-mode \nDRI counterpart. Whether or not the 100% mass recovery method allows for the necessary solvent equilibration within the \nimmediate vicinity of the polymer chain during a chromatographic run, so as to allow for accurate determination of ∂n /∂c \nin SEC/DRI experiments, is evaluated here. This is done using a set of three narrow-dispersity linear polystyrene standards \ncovering a 40-fold range in molar mass, dissolved in a 25:75 mix of tetrahydrofuran and N ,N-dimethyl formamide. Results \nare compared to those previously obtained by the batch-mode method and from calculations involving the accurately known \nmolar masses of the polymers and refractive indices of the solvents. The 100% mass recovery method of obtaining ∂n /∂c \nvalues, while of great help for determining the ∂n/∂c of, e.g., polyelectrolytes, does not appear able to overcome the obstacle \nof preferential solvation when analyzing macromolecules in a mix of non-isorefractive solvents with dissimilar second virial \ncoefficients.\nKeywords Size-exclusion chromatography · Specific refractive index increment · 100% mass recovery method · Absolute \nmolar mass · Preferential solvation\nIntroduction\nAccurate determination of macromolecular molar mass (M) \naverages and distributions is crucial to evaluating novel syn-\nthetic procedures, as well as to optimizing the processing \nand end-use properties of materials [1]. Most M determina-\ntions are performed using size-based separation methods, \nmost commonly size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) but \nalso hydrodynamic chromatography (HDC) and flow field-\nflow fractionation (flow FFF) techniques [2–4]. In combina-\ntion with these, the most accurate means of determining M \nis generally through the use of online static light scattering \ndetection, most commonly multi-angle static light scatter -\ning (MALS) in combination with concentration-sensitive \ndetection such as differential refractometry (DRI) [1 , 5]. A \ncrucial value in static light scattering and DRI calculations \nis the specific refractive index increment (∂n/∂c) of the ana-\nlyte solution. This value corresponds to the change in the \nrefractive index of a dilute analyte solution as a function \nof analyte concentration, at a given solvent, temperature, \nand wavelength of incident light. The accuracy with which \nthe ∂n/∂c is known directly translates into the accuracy of \ncalculated M and related values. As such, an error of E % in \n∂n/∂c will translate into an error of E  % in weight-average \nmolar mass (M w), when the latter is determined by SEC/\nDisclaimer Commercial products are identified to specify the \nexperimental procedure adequately. Such identification does not \nimply endorsement or recommendation by the National Institute \nof Standards and Technology, nor does it imply that the materials \nidentified are necessarily the best available for the purpose.\n * André M. Striegel \n andre.striegel@nist.gov\n1 Chemical Sciences Division, National Institute of Standards \nand Technology (NIST), 100 Bureau Drive, MS 8390, \nGaithersburg, MD 20899-8390, USA\n\n802 A. M. Striegel \nMALS/DRI. Additionally, most size-based experiments are \nconducted in neat solvents or in solvents with only a mod-\nest amount of additive (e.g., salts). While the use of mixed \nsolvents is common in interaction polymer chromatography \nmethods (e.g., gradient polymer elution chromatography \n[6]), which have traditionally employed evaporative mass \ndetectors, this is not the case in size-based methods [7]. The \nlatter is due to the widespread use of differential detectors \nin size-based methods and to the propensity for preferential \nsolvation of macromolecules in mixed solvents. Preferential \nsolvation refers to the greater “affinity” of the macromol-\necule toward one solvent over the other in a mix, as initially \ndemonstrated by the classic work of H. Kneebone Tompkins \nin 1896 [8]. When employing differential detection methods \nsuch as MALS or DRI, preferential solvation translates into \nthe solvent baseline no longer accurately representing the \nsolvent contribution to the peak height of chromatographic \n(or fractographic, henceforth implied) slices.\nRecent work toward the determination of accurate M \naverages and distributions by SEC/MALS/DRI in mixed sol-\nvents has shown that it is possible to obtain accurate values \nunder certain conditions. These conditions include the use \nof an isorefractive solvent pair, and also, the use of a near-\nisovirial solvent pair, i.e., when using solvents which, at the \nexperimental conditions, possess either identical refractive \nindices and/or which allow for dilute polymer solutions with \nsimilar second virial coefficients. (The second virial coef-\nficient serves to provide a quantitative measure of analyte \nsolvation at a particular set of solvent/temperature condi-\ntions). Details, requirements, and caveats in each case can \nbe found in references [ 9, 10]. Also examined in reference \n[10] was the amount of preferential solvation undergone by \npolystyrene (PS) in a 25:75 mix of tetrahydrofuran (THF) \nand N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF), two solvents which \nare neither isorefractive nor near-isovirial. Employing poly-\nstyrene standards with accurately determined M  averages \nand distributions and ∂n/∂c values obtained by offline, batch-\nmode DRI (otherwise considered a benchmark method of \ndetermining ∂n /∂c), it was shown that these ∂n /∂c values \nwere biased due to preferential solvation. Moreover, it was \nshown that in the 25:75 THF:DMF mix, the solvent ratio in \nthe immediate vicinity of the macromolecules examined was \nactually 75:25 THF:DMF, due to the greater affinity of PS \ntoward THF over DMF. This resulted in errors in calculated \nM, of up to 1 ×  105 g  mol−1 for PS with M = 8 ×  105 g  mol−1.\nAnother method for determining the ∂ n/∂c of a dilute \nmacromolecular solution at a particular set of experimental \nconditions (wavelength, temperature, and solvent composi-\ntion) is to assume that the concentration of the solution has \nbeen determined accurately and that 100% of the injected \npolymer has eluted from the SEC column (or appropriate \nseparation device) and is contained within the integration \nlimits and baseline of the DRI peak (it is also assumed that \nthe calibration constant of the DRI detector is accurately \nknown). This is generally referred to as the “100% mass \nrecovery method” of determining ∂n/∂c, or sometimes as the \n“∂n/∂c from peak method” [11] and has been employed to \ndetermine this parameter for dilute polyelectrolyte solutions. \nWhen studying polyelectrolytes, it is often assumed that the \nchromatographic column acts as a type of dialysis chamber \nso that, over the course of thousands of theoretical plates, \nequilibration occurs within the solvated region of the macro-\nmolecule [12]. The method is generally quicker, less sample-\nintensive, and easier to perform than its offline, batch-mode \nDRI counterpart and has found to yield, in a great many \ncases, ∂n /∂c values almost identical to those obtained by \noffline, batch-mode DRI with sample dialysis and other \nappropriate procedures [12– 15]. Given the method’s suc-\ncess for polyelectrolytes, it can naturally be asked whether \nthe same type of equilibration during a chromatographic run \noccurs when analyzing a neutral macromolecule in a mix \nof two solvents so that, at the end of the run, the effects \nof preferential solvation are obviated within the immediate \nvicinity of the polymer chain. Because the accuracy of the \n100% mass recovery option was not evaluated in [10], it is \ndone here, for the three narrow-dispersity linear PS stand-\nards previously analyzed, in a 25:75 THF:DMF mix and \ncovering a 40-fold range in M.\nExperimental\nThe SEC/MALS/DRI; absolute refractive index (aRI); and \noffline, batch-mode DRI ∂n /∂c methods; along with the PS \nstandards and the solvents employed; have all been described \nin detail in [10]. As such, only the 100% mass recovery \nmethod is described here.\nThe determination of ∂ n/∂c by the 100% mass recovery \nmethod employed the same experimental runs as did the \nSEC/MALS/DRI determinations of the M  averages and \nmolar mass distributions (MMDs) of the PS standards. For \nall analyses, concentrations were well below the critical \noverlap concentration c *. The calibration constant of the \nDRI was determined by the instrument manufacturer using \na series of NaCl solutions, the ∂n/∂c of which is well known \n(0.1740 mL   g−1 in water at 25 °C at a vacuum wavelength \nλ0 of 658 nm). The aRI of the 25:75 THF:DMF mix was \n1.4224, measured using the aRI capability of the same DRI \nas employed in the SEC experiments, at the same experi-\nmental conditions (λ 0 = 658 nm, temperature = (25.0 ± 0.1) \n°C). At these conditions, the ∂n /∂c of PS as determined by \noffline, batch-mode DRI experiments was (0.168 ± 0.001) \n mL−1 g (note a typo in Table 1 of reference [10], where the \nunits of ∂n/∂c are incorrectly stated in the table footnote as \nbeing mg  mL−1).\n\n803\nAbsolute Molar Mass Determination in Mixed Solvents. 3. Accuracy of ∂n/∂c Values Obtained…\nAll data acquisition and processing were performed using \nAstra software (Waters/Wyatt, version 7.3.2.21).\nResults and Discussion\nThree narrow-dispersity (Ð ≤ 1.01), linear PS standards were \nexamined, with nominal molar masses of 1.8 ×  104 g  mol−1, \n4.20 ×  105 g  mol−1, and 8.00 ×  105 g  mol−1; exact values of \nthe various M averages are given for each standard in [10], \nas are their MMDs. As was shown in [10], for the SEC/\nMALS/DRI analysis of each PS, the ∂n/∂c value which pro-\nvides accurate M  values in 25:75 THF:DMF at 25 °C and \n658 nm is (0.185 ± 0.001) mL  g−1. This value was consist-\nent across all runs of all three standards (each standard was \nanalyzed at least in triplicate) and was arrived at by incre-\nmentally changing the ∂n /∂c in the Astra software until a \nvalue was found which yielded M averages in agreement, to \nwithin ± 100 g  mol−1, with those obtained in either neat THF \nor neat toluene (as has been shown, both the latter values \ncoincided with each other remarkably well).\nThe above, calculated, ∂n /∂c value of 0.185 mL   g−1 dif-\nfers markedly from the value of 0.168 mL   g−1 determined \nfrom offline, batch-mode DRI, i.e., by injecting solutions \nof carefully measured concentration directly into the DRI, \nwith the DRI decoupled from the SEC column.
