130: Order of magnitude
131: The order of magnitude ofanumberisthepowerof10thatmostcloselyapproximatesit.Thus,theorderofmagnitude
132: refers to the scale (or size) of a value. Each power of 10 represents a different order of magnitude. For example,
133: 101, 102, 103, and so forth, are all different orders of magnitude, as are100 = 1, 10−1, 10−2, and 10−3. To find the
134: order of magnitude of a number, take the base-10 logarithm of the number and round it to the nearest integer, then the order
135: of magnitude of the number is simply the resulting power of 10. For example, the order of magnitude of 800 is 103because
136: log10 800 ≈ 2.903, which rounds to 3. Similarly, the order of magnitude of 450 is 103 because log10 450 ≈ 2.653,
137: which rounds to 3 as well. Thus, we say the numbers 800 and 450 are of the same order of magnitude: 103.However,the
138: order of magnitude of 250 is 102because log10 250 ≈ 2.397, which rounds to 2.
139: An equivalent but quicker way to find the order of magnitude of a number is first to write it in scientific notation and then
140: check to see whether the first factor is greater than or less than10 = 100.5 ≈ 3. The idea is that10 = 100.5 is halfway
141: between 1 = 100 and 10 = 101 on a log base-10 scale. Thus, if the first factor is less than10, then we round it down
142: to 1 and the order of magnitude is simply whatever power of 10 is required to write the number in scientific notation. On
143: the other hand, if the first factor is greater than10, then we round it up to 10 and the order of magnitude is one power of
144: 10 higher than the power needed to write the number in scientific notation. For example, the number 800 can be written in
145: scientific notation as8 × 102. Because 8 is bigger than10 ≈ 3, we say the order of magnitude of 800 is102 + 1= 103.
146: The number 450 can be written as4.5 × 102, so its order of magnitude is also 103because4.5isgreaterthan3.However,
147: 250 written in scientific notation is 2.5 × 102 and 2.5 is less than 3, so its order of magnitude is 102.
148: The order of magnitude of a number is designed to be a ballpark estimate for the scale (or size) of its value. It is simply a
149: way of rounding numbers consistently to the nearest power of 10. This makes doing rough mental math with very big and
150: very small numbers easier. For example, the diameter of a hydrogen atom is on the order of 10−10m,whereasthediameter
151: of the Sun is on the order of 109 m, so it would take roughly109 /10−10 = 1019 hydrogen atoms to stretch across the

196: A modelis arepresentation ofsomething that is often toodifficult (orimpossible) todisplay directly.Although amodel

212: The wordtheory means something different to scientists than what is often meant when the word is used in everyday
213: conversation. In particular, to a scientist a theory is not the same as a “guess” or an “idea” or even a “hypothesis.” The
214: phrase“it’sjustatheory”seemsmeaninglessandsillytoscientistsbecausescienceisfoundedonthenotionoftheories.To
215: ascientist,a theoryisatestableexplanationforpatternsinnaturesupportedbyscientificevidenceandverifiedmultiple
216: timesbyvariousgroupsofresearchers.Sometheoriesincludemodelstohelpvisualizephenomenawhereasothersdonot.
217: Newton’s theory of gravity, for example, does not require a model or mental image, because we can observe the objects
218: directlywithourownsenses.Thekinetictheoryofgases,ontheotherhand,isamodelinwhichagasisviewedasbeing
219: composedofatomsandmolecules.Atomsandmoleculesaretoosmalltobeobserveddirectlywithoursenses—thus,we
220: picturethemmentallytounderstandwhattheinstrumentstellusaboutthebehaviorofgases.Althoughmodelsaremeant
221: onlytodescribecertainaspectsofaphysicalsystemaccurately,atheoryshoulddescribeallaspectsofanysystemthatfalls
222: withinitsdomainofapplicability.Inparticular,anyexperimentallytestableimplicationofatheoryshouldbeverified.Ifan
223: experimentevershowsanimplicationofatheorytobefalse,thenthetheoryiseitherthrownoutormodifiedsuitably(for
224: example, by limiting its domain of applicability).
225: A law uses concise language to describe a generalized pattern in nature supported by scientific evidence and repeated
226: experiments. Often,alawcanbeexpressed intheformofasingle mathematical equation. Laws andtheories aresimilar
227: in that they are both scientific statements that result from a tested hypothesis and are supported by scientific evidence.
228: However, the designationlaw is usually reserved for a concise and very general statement that describes phenomena in
229: nature,suchasthelawthatenergyisconservedduringanyprocess,orNewton’ssecondlawofmotion,whichrelatesforce
230: (F), mass (m), and acceleration (a) by the simple equationF = ma. A theory, in contrast, is a less concise statement of
231: observed behavior. For example, the theory of evolution and the theory of relativity cannot be expressed concisely enough to
232: be considered laws. The biggest difference between a law and a theory is that a theory is much more complex and dynamic.
233: A law describes a single action whereas a theory explains an entire group of related phenomena. Less broadly applicable
234: statements are usually called principles (such as Pascal’s principle, which is applicable only in fluids), but the distinction
235: between laws and principles often is not made carefully.
236: The models, theories, and laws we devise sometimes imply the existence of objects or phenomena that are as yet
237: unobserved. These predictions are remarkable triumphs and tributes to the power of science. It is the underlying order in
238: the universe that enables scientists to make such spectacular predictions. However, if experimentation does not verify our
239: predictions, then the theory or law is wrong, no matter how elegant or convenient it is. Laws can never be known with
240: absolute certainty because it is impossible to perform every imaginable experiment to confirm a law for every possible
241: scenario. Physicists operate under the assumption that all scientific laws and theories are valid until a counterexample is
242: observed. If a good-quality, verifiable experiment contradicts a well-established law or theory, then the law or theory must
243: be modified or overthrown completely.
244: The study of science in general, and physics in particular, is an adventure much like the exploration of an uncharted ocean.
245: Discoveries are made; models, theories, and laws are formulated; and the beauty of the physical universe is made more
246: sublime for the insights gained.

264: We define aphysical quantity either by specifying how it is measured or by stating how it is calculated from other
265: measurements.Forexample,wemightdefinedistanceandtimebyspecifyingmethodsformeasuringthem,suchasusing
266: a meter stick and a stopwatch. Then, we could defineaverage speedby stating that it is calculated as the total distance
267: traveled divided by time of travel.

269: ofarace,whichisaphysicalquantity,canbeexpressedinunitsofmeters(forsprinters)orkilometers(fordistancerunners).
270: Without standardized units, it would be extremely difficult for scientists to express and compare measured values in a
271: meaningful way (Figure 1.7).

283: SI Units: Base and Derived Units
284: Inanysystemofunits,theunitsforsomephysicalquantitiesmustbedefinedthroughameasurementprocess.Theseare
285: called thebase quantities for that system and their units are the system’sbase units. All other physical quantities can
286: then be expressed as algebraic combinations of the base quantities. Each of these physical quantities is then known as a
287: derived quantityandeachunitiscalleda derived unit.Thechoiceofbasequantitiesissomewhatarbitrary,aslongasthey
288: areindependentofeachotherandallotherquantitiescanbederivedfromthem.Typically,thegoalistochoosephysical
289: quantitiesthatcanbemeasuredaccuratelytoahighprecisionasthebasequantities.Thereasonforthisissimple.Sincethe
290: derivedunitscanbeexpressedasalgebraiccombinationsofthebaseunits,theycanonlybeasaccurateandpreciseasthe
291: base units from which they are derived.
292: Based on such considerations, the International Standards Organization recommends using seven base quantities, which
293: formtheInternationalSystemofQuantities(ISQ).ThesearethebasequantitiesusedtodefinetheSIbaseunits. Table 1.1
294: lists these seven ISQ base quantities and the corresponding SI base units.

308: Youareprobablyalreadyfamiliarwithsomederivedquantitiesthatcanbeformedfromthebasequantitiesin Table 1.1.
309: For example, the geometric concept of area is always calculated as the product of two lengths. Thus, area is a derived
310: quantitythatcanbeexpressedintermsofSIbaseunitsusingsquaremeters (m × m = m2). Similarly, volume is a derived

562: 1.4 | Dimensional Analysis
563: Learning Objectives
564: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
565: • Find the dimensions of a mathematical expression involving physical quantities.
566: • Determine whether an equation involving physical quantities is dimensionally consistent.
567: The dimensionofanyphysicalquantityexpressesitsdependenceonthebasequantitiesasaproductofsymbols(orpowers
568: ofsymbols)representingthebasequantities. Table 1.3liststhebasequantitiesandthesymbolsusedfortheirdimension.
569: For example, a measurement of length is said to have dimension L or L1, a measurement of mass has dimension M or
570: M1, and a measurement of time has dimension T or T1. Like units, dimensions obey the rules of algebra. Thus, area is
571: the product of two lengths and so has dimension L2, or length squared. Similarly, volume is the product of three lengths
572: andhasdimensionL 3,orlengthcubed.Speedhasdimensionlengthovertime,L/TorLT –1.Volumetricmassdensityhas
573: dimensionM/L 3orML –3,ormassoverlengthcubed.Ingeneral,thedimensionofanyphysicalquantitycanbewrittenas
574: La Mb Tc Id Θe Nf Jg forsomepowers a, b, c, d, e, f , andg.Wecanwritethedimensionsofalengthinthisformwith
575: a = 1 and the remaining six powers all set equal to zero:L1 = L1 M0 T0 I0 Θ0 N0 J0. Any quantity with a dimension that
576: can be written so that all seven powers are zero (that is, its dimension isL0 M0 T0 I0 Θ0 N0 J0 ) is calleddimensionless
577: (or sometimes “of dimension 1,” because anything raised to the zero power is one). Physicists often call dimensionless
578: quantitiespure numbers.
579: Base Quantity Symbol for Dimension
580: Length L
581: Mass M
582: Time T
583: Current I
584: Thermodynamic temperature Θ
585: Amount of substance N
586: Luminous intensity J
587: Table 1.3 Base Quantities and Their Dimensions
588: Physicistsoftenusesquarebracketsaroundthesymbolforaphysicalquantitytorepresentthedimensionsofthatquantity.
589: For example, ifr is the radius of a cylinder andh is its height, then we write[r] = L and [h] = L to indicate the
590: dimensions of the radius and height are both those of length, or L. Similarly, if we use the symbolA for the surface area of
591: a cylinder andV for its volume, then [A]=L 2and[V]=L 3.Ifweusethesymbol m for the mass of the cylinder andρ
592: 22 Chapter 1 | Units and Measurement
593: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
594: 
595: for the density of the material from which the cylinder is made, then [m] = Mand [ρ] = ML−3.
596: The importance of the concept of dimension arises from the fact that any mathematical equation relating physical quantities
597: must be dimensionally consistent, which means the equation must obey the following rules:
598: • Everyterminanexpressionmusthavethesamedimensions;itdoesnotmakesensetoaddorsubtractquantitiesof
599: differingdimension(thinkoftheoldsaying:“Youcan’taddapplesandoranges”).Inparticular,theexpressionson
600: each side of the equality in an equation must have the same dimensions.
601: • The arguments of any of the standard mathematical functions such as trigonometric functions (such as sine and
602: cosine), logarithms, or exponential functions that appear in the equation must be dimensionless. These functions
603: require pure numbers as inputs and give pure numbers as outputs.
604: Ifeitheroftheserulesisviolated,anequationisnotdimensionally consistentandcannotpossiblybeacorrectstatement
605: ofphysicallaw.Thissimplefactcanbeusedtocheckfortyposoralgebramistakes,tohelprememberthevariouslawsof
606: physics,andeventosuggesttheformthatnewlawsofphysicsmighttake.Thislastuseofdimensionsisbeyondthescope
607: of this text, but is something you will undoubtedly learn later in your academic career.
608: Example 1.4
609: Using Dimensions to Remember an Equation
610: Suppose we need the formula for the area of a circle for some computation. Like many people who learned
611: geometry too long ago to recall with any certainty, two expressions may pop into our mind when we think of
612: circles: πr 2 and 2πr. One expression is the circumference of a circle of radiusrandtheotherisitsarea.But
613: which is which?
614: Strategy
615: Onenaturalstrategyistolookitup,butthiscouldtaketimetofindinformationfromareputablesource.Besides,
616: evenifwethinkthesourceisreputable,weshouldn’ttrusteverythingweread.Itisnicetohaveawaytodouble-
617: checkjustbythinkingaboutit.Also,wemightbeinasituationinwhichwecannotlookthingsup(suchasduring
618: atest).Thus,thestrategyistofindthedimensionsofbothexpressionsbymakinguseofthefactthatdimensions
619: followtherulesofalgebra.Ifeitherexpressiondoesnothavethesamedimensionsasarea,thenitcannotpossibly
620: be the correct equation for the area of a circle.
621: Solution
622: We know the dimension of area is L2. Now, the dimension of the expression πr 2 is
623: [πr 2] = [π] · [r]2 = 1 · L2 = L2,
624: since the constantπ is a pure number and the radiusr is a length. Therefore,πr 2 has the dimension of area.
625: Similarly, the dimension of the expression 2πr is
626: [2πr] = [2] · [π] · [r] = 1 · 1 · L = L,
627: since the constants2 and π are both dimensionless and the radiusr is a length. We see that2πr has the
628: dimension of length, which means it cannot possibly be an area.
629: We rule out2πr because it is not dimensionally consistent with being an area. We see thatπr 2 is dimensionally
630: consistent with being an area, so if we have to choose between these two expressions, πr 2 is the one to choose.
631: Significance
632: Thismayseemlikekindofasillyexample,buttheideasareverygeneral.Aslongasweknowthedimensions
633: of the individual physical quantities that appear in an equation, we can check to see whether the equation is
634: dimensionally consistent. On the other hand, knowing that true equations are dimensionally consistent, we can
635: matchexpressionsfromourimperfectmemoriestothequantitiesforwhichtheymightbeexpressions.Doingthis
636: willnothelpusrememberdimensionlessfactorsthatappearintheequations(forexample,ifyouhadaccidentally
637: conflated the two expressions from the example into2πr 2, then dimensional analysis is no help), but it does
638: help us remember the correct basic form of equations.

641: 1.5 Check Your Understanding Suppose we want the formula for the volume of a sphere. The two

644: Example 1.5
645: Checking Equations for Dimensional Consistency
646: Consider the physical quantitiess, v, a, and t with dimensions [s] = L, [v] = LT−1, [a] = LT−2,
647: and [t] = T. Determine whether each of the following equations is dimensionally consistent: (a)
648: s = vt + 0.5at2; (b) s = vt2 + 0.5at; and (c) v = sin(at2 /s).
649: Strategy
650: Bythedefinitionofdimensionalconsistency,weneedtocheckthateachterminagivenequationhasthesame
651: dimensionsastheothertermsinthatequationandthattheargumentsofanystandardmathematicalfunctionsare
652: dimensionless.
653: Solution
654: a. Therearenotrigonometric,logarithmic,orexponentialfunctionstoworryaboutinthisequation,sowe
655: needonlylookatthedimensionsofeachtermappearingintheequation.Therearethreeterms,oneinthe
656: left expression and two in the expression on the right, so we look at each in turn:
657: [s] = L
658: [vt] = [v] · [t] = LT−1 · T = LT0 = L
659: [0.5at2] = [a] · [t]2 = LT−2 · T2 = LT0 = L.
660: All three terms have the same dimension, so this equation is dimensionally consistent.
661: b. Again,therearenotrigonometric,exponential,orlogarithmicfunctions,soweonlyneedtolookatthe
662: dimensions of each of the three terms appearing in the equation:
663: [s] = L
664: [vt2] = [v] · [t]2 = LT−1 · T2 = LT
665: [at] = [a] · [t] = LT−2 · T = LT−1.
666: None of the three terms has the same dimension as any other, so this is about as far from being
667: dimensionally consistent as you can get. The technical term for an equation like this isnonsense.
668: c. This equation has a trigonometric function in it, so first we should check that the argument of the sine
669: function is dimensionless:

47: Estimate the total mass of the oceans on Earth.
48: Strategy

50: andvolumes.”Thus,weneedtoestimatethevolumeoftheplanet’soceans.Usingtheadviceto“getareasand

53: so we can estimate the surface area of the oceans as being roughly equal to the surface area of the planet. By

60: the oceans. Now we just need to estimate the average depth of the oceans. For this, we use the advice: “If all else
61: fails, bound it.” We happen to know the deepest points in the ocean are around 10 km and that it is not uncommon
62: for the ocean to be deeper than 1 km, so we take the average depth to be around(103 × 104)0.5 ≈ 3 × 103 m.
63: Now we just need to put it all together, heeding the advice that “one ‘sig. fig.’ is fine.”
64: Solution
65: We estimate the surface area of Earth (and hence the surface area of Earth’s oceans) to be roughly
66: A = πd 2 = π(107 m)2 ≈ 3 × 1014 m2.
67: Next, using our average depth estimate ofD = 3 × 103 m, which was obtained by bounding, we estimate the
68: volume of Earth’s oceans to be
69: V = AD = (3 × 1014 m2)(3 × 103 m) = 9 × 1017 m3.
70: Last, we estimate the mass of the world’s oceans to be
71: M = ρV = (103 kg/m3)(9 × 1017 m3) = 9 × 1020 kg.
72: Thus, we estimate that the order of magnitude of the mass of the planet’s oceans is 1021kg.

244: significant, depending on the style of writing numbers. They could mean the number is known to the last digit or they
245: couldbeplaceholders.So1300couldhavetwo,three,orfoursignificantfigures.Toavoidthisambiguity,weshouldwrite
246: 1300inscientificnotationas 1.3 × 103, 1.30 × 103, or 1.300 × 103, depending on whether it has two, three, or four
247: significant figures.Zeros are significant except when they serve only as placeholders.

446: SUMMARY
447: 1.1 The Scope and Scale of Physics
448: • Physics is about trying to find the simple laws that describe all natural phenomena.
449: • Physics operates on a vast range of scales of length, mass, and time. Scientists use the concept of the order of
450: magnitude of a number to track which phenomena occur on which scales. They also use orders of magnitude to
451: compare the various scales.
452: • Scientists attempt to describe the world by formulating models, theories, and laws.
453: 1.2 Units and Standards
454: • Systems of units are built up from a small number of base units, which are defined by accurate and precise
455: measurementsofconventionallychosenbasequantities.Otherunitsarethenderivedasalgebraiccombinationsof
456: the base units.
457: • TwocommonlyusedsystemsofunitsareEnglishunitsandSIunits.Allscientistsandmostoftheotherpeoplein
458: the world use SI, whereas nonscientists in the United States still tend to use English units.
459: • The SI base units of length, mass, and time are the meter (m), kilogram (kg), and second (s), respectively.
460: • SI units are a metric system of units, meaning values can be calculated by factors of 10. Metric prefixes may be
461: used with metric units to scale the base units to sizes appropriate for almost any application.
462: 1.3 Unit Conversion
463: • Toconvertaquantityfromoneunittoanother,multiplybyconversionsfactorsinsuchawaythatyoucancelthe
464: units you want to get rid of and introduce the units you want to end up with.
465: • Becarefulwithareasandvolumes.Unitsobeytherulesofalgebraso,forexample,ifaunitissquaredweneedtwo
466: factors to cancel it.
467: 1.4 Dimensional Analysis
468: • The dimension of a physical quantity is just an expression of the base quantities from which it is derived.
469: • Allequationsexpressingphysicallawsorprinciplesmustbedimensionallyconsistent.Thisfactcanbeusedasan
470: aidinrememberingphysicallaws,asawaytocheckwhetherclaimedrelationshipsbetweenphysicalquantitiesare
471: possible, and even to derive new physical laws.
472: 1.5 Estimates and Fermi Calculations
473: • An estimate is a rough educated guess at the value of a physical quantity based on prior experience and sound
474: physical reasoning. Some strategies that may help when making an estimate are as follows:
475: ◦ Get big lengths from smaller lengths.
476: ◦ Get areas and volumes from lengths.
477: ◦ Get masses from volumes and densities.
478: ◦ If all else fails, bound it.
479: 36 Chapter 1 | Units and Measurement
480: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
481: 
482: ◦ One “sig. fig.” is fine.
483: ◦ Ask yourself: Does this make any sense?
484: 1.6 Significant Figures
485: • Accuracyofameasuredvaluereferstohowcloseameasurementistoanacceptedreferencevalue.Thediscrepancy
486: in a measurement is the amount by which the measurement result differs from this value.
487: • Precisionofmeasuredvaluesreferstohowclosetheagreementisbetweenrepeatedmeasurements.Theuncertainty
488: of a measurement is a quantification of this.
489: • Theprecisionofameasuringtoolisrelatedtothesizeofitsmeasurementincrements.Thesmallerthemeasurement
490: increment, the more precise the tool.
491: • Significant figures express the precision of a measuring tool.
492: • Whenmultiplyingordividingmeasuredvalues,thefinalanswercancontainonlyasmanysignificantfiguresasthe
493: value with the least number of significant figures.
494: • Whenaddingorsubtractingmeasuredvalues,thefinalanswercannotcontainmoredecimalplacesthantheleast-
495: precise value.
496: 1.7 Solving Problems in Physics
497: The three stages of the process for solving physics problems used in this book are as follows:
498: • Strategy: Determine which physical principles are involved and develop a strategy for using them to solve the
499: problem.
500: • Solution: Do the math necessary to obtain a numerical solution complete with units.
501: • Significance: Check the solution to make sure it makes sense (correct units, reasonable magnitude and sign) and
502: assess its significance.

953: 
954: 2.1 | Scalars and Vectors
955: Learning Objectives
956: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
957: • Describe the difference between vector and scalar quantities.
958: • Identify the magnitude and direction of a vector.
959: • Explain the effect of multiplying a vector quantity by a scalar.
960: • Describe how one-dimensional vector quantities are added or subtracted.
961: • Explain the geometric construction for the addition or subtraction of vectors in a plane.
962: • Distinguish between a vector equation and a scalar equation.
963: Many familiar physical quantities can be specified completely by giving a single number and the appropriate unit. For
964: example, “a class period lasts 50min” or“the gas tank in my car holds 65L” or“the distance between two posts is 100
965: m.”Aphysicalquantitythatcanbespecifiedcompletelyinthismanneriscalleda scalar quantity.Scalarisasynonymof
966: “number.” Time, mass, distance, length, volume, temperature, and energy are examples of scalarquantities.
967: Scalar quantities that have the same physical units can be added or subtracted according to the usual rules of algebra for
968: numbers. For example, a class ending 10 min earlier than 50 min lasts50 min − 10 min = 40 min. Similarly, a 60-cal
969: serving of corn followed by a 200-cal serving of donuts gives60 cal + 200 cal = 260 calof energy. When we multiply
970: a scalar quantity by a number, we obtain the same scalar quantity but with a larger (or smaller) value. For example, if
971: yesterday’s breakfast had 200 cal of energy and today’s breakfast has four times as much energy as it had yesterday, then
972: today’s breakfast has4(200 cal) = 800 calof energy. Two scalar quantities can also be multiplied or divided by each other
973: to form a derived scalar quantity. For example, if a train covers a distance of 100 km in 1.0 h, its speed is 100.0 km/1.0 h =
974: 27.8 m/s, where the speed is a derived scalar quantity obtained by dividing distance by time.
975: Many physical quantities, however, cannot be described completely by just a single number of physical units. For example,
976: when the U.S. Coast Guard dispatches a ship or a helicopter for a rescue mission, the rescue team must know not only the
977: distance to the distress signal, but also the direction from which the signal is coming so they can get to its origin as quickly
978: as possible. Physical quantities specified completely by giving a number of units (magnitude) and a direction are called
979: vector quantities.Examplesofvectorquantitiesincludedisplacement,velocity,position,force,andtorque.Inthelanguage
980: of mathematics, physical vector quantities are represented by mathematical objects calledvectors(Figure 2.2). We can
981: addorsubtracttwovectors,andwecanmultiplyavectorbyascalarorbyanothervector,butwecannotdividebyavector.
982: The operation of division by a vector is not defined.
983: Figure 2.2 We draw a vector from the initial point or origin
984: (called the “tail” of a vector) to the end or terminal point (called
985: the “head” of a vector), marked by an arrowhead. Magnitude is
986: the length of a vector and is always a positive scalar quantity.
987: (credit "photo": modification of work by Cate Sevilla)

989: understanding.Inpractice,however,whenitcomestosolvingphysicsproblems,weuseanalyticalmethods,whichwe’ll
990: see in the next section. Analytical methods are more simple computationally and more accurate than graphical methods.
991: Fromnowon,todistinguishbetweenavectorandascalarquantity,weadoptthecommonconventionthataletterinbold

170: When vectors A→ and B→ lie along a line (that is, in one dimension), such as in the camping example, their resultant
171: R→ = A→ + B→ and their differenceD→ = A→ − B→ both lie along the same direction. We can illustrate the addition
172: or subtraction of vectors by drawing the corresponding vectors to scale in one dimension, as shown in Figure 2.7.
173: Toillustratetheresultantwhen A→ and B→ are two parallel vectors, we draw them along one line by placing the origin
174: of one vector at the end of the other vector in head-to-tail fashion (seeFigure 2.7(b)). The magnitude of this resultant
175: is the sum of their magnitudes:R =A +B. The direction of the resultant is parallel to both vectors. When vectorA→
176: is antiparallel to vector B→ , we draw them along one line in either head-to-head fashion (Figure 2.7(c)) or tail-to-
177: tail fashion. The magnitude of the vector difference, then, is theabsolute valueD = |A −B| of the difference of their
178: magnitudes. The direction of the difference vector D→ is parallel to the direction of the longer vector.
179: In general, in one dimension—as well as in higher dimensions, such as in a plane or in space—we can add any number of
180: vectors and we can do so in any order because the addition of vectors is commutative,
181: (2.7)A→ + B→ = B→ + A→ ,
182: and associative,
183: (2.8)( A→ + B→ ) + C→ = A→ + ( B→ + C→ ).
184: Moreover, multiplication by a scalar is distributive:
185: (2.9)α1 A→ +α2 A→ = (α1 +α2) A→ .
186: We used the distributive property in Equation 2.4and Equation 2.6.
187: When adding many vectors in one dimension, it is convenient to use the concept of aunit vector. A unit vector, which
188: isdenotedbyalettersymbolwithahat,suchas u^ , has a magnitude of one and does not have any physical unit so that
189: |u^
190: | ≡ u = 1. The only role of a unit vector is to specify direction. For example, instead of saying vectorD→
191: AB has a

286: If we need to add three or more vectors, we repeat the parallelogram rule for the pairs of vectors until we find the resultant

289: the operation of vector addition is commutative and associative (seeEquation 2.7and Equation 2.8).Beforewestatea
290: general rule that follows from repetitive applications of the parallelogram rule, let’s look at the following example.

633: Polar Coordinates
634: Todescribelocationsofpointsorvectorsinaplane,weneedtwoorthogonaldirections.IntheCartesiancoordinatesystem
635: thesedirectionsaregivenbyunitvectors i^ and j^ along thex-axisandthe y-axis,respectively.TheCartesiancoordinate
636: system is very convenient to use in describing displacements and velocities of objects and the forces acting on them.
637: However,itbecomescumbersomewhenweneedtodescribetherotationofobjects.Whendescribingrotation,weusually
638: work in the polar coordinate system.
639: Inthepolarcoordinatesystem,thelocationofpoint Pinaplaneisgivenbytwo polar coordinates(Figure 2.20).Thefirst
640: polarcoordinateisthe radial coordinater,whichisthedistanceofpoint Pfromtheorigin.Thesecondpolarcoordinateis
641: anangle φ that the radial vector makes with some chosen direction, usually the positivex-direction.Inpolarcoordinates,
642: anglesaremeasuredinradians,orrads.Theradialvectorisattachedattheoriginandpointsawayfromtheorigintopoint
643: P.This radial direction is described by a unit radial vectorr^ . The second unit vectort^ is a vector orthogonal to the
644: radial direction r^ . The positive+ t^ direction indicates how the angleφ changes in the counterclockwise direction. In
645: this way,apointPthathascoordinates(x ,y)intherectangularsystemcanbedescribedequivalentlyinthepolarcoordinate
646: system by the two polar coordinates(r, φ) . Equation 2.17 is valid for any vector, so we can use it to express thex-
647: and y-coordinates of vector r→ . In this way, we obtain the connection between the polar coordinates and rectangular
648: coordinates of pointP:
649: (2.18)⎧
650: ⎩
651: ⎨
652: x = r cosφ
653: y = r sinφ.
654: 64 Chapter 2 | Vectors

656: 
657: Figure 2.20 Using polar coordinates, the unit vector r^ defines
658: the positive direction along the radiusr(radial direction) and,
659: orthogonal to it, the unit vector t^ defines the positive direction of
660: rotation by the angle φ.

80: Example 2.8
81: Direction of Motion
82: In a Cartesian coordinate system wherei^ denotes geographic east, j^ denotes geographic north, andk^
83: denotes altitude above sea level, a military convoy advances its position through unknown territory with velocity
84: v→ = (4.0i^ + 3.0j^ + 0.1k^)km/h . If the convoy had to retreat, in what geographic direction would it be
85: moving?
86: Solution
87: Thevelocityvectorhasthethirdcomponent v→ z = ( + 0.1km/h)k^ , which says the convoy is climbing at a rate
88: of 100 m/h through mountainous terrain. At the same time, its velocity is 4.0 km/h to the east and 3.0 km/h to
89: the north, so it moves on the ground in directiontan−1(3 /4) ≈ 37°north of east. If the convoy had to retreat,
90: its new velocity vectoru→ would have to be antiparallel tov→ and be in the formu→ = −α v→ , where
91: α is a positive number. Thus, the velocity of the retreat would beu→ = α(−4.0 i^ − 3.0j^ − 0.1k^)km/h . The
92: negative sign of the third component indicates the convoy would be descending. The direction angle of the retreat
93: velocity is tan−1(−3α/ − 4α) ≈ 37° south of west. Therefore, the convoy would be moving on the ground in
94: direction 37° south of west while descending on its way back.
95: The generalization of the number zero to vector algebra is called thenull vector,denotedby 0→ . All components of the
96: null vector are zero, 0→ = 0i^ + 0j^ + 0k^ , so the null vector has no length and no direction.

100: write A→ = B→ if and only if the corresponding components of vectors A→ and B→ are equal:

547: 2.4 | Products of Vectors
548: Learning Objectives
549: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
550: • Explain the difference between the scalar product and the vector product of two vectors.
551: • Determine the scalar product of two vectors.
552: • Determine the vector product of two vectors.
553: • Describe how the products of vectors are used in physics.
554: A vector can be multiplied by another vector but may not be divided by another vector. There are two kinds of products
555: of vectors used broadly in physics and engineering. One kind of multiplication is ascalarmultiplicationoftwovectors .
556: Chapter 2 | Vectors 77
557: 
558: Taking a scalar product of two vectors results in a number (a scalar), as its name indicates. Scalar products are used to
559: define work and energy relations. For example, the work that a force (a vector) performs on an object while causing its
560: displacement(avector)isdefinedasascalarproductoftheforcevectorwiththedisplacementvector.Aquitedifferentkind
561: ofmultiplicationisa vectormultiplicationofvectors .Takingavectorproductoftwovectorsreturnsasaresultavector,as
562: itsnamesuggests.Vectorproductsareusedtodefineotherderivedvectorquantities.Forexample,indescribingrotations,
563: avectorquantitycalled torqueisdefinedasavectorproductofanappliedforce(avector)anditsdistancefrompivotto
564: force(avector).Itisimportanttodistinguishbetweenthesetwokindsofvectormultiplicationsbecausethescalarproduct
565: is a scalar quantity and a vector product is a vector quantity.
566: The Scalar Product of Two Vectors (the Dot Product)
567: Scalar multiplication of two vectors yields a scalar product.
568: Scalar Product (Dot Product)
569: The scalar product A→ · B→ of two vectors A→ and B→ is a number defined by the equation
570: (2.27)A→ · B→ = AB cosφ,
571: where φ is the angle between the vectors (shown inFigure 2.27).Thescalarproductisalsocalledthe dot product
572: because of the dot notation that indicates it.
573: In the definition of the dot product, the direction of angleφ does not matter, andφ can be measured from either of
574: the two vectors to the other becausecosφ = cos (−φ) = cos (2π−φ) . The dot product is a negative number when
575: 90° <φ ≤ 180° and is a positive number when0° ≤φ < 90°. Moreover, the dot product of two parallel vectors is
576: A→ · B→ = AB cos 0° =AB, and the dot product of two antiparallel vectors isA→ · B→ = AB cos 180° = −AB. The
577: scalar product of twoorthogonalvectors vanishes: A→ · B→ = AB cos 90° = 0. The scalar product of a vector with itself
578: is the square of its magnitude:
579: (2.28)A→ 2 ≡ A→ · A→ = AA cos 0° =A2.
580: Figure 2.27 The scalar product of two vectors. (a) The angle between the two vectors. (b) The orthogonal projection A⊥ of
581: vector A→ onto the direction of vector B→ . (c) The orthogonal projection B⊥ of vector B→ onto the direction of vector
582: A→ .

755: The Work of a Force
756: Whenforce F→ pulls on an object and when it causes its displacementD→ , we say the force performs work.
757: The amount of work the force does is the scalar productF→ · D→ . If the stick inExample 2.16 moves
758: momentarilyandgetsdisplacedbyvector D→ = (−7.9j^ − 4.2k^) cm, how much work is done by the third dog
759: in Example 2.16?
760: Strategy
761: Wecomputethescalarproductofdisplacementvector D→ with force vectorF→
762: 3 = (5.0i^ + 12.5j^)N , which
763: is the pull from the third dog. Let’s use W3 to denote the work done by force F→
764: 3 on displacement D→ .
765: Solution
766: Calculating the work is a straightforward application of the dot product:
767: W3 = F→
768: 3 · D→ = F3xDx +F3yDy +F3zDz
769: = (5.0 N)(0.0 cm) + (12.5 N)(−7.9 cm) + (0.0 N)(−4.2 cm)
770: = −98.7 N · cm.
771: Significance
772: The SI unit of work is called the joule(J) , where 1 J = 1N · m. The unit cm · Ncan be written as
773: 10−2 m · N = 10−2 J , so the answer can be expressed as W3 = −0.9875 J ≈ −1.0 J.

776: The Vector Product of Two Vectors (the Cross Product)
777: Vector multiplication of two vectors yields a vector product.
778: Vector Product (Cross Product)
779: The vector product of two vectors A→ and B→ is denoted by A→ × B→ and is often referred to as across
780: product.The vector product is a vector that has its direction perpendicular to both vectorsA→ and B→ . In other
781: words, vector A→ × B→ is perpendicular to the plane that contains vectorsA→ and B→ , as shown inFigure 2.29.
782: The magnitude of the vector product is defined as
783: (2.35)
784: | A→ × B→
785: | = AB sinφ,
786: where angleφ, between the two vectors, is measured from vectorA→ (first vector in the product) to vectorB→
787: (second vector in the product), as indicated in Figure 2.29, and is between 0° and 180° .
788: 82 Chapter 2 | Vectors
789: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
790: 
791: According to Equation 2.35, the vector product vanishes for pairs of vectors that are either parallel
792: ⎛
793: ⎝φ = 0°
794: ⎞
795: ⎠ or
796: antiparallel
797: ⎛
798: ⎝φ = 180°
799: ⎞
800: ⎠because sin 0° = sin 180° = 0.
801: Figure 2.29 The vector product of two vectors is drawn in three-
802: dimensional space. (a) The vector product A→ × B→ is a vector
803: perpendicular to the plane that contains vectors A→ and B→ . Small
804: squares drawn in perspective mark right angles between A→ and C→ ,
805: and between B→ and C→ so that if A→ and B→ lie on the floor,
806: vector C→ points vertically upward to the ceiling. (b) The vector
807: product B→ × A→ is a vector antiparallel to vector A→ × B→ .
808: Onthelineperpendiculartotheplanethatcontainsvectors A→ and B→ there are two alternative directions—either up or
809: down, as shown inFigure 2.29—andthedirectionofthevectorproductmaybeeitheroneofthem.Inthestandardright-
810: handedorientation,wheretheanglebetweenvectorsismeasuredcounterclockwisefromthefirstvector,vector A→ × B→
811: pointsupward, as seen inFigure 2.29(a). If we reverse the order of multiplication, so that nowB→ comes first in the
812: product, then vector B→ × A→ must pointdownward, as seen inFigure 2.29(b). This means that vectorsA→ × B→
813: and B→ × A→ areantiparalleltoeachotherandthatvectormultiplicationis notcommutativebut anticommutative.The
814: anticommutative propertymeans the vector product reverses the sign when the order of multiplication is reversed:
815: (2.36)A→ × B→ = − B→ × A→ .
816: The corkscrew right-hand rule isacommonmnemonicusedtodeterminethedirectionofthevectorproduct.Asshown
817: in Figure 2.30,acorkscrewisplacedinadirectionperpendiculartotheplanethatcontainsvectors A→ and B→ , and
818: its handle is turned in the direction from the first to the second vector in the product. The direction of the cross product is
819: given by the progression of the corkscrew.
820: Chapter 2 | Vectors 83
821: 
822: Figure 2.30 The corkscrew right-hand rule can be used to determine
823: the direction of the cross product A→ × B→ . Place a corkscrew in the
824: direction perpendicular to the plane that contains vectors A→ and B→
825: , and turn it in the direction from the first to the second vector in the
826: product. The direction of the cross product is given by the progression of
827: the corkscrew. (a) Upward movement means the cross-product vector
828: points up. (b) Downward movement means the cross-product vector
829: points downward.

831: The Torque of a Force
832: Themechanicaladvantagethatafamiliartoolcalleda wrenchprovides(Figure 2.31)dependsonmagnitude F
833: oftheappliedforce,onitsdirectionwithrespecttothewrenchhandle,andonhowfarfromthenutthisforceis
834: applied.Thedistance Rfromthenuttothepointwhereforcevector F→ is attached is represented by the radial
835: vector R→ . The physical vector quantity that makes the nut turn is calledtorque(denotedby τ→ ) , and it is the
836: vector product of the distance between the pivot to force with the force: τ→ = R→ × F→ .
837: To loosen a rusty nut, a 20.00-N force is applied to the wrench handle at angleφ = 40° and at a distance of 0.25
838: m from the nut, as shown inFigure 2.31(a).Findthemagnitudeanddirectionofthetorqueappliedtothenut.
839: Whatwouldthemagnitudeanddirectionofthetorquebeiftheforcewereappliedatangle φ = 45°, as shown
840: in Figure 2.31(b)? For what value of angle φ does the torque have the largest magnitude?
841: 84 Chapter 2 | Vectors
842: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
843: 
844: Figure 2.31 A wrench provides grip and mechanical advantage in applying torque to turn a nut. (a) Turn
845: counterclockwise to loosen the nut. (b) Turn clockwise to tighten the nut.
846: Strategy
847: We adopt the frame of reference shown inFigure 2.31, where vectors R→ and F→ lie in thexy-plane and
848: the origin is at the position of the nut. The radial direction along vectorR→ (pointing away from the origin)
849: is the reference direction for measuring the angleφ because R→ is the first vector in the vector product
850: τ→ = R→ × F→ . Vector τ→ must lie along thez-axis because this is the axis that is perpendicular to the
851: xy-plane, where both R→ and F→ lie. To compute the magnitudeτ, we useEquation 2.35. To find the
852: direction of τ→ , we use the corkscrew right-hand rule (Figure 2.30).
853: Solution
854: Forthesituationin(a),thecorkscrewrulegivesthedirectionof R→ × F→ in the positive direction of thez-axis.
855: Physically,itmeansthetorquevector τ→ pointsoutofthepage,perpendiculartothewrenchhandle.Weidentify
856: F= 20.00 N andR= 0.25 m, and compute the magnitude using Equation 2.35:
857: τ = | R→ × F→
858: | = RF sinφ = (0.25 m)(20.00 N) sin 40° = 3.21 N · m.
859: For the situation in (b), the corkscrew rule gives the direction ofR→ × F→ in the negative direction of
860: the z-axis. Physically, it means the vectorτ→ points into the page, perpendicular to the wrench handle. The
861: magnitude of this torque is
862: τ = | R→ × F→
863: | = RF sinφ = (0.25 m)(20.00 N) sin 45° = 3.53 N · m.
864: The torque has the largest value whensinφ = 1, which happens whenφ = 90°. Physically, it means the
865: wrench is most effective—giving us the best mechanical advantage—when we apply the force perpendicular
866: to the wrench handle. For the situation in this example, this best-torque value is
867: τbest = RF = (0.25 m)(20.00 N) = 5.00 N · m.

374: SUMMARY
375: 2.1 Scalars and Vectors
376: • A vector quantity is any quantity that has magnitude and direction, such as displacement or velocity. Vector
377: quantities are represented by mathematical objects called vectors.
378: • Geometrically,vectorsarerepresentedbyarrows,withtheendmarkedbyanarrowhead.Thelengthofthevectoris
379: itsmagnitude,whichisapositivescalar.Onaplane,thedirectionofavectorisgivenbytheanglethevectormakes
380: Chapter 2 | Vectors 93
381: 
382: with a reference direction, often an angle with the horizontal. The direction angle of a vector is a scalar.
383: • Twovectorsareequalifandonlyiftheyhavethesamemagnitudesanddirections.Parallelvectorshavethesame
384: directionanglesbutmayhavedifferentmagnitudes.Antiparallelvectorshavedirectionanglesthatdifferby 180° .
385: Orthogonal vectors have direction angles that differ by 90° .
386: • Whenavectorismultipliedbyascalar,theresultisanothervectorofadifferentlengththanthelengthoftheoriginal
387: vector. Multiplication by a positive scalar does not change the original direction; only the magnitude is affected.
388: Multiplicationbyanegativescalarreversestheoriginaldirection.Theresultingvectorisantiparalleltotheoriginal
389: vector.Multiplicationbyascalarisdistributive.Vectorscanbedividedbynonzeroscalarsbutcannotbedividedby
390: vectors.
391: • Twoormorevectorscanbeaddedtoformanothervector.Thevectorsumiscalledtheresultantvector.Wecanadd
392: vectors to vectors or scalars to scalars, but we cannot add scalars to vectors. Vector addition is commutative and
393: associative.
394: • Toconstructaresultantvectoroftwovectorsinaplanegeometrically,weusetheparallelogramrule.Toconstruct
395: a resultant vector of many vectors in a plane geometrically, we use the tail-to-head method.
396: 2.2 Coordinate Systems and Components of a Vector
397: • Vectorsaredescribedintermsoftheircomponentsinacoordinatesystem.Intwodimensions(inaplane),vectors
398: have two components. In three dimensions (in space), vectors have three components.
399: • Avectorcomponentofavectorisitspartinanaxisdirection.Thevectorcomponentistheproductoftheunitvector
400: of an axis with its scalar component along this axis. A vector is the resultant of its vector components.
401: • Scalarcomponentsofavectoraredifferencesofcoordinates,wherecoordinatesoftheoriginaresubtractedfrom
402: endpointcoordinatesofavector.Inarectangularsystem,themagnitudeofavectoristhesquarerootofthesumof
403: the squares of its components.
404: • Inaplane,thedirectionofavectorisgivenbyananglethevectorhaswiththepositive x-axis.Thisdirectionangle
405: ismeasuredcounterclockwise.Thescalar x-componentofavectorcanbeexpressedastheproductofitsmagnitude
406: withthecosineofitsdirectionangle,andthescalar y-componentcanbeexpressedastheproductofitsmagnitude
407: with the sine of its direction angle.
408: • Inaplane,therearetwoequivalentcoordinatesystems.TheCartesiancoordinatesystemisdefinedbyunitvectors
409: i^ and j^ along thex-axisandthe y-axis,respectively.Thepolarcoordinatesystemisdefinedbytheradialunit
410: vector r^ , which gives the direction from the origin, and a unit vectort^ , which is perpendicular (orthogonal) to
411: the radial direction.
412: 2.3 Algebra of Vectors
413: • Analyticalmethodsofvectoralgebraallowustofindresultantsofsumsordifferencesofvectorswithouthavingto
414: drawthem.Analyticalmethodsofvectoradditionareexact,contrarytographicalmethods,whichareapproximate.
415: • Analytical methods of vector algebra are used routinely in mechanics, electricity, and magnetism. They are
416: important mathematical tools of physics.
417: 2.4 Products of Vectors
418: • Therearetwokindsofmultiplication forvectors.Onekindofmultiplication isthescalarproduct,alsoknownas
419: thedotproduct.Theotherkindofmultiplicationisthevectorproduct,alsoknownasthecrossproduct.Thescalar
420: product of vectors is a number (scalar). The vector product of vectors is a vector.
421: • Both kinds of multiplication have the distributive property, but only the scalar product has the commutative
422: property. The vector product has the anticommutative property, which means that when we change the order in
423: which two vectors are multiplied, the result acquires a minus sign.
424: • Thescalarproductoftwovectorsisobtainedbymultiplyingtheirmagnitudeswiththecosineoftheanglebetween
425: them. The scalar product of orthogonal vectors vanishes; the scalar product of antiparallel vectors is negative.
426: • Thevectorproductoftwovectorsisavectorperpendiculartobothofthem.Itsmagnitudeisobtainedbymultiplying
427: 94 Chapter 2 | Vectors
428: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
429: 
430: theirmagnitudesbythesineoftheanglebetweenthem.Thedirectionofthevectorproductcanbedeterminedbythe
431: corkscrewright-handrule.Thevectorproductoftwoeitherparallelorantiparallelvectorsvanishes.Themagnitude
432: of the vector product is largest for orthogonal vectors.
433: • Thescalarproductofvectorsisusedtofindanglesbetweenvectorsandinthedefinitionsofderivedscalarphysical
434: quantities such as work or energy.
435: • Thecrossproductofvectorsisusedindefinitionsofderivedvectorphysicalquantitiessuchastorqueormagnetic
436: force, and in describing rotations.

1: 3.1 | Position, Displacement, and Average Velocity
2: Learning Objectives
3: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
4: • Define position, displacement, and distance traveled.
5: • Calculate the total displacement given the position as a function of time.
6: • Determine the total distance traveled.
7: • Calculate the average velocity given the displacement and elapsed time.
8: When you’re in motion, the basic questions to ask are: Where are you? Where are you going? How fast are you getting
9: there? The answers to these questions require that you specify your position, your displacement, and your average
10: velocity—the terms we define in this section.
11: Position
12: Todescribethemotionofanobject,youmustfirstbeabletodescribeits position(x):whereitisatanyparticulartime .
13: More precisely, we need to specify its position relative to a convenient frame of reference. A frame of reference is an
14: arbitrary set of axes from which the position and motion of an object are described. Earth is often used as a frame of
15: reference,andweoftendescribethepositionofanobjectasitrelatestostationaryobjectsonEarth.Forexample,arocket
16: launchcouldbedescribedintermsofthepositionoftherocketwithrespecttoEarthasawhole,whereasacyclist’sposition
17: could be described in terms of where she is in relation to the buildings she passesFigure 3.2. In other cases, we use
18: referenceframesthatarenotstationarybutareinmotionrelativetoEarth.Todescribethepositionofapersoninanairplane,
19: forexample,weusetheairplane,notEarth,asthereferenceframe.Todescribethepositionofanobjectundergoingone-
20: dimensionalmotion,weoftenusethevariable x.Laterinthechapter,duringthediscussionoffreefall,weusethevariable
21: y.
22: Figure 3.2 These cyclists in Vietnam can be described by
23: their position relative to buildings or a canal. Their motion can
24: be described by their change in position, or displacement, in a
25: frame of reference. (credit: modification of work by Suzan
26: Black)
27: Displacement
28: Ifanobjectmovesrelativetoaframeofreference—forexample,ifaprofessormovestotherightrelativetoawhiteboard

30: impliesthatanobjecthasmoved,orhasbeendisplaced.Althoughpositionisthenumericalvalueof xalongastraightline
31: whereanobjectmightbelocated,displacementgivesthe changeinpositionalongthisline.Sincedisplacementindicates
32: direction,itisavectorandcanbeeitherpositiveornegative,dependingonthechoiceofpositivedirection.Also,ananalysis
33: ofmotioncanhavemanydisplacementsembeddedinit.Ifrightispositiveandanobjectmoves2mtotheright,then4m

41: Displacement
42: Displacement Δx is the change in position of an object:
43: (3.1)Δx = xf −x0,
44: where Δx is displacement, xf is the final position, and x0 is the initial position.
45: We use the uppercase Greek letter delta (Δ) to mean “change in” whatever quantity follows it; thus,Δx meanschangein
46: position(finalpositionlessinitialposition).Wealwayssolvefordisplacementbysubtractinginitialposition x0 from final
47: position xf . Note that the SI unit for displacement is the meter, but sometimes we use kilometers or other units of length.
48: Keep in mind that when units other than meters are used in a problem, you may need to convert them to meters to complete
49: the calculation (see Appendix B).
50: Objectsinmotioncanalsohaveaseriesofdisplacements.Inthepreviousexampleofthepacingprofessor,theindividual
51: displacementsare2mand −4 m, giving a total displacement of −2 m. We definetotal displacement ΔxTotal,as thesum
52: of the individual displacements, and express this mathematically with the equation
53: (3.2)ΔxTotal = ∑ Δxi,
54: where Δxi are the individual displacements. In the earlier example,
55: Δx1 = x1 −x0 = 2 − 0 = 2 m.
56: Similarly,
57: Δx2 = x2 −x1 = −2 − (2) = −4 m.
58: Chapter 3 | Motion Along a Straight Line 107
59: 
60: Thus,
61: ΔxTotal = Δx1 + Δx2 = 2 − 4 = −2 m.
62: The total displacement is 2 − 4 = −2 m to the left, or in the negative direction. It is also useful to calculate the magnitude
63: of the displacement, or its size. The magnitude of the displacement is always positive. This is the absolute value of
64: the displacement, because displacement is a vector and cannot have a negative value of magnitude. In our example, the
65: magnitude of the total displacement is 2 m, whereas the magnitudes of the individual displacements are 2 m and 4 m.
66: The magnitude of the total displacement should not be confused with the distance traveled. Distance traveledxTotal , is the
67: total length of the path traveled between two positions. In the previous problem, thedistance traveled is the sum of the
68: magnitudes of the individual displacements:
69: xTotal = |Δx1| + |Δx2| = 2 + 4 = 6 m.

73: is given by the rate at which the position changes with time.

156: Instantaneous Velocity
157: The quantity that tells us how fast an object is moving anywhere along its path is theinstantaneous velocity, usually
158: calledsimply velocity.Itistheaveragevelocitybetweentwopointsonthepathinthelimitthatthetime(andthereforethe
159: displacement)betweenthetwopointsapproacheszero.Toillustratethisideamathematically,weneedtoexpressposition x
160: asacontinuousfunctionof tdenotedby x(t).Theexpressionfortheaveragevelocitybetweentwopointsusingthisnotation
161: is v– = x(t2) −x(t1)
162: t2 −t1
163: . To find the instantaneous velocity at any position, we lett1 = t and t2 = t + Δt. After inserting
164: these expressions into the equation for the average velocity and taking the limit asΔt → 0, we find the expression for the
165: instantaneous velocity:
166: v(t) = limΔt → 0
167: x(t + Δt) −x(t)
168: Δt = dx(t)
169: dt .
170: Instantaneous Velocity
171: Theinstantaneousvelocityofanobjectisthelimitoftheaveragevelocityastheelapsedtimeapproacheszero,orthe
172: derivative ofxwith respect tot:
173: (3.4)v(t) = d
174: dtx(t).
175: Likeaveragevelocity,instantaneousvelocityisavectorwithdimensionoflengthpertime.Theinstantaneousvelocityat
176: aspecifictimepoint t0 is the rate of change of the position function, which is the slope of the position functionx(t) at
177: t0 . Figure 3.6showshowtheaveragevelocity v– = Δx
178: Δt between two times approaches the instantaneous velocity att0.
179: The instantaneous velocity is shown at timet0 , which happens to be at the maximum of the position function. The slope
180: of the position graph is zero at this point, and thus the instantaneous velocity is zero. At other times,t1, t2 , and so on,
181: the instantaneous velocity is not zero because the slope of the position graph would be positive or negative. If the position
182: function had a minimum, the slope of the position graph would also be zero, giving an instantaneous velocity of zero there
183: as well. Thus, the zeros of the velocity function give the minimum and maximum of the position function.
184: Figure 3.6 In a graph of position versus time, the

334: 3.3 | Average and Instantaneous Acceleration
335: Learning Objectives
336: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
337: • Calculate the average acceleration between two points in time.
338: • Calculate the instantaneous acceleration given the functional form of velocity.
339: • Explain the vector nature of instantaneous acceleration and velocity.
340: • Explain the difference between average acceleration and instantaneous acceleration.
341: • Find instantaneous acceleration at a specified time on a graph of velocity versus time.
342: Theimportanceofunderstandingaccelerationspansourday-to-dayexperience,aswellasthevastreachesofouterspace
343: and the tiny world of subatomic physics. In everyday conversation, toaccelerate means to speed up; applying the brake
344: pedal causes a vehicle to slow down. We are familiar with the acceleration of our car, for example. The greater the
345: acceleration,thegreaterthechangeinvelocityoveragiventime.Accelerationiswidelyseeninexperimentalphysics.In
346: linearparticleacceleratorexperiments,forexample,subatomicparticlesareacceleratedtoveryhighvelocitiesincollision
347: experiments, which tell us information about the structure of the subatomic world as well as the origin of the universe.
348: In space, cosmic rays are subatomic particles that have been accelerated to very high energies in supernovas (exploding
349: massive stars) and active galactic nuclei. It is important to understand the processes that accelerate cosmic rays because
350: these rays contain highly penetrating radiation that can damage electronics flown on spacecraft, for example.
351: Average Acceleration
352: The formal definition of acceleration is consistent with these notions just described, but is more inclusive.
353: Average Acceleration
354: Average acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes:
355: (3.8)a– = Δv
356: Δt = vf −v0
357: tf −t0
358: ,
359: 116 Chapter 3 | Motion Along a Straight Line
360: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
361: 
362: where a− is average acceleration,vis velocity, andtis time. (The bar over theameansaverageacceleration.)
363: Because acceleration is velocity in meters per second divided by time in seconds, the SI units for acceleration are often
364: abbreviated m/s2—that is, meters per second squared or meters per second per second. This literally means by how
365: many meters per second the velocity changes every second. Recall that velocity is a vector—it has both magnitude and
366: direction—whichmeansthatachangeinvelocitycanbeachangeinmagnitude(orspeed),butitcanalsobeachangein
367: direction.Forexample,ifarunnertravelingat10km/hdueeastslowstoastop,reversesdirection,andcontinuesherrun
368: at10km/hduewest,hervelocityhaschangedasaresultofthechangeindirection,althoughthe magnitudeofthevelocity
369: isthe same inbothdirections. Thus,acceleration occurs whenvelocity changes inmagnitude (anincrease ordecrease in
370: speed) or in direction, or both.
371: Acceleration as a Vector
372: Accelerationisavectorinthesamedirectionasthe changeinvelocity, Δv. Since velocity is a vector, it can change
373: in magnitude or in direction, or both. Acceleration is, therefore, a change in speed or direction, or both.
374: Keep in mind that although acceleration is in the direction of the change in velocity, it is not always in the direction of
375: motion. When an object slows down, its acceleration is opposite to the direction of its motion. Although this is commonly
376: referred to asdeceleration Figure 3.10, we say the train is accelerating in a direction opposite to its direction of motion.
377: Figure 3.10 A subway train in Sao Paulo, Brazil, decelerates
378: as it comes into a station. It is accelerating in a direction
379: opposite to its direction of motion. (credit: modification of work
380: by Yusuke Kawasaki)
381: The termdeceleration can cause confusion in our analysis because it is not a vector and it does not point to a specific
382: directionwithrespecttoacoordinatesystem,sowedonotuseit.Accelerationisavector,sowemustchoosetheappropriate
383: signforitinourchosencoordinatesystem.Inthecaseofthetrainin Figure 3.10,accelerationis inthenegativedirection
384: in the chosen coordinate system, so we say the train is undergoing negative acceleration.
385: If an object in motion has a velocity in the positive direction with respect to a chosen origin and it acquires a constant
386: negativeacceleration,theobjecteventuallycomestoarestandreversesdirection.Ifwewaitlongenough,theobjectpasses
387: through the origin going in the opposite direction. This is illustrated in Figure 3.11.
388: Chapter 3 | Motion Along a Straight Line 117
389: 
390: Figure 3.11 An object in motion with a velocity vector toward the east under
391: negative acceleration comes to a rest and reverses direction. It passes the origin going
392: in the opposite direction after a long enough time.

432: Instantaneous Acceleration
433: Instantaneousacceleration a,or accelerationataspecificinstantintime ,isobtainedusingthesameprocessdiscussedfor
434: instantaneousvelocity.Thatis,wecalculatetheaverageaccelerationbetweentwopointsintimeseparatedby Δt and let
435: Δt approach zero. The result is the derivative of the velocity functionv(t), which isinstantaneous acceleration and is

439: Thus, similar to velocity being the derivative of the position function, instantaneous acceleration is the derivative of the

441: acceleration at timet0 is the slope of the tangent line to the velocity-versus-time graph at timet0. We see that average
442: acceleration a– = Δv

444: that velocity has a maximum when its slope is zero. This time corresponds to the zero of the acceleration function. In
445: part (b), instantaneous acceleration at the minimum velocity is shown, which is also zero, since the slope of the curve is
446: zero there, too. Thus, for a given velocity function, the zeros of the acceleration function give either the minimum or the
447: maximum velocity.

559: 3.4 | Motion with Constant Acceleration
560: Learning Objectives
561: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
562: • Identify which equations of motion are to be used to solve for unknowns.
563: • Use appropriate equations of motion to solve a two-body pursuit problem.
564: You might guess that the greater the acceleration of, say, a car moving away from a stop sign, the greater the car’s
565: displacementinagiventime.But,wehavenotdevelopedaspecificequationthatrelatesaccelerationanddisplacement.In
566: thissection,welookatsomeconvenientequationsforkinematicrelationships,startingfromthedefinitionsofdisplacement,
567: velocity,andacceleration.Wefirstinvestigateasingleobjectinmotion,calledsingle-bodymotion.Thenweinvestigatethe
568: motion of two objects, called two-body pursuit problems.
569: Notation
570: First,letusmakesomesimplificationsinnotation.Takingtheinitialtimetobezero,asiftimeismeasuredwithastopwatch,
571: is a great simplification. Since elapsed time isΔt = tf −t0 , taking t0 = 0 means thatΔt = tf , the final time on the
572: stopwatch. When initial time is taken to be zero, we use the subscript 0 to denote initial values of position and velocity.
573: That is,x0 istheinitialposition and v0 istheinitialvelocity .Weputnosubscriptsonthefinalvalues.Thatis, tisthe
574: finaltime,xisthefinalposition ,and visthefinalvelocity .Thisgivesasimplerexpressionforelapsedtime, Δt = t. It also
575: simplifies the expression forxdisplacement,whichisnow Δx = x −x0 . Also, it simplifies the expression for change in
576: velocity, which is now Δv = v −v0 . To summarize, using the simplified notation, with the initial time taken to be zero,
577: 124 Chapter 3 | Motion Along a Straight Line
578: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
579: 
580: Δt = t
581: Δx = x −x0
582: Δv = v −v0,
583: where the subscript 0 denotes an initial value and the absence of a subscript denotes a final value in whatever motion is
584: under consideration.
585: Wenowmaketheimportantassumptionthat accelerationisconstant .Thisassumptionallowsustoavoidusingcalculusto
586: findinstantaneousacceleration.Sinceaccelerationisconstant,theaverageandinstantaneousaccelerationsareequal—that
587: is,
588: a– = a = constant.
589: Thus, we can use the symbolaforaccelerationatalltimes.Assumingaccelerationtobeconstantdoesnotseriouslylimit
590: the situations we can study nor does it degrade the accuracy of our treatment. For one thing, accelerationis constant in
591: a great number of situations. Furthermore, in many other situations we can describe motion accurately by assuming a
592: constantaccelerationequaltotheaverageaccelerationforthatmotion.Lastly,formotionduringwhichaccelerationchanges
593: drastically,suchasacaracceleratingtotopspeedandthenbrakingtoastop,motioncanbeconsideredinseparateparts,
594: each of which has its own constant acceleration.
595: Displacement and Position from Velocity
596: To get our first two equations, we start with the definition of average velocity:
597: v– = Δx
598: Δt .
599: Substituting the simplified notation for Δx and Δt yields
600: v– = x −x0
601: t .
602: Solving forxgives us
603: (3.10)x = x0 +v–t,
604: where the average velocity is
605: (3.11)v– = v0 +v
606: 2 .
607: The equationv– = v0 +v
608: 2 reflects the fact that when acceleration is constant,v– is just the simple average of the initial
609: and final velocities.Figure 3.18illustratesthisconceptgraphically.Inpart(a)ofthefigure,accelerationisconstant,with
610: velocity increasing at a constant rate. The average velocity during the 1-h interval from 40 km/h to 80 km/h is 60 km/h:
611: v– = v0 +v
612: 2 = 40 km/h + 80 km/h
613: 2 = 60 km/h.
614: In part (b), acceleration is not constant. During the 1-h interval, velocity is closer to 80 km/h than 40 km/h. Thus, the average
615: velocity is greater than in part (a).

163: a = v −v0
164: t .

166: small, approaching zero in the limit that the initial and final velocities are equal. On the contrary, in the limitt → 0 for a

171: 2(x −x0).

173: displacement approaches zero. Acceleration approaches zero in the limit the difference in initial and final velocities
174: approaches zero for a finite displacement.

378: 3.5 | Free Fall
379: Learning Objectives
380: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
381: • Use the kinematic equations with the variables y and g to analyze free-fall motion.
382: • Describe how the values of the position, velocity, and acceleration change during a free fall.
383: • Solve for the position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time when an object is in a free
384: fall.
385: Aninterestingapplicationof Equation 3.4 through Equation 3.14 iscalled freefall,whichdescribesthemotionofan
386: object falling in a gravitational field, such as near the surface of Earth or other celestial objects of planetary size. Let’s
387: assumethebodyisfallinginastraightlineperpendiculartothesurface,soitsmotionisone-dimensional.Forexample,we
388: canestimatethedepthofaverticalmineshaftbydroppingarockintoitandlisteningfortherocktohitthebottom.But
389: “falling,”inthecontextoffreefall,doesnotnecessarilyimplythebodyismovingfromagreaterheighttoalesserheight.
390: If a ball is thrown upward, the equations of free fall apply equally to its ascent as well as its descent.
391: Gravity
392: Themostremarkable andunexpected fact aboutfalling objects isthat ifairresistance andfriction arenegligible, thenin
393: agivenlocationallobjectsfalltowardthecenterofEarthwiththe sameconstantacceleration ,independentoftheirmass.
394: Thisexperimentallydeterminedfactisunexpectedbecausewearesoaccustomedtotheeffectsofairresistanceandfriction
395: that we expect light objects to fall slower than heavy ones. Until Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) proved otherwise, people
396: believedthataheavierobjecthasagreateraccelerationinafreefall.Wenowknowthisisnotthecase.Intheabsenceof
397: air resistance, heavy objects arrive at the ground at the same time as lighter objects when dropped from the same height
398: Figure 3.26.
399: 136 Chapter 3 | Motion Along a Straight Line
400: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
401: 
402: Figure 3.26 A hammer and a feather fall with the same constant acceleration if air resistance is negligible. This is a general
403: characteristic of gravity not unique to Earth, as astronaut David R. Scott demonstrated in 1971 on the Moon, where the
404: acceleration from gravity is only 1.67 m/s2and there is no atmosphere.
405: Intherealworld,airresistancecancausealighterobjecttofallslowerthanaheavierobjectofthesamesize.Atennisball
406: reachesthegroundafterabaseballdroppedatthesametime.(Itmightbedifficulttoobservethedifferenceiftheheightis
407: notlarge.)Airresistanceopposesthemotionofanobjectthroughtheair,andfrictionbetweenobjects—suchasbetween
408: clothes and a laundry chute or between a stone and a pool into which it is dropped—also opposes motion between them.
409: For the ideal situations of these first few chapters, an objectfallingwithoutairresistance orfriction is defined to be in
410: free fall. The force of gravity causes objects to fall toward the center of Earth. The acceleration of free-falling objects
411: is therefore calledacceleration due to gravity. Acceleration due to gravity is constant, which means we can apply the
412: kinematicequationstoanyfallingobjectwhereairresistanceandfrictionarenegligible.Thisopenstousabroadclassof
413: interesting situations.
414: Accelerationduetogravityissoimportantthatitsmagnitudeisgivenitsownsymbol, g.Itisconstantatanygivenlocation
415: on Earth and has the average value
416: g = 9.81 m/s2 (or 32.2 ft/s2).
417: Although g varies from 9.78 m/s2 to 9.83 m/s2, depending on latitude, altitude, underlying geological formations, and
418: local topography, let’s use an average value of 9.8 m/s2 rounded to two significant figures in this text unless specified
419: otherwise.Neglectingtheseeffectsonthevalueof gasaresultofpositiononEarth’ssurface,aswellaseffectsresulting
420: from Earth’s rotation, we take the direction of acceleration due to gravity to be downward (toward the center of Earth).
421: In fact, its directiondefines what we call vertical. Note that whether accelerationa in the kinematic equations has the
422: value +g or −g depends on how we define our coordinate system. If we define the upward direction as positive, then
423: a = −g = −9.8 m/s2, and if we define the downward direction as positive, then a = g = 9.8 m/s2 .

68: SUMMARY
69: 3.1 Position, Displacement, and Average Velocity
70: • Kinematicsisthedescriptionofmotionwithoutconsideringitscauses.Inthischapter,itislimitedtomotionalong
71: a straight line, called one-dimensional motion.
72: • Displacement is the change in position of an object. The SI unit for displacement is the meter. Displacement has
73: direction as well as magnitude.
74: • Distance traveled is the total length of the path traveled between two positions.
75: • Timeismeasuredintermsofchange.Thetimebetweentwopositionpoints x1 and x2 is Δt = t2 −t1 . Elapsed
76: time for an event isΔt = tf −t0 , wheretf is the final time andt0 is the initial time. The initial time is often taken
77: to be zero.
78: • Averagevelocity v– is defined as displacement divided by elapsed time. Ifx1, t1 and x2, t2 are two position time
79: points, the average velocity between these points is
80: v– = Δx
81: Δt = x2 −x1
82: t2 −t1
83: .
84: 3.2 Instantaneous Velocity and Speed
85: • Instantaneousvelocityisacontinuousfunctionoftimeandgivesthevelocityatanypointintimeduringaparticle’s
86: motion. We can calculate the instantaneous velocity at a specific time by taking the derivative of the position
87: function, which gives us the functional form of instantaneous velocityv(t).
88: • Instantaneous velocity is a vector and can be negative.
89: • Instantaneous speed is found by taking the absolute value of instantaneous velocity, and it is always positive.
90: • Average speed is total distance traveled divided by elapsed time.
91: • The slope of a position-versus-time graph at a specific time gives instantaneous velocity at that time.
92: 3.3 Average and Instantaneous Acceleration
93: • Accelerationistherateatwhichvelocitychanges.Accelerationisavector;ithasbothamagnitudeanddirection.
94: The SI unit for acceleration is meters per second squared.
95: • Acceleration can be caused by a change in the magnitude or the direction of the velocity, or both.
96: • Instantaneousacceleration a(t)isacontinuousfunctionoftimeandgivestheaccelerationatanyspecifictimeduring
97: themotion.Itiscalculated fromthederivativeofthevelocityfunction.Instantaneousacceleration istheslopeof
98: the velocity-versus-time graph.
99: Chapter 3 | Motion Along a Straight Line 147
100: 
101: • Negative acceleration (sometimes called deceleration) is acceleration in the negative direction in the chosen
102: coordinate system.
103: 3.4 Motion with Constant Acceleration
104: • Whenanalyzingone-dimensionalmotionwithconstantacceleration,identifytheknownquantitiesandchoosethe
105: appropriateequationstosolvefortheunknowns.Eitheroneortwoofthekinematicequationsareneededtosolve
106: for the unknowns, depending on the known and unknown quantities.
107: • Two-body pursuit problems always require two equations to be solved simultaneously for the unknowns.
108: 3.5 Free Fall
109: • An object in free fall experiences constant acceleration if air resistance is negligible.
110: • On Earth, all free-falling objects have an accelerationgdue to gravity, which averages g = 9.81 m/s2 .
111: • For objects in free fall, the upward direction is normally taken as positive for displacement, velocity, and
112: acceleration.
113: 3.6 Finding Velocity and Displacement from Acceleration
114: • Integral calculus gives us a more complete formulation of kinematics.
115: • If accelerationa(t) is known, we can use integral calculus to derive expressions for velocityv(t) and positionx(t).
116: • If acceleration is constant, the integral equations reduce toEquation 3.12 and Equation 3.13 for motion with
117: constant acceleration.

776: 4.1 | Displacement and Velocity Vectors
777: Learning Objectives
778: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
779: • Calculate position vectors in a multidimensional displacement problem.
780: • Solve for the displacement in two or three dimensions.
781: • Calculate the velocity vector given the position vector as a function of time.
782: • Calculate the average velocity in multiple dimensions.
783: Displacement and velocity in two or three dimensions are straightforward extensions of the one-dimensional definitions.
784: However, now they are vector quantities, so calculations with them have to follow the rules of vector algebra, not scalar
785: algebra.

968: The Independence of Perpendicular Motions
969: Whenwelookatthethree-dimensionalequationsforpositionandvelocitywritteninunitvectornotation, Equation 4.2
970: and Equation 4.5,weseethecomponentsoftheseequationsareseparateanduniquefunctionsoftimethatdonotdepend
971: ononeanother.Motionalongthe xdirectionhasnopartofitsmotionalongthe yandzdirections,andsimilarlyfortheother
972: two coordinate axes. Thus, the motion of an object in two or three dimensions can be divided into separate, independent
973: motions along the perpendicular axes of the coordinate system in which the motion takes place.
974: To illustrate this concept with respect to displacement, consider a woman walking from pointAto pointBin a city with
975: squareblocks.Thewomantakingthepathfrom AtoBmaywalkeastforsomanyblocksandthennorth(twoperpendicular
976: directions)foranothersetofblockstoarriveat B.Howfarshewalkseastisaffectedonlybyhermotioneastward.Similarly,
977: how far she walks north is affected only by her motion northward.
978: Independence of Motion
979: Inthekinematicdescriptionofmotion,weareabletotreatthehorizontalandverticalcomponentsofmotionseparately.
980: In many cases, motion in the horizontal direction does not affect motion in the vertical direction, and vice versa.
981: An example illustrating the independence of vertical and horizontal motions is given by two baseballs. One baseball is
982: droppedfromrest.Atthesameinstant,anotheristhrownhorizontallyfromthesameheightanditfollowsacurvedpath.A
983: stroboscope captures the positions of the balls at fixed time intervals as they fall (Figure 4.8).
984: 164 Chapter 4 | Motion in Two and Three Dimensions

989: velocity. Each subsequent position is an equal time interval.

1: 4.2 | Acceleration Vector
2: Learning Objectives
3: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
4: • Calculate the acceleration vector given the velocity function in unit vector notation.
5: • Describe the motion of a particle with a constant acceleration in three dimensions.
6: • Use the one-dimensional motion equations along perpendicular axes to solve a problem in two
7: or three dimensions with a constant acceleration.
8: • Express the acceleration in unit vector notation.
9: Instantaneous Acceleration
10: Inadditiontoobtainingthedisplacementandvelocityvectorsofanobjectinmotion,weoftenwanttoknowits acceleration
11: vector at any point in time along its trajectory. This acceleration vector is the instantaneous acceleration and it can be
12: obtainedfromthederivativewithrespecttotimeofthevelocityfunction,aswehaveseeninapreviouschapter.Theonly
13: difference in two or three dimensions is that these are now vector quantities. Taking the derivative with respect to time
14: v→ (t), we find
15: (4.8)a→ (t) = limt → 0
16: v→ (t + Δt) − v→ (t)
17: Δt = d v→ (t)
18: dt .
19: The acceleration in terms of components is
20: (4.9)a→ (t) =dvx(t)
21: dt i^ + dvy(t)
22: dt j^ + dvz(t)
23: dt k^.
24: Also, since the velocity is the derivative of the position function, we can write the acceleration in terms of the second
25: derivative of the position function:
26: (4.10)
27: a→ (t) =d2x(t)
28: dt 2 i^ + d2y(t)
29: dt 2 j^ + d2z(t)
30: dt 2 k^.
31: Example 4.4
32: Finding an Acceleration Vector

34: What is the acceleration vector att= 2.0 s? Find its magnitude and direction.
35: Solution
36: (a)Wetakethefirstderivativewithrespecttotimeofthevelocityfunctiontofindtheacceleration.Thederivative
37: is taken component by component:
38: a→ (t) = 5.0i^ + 2.0tj^ − 6.0t2 k^m/s2.
39: 166 Chapter 4 | Motion in Two and Three Dimensions
40: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
41: 
42: (b) Evaluating a→ (2.0 s) = 5.0i^ + 4.0j^ − 24.0k^m/s2 gives us the direction in unit vector notation. The
43: magnitude of the acceleration is | a→ (2.0 s)| = 5.0 2 + 4.02 + (−24.0)2 = 24.8 m/s2.
44: Significance
45: In this example we find that acceleration has a time dependence and is changing throughout the motion. Let’s
46: consider a different velocity function for the particle.

171: 4.3 | Projectile Motion
172: Learning Objectives
173: By the end of this section, you will be able to:
174: • Use one-dimensional motion in perpendicular directions to analyze projectile motion.
175: • Calculate the range, time of flight, and maximum height of a projectile that is launched and
176: impacts a flat, horizontal surface.
177: • Find the time of flight and impact velocity of a projectile that lands at a different height from that
178: of launch.
179: • Calculate the trajectory of a projectile.
180: Projectile motion is the motion of an object thrown or projected into the air, subject only to acceleration as a result of
181: gravity. The applications of projectile motion in physics and engineering are numerous. Some examples include meteors
182: as they enter Earth’s atmosphere, fireworks, and the motion of any ball in sports. Such objects are calledprojectilesand
183: theirpathiscalleda trajectory.Themotionoffallingobjectsasdiscussedin Motion Along a Straight Lineisasimple
184: one-dimensional type of projectile motion in which there is no horizontal movement. In this section, we consider two-
185: dimensional projectile motion, and our treatment neglects the effects of air resistance.
186: The most important fact to remember here is thatmotions along perpendicular axes are independentand thus can be
187: analyzed separately. We discussed this fact inDisplacement and Velocity Vectors, where we saw that vertical and
188: horizontalmotionsareindependent.Thekeytoanalyzingtwo-dimensionalprojectilemotionistobreakitintotwomotions:
189: onealongthehorizontalaxisandtheotheralongthevertical.(Thischoiceofaxesisthemostsensiblebecauseacceleration
190: resultingfromgravityisvertical;thus,thereisnoaccelerationalongthehorizontalaxiswhenairresistanceisnegligible.)
191: As is customary, we call the horizontal axis thex-axis and the vertical axis they-axis. It is not required that we use this
192: choiceofaxes;itissimplyconvenientinthecaseofgravitationalacceleration.Inothercaseswemaychooseadifferentset
193: ofaxes. Figure 4.11illustratesthenotationfordisplacement,wherewedefine s→ to be the total displacement, andx→
194: and y→ are its component vectors along the horizontal and vertical axes, respectively. The magnitudes of these vectors are
195: Chapter 4 | Motion in Two and Three Dimensions 171
