198: Figure 4.11 The total displacementsof a soccer ball at a point along its path. The vector s→ has
199: components x→ and y→ along the horizontal and vertical axes. Its magnitude issand it makes an angle
200: θwith the horizontal.
201: Todescribeprojectilemotioncompletely,wemustincludevelocityandacceleration,aswellasdisplacement.Wemustfind
202: their components along thex- andy-axes. Let’s assume all forces except gravity (such as air resistance and friction, for
203: example)arenegligible.Definingthepositivedirectiontobeupward,thecomponentsofaccelerationarethenverysimple:
204: ay = −g = −9.8 m/s2 ( − 32 ft/s2).

593: 4.4 | Uniform Circular Motion
594: Learning Objectives

603: Uniform circular motion is a specific type of motion in which an object travels in a circle with a constant speed. For
604: example,anypointonapropellerspinningataconstantrateisexecutinguniformcircularmotion.Otherexamplesarethe
605: second,minute,andhourhandsofawatch.Itisremarkablethatpointsontheserotatingobjectsareactuallyaccelerating,
606: although the rotation rate is a constant. To see this, we must analyze the motion in terms of vectors.
607: Centripetal Acceleration
608: In one-dimensional kinematics, objects with a constant speed have zero acceleration. However, in two- and three-
609: dimensionalkinematics,evenifthespeedisaconstant,aparticlecanhaveaccelerationifitmovesalongacurvedtrajectory
610: suchasacircle.Inthiscasethevelocityvectorischanging,or d v→ /dt ≠ 0. This is shown inFigure 4.18.Astheparticle
611: moves counterclockwise in timeΔt on the circular path, its position vector moves fromr→ (t) to r→ (t + Δt). The
612: velocity vector has constant magnitude and is tangent to the path as it changes fromv→ (t) to v→ (t + Δt), changing its
613: direction only. Since the velocity vectorv→ (t) is perpendicular to the position vectorr→ (t), the triangles formed by the
614: position vectors andΔ r→ , and the velocity vectors andΔ v→ are similar. Furthermore, since| r→ (t)| = | r→ (t + Δt)|
615: and | v→ (t)| = | v→ (t + Δt)|, the two triangles are isosceles. From these facts we can make the assertion
616: Δvv = Δrr or Δv = vrΔr.

622: points toward the center of the circle in the limit Δt → 0.

423: SUMMARY
424: 4.1 Displacement and Velocity Vectors
425: • The position function r→ (t) gives the position as a function of time of a particle moving in two or three
426: dimensions. Graphically, it is a vector from the origin of a chosen coordinate system to the point where the particle
427: is located at a specific time.
428: • Thedisplacementvector Δ r→ gives the shortest distance between any two points on the trajectory of a particle in
429: two or three dimensions.
430: • Instantaneousvelocitygivesthespeedanddirectionofaparticleataspecifictimeonitstrajectoryintwoorthree
431: dimensions, and is a vector in two and three dimensions.
432: • The velocity vector is tangent to the trajectory of the particle.
433: • Displacement r→ (t) can be written as a vector sum of the one-dimensional displacementsx→ (t), y→ (t), z→ (t)
434: along thex,y, andzdirections.
435: • Velocity v→ (t) can be written as a vector sum of the one-dimensional velocitiesvx(t), vy(t), vz(t) along thex,y,
436: andzdirections.
437: 196 Chapter 4 | Motion in Two and Three Dimensions
438: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
439: 
440: • Motion in any given direction is independent of motion in a perpendicular direction.
441: 4.2 Acceleration Vector
442: • Intwoandthreedimensions,theaccelerationvectorcanhaveanarbitrarydirectionanddoesnotnecessarilypoint
443: along a given component of the velocity.
444: • The instantaneous acceleration is produced by a change in velocity taken over a very short (infinitesimal) time
445: period.Instantaneousaccelerationisavectorintwoorthreedimensions.Itisfoundbytakingthederivativeofthe
446: velocity function with respect to time.
447: • In three dimensions, acceleration a→ (t) can be written as a vector sum of the one-dimensional accelerations
448: ax(t), ay(t), andaz(t) along thex-,y-, andz-axes.
449: • The kinematic equations for constant acceleration can be written as the vector sum of the constant acceleration
450: equations in thex,y, andzdirections.
451: 4.3 Projectile Motion
452: • Projectile motion is the motion of an object subject only to the acceleration of gravity, where the acceleration is
453: constant, as near the surface of Earth.
454: • Tosolveprojectilemotionproblems,weanalyzethemotionoftheprojectileinthehorizontalandverticaldirections
455: using the one-dimensional kinematic equations forxandy.
456: • The time of flight of a projectile launched with initial vertical velocity v0y on an even surface is given by
457: Ttof = 2(v0 sinθ)
458: g .
459: This equation is valid only when the projectile lands at the same elevation from which it was launched.
460: • Themaximumhorizontaldistancetraveledbyaprojectileiscalledtherange.Again,theequationforrangeisvalid
461: only when the projectile lands at the same elevation from which it was launched.
462: 4.4 Uniform Circular Motion
463: • Uniform circular motion is motion in a circle at constant speed.
464: • Centripetal acceleration a→
465: C is the acceleration a particle must have to follow a circular path. Centripetal
466: acceleration always points toward the center of rotation and has magnitude aC = v2/r.
467: • Nonuniformcircularmotionoccurswhenthereistangentialaccelerationofanobjectexecutingcircularmotionsuch
468: thatthespeedoftheobjectischanging.Thisaccelerationiscalledtangentialacceleration a→
469: T. The magnitude of
470: tangential acceleration is the time rate of change of the magnitude of the velocity. The tangential acceleration vector
471: is tangential to the circle, whereas the centripetal acceleration vector points radially inward toward the center of the
472: circle. The total acceleration is the vector sum of tangential and centripetal accelerations.
473: • Anobjectexecutinguniformcircularmotioncanbedescribedwithequationsofmotion.Thepositionvectorofthe
474: objectis r→ (t) =A cosωt i^ + A sinωt j^, whereAisthemagnitude | r→ (t)|, which is also the radius of the
475: circle, and ω is the angular frequency.
476: 4.5 Relative Motion in One and Two Dimensions
477: • Whenanalyzingmotionofanobject,thereferenceframeintermsofposition,velocity,andaccelerationneedstobe
478: specified.
479: • Relativevelocityisthevelocityofanobjectasobservedfromaparticularreferenceframe,anditvarieswiththe
480: choice of reference frame.
481: Chapter 4 | Motion in Two and Three Dimensions 197
482: 
483: • IfSand S′ are two reference frames moving relative to each other at a constant velocity, then the velocity of an
484: object relative toSis equal to its velocity relative to S′ plus the velocity of S′ relative toS.
485: • Iftworeferenceframesaremovingrelativetoeachotherataconstantvelocity,thentheaccelerationsofanobject
486: as observed in both reference frames are equal.

37: The study of motion is calledkinematics, but kinematics only describes the way objects move—their velocity and their
38: acceleration. Dynamicsisthestudyofhowforcesaffectthemotionofobjectsandsystems.Itconsidersthecausesofmotion
39: ofobjectsandsystemsofinterest,whereasystemisanythingbeinganalyzed.Thefoundationofdynamicsarethelawsof
40: motion stated by Isaac Newton (1642–1727). These laws provide an example of the breadth and simplicity of principles
41: under which nature functions. They are also universal laws in that they apply to situations on Earth and in space.
42: Newton’s laws of motion were just one part of the monumental work that has made him legendary (Figure 5.2). The
43: developmentofNewton’slawsmarksthetransitionfromtheRenaissancetothemodernera.Notuntiltheadventofmodern
44: physicswasitdiscoveredthatNewton’slawsproduceagooddescriptionofmotiononlywhentheobjectsaremovingat
45: speedsmuchlessthanthespeedoflightandwhenthoseobjectsarelargerthanthesizeofmostmolecules(about 10−9
46: m in diameter). These constraints define the realm of Newtonian mechanics. At the beginning of the twentieth century,
47: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) developed the theory of relativity and, along with many other scientists, quantum mechanics.
48: Quantum mechanics does not have the constraints present in Newtonian physics. All of the situations we consider in this
49: chapter, and all those preceding the introduction of relativity inRelativity (http://cnx.org/content/m58555/latest/) ,
50: are in the realm of Newtonian physics.
51: Figure 5.2 Isaac Newton (1642–1727) published his amazing

99: Development of the Force Concept
100: Aquantitative definition offorce can be based onsome standard force, just as distance is measured in units relative to a
101: standardlength.Onepossibilityistostretchaspringacertainfixeddistance(Figure 5.5 )andusetheforceitexertstopull
102: itselfbacktoitsrelaxedshape—calleda restoringforce—asastandard.Themagnitudeofallotherforcescanbeconsidered
103: asmultiplesofthisstandardunitofforce.Manyotherpossibilitiesexistforstandardforces.Somealternativedefinitionsof
104: force will be given later in this chapter.
105: Figure 5.5 The force exerted by a stretched spring can be used as a standard unit of force. (a)
106: This spring has a lengthxwhen undistorted. (b) When stretched a distance Δx, the spring exerts
107: a restoring force F→
108: restore, which is reproducible. (c) A spring scale is one device that uses a
109: spring to measure force. The force F→
110: restore is exerted on whatever is attached to the hook.
111: Here, this force has a magnitude of six units of the force standard being employed.
112: Let’s analyze force more deeply. Suppose a physics student sits at a table, working diligently on his homework (Figure
113: 5.6). What external forces act on him? Can we determine the origin of these forces?
114: 210 Chapter 5 | Newton's Laws of Motion
115: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
116: 
117: Figure 5.6 (a) The forces acting on the student are due to the
118: chair, the table, the floor, and Earth’s gravitational attraction. (b) In
119: solving a problem involving the student, we may want to consider
120: only the forces acting along the line running through his torso. A
121: free-body diagram for this situation is shown.
122: In most situations, forces are grouped into two categories:contact forcesand field forces. As you might guess, contact
123: forcesareduetodirectphysicalcontactbetweenobjects.Forexample,thestudentin Figure 5.6 experiencesthecontact
124: forces C→ , F→ , and T→ , which are exerted by the chair on his posterior, the floor on his feet, and the table on his
125: forearms, respectively. Field forces, however, act without the necessity of physical contact between objects. They depend
126: on the presence of a “field” in the region of space surrounding the body under consideration. Since the student is in Earth’s
127: gravitational field, he feels a gravitational force w→ ; in other words, he has weight.
128: You can think of a field as a property of space that is detectable by the forces it exerts. Scientists think there are only four
129: fundamental force fields in nature. These are the gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear, and weak fields (we consider
130: these four forces in nature later in this text). As noted forw→ in Figure 5.6,thegravitationalfieldisresponsibleforthe
131: weight of a body. The forces of the electromagnetic field include those of static electricity and magnetism; they are also
132: responsiblefortheattractionamongatomsinbulkmatter.Boththestrongnuclearandtheweakforcefieldsareeffective
133: onlyoverdistancesroughlyequaltoalengthofscalenolargerthananatomicnucleus( 10−15 m ). Their range is so small
134: that neither field has influence in the macroscopic world of Newtonian mechanics.
135: Contact forces are fundamentally electromagnetic. While the elbow of the student inFigure 5.6 is in contact with the
136: tabletop, the atomic charges in his skin interact electromagnetically with the charges in the surface of the table. The net
137: (total)resultistheforce T→ . Similarly, when adhesive tape sticks to a piece of paper, the atoms of the tape are intermingled
138: with those of the paper to cause a net electromagnetic force between the two objects. However, in the context of Newtonian
139: mechanics, the electromagnetic origin of contact forces is not an important concern.
140: Vector Notation for Force
141: As previously discussed, force is a vector; it has both magnitude and direction. The SI unit of force is called the

213: Experience suggests that an object at rest remains at rest if left alone and that an object in motion tends to slow down
214: and stop unless some effort is made to keep it moving. However,Newton’s first lawgives a deeper explanation of this
215: observation.
216: Newton’s First Law of Motion
217: Abodyatrestremainsatrestor,ifinmotion,remainsinmotionatconstantvelocityunlessactedonbyanetexternal
218: force.

221: nor the direction of the velocity vector changes. We can use Figure 5.7to consider the two parts of Newton’s first law.
222: Figure 5.7 (a) A hockey puck is shown at rest; it remains at rest until an outside

224: motion; it continues in motion in a straight line until an outside force causes it to

228: (a change in either magnitude or direction) to occur. This cause is a net external force, which we defined earlier in the
229: chapter.Anobjectslidingacrossatableorfloorslowsdownduetothenetforceoffrictionactingontheobject.Iffriction
230: disappears, will the object still slow down?

232: what happens to an object sliding along a rough horizontal surface. The object quickly grinds to a halt. If we spray the
233: surfacewithtalcumpowdertomakethesurfacesmoother,theobjectslidesfarther.Ifwemakethesurfaceevensmootherby
234: rubbinglubricatingoilonit,theobjectslidesfartheryet.Extrapolatingtoafrictionlesssurfaceandignoringairresistance,
235: Chapter 5 | Newton's Laws of Motion 213

238: Newton’s first law). The object would not slow down if friction were eliminated.
239: Consideranairhockeytable(Figure 5.8 ).Whentheairisturnedoff,thepuckslidesonlyashortdistancebeforefriction

246: Newton’s first law is general and can be applied to anything from an object sliding on a table to a satellite in orbit to
247: bloodpumpedfromtheheart.Experimentshaveverifiedthatanychangeinvelocity(speedordirection)mustbecaused

266: Earlier,westatedNewton’sfirstlawas“Abodyatrestremainsatrestor,ifinmotion,remainsinmotionatconstantvelocity

273: itsvelocityrelativetoagivenframeisconstant,thenthatframeissaidtobeinertial.Sobydefinition,aninertialreference

279: Inertial Reference Frame
280: A reference frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial. A reference frame
281: accelerating relative to an inertial frame is not inertial.
282: Are inertial frames common in nature? It turns out that well within experimental error, a reference frame at rest relative
283: tothemostdistant,or“fixed,”starsisinertial.Allframesmovinguniformlywithrespecttothisfixed-starframearealso
284: inertial. Forexample, anonrotating reference frameattached totheSunis,forallpractical purposes,inertial, because its
285: velocityrelativetothefixedstarsdoesnotvarybymorethanonepartin 1010. Earth accelerates relative to the fixed stars
286: because it rotates on its axis and revolves around the Sun; hence, a reference frame attached to its surface is not inertial.
287: For most problems, however, such a frame serves as a sufficiently accurate approximation to an inertial frame, because
288: the acceleration of a point on Earth’s surface relative to the fixed stars is rather small (< 3.4 × 10−2 m/s2 ). Thus, unless
289: indicated otherwise, we consider reference frames fixed on Earth to be inertial.
290: Finally, no particular inertial frame is more special than any other. As far as the laws of nature are concerned, all
291: inertial frames are equivalent. In analyzing a problem, we choose one inertial frame over another simply on the basis of
292: convenience.

538: Strategy
539: Although forces are acting both vertically and horizontally, we assume the vertical forces cancel because there

541: Directions are indicated with plus or minus signs, with right taken as the positive direction. See the free-body
542: diagram in Figure 5.14.

545: to find the thrust of the engines. We have defined the direction of the force and acceleration as acting “to the
546: right,” so we need to consider only the magnitudes of these quantities in the calculations. Hence we begin with
547: Fnet = ma
548: where Fnet is the net force along the horizontal direction. We can see from the figure that the engine thrusts add,
549: whereas friction opposes the thrust. In equation form, the net external force is
550: Fnet = 4T − f .

581: the system of interest is crucial—and the choice is not always obvious.
582: Newton’s second law is more than a definition; it is a relationship among acceleration, force, and mass. It can
583: help us make predictions. Each of those physical quantities can be defined independently, so the second law tells
584: us something basic and universal about nature.

44: 5.4 | Mass and Weight
45: Learning Objectives
46: By the end of the section, you will be able to:
47: • Explain the difference between mass and weight
48: • Explain why falling objects on Earth are never truly in free fall
49: • Describe the concept of weightlessness
50: Mass and weight are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation. Forexample, ourmedical records often show
51: our weight in kilograms but never in the correct units of newtons. In physics, however, there is an important distinction.
52: WeightisthepullofEarthonanobject.ItdependsonthedistancefromthecenterofEarth.Unlikeweight,massdoesnot
53: vary with location. The mass of an object is the same on Earth, in orbit, or on the surface of the Moon.
54: Units of Force
55: Theequation Fnet = ma is used to define net force in terms of mass, length, and time. As explained earlier, the SI unit of
56: force is the newton. Since Fnet = ma,
57: 1 N = 1 kg · m/s2.
58: Although almost the entire world uses the newton for the unit of force, in the United States, the most familiar unit of force
59: is the pound (lb), where 1 N = 0.225 lb. Thus, a 225-lb person weighs 1000 N.
60: Weight and Gravitational Force
61: Whenanobjectisdropped,itacceleratestowardthecenterofEarth.Newton’ssecondlawsaysthatanetforceonanobject
62: isresponsibleforitsacceleration.Ifairresistanceisnegligible,thenetforceonafallingobjectisthegravitationalforce,
63: commonly called itsweight w→ , or its force due to gravity acting on an object of massm. Weight can be denoted as a
64: vectorbecauseithasadirection; downis,bydefinition,thedirectionofgravity,andhence,weightisadownwardforce.The
65: magnitudeofweightisdenotedas w.Galileowasinstrumentalinshowingthat,intheabsenceofairresistance,allobjects
66: fall with the same accelerationg. Using Galileo’s result and Newton’s second law, we can derive an equation for weight.
67: Consideranobjectwithmass mfallingtowardEarth.Itexperiencesonlythedownwardforceofgravity,whichistheweight
68: w→ . Newton’s second law says that the magnitude of the net external force on an object isF→
69: net = m a→ . We know that
70: the acceleration of an object due to gravity isg→ , or a→ = g→ . Substituting these into Newton’s second law gives us
71: the following equations.
72: Weight
73: Thegravitationalforceonamassisitsweight.Wecanwritethisinvectorform,where w→ is weight andmismass,
74: as
75: (5.8)w→ = m g→ .
76: In scalar form, we can write
77: (5.9)w = mg.
78: Chapter 5 | Newton's Laws of Motion 227
79: 
80: Since g = 9.80 m/s2 on Earth, the weight of a 1.00-kg object on Earth is 9.80 N:
81: w = mg = (1.00 kg)(9.80 m/s2) = 9.80 N.
82: When the net external force on an object is its weight, we say that it is infree fall,thatis,theonlyforceactingontheobject
83: isgravity.However,whenobjects onEarth fall downward,they are never truly infree fall because there isalways some
84: upward resistance force from the air acting on the object.
85: Accelerationduetogravity gvariesslightlyoverthesurfaceofEarth,sotheweightofanobjectdependsonitslocationand
86: isnotanintrinsicpropertyoftheobject.WeightvariesdramaticallyifweleaveEarth’ssurface.OntheMoon,forexample,
87: accelerationduetogravityisonly 1.67 m/s2 . A 1.0-kg mass thus has a weight of 9.8 N on Earth and only about 1.7 N on
88: the Moon.
89: The broadest definition of weight in this sense is that the weight of an object is the gravitational force on it from the nearest
90: large body, such as Earth, the Moon, or the Sun. This is the most common and useful definition of weight in physics. It
91: differs dramatically, however, from the definition of weight used by NASA and the popular media in relation to space travel
92: and exploration. When they speak of “weightlessness” and “microgravity,” they are referring to the phenomenon we call
93: “free fall” in physics. We use the preceding definition of weight, forcew→ due to gravity acting on an object of massm,
94: and we make careful distinctions between free fall and actual weightlessness.
95: Be aware that weight and mass are different physical quantities, although they are closely related. Mass is an intrinsic
96: propertyofanobject:Itisaquantityofmatter.Thequantityoramountofmatterofanobjectisdeterminedbythenumbers
97: ofatomsandmoleculesofvarioustypesitcontains.Becausethesenumbersdonotvary,inNewtonianphysics,massdoes
98: notvary;therefore,itsresponsetoanappliedforcedoesnotvary.Incontrast,weightisthegravitationalforceactingonan
99: object,soitdoesvarydependingongravity.Forexample,apersonclosertothecenterofEarth,atalowelevationsuchas
100: NewOrleans,weighsslightlymorethanapersonwhoislocatedinthehigherelevationofDenver,eventhoughtheymay
101: have the same mass.
102: Itistemptingtoequatemasstoweight,becausemostofourexamplestakeplaceonEarth,wheretheweightofanobject
103: varies only a little with the location of the object. In addition, it is difficult to count and identify all of the atoms and
104: moleculesinanobject,somassisrarelydeterminedinthismanner.Ifweconsidersituationsinwhich g→ is a constant on
105: Earth, we see that weightw→ is directly proportional to massm,since w→ = m g→ , that is, the more massive an object
106: is, the more it weighs. Operationally, the masses of objects are determined by comparison with the standard kilogram, as
107: we discussed inUnits and Measurement.ButbycomparinganobjectonEarthwithoneontheMoon,wecaneasily
108: see a variation in weight but not in mass. For instance, on Earth, a 5.0-kg object weighs 49 N; on the Moon, wheregis
109: 1.67 m/s2 , the object weighs 8.4 N. However, the mass of the object is still 5.0 kg on the Moon.

154: Newton’s Third Law of Motion
155: Wheneveronebodyexertsaforceonasecondbody,thefirstbodyexperiencesaforcethatisequalinmagnitudeand
156: opposite in direction to the force that it exerts. Mathematically, if a bodyA exerts a force F→ on bodyB, thenB
157: Chapter 5 | Newton's Laws of Motion 229
158:

160: (5.10)F→
161: AB = − F→
162: BA.
163: Newton’sthirdlawrepresentsacertainsymmetryinnature:Forcesalwaysoccurinpairs,andonebodycannotexertaforce
164: onanotherwithoutexperiencingaforceitself.Wesometimesrefertothislawlooselyas“action-reaction,”wheretheforce
165: exertedistheactionandtheforceexperienced asaconsequence isthereaction. Newton’sthirdlawhaspractical usesin
166: analyzing the origin of forces and understanding which forces are external to a system.
167: WecanreadilyseeNewton’sthirdlawatworkbytakingalookathowpeoplemoveabout.Consideraswimmerpushing
168: offthesideofapool(Figure 5.16 ).Shepushesagainstthewallofthepoolwithherfeetandacceleratesinthedirection
169: oppositethatofherpush.Thewallhasexertedanequalandoppositeforceontheswimmer.Youmightthinkthattwoequal
170: andoppositeforceswouldcancel,buttheydonot becausetheyactondifferentsystems .Inthiscase,therearetwosystems
171: thatwecouldinvestigate:theswimmerandthewall.Ifweselecttheswimmertobethesystemofinterest,asinthefigure,
172: then Fwall on feet is an external force on this system and affects its motion. The swimmer moves in the direction of this
173: force. In contrast, the forceFfeet on wall acts on the wall, not on our system of interest. Thus,Ffeet on wall does not directly
174: affect the motion of the system and does not cancelFwall on feet. The swimmer pushes in the direction opposite that in
175: which she wishes to move. The reaction to her push is thus in the desired direction. In a free-body diagram, such as the one
176: shown inFigure 5.16,weneverincludebothforcesofanaction-reactionpair;inthiscase,weonlyuse Fwall on feet , not
177: Ffeet on wall .
178: Figure 5.16 When the swimmer exerts a force on the wall, she accelerates in the opposite direction; in other
179: words, the net external force on her is in the direction opposite of Ffeet on wall. This opposition occurs because,
180: in accordance with Newton’s third law, the wall exerts a force Fwall on feet on the swimmer that is equal in
181: magnitude but in the direction opposite to the one she exerts on it. The line around the swimmer indicates the
182: system of interest. Thus, the free-body diagram shows only Fwall on feet, w(the gravitational force), andBF,
183: which is the buoyant force of the water supporting the swimmer’s weight. The vertical forceswandBFcancel
184: because there is no vertical acceleration.

385: Consider the skier on the slope inFigure 5.22. Her mass including equipment is 60.0 kg. (a) What is her
386: acceleration if friction is negligible? (b) What is her acceleration if friction is 45.0 N?
387: Figure 5.22 Since the acceleration is parallel to the slope and acting down the slope, it is most convenient to
388: project all forces onto a coordinate system where one axis is parallel to the slope and the other is perpendicular to it
389: (axes shown to the left of the skier). N→ is perpendicular to the slope and f→ is parallel to the slope, but w→
390: has components along both axes, namely, wy and wx. Here, w→ has a squiggly line to show that it has been
391: replaced by these components. The force N→ is equal in magnitude to wy, so there is no acceleration
392: perpendicular to the slope, butfis less than wx, so there is a downslope acceleration (along the axis parallel to the
393: slope).

395: This is a two-dimensional problem, since not all forces on the skier (the system of interest) are parallel. The
396: approach we have used in two-dimensional kinematics also works well here. Choose a convenient coordinate

481: Tension
482: A tension is a force along the length of a medium; in particular, it is a pulling force that acts along a stretched flexible
483: connector,suchasaropeorcable.Theword“tension”comesfromaLatinwordmeaning“tostretch.”Notcoincidentally,
484: the flexible cords that carry muscle forces to other parts of the body are calledtendons.
485: Any flexible connector, such as a string, rope, chain, wire, or cable, can only exert a pull parallel to its length; thus, a
486: forcecarriedbyaflexibleconnectorisatensionwithadirectionparalleltotheconnector.Tensionisapullinaconnector.
487: Consider the phrase: “You can’t push a rope.” Instead, tension force pulls outward along the two ends of a rope.
488: Considerapersonholdingamassonarope,asshownin Figure 5.24.Ifthe5.00-kgmassinthefigureisstationary,then
489: itsaccelerationiszeroandthenetforceiszero.Theonlyexternalforcesactingonthemassareitsweightandthetension
490: supplied by the rope. Thus,
491: Fnet = T −w = 0,
492: whereTandwarethemagnitudesofthetensionandweight,respectively,andtheirsignsindicatedirection,withupbeing
493: positive. As we proved using Newton’s second law, the tension equals the weight of the supported mass:
494: 240 Chapter 5 | Newton's Laws of Motion
495: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
496: 
497: (5.14)T = w = mg.
498: Thus, for a 5.00-kg mass (neglecting the mass of the rope), we see that
499: T = mg =
500: ⎛
501: ⎝5.00 kg
502: ⎞
503: ⎠

506: ⎠ = 49.0 N.
507: If we cut the rope and insert a spring, the spring would extend a length corresponding to a force of 49.0 N, providing a direct
508: observation and measure of the tension force in the rope.
509: Figure 5.24 When a perfectly flexible connector (one
510: requiring no force to bend it) such as this rope transmits a force
511: T→ , that force must be parallel to the length of the rope, as
512: shown. By Newton’s third law, the rope pulls with equal force
513: but in opposite directions on the hand and the supported mass
514: (neglecting the weight of the rope). The rope is the medium that
515: carries the equal and opposite forces between the two objects.
516: The tension anywhere in the rope between the hand and the
517: mass is equal. Once you have determined the tension in one
518: location, you have determined the tension at all locations along
519: the rope.
520: Flexible connectorsareoftenusedtotransmit forcesaroundcorners,suchasinahospitaltraction system,atendon,ora
521: bicycle brake cable. If there is no friction, the tension transmission is undiminished; only its direction changes, and it is
522: always parallel to the flexible connector, as shown in Figure 5.25.

1: Real Forces and Inertial Frames
2: There is another distinction among forces: Some forces are real, whereas others are not.Realforces have some physical
3: origin, such as a gravitational pull. In contrast,fictitiousforces arise simply because an observer is in an accelerating or
4: noninertialframeofreference,suchasonethatrotates(likeamerry-go-round)orundergoeslinearacceleration(likeacar
5: slowingdown).Forexample,ifasatelliteisheadingduenorthaboveEarth’sNorthernHemisphere,thentoanobserveron
6: Earth,itwillappeartoexperienceaforcetothewestthathasnophysicalorigin.Instead,Earthisrotatingtowardtheeast
7: andmoveseastunderthesatellite.InEarth’sframe,thislookslikeawestwardforceonthesatellite,oritcanbeinterpreted
8: asaviolationofNewton’sfirstlaw(thelawofinertia).Wecanidentifyafictitiousforcebyaskingthequestion,“Whatis
9: thereactionforce?”Ifwecannotnamethereactionforce,thentheforceweareconsideringisfictitious.Intheexampleof
10: thesatellite,thereactionforcewouldhavetobeaneastwardforceonEarth.Recallthataninertialframeofreferenceisone
11: in which all forces are real and, equivalently, one in which Newton’s laws have the simple forms given in this chapter.
12: Earth’srotationisslowenoughthatEarthisnearlyaninertialframe.Youordinarilymustperformpreciseexperimentsto
13: observefictitiousforcesandtheslightdeparturesfromNewton’slaws,suchastheeffectjustdescribed.Onalargescale,
14: such as for the rotation of weather systems and ocean currents, the effects can be easily observed (Figure 5.30).
15: Figure 5.30 Hurricane Fran is shown heading toward the
16: southeastern coast of the United States in September 1996.
17: Notice the characteristic “eye” shape of the hurricane. This is a
18: result of the Coriolis effect, which is the deflection of objects (in
19: this case, air) when considered in a rotating frame of reference,
20: like the spin of Earth. This hurricane shows a counter-clockwise
21: rotation because it is a low pressure storm. (credit "runner":
22: modification of work by "Greenwich Photography"/Flickr)
23: The crucial factor in determining whether a frame of reference is inertial is whether it accelerates or rotates relative to a
24: known inertial frame. Unless stated otherwise, all phenomena discussed in this text are in inertial frames.

38: 5.7 | Drawing Free-Body Diagrams
39: Learning Objectives
40: By the end of the section, you will be able to:
41: • Explain the rules for drawing a free-body diagram
42: • Construct free-body diagrams for different situations
43: Thefirststepindescribingandanalyzingmostphenomenainphysicsinvolvesthecarefuldrawingofafree-bodydiagram.
44: Free-body diagrams have been used in examples throughout this chapter. Remember that a free-body diagram must only
45: includetheexternalforcesactingonthebodyofinterest.Oncewehavedrawnanaccuratefree-bodydiagram,wecanapply
46: Newton’sfirstlawifthebodyisinequilibrium(balancedforces;thatis, Fnet = 0) or Newton’s second law if the body is
47: accelerating (unbalanced force; that is, Fnet ≠ 0).
48: In Forces,wegaveabriefproblem-solvingstrategytohelpyouunderstandfree-bodydiagrams.Here,weaddsomedetails
49: to the strategy that will help you in constructing these diagrams.
50: Problem-Solving Strategy: Constructing Free-Body Diagrams
51: Observe the following rules when constructing a free-body diagram:
52: 1. Draw the object under consideration; it does not have to be artistic. At first, you may want to draw a circle
53: aroundtheobjectofinteresttobesureyoufocusonlabelingtheforcesactingontheobject.Ifyouaretreating
54: theobjectasaparticle(nosizeorshapeandnorotation),representtheobjectasapoint.Weoftenplacethis
55: point at the origin of anxy-coordinate system.
56: 2. Include all forces that act on the object, representing these forces as vectors. Consider the types of forces
57: described inCommon Forces—normal force, friction, tension, and spring force—as well as weight and
58: applied force. Do not include the net force on the object. With the exception of gravity, all of the forces we
59: havediscussedrequiredirectcontactwiththeobject.However,forcesthattheobjectexertsonitsenvironment
60: must not be included. We never include both forces of an action-reaction pair.
61: 3. Convert the free-body diagram into a more detailed diagram showing thex- andy-components of a given
62: force(thisisoftenhelpfulwhensolvingaproblemusingNewton’sfirstorsecondlaw).Inthiscase,placea
63: squigglylinethroughtheoriginalvectortoshowthatitisnolongerinplay—ithasbeenreplacedbyits x-and
64: y-components.
65: 4. If there are two or more objects, or bodies, in the problem, draw a separate free-body diagram for each object.
66: Note:Ifthereisacceleration,wedonotdirectlyincludeitinthefree-bodydiagram;however,itmayhelptoindicate
67: accelerationoutsidethefree-bodydiagram.Youcanlabelitinadifferentcolortoindicatethatitisseparatefromthe
68: free-body diagram.
69: Let’sapplytheproblem-solvingstrategyindrawingafree-bodydiagramforasled.In Figure 5.31(a),asledispulledby
70: force Patanangleof 30° . In part (b), we show a free-body diagram for this situation, as described by steps 1 and 2 of the
71: problem-solving strategy. In part (c), we show all forces in terms of theirx- andy-components, in keeping with step 3.

236: SUMMARY
237: 5.1 Forces
238: • Dynamics is the study of how forces affect the motion of objects, whereas kinematics simply describes the way
239: objects move.
240: • Forceisapushorpullthatcanbedefinedintermsofvariousstandards,anditisavectorthathasbothmagnitude
241: and direction.
242: • Externalforcesareanyoutsideforcesthatactonabody.Afree-bodydiagramisadrawingofallexternalforces
243: acting on a body.
244: • The SI unit of force is the newton (N).
245: 5.2 Newton's First Law
246: • AccordingtoNewton’sfirstlaw,theremustbeacauseforanychangeinvelocity(achangeineithermagnitudeor
247: direction) to occur. This law is also known as the law of inertia.
248: • Friction is an external force that causes an object to slow down.
249: • Inertia is the tendency of an object to remain at rest or remain in motion. Inertia is related to an object’s mass.
250: • Ifanobject’svelocityrelativetoagivenframeisconstant,thentheframeisinertial.Thismeansthatforaninertial
251: reference frame, Newton’s first law is valid.
252: • Equilibrium is achieved when the forces on a system are balanced.
253: • A net force of zero means that an object is either at rest or moving with constant velocity; that is, it is not
254: accelerating.
255: 5.3 Newton's Second Law
256: • An external force acts on a system from outside the system, as opposed to internal forces, which act between
257: components within the system.
258: • Newton’s second law of motion says that the net external force on an object with a certain mass is directly
259: proportional to and in the same direction as the acceleration of the object.
260: • Newton’s second law can also describe net force as the instantaneous rate of change of momentum. Thus, a net
261: external force causes nonzero acceleration.
262: 5.4 Mass and Weight
263: • Mass is the quantity of matter in a substance.
264: • The weight of an object is the net force on a falling object, or its gravitational force. The object experiences
265: acceleration due to gravity.
266: • SomeupwardresistanceforcefromtheairactsonallfallingobjectsonEarth,sotheycannevertrulybeinfreefall.
267: Chapter 5 | Newton's Laws of Motion 253
268: 
269: • Carefuldistinctionsmustbemadebetweenfreefallandweightlessnessusingthedefinitionofweightasforcedue
270: to gravity acting on an object of a certain mass.
271: 5.5 Newton’s Third Law
272: • Newton’sthirdlawofmotionrepresentsabasicsymmetryinnature,withanexperiencedforceequalinmagnitude
273: and opposite in direction to an exerted force.
274: • Two equal and opposite forces do not cancel because they act on different systems.
275: • Action-reactionpairsincludeaswimmerpushingoffawall,helicopterscreatingliftbypushingairdown,andan
276: octopuspropellingitselfforwardbyejectingwaterfromitsbody.Rockets,airplanes,andcarsarepushedforward
277: by a thrust reaction force.
278: • Choosing a system is an important analytical step in understanding the physics of a problem and solving it.
279: 5.6 Common Forces
280: • Whenanobjectrestsonasurface,thesurfaceappliesaforcetotheobjectthatsupportstheweightoftheobject.
281: This supporting force acts perpendicular to and away from the surface. It is called a normal force.
282: • When an object rests on a nonaccelerating horizontal surface, the magnitude of the normal force is equal to the
283: weight of the object.
284: • When an object rests on an inclined plane that makes an angleθ with the horizontal surface, the weight of the
285: object can be resolved into components that act perpendicular and parallel to the surface of the plane.
286: • Thepullingforcethatactsalongastretchedflexibleconnector,suchasaropeorcable,iscalledtension.Whena
287: ropesupportstheweightofanobjectatrest,thetensionintheropeisequaltotheweightoftheobject.Iftheobject
288: is accelerating, tension is greater than weight, and if it is decelerating, tension is less than weight.
289: • Theforceoffrictionisaforceexperiencedbyamovingobject(oranobjectthathasatendencytomove)parallelto
290: the interface opposing the motion (or its tendency).
291: • The force developed in a spring obeys Hooke’s law, according to which its magnitude is proportional to the
292: displacement and has a sense in the opposite direction of the displacement.
293: • Real forces have a physical origin, whereas fictitious forces occur because the observer is in an accelerating or
294: noninertial frame of reference.
295: 5.7 Drawing Free-Body Diagrams
296: • Todrawafree-bodydiagram,wedrawtheobjectofinterest,drawallforcesactingonthatobject,andresolveall
297: forcevectorsinto x-and y-components.Wemustdrawaseparatefree-bodydiagramforeachobjectintheproblem.
298: • Afree-bodydiagramisausefulmeansofdescribingandanalyzingalltheforcesthatactonabodytodetermine
299: equilibrium according to Newton’s first law or acceleration according to Newton’s second law.

1: 6.1 | Solving Problems with Newton’s Laws
2: Learning Objectives
3: By the end of the section, you will be able to:
4: • Apply problem-solving techniques to solve for quantities in more complex systems of forces
5: • Use concepts from kinematics to solve problems using Newton’s laws of motion
6: • Solve more complex equilibrium problems
7: • Solve more complex acceleration problems
8: • Apply calculus to more advanced dynamics problems
9: Successinproblemsolvingisnecessarytounderstandandapplyphysicalprinciples.Wedevelopedapatternofanalyzing
10: and setting up the solutions to problems involving Newton’s laws inNewton’s Laws of Motion; in this chapter, we
11: continue to discuss these strategies and apply a step-by-step process.
12: Problem-Solving Strategies
13: We follow here the basics of problem solving presented earlier in this text, but we emphasize specific strategies that
14: are useful in applying Newton’s laws of motion. Once you identify the physical principles involved in the problem and
15: determinethattheyincludeNewton’slawsofmotion,youcanapplythesestepstofindasolution.Thesetechniquesalso
16: reinforceconceptsthatareusefulinmanyotherareasofphysics.Manyproblem-solvingstrategiesarestatedoutrightinthe
17: worked examples, so the following techniques should reinforce skills you have already begun to develop.
18: Problem-Solving Strategy: Applying Newton’s Laws of Motion
19: 1. Identify the physical principles involved by listing the givens and the quantities to be calculated.
20: 2. Sketch the situation, using arrows to represent all forces.
21: 3. Determine the system of interest. The result is afree-body diagramthat is essential to solving the problem.
22: 4. ApplyNewton’ssecondlawtosolvetheproblem.Ifnecessary,applyappropriatekinematicequationsfromthe
23: chapter on motion along a straight line.
24: 5. Check the solution to see whether it is reasonable.
25: Let’sapplythisproblem-solvingstrategytothechallengeofliftingagrandpianointoasecond-storyapartment.Oncewe
26: havedeterminedthatNewton’slawsofmotionareinvolved(iftheprobleminvolvesforces),itisparticularlyimportantto
27: drawacarefulsketchofthesituation.Suchasketchisshownin Figure 6.2(a).Then,asin Figure 6.2(b),wecanrepresent
28: allforceswitharrows.Wheneversufficientinformationexists,itisbesttolabelthesearrowscarefullyandmakethelength
29: and direction of each correspond to the represented force.

71: These serve also to illustrate some further subtleties of physics and to help build problem-solving skills. We look first at
72: problems involving particle equilibrium, which make use of Newton’s first law, and then consider particle acceleration,
73: which involves Newton’s second law.

100: Solution
101: First consider the horizontal orx-axis:

110: that T2 ends up being greater than T1 because it is exerted more vertically than T1.

112: Fnety = T1y +T2y −w = 0.

125: we obtain

370: Example 6.5
371: Atwood Machine
372: Aclassicprobleminphysics,similartotheonewejustsolved,isthatoftheAtwoodmachine,whichconsistsof
373: aroperunningoverapulley,withtwoobjectsofdifferentmassattached.Itisparticularlyusefulinunderstanding
374: the connection between force and motion. InFigure 6.7, m1 = 2.00 kg and m2 = 4.00 kg. Consider the
375: pulley to be frictionless. (a) Ifm2 is released, what will its acceleration be? (b) What is the tension in the string?
376: Chapter 6 | Applications of Newton's Laws 275
377: 
378: Figure 6.7 An Atwood machine and free-body diagrams for each of the two
379: blocks.
380: Strategy
381: Wedrawafree-bodydiagramforeachmassseparately,asshowninthefigure.Thenweanalyzeeachdiagramto
382: findtherequiredunknowns.Thismayinvolvethesolutionofsimultaneousequations.Itisalsoimportanttonote
383: thesimilaritywiththepreviousexample.Asblock2accelerateswithacceleration a2 in the downward direction,
384: block 1 accelerates upward with acceleration a1 . Thus, a = a1 = −a2.
385: Solution
386: a. We have
387: Form1, ∑Fy = T −m1g = m1a. For m2, ∑Fy = T −m2g = −m2a.
388: (The negative sign in front ofm2a indicates thatm2 accelerates downward; both blocks accelerate at
389: the same rate, but in opposite directions.) Solve the two equations simultaneously (subtract them) and the
390: result is
391: (m2 −m1)g = (m1 +m2)a.
392: Solving fora:
393: a = m2 −m1
394: m1 +m2
395: g = 4 kg − 2 kg
396: 4 kg + 2 kg(9.8 m/s2) = 3.27 m/s2.
397: b. Observing the first block, we see that
398: T −m1g = m1a
399: T = m1(g +a) = (2 kg)(9.8 m/s2 + 3.27 m/s2) = 26.1 N.
400: Significance
401: The result for the acceleration given in the solution can be interpreted as the ratio of the unbalanced force on
402: the system, (m2 −m1)g, to the total mass of the system,m1 +m2 . We can also use the Atwood machine to
403: measure local gravitational field strength.

409: Newton’s Laws of Motion and Kinematics
410: Physics is most interesting and most powerful when applied to general situations that involve more than a narrow set of
411: physicalprinciples.Newton’slawsofmotioncanalsobeintegratedwithotherconceptsthathavebeendiscussedpreviously

604: 6.2 | Friction
605: Learning Objectives
606: By the end of the section, you will be able to:
607: • Describe the general characteristics of friction
608: • List the various types of friction
609: • Calculate the magnitude of static and kinetic friction, and use these in problems involving
610: Newton’s laws of motion
611: Whenabodyisinmotion,ithasresistancebecausethebodyinteractswithitssurroundings.Thisresistanceisaforceof
612: friction.Frictionopposesrelativemotionbetweensystemsincontactbutalsoallowsustomove,aconceptthatbecomes
613: obviousifyoutrytowalkonice.Frictionisacommonyetcomplexforce,anditsbehaviorstillnotcompletelyunderstood.
614: Chapter 6 | Applications of Newton's Laws 281
615: 
616: Still, it is possible to understand the circumstances in which it behaves.
617: Static and Kinetic Friction
618: The basic definition of frictionis relatively simple to state.
619: Friction
620: Friction is a force that opposes relative motion between systems in contact.
621: Thereareseveralformsoffriction.Oneofthesimplercharacteristicsofslidingfrictionisthatitisparalleltothecontact
622: surfaces between systems and is always in a direction that opposes motion or attempted motion of the systems relative
623: to each other. If two systems are in contact and moving relative to one another, then the friction between them is called
624: kineticfriction.Forexample,frictionslowsahockeypuckslidingonice.Whenobjectsarestationary,staticfrictioncanact
625: between them; the static friction is usually greater than the kinetic friction between two objects.
626: Static and Kinetic Friction
627: If two systems are in contact and stationary relative to one another, then the friction between them is calledstatic
628: friction. If two systems are in contact and moving relative to one another, then the friction between them is called
629: kinetic friction.
630: Imagine,forexample,tryingtoslideaheavycrateacrossaconcretefloor—youmightpushveryhardonthecrateandnot
631: moveitatall.Thismeansthatthestaticfrictionrespondstowhatyoudo—itincreasestobeequaltoandintheopposite
632: direction of your push. If you finally push hard enough, the crate seems to slip suddenly and starts to move. Now static
633: frictiongiveswaytokineticfriction.Onceinmotion,itiseasiertokeepitinmotionthanitwastogetitstarted,indicating
634: thatthekineticfrictionalforceislessthanthestaticfrictionalforce.Ifyouaddmasstothecrate,saybyplacingaboxon
635: topofit,youneedtopushevenhardertogetitstartedandalsotokeepitmoving.Furthermore,ifyouoiledtheconcrete
636: you would find it easier to get the crate started and keep it going (as you might expect).
637: Figure 6.10 is a crude pictorial representation of how friction occurs at the interface between two objects. Close-up
638: inspectionofthesesurfacesshowsthemtoberough.Thus,whenyoupushtogetanobjectmoving(inthiscase,acrate),
639: youmustraisetheobjectuntilitcanskipalongwithjustthetipsofthesurfacehitting,breakingoffthepoints,orboth.A
640: considerableforcecanberesistedbyfrictionwithnoapparentmotion.Theharderthesurfacesarepushedtogether(suchas
641: ifanotherboxisplacedonthecrate),themoreforceisneededtomovethem.Partofthefrictionisduetoadhesiveforces
642: betweenthesurfacemoleculesofthetwoobjects,whichexplainsthedependenceoffrictiononthenatureofthesubstances.
643: For example, rubber-soled shoes slip less than those with leather soles. Adhesion varies with substances in contact and
644: is a complicated aspect ofsurface physics. Once an object is moving, there are fewer points ofcontact (fewer molecules
645: adhering),solessforceisrequiredtokeeptheobjectmoving.Atsmallbutnonzerospeeds,frictionisnearlyindependent
646: of speed.
647: 282 Chapter 6 | Applications of Newton's Laws
648: This OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10
649: 
650: Figure 6.10 Frictional forces, such as f→ , always oppose motion or
651: attempted motion between objects in contact. Friction arises in part because
652: of the roughness of the surfaces in contact, as seen in the expanded view.
653: For the object to move, it must rise to where the peaks of the top surface can
654: skip along the bottom surface. Thus, a force is required just to set the object
655: in motion. Some of the peaks will be broken off, also requiring a force to
656: maintain motion. Much of the friction is actually due to attractive forces
657: between molecules making up the two objects, so that even perfectly
658: smooth surfaces are not friction-free. (In fact, perfectly smooth, clean
659: surfaces of similar materials would adhere, forming a bond called a “cold
660: weld.”)
661: The magnitude of the frictional force has two forms: one for static situations (static friction), the other for situations
662: involving motion (kinetic friction). What follows is an approximate empirical (experimentally determined) model only.
663: These equations for static and kinetic friction are not vector equations.
664: Magnitude of Static Friction
665: The magnitude of static friction fs is
666: (6.1)fs ≤ µsN,
667: where µs is the coefficient of static friction andNis the magnitude of the normal force.
668: The symbol ≤ means less than or equal to, implying that static friction can have a maximum value ofµsN. Static
669: friction is a responsive force that increases to be equal and opposite to whatever force is exerted, up to its maximum limit.
670: Once the applied force exceeds
671: fs (max), the object moves. Thus,
672: fs(max) =µsN.
673: Magnitude of Kinetic Friction
674: The magnitude of kinetic friction fk is given by
675: (6.2)fk = µkN,
676: where µk is the coefficient of kinetic friction.
677: A system in whichfk = µkN is described as a system in whichfrictionbehavessimply .Thetransitionfromstaticfriction
678: to kinetic friction is illustrated in Figure 6.11.
679: Chapter 6 | Applications of Newton's Laws 283
680: 
681: Figure 6.11 (a) The force of friction f→ between the block and the rough surface opposes the direction of the applied force
682: F→ . The magnitude of the static friction balances that of the applied force. This is shown in the left side of the graph in (c). (b)
683: At some point, the magnitude of the applied force is greater than the force of kinetic friction, and the block moves to the right.
684: This is shown in the right side of the graph. (c) The graph of the frictional force versus the applied force; note that
685: fs(max) > fk. This means that µs > µk.
686: As you can see inTable 6.1, the coefficients of kinetic friction are less than their static counterparts. The approximate
687: valuesof µ are stated to only one or two digits to indicate the approximate description of friction given by the preceding
688: two equations.
689: System Static Friction µs Kinetic Friction µk

692: Wood on wood 0.5 0.3
693: Waxed wood on wet snow 0.14 0.1
694: Metal on wood 0.5 0.3
695: Steel on steel (dry) 0.6 0.3

[{"suffix": "", "text": "16.2 | Plane Electromagnetic Waves\r\nLearning Objectives\r\nBy the end of this section, you will be able to:\r\n• Describe how Maxwell’s equations predict the relative directions of the electric fields and\r\nmagnetic fields, and the direction of propagation of plane electromagnetic waves\r\n• Explain how Maxwell’s equations predict that the speed of propagation of electromagnetic\r\nwaves in free space is exactly the speed of light\r\n• Calculate the relative magnitude of the electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic plane\r\nwave\r\n• Describe how electromagnetic waves are produced and detected\r\nMechanical waves travel through a medium such as a string, water, or air. Perhaps the most significant prediction of\r\nMaxwell’sequationsistheexistenceofcombinedelectricandmagnetic(orelectromagnetic)fieldsthatpropagatethrough\r\nspace as electromagnetic waves. Because Maxwell’s equations hold in free space, the predicted electromagnetic waves,\r\nunlike mechanical waves, do not require a medium for their propagation.\r\nA general treatment of the physics of electromagnetic waves is beyond the scope of this textbook. We can, however,\r\ninvestigate the special case of an electromagnetic wave that propagates through free space along thex-axis of a given\r\ncoordinate system.\r\nElectromagnetic Waves in One Direction\r\nAn electromagnetic wave consists of an electric field, defined as usual in terms of the force per charge on a stationary\r\ncharge, and a magnetic field, defined in terms of the force per charge on a moving charge. The electromagnetic field\r\nis assumed to be a function of only thex-coordinate and time. For any other thermodynamic system, when the process is reversible, the change of the entropy is given by\r\nΔS = Q/T . But what happens if the temperature goes to zero,T → 0? It turns out this is not a question that can be\r\nanswered by the second law.\r\nA fundamental issue still remains: Is it possible to cool a system all the way down to zero kelvin? We understand that\r\nthe system must be at its lowest energy state because lowering temperature reduces the kinetic energy of the constituents\r\nin the system. What happens to the entropy of a system at the absolute zero temperature? It turns out the absolute zero\r\ntemperature is not reachable—at least, not though a finite number of cooling steps. This is a statement of thethird law of\r\nthermodynamics,whoseproofrequiresquantummechanicsthatwedonotpresenthere.Inactualexperiments,physicists\r\nhave continuously pushed that limit downward, with the lowest temperature achieved at about1 × 10−10 K in a low-\r\ntemperature lab at the Helsinki University of Technology in 2008.\r\nLike the second law of thermodynamics, the third law of thermodynamics can be stated in different ways. One of the\r\ncommon statements of the third law of thermodynamics is:The absolute zero temperature cannot be reached through any\r\nfinite number of cooling steps.\r\nInotherwords,thetemperatureofanygivenphysicalsystemmustbefinite,thatis, T > 0. This produces a very interesting\r\nquestion in physics: Do we know how a system would behave if it were at the absolute zero temperature?\r\nThe reason a system is unable to reach 0 K is fundamental and requires quantum mechanics to fully understand its origin.\r\nBut we can certainly ask what happens to the entropy of a system when we try to cool it down to 0 K. Because the amount\r\nof heat that can be removed from the system becomes vanishingly small, we expect that the change in entropy of the system\r\nalong an isotherm approaches zero, that is,\r\n(4.13)limT → 0(ΔS)T = 0.\r\nThiscanbeviewedasanotherstatementofthethirdlaw,withalltheisothermsbecoming isentropic,orintoareversible\r\nidealadiabat.Wecanputthisexpressioninwords: A system becomes perfectly ordered when its temperature approaches\r\nabsolute zero and its entropy approaches its absolute minimum.\r\nThethirdlawofthermodynamicsputsanotherlimitonwhatcanbedonewhenwelookforenergyresources.Iftherecould\r\nbeareservoirattheabsolutezerotemperature,wecouldhaveengineswithefficiencyof 100% , which would, of course,\r\nviolate the second law of thermodynamics.\r\nExample 4.8\r\nEntropy Change of an Ideal Gas in Free Expansion\r\nAnidealgasoccupiesapartitionedvolume V1 inside a box whose walls are thermally insulating, as shown in\r\nFigure 4.18(a).Whenthepartitionisremoved,thegasexpandsandfillstheentirevolume V2 of the box, as\r\nshown in part (b). When a trough and a crest coincide, destructive interference\r\noccurs, marked by black dots. The phase difference is due to the path lengths traveled by the\r\nindividual waves. Two identical waves travel two different path lengths to a pointP. (a) The\r\ndifference in the path lengths is one wavelength, resulting in total constructive interference and\r\na resulting amplitude equal to twice the original amplitude. The equationp2 − p1 = RQ is valid for both laminar and\r\nturbulent flows.\r\nFigure 14.39 During times of heavy use, there is a significant\r\npressure drop in a water main, and p1 supplied to users is\r\nsignificantly less than p2 created at the water works. If the\r\nflow is very small, then the pressure drop is negligible, and\r\np2 ≈ p1 .\r\n728 Chapter 14 | Fluid Mechanics\r\nThis OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10\r\n\r\nWe can also usep2 − p1 = RQ to analyze pressure drops occurring in more complex systems in which the tube radius\r\nis not the same everywhere. Plaque in an artery reduces pressure and hence flow, both by its resistance and by the turbulence it creates.\r\nMeasuring Turbulence\r\nAn indicator called theReynolds number NR can reveal whether flow is laminar or turbulent. For flow in a tube of\r\nuniform diameter, the Reynolds number is defined as\r\n(14.20)NR = 2ρvr\r\nη (fl w in tube)\r\nwhere ρ is the fluid density,vitsspeed, η its viscosity, andrthetuberadius.TheReynoldsnumberisadimensionless\r\nquantity. Experiments have revealed thatNR is related to the onset of turbulence. ForNR below about 2000, flow is\r\nlaminar. For NR above about 3000, flow is turbulent.\r\nFor values ofNR between about 2000 and 3000, flow is unstable—that is, it can be laminar, but small obstructions and\r\nsurface roughness can make it turbulent, and it may oscillate randomly between being laminar and turbulent. In fact, the\r\nflow of a fluid with a Reynolds number between 2000 and 3000 is a good example of chaotic behavior. A system is defined\r\nto be chaotic when its behavior is so sensitive to some factor that it is extremely difficult to predict. It is difficult, but not\r\nimpossible, to predict whether flow is turbulent or not when a fluid’s Reynold’s number falls in this range due to extremely\r\nsensitive dependence on factors like roughness and obstructions on the nature of the flow. A tiny variation in one factor has\r\nan exaggerated (or nonlinear) effect on the flow.\r\nExample 14.9\r\nUsing Flow Rate: Turbulent Flow or Laminar Flow\r\nIn Example 14.8,wefoundthevolumeflowrateofanairconditioningsystemtobe Q = 3.84 × 10−3 m3 /s.\r\nThis calculation assumed laminar flow. (a) The mass is displaced to a position x = A and released from\r\nrest. (b) The mass accelerates as it moves in the negativex-direction, reaching a maximum\r\nnegative velocity at x = 0. (c) The mass continues to move in the negativex-direction, slowing\r\nuntil it comes to a stop at x = −A. (d) The mass now begins to accelerate in the positive\r\nx-direction, reaching a positive maximum velocity at x = 0. (e) The mass then continues to\r\nmove in the positive direction until it stops at x = A. The mass continues in SHM that has an\r\namplitudeAand a periodT. The object’s maximum speed occurs as it passes through\r\nequilibrium. The stiffer the spring is, the smaller the periodT. The greater the mass of the object\r\nis, the greater the periodT.\r\nWhat is so significant about SHM? For one thing, the periodT and frequencyf of a simple harmonic oscillator are\r\nindependentofamplitude.Thestringofaguitar,forexample,oscillateswiththesamefrequencywhetherpluckedgentlyor\r\nhard.\r\nTwoimportantfactorsdoaffecttheperiodofasimpleharmonicoscillator.Theperiodisrelatedtohowstiffthesystemis.\r\nAverystiffobjecthasalarge force constant (k),whichcausesthesystemtohaveasmallerperiod.Forexample,youcan\r\nadjustadivingboard’sstiffness—thestifferitis,thefasteritvibrates,andtheshorteritsperiod.Periodalsodependsonthe\r\nmassoftheoscillatingsystem.Themoremassivethesystemis,thelongertheperiod.Forexample,aheavypersonona\r\ndivingboardbouncesupanddownmoreslowlythanalightone.Infact,themass mandtheforceconstant karethe only\r\nfactorsthataffecttheperiodandfrequencyofSHM.Toderiveanequationfortheperiodandthefrequency,wemustfirst\r\ndefine and analyze the equations of motion. For example, if we are to sum up\r\nN vectors F→\r\n1, F→\r\n2, F→\r\n3, … , F→\r\nN , where each vector isF→\r\nk = Fkx i^ +Fky j^ +Fkz k^ , the resultant vector\r\nF→\r\nR is\r\nF→\r\nR = F→\r\n1 + F→\r\n2 + F→\r\n3 + … + F→\r\nN = ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nF→\r\nk = ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN ⎛\r\n⎝Fkx i^ +Fky j^ +Fkz k^⎞\r\n⎠\r\n=\r\n⎛\r\n⎝\r\n⎜ ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nFkx\r\n⎞\r\n⎠\r\n⎟ i^ +\r\n⎛\r\n⎝\r\n⎜ ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nFky\r\n⎞\r\n⎠\r\n⎟ j^ +\r\n⎛\r\n⎝\r\n⎜ ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nFkz\r\n⎞\r\n⎠\r\n⎟k^.\r\nTherefore, scalar components of the resultant vector are\r\n(2.25)⎧\r\n⎩\r\n⎨\r\n⎪\r\n⎪\r\n⎪\r\n⎪\r\n⎪\r\n⎪\r\nFRx = ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nFkx = F1x +F2x + … +FNx\r\nFRy = ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nFky = F1y +F2y + … +FNy\r\nFRz = ∑\r\nk = 1\r\nN\r\nFkz = F1z +F2z + … +FNz.\r\nHaving found the scalar components, we can write the resultant in vector component form:\r\nF→\r\nR = FRx i^ +FRy j^ +FRz k^.\r\nAnalytical methods for finding the resultant and, in general, for solving vector equations are very important in physics\r\nbecause many physical quantities are vectors. Alternating current (ac) refers to systems in which the source voltage varies periodically, particularly sinusoidally.\r\n• Thevoltagesourceofanacsystemputsoutavoltagethatiscalculatedfromthetime,thepeakvoltage,andthe\r\nangular frequency.\r\n• Inasimplecircuit,thecurrentisfoundbydividingthevoltagebytheresistance.Anaccurrentiscalculatedusing\r\nthe peak current (determined by dividing the peak voltage by the resistance), the angular frequency, and the time.\r\n15.2 Simple AC Circuits\r\n• For resistors, the current through and the voltage across are in phase.\r\n• Forcapacitors,wefindthatwhenasinusoidalvoltageisappliedtoacapacitor,thevoltagefollowsthecurrentby\r\none-fourthofacycle.Sinceacapacitorcanstopcurrentwhenfullycharged,itlimitscurrentandoffersanotherform\r\nof ac resistance, called capacitive reactance, which has units of ohms.\r\n• Forinductorsinaccircuits,wefindthatwhenasinusoidalvoltageisappliedtoaninductor,thevoltageleadsthe\r\ncurrent by one-fourth of a cycle.\r\n• Theoppositionofaninductortoachangeincurrentisexpressedasatypeofacreactance.Thisinductivereactance,\r\nwhich has units of ohms, varies with the frequency of the ac source.\r\n15.3 RLC Series Circuits with AC\r\n• AnRLCseries circuit is a resistor, capacitor, and inductor series combination across an ac source.\r\n• The same current flows through each element of anRLCseries circuit at all points in time.\r\n• The counterpart of resistance in a dc circuit is impedance, which measures the combined effect of resistors,\r\ncapacitors, and inductors. The maximum current is defined by the ac version of Ohm’s law.\r\n690 Chapter 15 | Alternating-Current Circuits\r\nThis OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12074/1.9\r\n\r\n• Impedancehasunitsofohmsandisfoundusingtheresistance,thecapacitivereactance,andtheinductivereactance.\r\n15.4 Power in an AC Circuit\r\n• The average ac power is found by multiplying the rms values of current and voltage.\r\n• Ohm’s law for the rms ac is found by dividing the rms voltage by the impedance.\r\n• Inanaccircuit,thereisaphaseanglebetweenthesourcevoltageandthecurrent,whichcanbefoundbydividing\r\nthe resistance by the impedance.\r\n• The average power delivered to anRLCcircuit is affected by the phase angle.\r\n• The power factor ranges from –1 to 1.\r\n15.5 Resonance in an AC Circuit\r\n• At the resonant frequency, inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance.\r\n• Theaveragepowerversusangularfrequencyplotfora RLCcircuithasapeaklocatedattheresonantfrequency;the\r\nsharpness or width of the peak is known as the bandwidth.\r\n• Thebandwidthisrelatedtoadimensionlessquantitycalledthequalityfactor.Ahighqualityfactorvalueisasharp\r\nor narrow peak.\r\n15.6 Transformers\r\n• Power plants transmit high voltages at low currents to achieve lower ohmic losses in their many kilometers of\r\ntransmission lines.\r\n• Transformers use induction to transform voltages from one value to another.\r\n• Foratransformer,thevoltagesacrosstheprimaryandsecondarycoils,orwindings,arerelatedbythetransformer\r\nequation.\r\n• Thecurrentsintheprimaryandsecondarywindingsarerelatedbythenumberofprimaryandsecondaryloops,or\r\nturns, in the windings of the transformer.\r\n• Astep-uptransformerincreasesvoltageanddecreasescurrent,whereasastep-downtransformerdecreasesvoltage\r\nand increases current.\r\nCONCEPTUAL QUESTIONS\r\n15.1 AC Sources\r\n1. The driver pushes the brake pedal, exerting a force\r\nthat is increased by the simple lever and again by the hydraulic system. Each of the identical wheel cylinders\r\nreceives the same pressure and, therefore, creates the same force output F2 . This\r\nmeansthattheupwardforceonthebottomofanobjectinafluidisgreaterthanthedownwardforceontopoftheobject.\r\nThereisanupwardforce,or buoyant force,onanyobjectinanyfluid(Figure 14.20 ).Ifthebuoyantforceisgreaterthan\r\ntheobject’sweight,theobjectrisestothesurfaceandfloats.Ifthebuoyantforceislessthantheobject’sweight,theobject\r\nsinks. If the buoyant force equals the object’s weight, the object can remain suspended at its present depth. The buoyant\r\nforce is always present, whether the object floats, sinks, or is suspended in a fluid.\r\nChapter 14 | Fluid Mechanics 707\r\n\r\nBuoyant Force\r\nThe buoyant force is the upward force on any object in any fluid.\r\nFigure 14.20 Pressure due to the weight of a fluid increases\r\nwith depth because p = hpg . This change in pressure and\r\nassociated upward force on the bottom of the cylinder are\r\ngreater than the downward force on the top of the cylinder. The\r\ndifferences in the force results in the buoyant force FB .\r\n(Horizontal forces cancel.)\r\nArchimedes’ Principle\r\nJust how large a force is buoyant force? To answer this question, think about what happens when a submerged object is\r\nremovedfromafluid,asin Figure 14.21.Iftheobjectwerenotinthefluid,thespacetheobjectoccupiedwouldbefilled\r\nbyfluidhavingaweight wfl. This weight is supported by the surrounding fluid, so the buoyant force must equalwfl, the\r\nweight of the fluid displaced by the object.\r\nArchimedes’ Principle\r\nThebuoyantforceonanobjectequalstheweightofthefluiditdisplaces.Inequationform, Archimedes’ principleis\r\nFB = wfl,\r\nwhere FB is the buoyant force and wfl is the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.\r\nThis principle is named after the Greek mathematician and inventor Archimedes (ca. 287–212 BCE), who stated this\r\nprinciple long before concepts of force were well established.\r\n708 Chapter 14 | Fluid Mechanics\r\nThis OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10\r\n\r\nFigure 14.21 (a) An object submerged in a fluid experiences a buoyant force FB. If FB is greater than the weight of the\r\nobject, the object rises. If FB is less than the weight of the object, the object sinks. (b) If the object is removed, it is replaced\r\nby fluid having weight wfl. The rest of this chapter deals with fluid\r\ndynamics,thestudyoffluidsinmotion.Eventhemostbasicformsoffluidmotioncanbequitecomplex.Forthisreason,\r\nwe limit our investigation toideal fluids in many of the examples. An ideal fluid is a fluid with negligibleviscosity.\r\nViscosityisameasureoftheinternalfrictioninafluid;weexamineitinmoredetailin Viscosity and Turbulence.In\r\na few examples, we examine an incompressible fluid—one for which an extremely large force is required to change the\r\nvolume—since the density in an incompressible fluid is constant throughout.\r\nCharacteristics of Flow\r\nVelocity vectors are often used to illustrate fluid motion in applications like meteorology. [{"suffix": "", "text": "6.10\r\nAssume the density of air isρ = 1.21 kg/m3. A 75-kg skydiver descending head first has a cross-sectional area of\r\napproximately A = 0.18 m2 and a drag coefficient of approximately C = 0.70. We find that\r\nvT = 2(75 kg)(9.80 m/s2)\r\n(1.21\r\nkg/m3)(0.70)(0.18 m2)\r\n= 98 m/s = 350 km/h.\r\nThis means a skydiver with a mass of 75 kg achieves a terminal velocity of about 350 km/h while traveling in a pike (head\r\nfirst) position, minimizing the area and his drag. In a spread-eagle position, that terminal velocity may decrease to about\r\n200 km/h as the area increases. Gases are not bonded to neighboring atoms and can have large separations between molecules. Gases have\r\nneitherspecificshapesnordefinitevolumes,sincetheirmoleculesmovetofillthecontainerinwhichtheyareheld(Figure\r\n14.2).\r\n686 Chapter 14 | Fluid Mechanics\r\nThis OpenStax book is available for free at http://cnx.org/content/col12031/1.10\r\n\r\nFigure 14.2 (a) Atoms in a solid are always in close contact with neighboring atoms, held in place by forces represented here\r\nby springs. (b) Atoms in a liquid are also in close contact but can slide over one another. Forces between the atoms strongly resist\r\nattempts to compress the atoms. of Energy\r\n• A conserved quantity is a physical property that stays constant regardless of the path taken.\r\n• Aformofthework-energytheoremsaysthatthechangeinthemechanicalenergyofaparticleequalstheworkdone\r\non it by non-conservative forces.\r\n• If non-conservative forces do no work and there are no external       - ./models:/models:ro

      "questions": [
        "Why does chromium improve corrosion resistance in steel?",
        "Why does chromium improve corrosion resistance?",
        "Why is stainless steel corrosion resistant?",
        "How does chromium protect stainless steel?"
      ],
      "answer": "Chromium enables stainless steel to form a thin passive surface film in oxidizing environments. That film limits corrosion reactions at the underlying metal. Protection depends on the alloy and exposure: aggressive conditions can break down the film and cause localized or uniform corrosion. Chromium therefore does not make every steel immune to corrosion, and this mechanism alone does not establish a corrosion rate or service life."
